## Proposition 1.38
**Statement:** Triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be triangles on equal bases BC and EF and in the same parallels BF and AD: the points B, C, E, F lie on one straight line BF, the vertices A and D lie on a straight line AD parallel to BF, and BC = EF. We must show that triangle ABC is equal to triangle DEF.

**Step 2.** Produce the straight line AD in both directions [P2]. Through B draw BG parallel to CA [1.31], and through F draw FH parallel to DE [1.31], G and H being the points in which these parallels meet the produced line AD.

**Step 3.** Each of the figures GBCA and DEFH is a parallelogram. In GBCA the side GB is parallel to the side CA by construction, and the side GA, lying on the line AD, is parallel to the side BC, lying on the line BF, by hypothesis. In DEFH the side FH is parallel to the side DE by construction, and the side DH, lying on the line AD, is parallel to the side EF, lying on the line BF, by hypothesis.

**Step 4.** The parallelograms GBCA and DEFH stand on the equal bases BC and EF and lie in the same parallels BF and GH. Therefore the parallelogram GBCA is equal to the parallelogram DEFH [1.36].

**Step 5.** AB is a diameter of the parallelogram GBCA, and the diameter bisects the parallelogram [1.34]; hence triangle ABG is equal to triangle ABC, and the parallelogram GBCA, being made up of these two equal triangles, is double of triangle ABC. Likewise DF is a diameter of the parallelogram DEFH, so triangle DFH is equal to triangle DEF [1.34], and the parallelogram DEFH is double of triangle DEF.

**Step 6.** The halves of equal things are equal; hence triangle ABC is equal to triangle DEF. In detail: suppose the triangles ABC and DEF were unequal, say ABC greater than DEF, so that ABC is equal to DEF together with some excess X. Then ABG, being equal to ABC (Step 5), is also equal to DEF together with X [CN1]; and since DEF is equal to DFH (Step 5), DEF together with X is equal to DFH together with X [CN2], so that ABG is equal to DFH together with X [CN1]. Adding these equals to equals [CN2], ABC together with ABG is equal to DEF together with DFH, together with X and X; that is, the parallelogram GBCA is equal to the parallelogram DEFH together with the excess X + X, so that GBCA is greater than DEFH, the whole being greater than the part [CN5]. This contradicts Step 4. The same contradiction arises if DEF is supposed greater than ABC. Therefore triangle ABC is equal to triangle DEF.

**Step 7.** Therefore triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* an alternative route transfers ABC congruently onto the base EF (through E draw a parallel to BA meeting AD at K; then ABC = KEF by 1.34, 1.29, 1.4, and KEF = DEF by 1.37). The parallelogram route above via 1.36 and 1.34 is shorter and reaches the result more directly, so it was chosen.

## Proposition 1.39
**Statement:** Equal triangles which are on the same base and on the same side are also in the same parallels.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DBC be equal triangles on the same base BC and on the same side of it. Join AD (P1). It is to be shown that AD is parallel to BC.

**Step 2.** Suppose, on the contrary, that AD is not parallel to BC. Through the point A draw the straight line AE parallel to BC (1.31). Since AD is not parallel to BC, the line AE is distinct from the line AD, and therefore the point D does not lie on AE.

**Step 3.** The line AE meets the line BD. For if AE and BD did not meet they would be parallel, and then, since AE is also parallel to BC, the lines BD and BC, being each parallel to AE, would be parallel to one another (1.30); but BD and BC meet at the point B, so they are not parallel (D1.23). Therefore BD, produced if necessary (P2), meets AE at some point; call it E. Join EC (P1).

**Step 4.** Since AE is parallel to BC it never meets BC (D1.23); hence the whole line AE, and in particular the point E, lies on the same side of BC as A, which is also the side on which D lies. Consequently E lies on the ray from B through D, and since E is not the point D (Step 2), either D falls between B and E or E falls between B and D.

**Step 5.** The triangles ABC and EBC are on the same base BC and in the same parallels BC, AE; therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle EBC (1.37).

**Step 6.** But the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DBC by hypothesis. Therefore the triangle DBC is equal to the triangle EBC (CN1).

**Step 7.** By Step 4, one of the triangles DBC, EBC is a part of the other: if D falls between B and E, the triangle DBC is a part of the triangle EBC; if E falls between B and D, the triangle EBC is a part of the triangle DBC. Thus a whole would be equal to its own part, which is impossible, since the whole is greater than the part (CN5).

**Step 8.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false, and AD is parallel to BC. Hence the equal triangles ABC and DBC, being on the same base BC and on the same side of it, are in the same parallels BC, AD. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.40
**Statement:** Equal triangles which are on equal bases and on the same side are also in the same parallels.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DCE be equal triangles on the equal bases BC and CE, where B, C, E lie in one straight line BE, and let the vertices A and D lie on the same side of BE. Join AD [P1]. I say that AD is parallel to BE, so that the two triangles are in the same parallels BE, AD.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AD is not parallel to BE. Through the point A draw the straight line AF parallel to BE [1.31]. Since AD is not parallel to BE, the line AF is distinct from AD, and the two lines AF, AD have only the point A in common.

**Step 3.** The straight line DC meets BE at C. The line DC, produced if necessary, must meet AF: for if it did not, then DC and AF, being produced indefinitely and never meeting, would be parallel [D1.23]; then DC and BE, being each parallel to AF, would be parallel to one another [1.30], which is impossible because DC meets BE at C. Let DC, produced if necessary, meet AF at the point F. The point F is distinct from D, for otherwise AF would pass through A and D and so coincide with AD. Join FE [P1].

**Step 4.** The triangle ABC is on the base BC, the triangle FCE is on the base CE, the bases BC and CE are equal, and both triangles lie in the same parallels BE and AF (their bases on BE, their vertices A and F on AF). Therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle FCE [1.38].

**Step 5.** But the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCE by hypothesis. Therefore the triangle DCE is equal to the triangle FCE [CN1].

**Step 6.** Now F and D are distinct points of the straight line DC on the same side of BE as A (since AF, being parallel to BE, never crosses BE). Hence either F lies between D and C, in which case the triangle FCE is a part of the triangle DCE, or D lies between F and C, in which case the triangle DCE is a part of the triangle FCE. In either case one of the two triangles is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part [CN5]; so the triangles DCE and FCE are unequal, which contradicts Step 5.

**Step 7.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is impossible, and AD is parallel to BE. Hence the equal triangles ABC and DCE, being on the equal bases BC and CE and on the same side of BE, are in the same parallels BE and AD. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.41
**Statement:** If a parallelogram have the same base with a triangle and be in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double of the triangle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a parallelogram and EBC a triangle having the same base BC and lying in the same parallels BC, AE, so that the vertex E lies on the straight line through A and D that is parallel to BC. I say that the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle EBC.

**Step 2.** Join AC. [P1]

**Step 3.** The triangle ABC is equal to the triangle EBC, for they are on the same base BC and in the same parallels BC, AE. [1.37]

**Step 4.** AC is a diameter of the parallelogram ABCD, and the diameter bisects the parallelogrammic area; therefore the triangle ACD is equal to the triangle ABC, and the parallelogram ABCD is made up of the two equal triangles ABC and ACD. [1.34]

**Step 5.** Since the triangle ACD is equal to the triangle ABC (Step 4) and the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle EBC (Step 3), the triangle ACD is also equal to the triangle EBC. [CN1]

**Step 6.** Therefore the parallelogram ABCD, being the sum of the triangles ABC and ACD, each of which is equal to the triangle EBC, is equal to the triangle EBC taken twice; that is, the parallelogram ABCD is double of the triangle EBC. [CN2]

**Step 7.** Therefore, if a parallelogram have the same base with a triangle and be in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double of the triangle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.42
**Statement:** To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given triangle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given triangle and D the given rectilineal angle. It is required to construct, in an angle equal to D, a parallelogram equal to the triangle ABC.

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at the point E [1.10], and join AE [P1]. Then BE is equal to EC.

**Step 3.** Through the point A draw the straight line AH parallel to BC [1.31].

**Step 4.** On the straight line EC, and at the point E on it, construct an angle equal to the angle D [1.23], its second arm being taken on that side of BC on which A lies.

**Step 5.** This second arm is not parallel to AH. For if it were, then it and EC, being each parallel to AH, would be parallel to one another [1.30]; but they meet one another at E, and so are not parallel [D1.23]. Hence the arm, produced if necessary [P2], meets AH [D1.23]; let it meet AH at F. Then the angle CEF is equal to the angle D.

**Step 6.** Through the point C draw CG parallel to EF [1.31]. CG is not parallel to AH; for otherwise EF and AH, being each parallel to CG, would be parallel to one another [1.30], which by Step 5 is not the case. Hence CG, produced if necessary [P2], meets AH [D1.23]; let it meet AH at G.

**Step 7.** In the quadrilateral FECG the side FE is parallel to the side CG (Step 6), and the side EC is parallel to the side FG, since F and G lie on AH, which is parallel to BC (Step 3). Therefore FECG is a parallelogram.

**Step 8.** Since BE is equal to EC (Step 2), the triangles ABE and AEC are on equal bases BE, EC and in the same parallels BC, AH; therefore the triangle ABE is equal to the triangle AEC [1.38].

**Step 9.** The triangle ABC is made up of the triangles ABE and AEC; hence, by Step 8, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle AEC taken twice, that is, the triangle ABC is double of the triangle AEC.

**Step 10.** The parallelogram FECG has the same base EC with the triangle AEC and is in the same parallels EC, AH (the points A, F, G all lying on AH); therefore the parallelogram FECG is double of the triangle AEC [1.41].

**Step 11.** The parallelogram FECG and the triangle ABC are each equal to the double of the same triangle AEC; therefore the parallelogram FECG is equal to the triangle ABC [CN1].

**Step 12.** And the angle CEF of the parallelogram FECG is equal to the given angle D (Step 5). Therefore the parallelogram FECG has been constructed equal to the given triangle ABC, in the angle CEF which is equal to the given angle D. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.43
**Statement:** In any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a parallelogram and AC its diameter. Let K be a point on AC, and let AEKH and KGCF be the parallelograms about the diameter AC, with E on AB, H on AD, G on BC and F on DC; thus AK is the diameter of AEKH and KC is the diameter of KGCF. The remaining two parallelograms EBGK and HKFD are the complements. It is required to prove that the complement EBGK is equal to the complement HKFD.

**Step 2.** Since ABCD is a parallelogram and AC is its diameter, the diameter bisects the area; therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle ACD [1.34].

**Step 3.** Since AEKH is a parallelogram and AK is its diameter, the triangle AEK is equal to the triangle AHK [1.34].

**Step 4.** Since KGCF is a parallelogram and KC is its diameter, the triangle KGC is equal to the triangle KFC [1.34].

**Step 5.** Since the triangle AEK is equal to the triangle AHK (Step 3) and the triangle KGC is equal to the triangle KFC (Step 4), the two triangles AEK, KGC taken together are equal to the two triangles AHK, KFC taken together [CN2].

**Step 6.** Now the whole triangle ABC is made up of the triangle AEK, the complement EBGK and the triangle KGC, since E lies on AB, G lies on BC and K lies on AC; and the whole triangle ACD is made up of the triangle AHK, the complement HKFD and the triangle KFC, since H lies on AD, F lies on DC and K lies on AC.

**Step 7.** The whole triangle ABC is equal to the whole triangle ACD (Step 2), and the parts AEK, KGC taken from ABC are equal to the parts AHK, KFC taken from ACD (Step 5). Subtracting these equals from the equal wholes, the remainders are equal; therefore the complement EBGK is equal to the complement HKFD [CN3].

**Step 8.** Therefore in any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.44
**Statement:** To a given straight line to apply, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given triangle.

Let AB be the given straight line, C the given triangle, and D the given rectilineal angle. It is required to apply to AB, in an angle equal to D, a parallelogram equal to C.

**Step 1.** Produce AB beyond B (P2). By 1.42, construct a parallelogram BEFG equal to the triangle C in an angle EBG equal to the angle D, and let it be placed so that BE lies along AB produced, with B between A and E; thus A, B, E lie in one straight line. Since BEFG is a parallelogram, BG is parallel to EF and BE (that is, the line AE) is parallel to GF.

**Step 2.** Produce FG beyond G (P2), and through A draw AH parallel to BG (1.31), H being the point in which this parallel meets FG produced.

**Step 3.** Since AH is parallel to BG and BG is parallel to EF, AH is parallel to EF (1.30). Join HB (P1).

**Step 4.** Since the straight line HF falls upon the parallel straight lines AH and EF, the interior angles AHF and HFE on the same side are together equal to two right angles (1.29).

**Step 5.** The point B lies between A and E, so HB falls within the angle AHF; hence the angle BHG is a part of the angle AHF and is therefore less than it (CN5). Moreover, G lies on HF, so the angle GFE is the same angle as HFE. Therefore the angles BHG and GFE are together less than two right angles.

**Step 6.** Hence the straight lines HB and FE, if produced indefinitely, meet on the side on which the angles BHG, GFE lie (P5). Produce HB and FE (P2) and let them meet at the point K.

**Step 7.** Through K draw KL parallel to EA (1.31). Since EA is parallel to FH (Step 1), KL is also parallel to FH (1.30). Produce HA and GB (P2) and let them meet KL at the points L and M respectively.

**Step 8.** HLKF is a parallelogram, for HL is parallel to KF (AH is parallel to EF, Step 3) and LK is parallel to HF (Step 7). HK is a diameter of it, and B lies on HK. HABG is a parallelogram (AH parallel to BG, HG parallel to AB) and BMKE is a parallelogram (BM parallel to EK, MK parallel to BE); these are the parallelograms about the diameter HK, and LABM and BEFG are their complements. Therefore the complement LABM is equal to the complement BEFG (1.43).

**Step 9.** But BEFG is equal to the triangle C (Step 1). Therefore the parallelogram LABM is equal to the triangle C (CN1).

**Step 10.** Since the straight lines AE and GM cut one another at B, the vertical angles ABM and GBE are equal (1.15). But the angle GBE is equal to the angle D (Step 1). Therefore the angle ABM is equal to the angle D (CN1).

**Step 11.** Therefore the parallelogram LABM, equal to the given triangle C, has been applied to the given straight line AB in the angle ABM, which is equal to the given angle D. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.45
**Statement:** To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure (taken as a quadrilateral; a figure with more sides is cut into triangles by diagonals and treated in the same way, applying Step 3 once for each further triangle) and let E be the given rectilineal angle. Join DB (P1). Then the figure ABCD is made up of the two triangles ABD and DBC.

**Step 2.** By 1.42, construct a parallelogram FKHG (written FH) equal to the triangle ABD, having the angle HKF equal to the angle E. In this parallelogram FK is parallel to GH and KH is parallel to FG.

**Step 3.** By 1.44, apply to the straight line GH, on the side of GH remote from FK, a parallelogram GHML (written GM) equal to the triangle DBC, having the angle GHM equal to the angle E. In this parallelogram GH is parallel to LM and HM is parallel to GL.

**Step 4.** Since the angle HKF is equal to E and the angle GHM is equal to E, the angle HKF is equal to the angle GHM (CN1).

**Step 5.** Add the angle KHG to each: the angles FKH, KHG together are equal to the angles KHG, GHM together (CN2).

**Step 6.** Since FK is parallel to GH and the straight line KH falls on them, the interior angles on the same side, FKH and KHG, are together equal to two right angles (1.29). Therefore the angles KHG, GHM are also together equal to two right angles (CN1).

**Step 7.** Thus with the straight line GH, and at the point H on it, the two straight lines HK and HM, which lie on opposite sides of GH, make the adjacent angles KHG, GHM equal to two right angles; therefore KH is in a straight line with HM (1.14). Call this straight line KM.

**Step 8.** Since KH is parallel to FG, and KM is the straight line KH produced, KM is parallel to FG (D1.23). The straight line HG falls on the parallels KM, FG; therefore the alternate angles MHG and HGF are equal to one another (1.29).

**Step 9.** Add the angle HGL to each: the angles MHG, HGL together are equal to the angles HGF, HGL together (CN2).

**Step 10.** Since HM is parallel to GL and the straight line HG falls on them, the interior angles on the same side, MHG and HGL, are together equal to two right angles (1.29). Therefore the angles HGF, HGL are also together equal to two right angles (CN1).

**Step 11.** Thus with the straight line HG, and at the point G on it, the two straight lines GF and GL, which lie on opposite sides of HG, make the adjacent angles HGF, HGL equal to two right angles; therefore FG is in a straight line with GL (1.14). Call this straight line FL.

**Step 12.** Now FK is parallel to GH, and LM is parallel to GH; therefore FK is parallel to LM (1.30). Also KM and FL are the parallel straight lines KH and FG produced, so KM is parallel to FL (D1.23). Therefore the quadrilateral KFLM, having each pair of opposite sides parallel, is a parallelogram, and it is made up of the two parallelograms FH and GM.

**Step 13.** Since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and the triangle DBC is equal to the parallelogram GM, the triangles ABD, DBC together are equal to the parallelograms FH, GM together (CN2). But the triangles ABD, DBC together make up the whole figure ABCD, and the parallelograms FH, GM together make up the whole parallelogram KFLM. Therefore the rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the parallelogram KFLM.

**Step 14.** The angle FKM of the parallelogram KFLM is the same as the angle FKH, since H lies on KM, and this angle was constructed equal to E. Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed in the given angle E and equal to the given rectilineal figure ABCD. Q.E.F.

*Path note:* Step 12 could alternatively be reached by showing FK equal and parallel to ML (1.34, 1.30) and then invoking 1.33 to make KM equal and parallel to FL. The route above via 1.30 and D1.23 is more direct, since only the parallelism of the opposite sides is needed to conclude that KFLM is a parallelogram.

## Proposition 1.46
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a square.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line. It is required to describe a square on AB.

**Step 2.** From the point A on AB draw the straight line AC at right angles to AB [1.11]; produce AC as far as necessary so that it is greater than AB [P2], and from AC cut off AD equal to AB [1.3]. Thus the angle BAD is a right angle and AD = AB.

**Step 3.** Through the point D draw DE parallel to AB, and through the point B draw BE parallel to AD [1.31]; let these two straight lines meet at the point E. Then ADEB is a parallelogram, since its opposite sides DE, AB are parallel and its opposite sides BE, AD are parallel.

**Step 4.** In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal [1.34]; therefore AB = DE and AD = BE.

**Step 5.** But AB = AD by construction (Step 2). Hence DE = AB = AD = BE, and since things equal to the same thing are equal to one another [CN1], the four straight lines BA, AD, DE, EB are all equal to one another. Therefore the parallelogram ADEB is equilateral.

**Step 6.** Next, the straight line AD falls on the two parallel straight lines AB, DE, so the interior angles on the same side, namely the angles BAD, ADE, are together equal to two right angles [1.29].

**Step 7.** The angle BAD is a right angle (Step 2). Subtracting this right angle from the two right angles [CN3], the remaining angle ADE equals the remaining right angle, and since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], the angle ADE is also a right angle.

**Step 8.** In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal [1.34]; therefore the angle ABE, opposite to ADE, equals the right angle ADE, and the angle BED, opposite to BAD, equals the right angle BAD. Hence each of the angles ABE, BED is also a right angle, and the parallelogram ADEB is right-angled.

**Step 9.** The quadrilateral ADEB has been shown to be both equilateral (Step 5) and right-angled (Step 8); therefore, by the definition of a square [D1.22], ADEB is a square, and it has been described on the given straight line AB. This is what was required.

## Proposition 1.47
**Statement:** In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a right-angled triangle having the angle BAC right. It is to be shown that the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA and AC taken together.

**Step 2.** On BC describe the square BDEC, and on BA and AC describe the squares GB (with vertices A, B, F, G) and HC (with vertices A, C, K, H), each described on the side of its base remote from the triangle [1.46]. Through A draw AL parallel to BD [1.31], and let it meet BC at M and DE at L. Join AD and FC [P1].

**Step 3.** Since GB is a square, it is right-angled [D1.22], so the angle BAG is right; and the angle BAC is right by hypothesis. Hence with the straight line BA, and at the point A on it, the two straight lines AC and AG, which do not lie on the same side of BA, make the adjacent angles BAC and BAG equal to two right angles. Therefore CA is in a straight line with AG [1.14].

**Step 4.** For the same reason, since the angles CAB and CAH are both right (the latter being an angle of the square HC [D1.22]), the straight lines AB and AH, which do not lie on the same side of CA, make with CA at the point A adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore BA is in a straight line with AH [1.14].

**Step 5.** The angle DBC is right, being an angle of the square BDEC, and the angle FBA is right, being an angle of the square GB [D1.22]; therefore the angle DBC is equal to the angle FBA [P4]. Since the squares lie on the sides of BC and BA remote from the triangle, the angle DBA is made up of the angles DBC and CBA, and the angle FBC is made up of the angles FBA and ABC. Adding the angle ABC to each of the equal angles DBC and FBA, the whole angle DBA is equal to the whole angle FBC [CN2].

**Step 6.** Since BDEC and GB are squares, they are equilateral [D1.22]; so DB is equal to BC and FB is equal to BA. Thus in the triangles ABD and FBC the two sides AB, BD are equal to the two sides FB, BC respectively, and the angle ABD contained by them is equal to the angle FBC [Step 5]. Therefore the base AD is equal to the base FC, and the triangle ABD is equal to the triangle FBC [1.4].

**Step 7.** In the figure BDLM, BD is parallel to ML by construction [Step 2], and BM is parallel to DL, since BC and DE are opposite sides of the square BDEC, which was constructed with its opposite sides parallel [1.46]; hence BDLM is a parallelogram, which we call BL. The parallelogram BL and the triangle ABD have the same base BD and are in the same parallels BD and AL. Therefore the parallelogram BL is double of the triangle ABD [1.41].

**Step 8.** The side FB of the square GB is parallel to the opposite side GA, by the construction of the square [1.46], and GA together with AC forms the single straight line GC [Step 3]. Hence the square GB and the triangle FBC have the same base FB and are in the same parallels FB and GC. Therefore the square GB is double of the triangle FBC [1.41].

**Step 9.** Since the triangle ABD is equal to the triangle FBC [Step 6], the double of the one, being the sum of two equals, is equal to the double of the other [CN2]. The parallelogram BL is equal to the double of the triangle ABD and the square GB is equal to the double of the triangle FBC [Steps 7, 8]; therefore the parallelogram BL is equal to the square GB [CN1].

**Step 10.** Join AE and BK [P1]. Since BD is parallel to CE, these being opposite sides of the square BDEC [1.46], and AL was drawn parallel to BD, AL is also parallel to CE [1.30]. Hence MCEL is a parallelogram (MC being parallel to LE, as in Step 7); call it CL.

**Step 11.** The angle BCE is right, being an angle of the square BDEC, and the angle ACK is right, being an angle of the square HC [D1.22]; therefore they are equal [P4]. ## Proposition 1.48
**Statement:** If in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle in which the square on the side BC is equal to the squares on the sides BA, AC. I say that the angle BAC is right.

**Step 2.** From the point A draw AD at right angles to the straight line AC (1.11); make AD equal to BA (1.3); and join DC (P1).

**Step 3.** Since DA is equal to AB (Step 2), the square on DA is equal to the square on AB; for these two squares have their sides equal and their angles right and therefore equal to one another (P4), so that, if the one be applied to the other, they coincide and are therefore equal (CN4).

**Step 4.** Let the square on AC be added to each; therefore the squares on DA, AC are equal to the squares on BA, AC (CN2).

**Step 5.** But the angle DAC is right (Step 2); therefore the square on DC is equal to the squares on DA, AC (1.47).

**Step 6.** And the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA, AC, by hypothesis (Step 1).

**Step 7.** Therefore the square on DC is equal to the square on BC, since each of them is equal to the squares on BA, AC (Steps 4, 5, 6; CN1).

**Step 8.** Hence the side DC is equal to the side BC. For if they were unequal, one of them would be greater, and the square on the less, being applied to the square on the greater along a common side and angle, would be a part of it; so that the square on the greater would be greater than the square on the less (CN5), which contradicts Step 7.

**Step 9.** Now in the triangles DAC, BAC, the side DA is equal to the side AB (Step 2), the side AC is common, and the base DC is equal to the base BC (Step 8); therefore the angle DAC is equal to the angle BAC (1.8).

**Step 10.** But the angle DAC is right (Step 2); therefore the angle BAC is also right.

**Step 11.** Therefore, if in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.1
**Statement:** If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments.

**Step 1.** Let A and BC be the two straight lines, and let BC be cut at random at the points D and E, so that BC is divided into the segments BD, DE, EC. (Two points of section are taken for definiteness; the argument below is the same for any number of points, one further parallel being drawn for each additional point of section.) It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by A, BC is equal to the rectangles contained by A, BD; by A, DE; and by A, EC together.

**Step 2.** From the point B draw BF at right angles to BC [1.11], so that the angle FBC is right.

**Step 3.** From BF cut off BG equal to A [1.3].

**Step 4.** Through G draw GH parallel to BC [1.31]; and through D, E, C draw DK, EL, CH parallel to BG [1.31], meeting GH at the points K, L, H respectively.

**Step 5.** Since DK, EL, CH are each parallel to BG, they are also parallel to one another [1.30]. Hence each of the figures BK, BL, BH, DL, EH is a parallelogram: its two sides lying along GH and BC are parallel (Step 4), and its two remaining sides are two of the parallels BG, DK, EL, CH.

**Step 6.** A parallelogram having one right angle has all its angles right. For each side of the parallelogram is a straight line falling upon the two parallels that form the adjacent sides, so that the two interior angles on the same side of it together equal two right angles [1.29]; hence each angle adjacent to the right angle is right, and, applying the same reasoning again, so is the angle opposite. Such a parallelogram is rectangular, and is the rectangle contained by the two straight lines about its right angle [D2.1].

**Step 7.** The angle GBC is right (Step 2), and it is an angle of the parallelogram BH; therefore BH is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6). It is contained by GB, BC, which contain the right angle GBC; and GB is equal to A (Step 3). Therefore BH is the rectangle contained by A, BC [D2.1].

**Step 8.** The angle GBD is the same right angle GBC, and it is an angle of the parallelogram BK; therefore BK is rectangular (Step 6), contained by GB, BD, and GB is equal to A. Therefore BK is the rectangle contained by A, BD [D2.1].

**Step 9.** Since BC falls upon the parallels BG, DK, the exterior angle KDE is equal to the interior and opposite angle GBD [1.29]; but GBD is right, so KDE is right, and DL is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6) contained by DK, DE. Now in the parallelogram BK the opposite sides BG, DK are equal [1.34]; and BG is equal to A; therefore DK is equal to A [CN1]. Therefore DL is the rectangle contained by A, DE [D2.1].

**Step 10.** In the same way, since BC falls upon the parallels BG, EL, the exterior angle LEC is equal to the interior and opposite angle GBE [1.29], which is right; so EH is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6) contained by EL, EC. In the parallelogram BL the opposite sides BG, EL are equal [1.34]; and BG is equal to A; therefore EL is equal to A [CN1]. Therefore EH is the rectangle contained by A, EC [D2.1].

**Step 11.** The straight lines DK, EL divide the rectangle BH into the three rectangles BK, DL, EH, and no part of BH lies outside them; therefore BH is equal to BK, DL, EH taken together, the whole being made up of its parts.

**Step 12.** Substituting the descriptions obtained in Steps 7–10: the rectangle contained by A, BC (which is BH) is equal to the rectangle contained by A, BD (which is BK), together with the rectangle contained by A, DE (which is DL) and the rectangle contained by A, EC (which is EH). For any number of points of section the same construction yields one rectangle for each segment, each contained by a straight line equal to A and that segment, and their sum is again the whole rectangle BH.

Therefore, if there be two straight lines and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments. Q.E.D.

Path note: the auxiliary lines DK, EL, CH were drawn as parallels to BG [1.31] rather than as perpendiculars to BC [1.11], since parallels give the parallelogram structure needed for 1.34 directly, and their right angles then follow from 1.29 in one step.

## Proposition 2.2
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by AB, AC together with the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the square on AB.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square ADEB [1.46], with the vertex D adjoining A and the vertex E adjoining B. By the construction of 1.46, the side DE is drawn parallel to AB and the side BE parallel to AD.

**Step 3.** Through C draw CF parallel to AD [1.31], and let it meet DE at F. The straight line CF divides the square AE into the two quadrilaterals AF (that is, ACFD) and CE (that is, CBEF); thus the square AE is made up of the figures AF and CE.

**Step 4.** AF is a parallelogram, for AD is parallel to CF by construction, and AC, DF are parts of the parallel sides AB, DE of the square. Its angles at A and D are angles of the square ADEB and are therefore right [D1.22]; hence its opposite angles at F and at C are also right [1.34], so that AF is a rectangular parallelogram. By D2.1 it is the rectangle contained by DA, AC; and since DA is equal to AB, being sides of the square [D1.22], AF is the rectangle contained by AB, AC.

**Step 5.** In the same way CE is a parallelogram, for CF is parallel to BE by construction, and CB, FE are parts of the parallel sides AB, DE. Its angles at B and E are angles of the square and are right [D1.22]; hence its opposite angles at F and at C are right [1.34], and CE is a rectangular parallelogram. By D2.1 it is the rectangle contained by BE, BC; and since BE is equal to AB [D1.22], CE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC.

**Step 6.** AE is the square on AB, by the construction of Step 2.

**Step 7.** Therefore, since the square AE is made up of AF and CE, the square on AB is equal to the rectangle contained by AB, AC together with the rectangle contained by AB, BC. That is, if a straight line AB is cut at random at C, the rectangles contained by the whole AB and each of the segments AC, CB together equal the square on AB. Q.E.D.

Path note: the result could also be derived from Proposition 2.1 by taking the uncut line equal to AB, but that route needs an extra lemma identifying the rectangle contained by two lines equal to AB with the square on AB; the direct division of the square is chosen because the statement itself concerns the square on AB, which this construction exhibits and divides.

## Proposition 2.3
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.

Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. I say that the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on CB.

**Step 1.** On CB describe the square CDEB [1.46], with CD and BE the sides standing on CB at C and B respectively, and DE the side opposite CB. Since CDEB is a square, its four sides CD, DE, EB, BC are equal to one another and its four angles DCB, CDE, DEB, EBC are right angles [D1.22].

**Step 2.** Since the angles DCB, CBE are right, the straight line CB falling on the two straight lines CD, BE makes the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles; therefore CD is parallel to BE [1.28]. In the same way, since the angles CDE, DCB are right, the straight line CD falling on DE, CB makes the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles; therefore DE is parallel to CB [1.28].

**Step 3.** Produce ED beyond D [P2], and through the point A draw AF parallel to CD [1.31], F being the point in which AF meets ED produced. Since AF is parallel to CD, and CD is parallel to BE (Step 2), AF is also parallel to BE [1.30].

**Step 4.** In the quadrilateral AFEB, AF is parallel to BE (Step 3), and FE, which lies along the straight line DE, is parallel to AB, which lies along the straight line CB (Step 2); therefore AFEB is a parallelogram. Since AF is parallel to BE and AB falls on them, the angles FAB, ABE are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; but the angle ABE is the angle EBC of the square, which is right (Step 1); therefore the angle FAB is right. Likewise FE falls on the parallels AF, BE, so the angles AFE, FEB are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; the angle FEB is the angle DEB of the square, which is right (Step 1); therefore the angle AFE is right. Thus AFEB is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AB, BE [D2.1]; call it AE.

**Step 5.** In the quadrilateral ACDF, AF is parallel to CD (Step 3), and FD, which lies along ED, is parallel to AC, which lies along CB (Step 2); therefore ACDF is a parallelogram. Since AF is parallel to CD and AC falls on them, the angles FAC, ACD are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; but the angle FAC is the angle FAB, which is right (Step 4); therefore the angle ACD is right. Thus ACDF is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AC, CD [D2.1]; call it AD. Call the square CDEB also CE.

**Step 6.** The straight line CD divides the figure AE into the two figures AD and CE, and AE is made up of these two parts; therefore AE is equal to AD together with CE.

**Step 7.** Now AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BE (Step 4), and BE is equal to BC (Step 1); therefore AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC. Again, AD is the rectangle contained by AC, CD (Step 5), and CD is equal to CB (Step 1); therefore AD is the rectangle contained by AC, CB. And CE is the square described on CB (Step 1).

**Step 8.** Therefore, by Step 6, the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on CB. Therefore, if a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.4
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the straight line, cut at random at the point C. I say that the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. On AB describe the square ADEB [1.46], and join DB [P1].

In the same way, since the angles ADE, DAB are right, DE is parallel to AB [1.28].

**Step 3.** Through C draw CF parallel to AD, meeting DB at G and DE at F; and through G draw HK parallel to AB, meeting AD at H and BE at K [1.31]. Since CF is parallel to AD and AD to BE, CF is also parallel to BE; and since HK is parallel to AB and AB to DE, HK is also parallel to DE [1.30]. Consequently AHGC, CGKB, HDFG and GFEK are all parallelograms, and ADEB is a parallelogram with diameter DB.

**Step 4.** Since CF is parallel to AD and the straight line DB falls on them, the exterior angle CGB is equal to the interior and opposite angle ADB [1.29].

**Step 5.** Since ADEB is a square, BA is equal to AD [D1.22]; so in the triangle ABD the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD [1.5]. Therefore the angle CGB is also equal to the angle CBG [CN1].

**Step 6.** In the triangle CGB the angle CGB is equal to the angle CBG; therefore the side CB, which subtends the angle CGB, is equal to the side CG, which subtends the angle CBG [1.6].

**Step 7.** CGKB is a parallelogram (Step 3); therefore its opposite sides are equal, CB to GK and CG to KB [1.34]. But CB is equal to CG (Step 6); therefore the four sides CB, CG, GK, KB are all equal to one another [CN1], and CGKB is equilateral.

**Step 8.** Since CG is parallel to BK and the straight line CB falls on them, the interior angles GCB, CBK on the same side are equal to two right angles [1.29]. But the angle CBK is right, being an angle of the square ADEB [D1.22]; therefore the angle GCB is also right. And the opposite angles of the parallelogram CGKB are equal [1.34], so the angles CGK, GKB are likewise right. Thus CGKB is both equilateral and right-angled, that is, a square [D1.22]; and it is the square described on CB.

**Step 9.** Similarly HDFG is a square. For, HK being parallel to AB and DB falling on them, the exterior angle DGH is equal to the interior and opposite angle DBA [1.29], which is equal to the angle GDH (Step 5) [CN1]; hence HD is equal to HG [1.6]. Since HDFG is a parallelogram, HD is equal to GF and HG to DF [1.34], so that HDFG is equilateral [CN1]. Also the angle HDF is right [D1.22]; DF being parallel to HG and DH falling on them, the angles HDF, DHG are equal to two right angles [1.29], so the angle DHG is right; and the opposite angles of the parallelogram are equal [1.34], so HDFG is right-angled. Hence HDFG is a square [D1.22]. Moreover HG is equal to AC, being opposite sides of the parallelogram AHGC [1.34]; so HDFG is the square on AC.

**Step 10.** Next, AHGC is a parallelogram, and since CF is parallel to AD and AB falls on them, the angles DAC, ACG are equal to two right angles [1.29]; the angle DAC is right [D1.22], so the angle ACG is right, and AHGC is a rectangular parallelogram. Hence AG is the rectangle contained by AC and CG [D2.1]; and CG is equal to CB (Step 6); therefore AG is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 11.** In the parallelogram ADEB with diameter DB, HF and CK are the parallelograms about the diameter and AG, GE are their complements; therefore AG is equal to GE [1.43]. Hence GE is also equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB, and AG together with GE is twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB [CN2].

**Step 12.** Now HF is the square on AC and CK is the square on CB (Steps 8, 9), while AG and GE together are twice the rectangle AC, CB (Step 11). Adding these equals, HF, CK, AG, GE together are equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB [CN2]. But HF, CK, AG, GE together make up the whole figure ADEB, which is the square on AB. Therefore the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB and twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. QED.

## Proposition 2.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut into equal segments at C, so that AC = CB, and into unequal segments at D, so that AD is not equal to DB; then D is a point of AB other than C. If D lies between A and C, interchange the names of A and B; so we may suppose that D lies between C and B. We must show that the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD is equal to the square on CB.

**Step 2.** On CB describe the square CEFB [1.46], with CE and BF the sides at right angles to CB and EF the side opposite to CB; by the construction of 1.46, CE is parallel to BF and CB is parallel to EF. Join BE [P1]; BE is a diameter of the square CEFB.

**Step 3.** Through D draw DG parallel to CE [1.31]. Since D lies between C and B, DG runs across the square from the side CB to the side EF and cuts the diameter BE; let H be the point where DG cuts BE, and G the point where it meets EF. Through H draw the straight line KM parallel to AB [1.31], meeting CE at L and BF at M. Through A draw AK parallel to CE [1.31], meeting KM at K.

**Step 4.** By construction DG and AK are parallel to CE, and KM is parallel to AB, while CE and BF are at right angles to CB; hence the quadrilaterals CDHL, DBMH, LHGE, HMFG, ACLK and ADHK cut off in the figure are all parallelograms, and their angles, like those of the square, are right angles. In the square CEFB with diameter BE, the parallelograms DBMH (call it DM) and LHGE (call it LG) are the parallelograms about the diameter, since their diameters HB and HE lie along BE; and CDHL (call it CH) and HMFG (call it HF) are their complements.

**Step 5.** Since CH and HF are the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter BE of the parallelogram CEFB, the complement CH is equal to the complement HF [1.43].

**Step 6.** Add the parallelogram DM to each. CH together with DM is the whole parallelogram CBML (call it CM), and HF together with DM is the whole parallelogram DBFG (call it DF). Therefore CM = DF [CN2].

**Step 7.** The parallelograms ACLK (call it AL) and CBML (that is, CM) stand on the equal bases AC, CB and lie in the same parallels AB, KM. Therefore AL = CM [1.36].

**Step 8.** Since AL = CM and CM = DF, AL = DF [CN1].

**Step 9.** Add CH to each. AL together with CH is the whole parallelogram ADHK (call it AH). DF together with CH consists of the parallelogram DM about the diameter together with its two complements CH and HF, which is a gnomon [D2.2]; call it the gnomon NOP. It is the square CEFB with LG removed. Therefore AH = gnomon NOP [CN2].

**Step 10.** DM is a parallelogram about the diameter BE of the square CEFB; therefore DM is itself a square [2.4, Porism: in square areas the parallelograms about the diameter are squares]. A square is equilateral [D1.22]; hence DH = DB.

**Step 11.** AH is a rectangular parallelogram whose right angle at D is contained by AD and DH; so AH is the rectangle contained by AD, DH [D2.1]. Since DH = DB, AH is the rectangle contained by AD, DB. Consequently, by Step 9, the gnomon NOP is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB.

**Step 12.** LG is also a parallelogram about the diameter BE of the square CEFB, so LG is a square [2.4, Porism]. Its side LH is equal to CD, because CD and LH are opposite sides of the parallelogram CH [1.34]. Therefore LG is a square described on a straight line equal to CD, that is, LG is equal to the square on CD.

**Step 13.** Add LG to each of the equals in Step 11. Then the gnomon NOP together with LG is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD [CN2].

**Step 14.** But the gnomon NOP together with LG is the whole square CEFB, which is the square described on CB. Therefore the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD is equal to the square on CB [CN1].

Therefore, if a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.6
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be bisected at C, so that AC = CB, and let the straight line BD be added to it in a straight line, so that A, C, B, D lie in this order on the single straight line AD. It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CB is equal to the square on CD.

**Step 2.** On CD describe the square CEFD [1.46], CE and DF being the sides drawn at right angles to CD and EF the side opposite to CD, and join DE [P1]. By its construction in 1.46 the square has its opposite sides parallel, CE ∥ DF and CD ∥ EF, so CEFD is a parallelogram with DE as a diameter; and all its sides are equal and all its angles are right [D1.22].

**Step 3.** Through B draw BG parallel to CE [1.31], meeting the diameter DE at H and the side EF at G; through H draw KM parallel to AD [1.31], meeting CE at L and DF at M; and through A draw AK parallel to DM [1.31], meeting KM at K.

**Step 4.** Since BG ∥ CE and CE ∥ DF, also BG ∥ DF; since AK ∥ DM and DM ∥ CE, also AK ∥ CE; and since KM ∥ AD and AD ∥ EF, also KM ∥ EF [1.30]. Hence each of the figures AL (= AKLC), CH (= CLHB), BM (= BHMD), LG (= LEGH), HF (= HGFM), CM (= CLMD) and AM (= AKMD) has its opposite sides parallel and is a parallelogram. Because H lies on the diameter DE, LG and BM are the parallelograms about the diameter DE of the parallelogram CEFD, and CH, HF are their complements; the parallelogram BM together with the two complements CH, HF is a gnomon [D2.2], which we call the gnomon NOP. The gnomon NOP together with LG makes up the whole square CEFD.

**Step 5.** Since AC = CB, the parallelograms AL and CH are on the equal bases AC, CB and in the same parallels AD, KM; therefore AL = CH [1.36].

**Step 6.** Since CH and HF are the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter DE of the parallelogram CEFD, CH = HF [1.43].

**Step 7.** Therefore AL = HF [CN1].

**Step 8.** Let CM be added to each. AL together with CM is the whole parallelogram AM, and HF together with CM (which is made up of CH and BM) is the gnomon NOP. Therefore AM = gnomon NOP [CN2].

**Step 9.** Now BM is a parallelogram about the diameter of the square CEFD; hence BM is itself a square [2.4, Porism], so that DM = DB [D1.22]. Further, AM is a parallelogram whose angle ADM is the angle CDF of the square and is therefore right [D1.22]; since AK ∥ DM and AD falls on them, the angle KAD together with the angle ADM equals two right angles [1.29], so KAD is right; and the angles AKM, KMD, being opposite to ADM, KAD in the parallelogram AM, are also right [1.34]. Thus AM is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AD, DM [D2.1]; and since DM = DB, AM is the rectangle contained by AD, DB.

**Step 10.** Therefore the gnomon NOP is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 11.** Again, LG is a parallelogram about the diameter of the square CEFD, so LG is a square [2.4, Porism]; and its side LH is equal to CB, these being opposite sides of the parallelogram CH [1.34]. Therefore LG is the square on a straight line equal to CB, that is, LG is equal to the square on CB.

**Step 12.** Let LG be added to each. Then the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CB is equal to the gnomon NOP together with LG [CN2]. ## Proposition 2.7
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.

Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. I say that the squares on AB, BC are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on CA.

**Step 2.** Again, since AB has been cut at random at C, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments AC, CB together with the square on BC [2.3].

**Step 3.** Adding the equals of Step 2 to themselves, twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with twice the square on BC [CN2].

**Step 4.** Let the square on AC be added to each; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together [CN2].

**Step 5.** But, by Step 1, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB; let the square on BC be added to each; therefore the square on AB together with the square on BC is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together [CN2].

**Step 6.** Now the two magnitudes obtained in Steps 4 and 5, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC, and the squares on AB, BC taken together, are each equal to the same thing, namely twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together; therefore they are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 7.** Therefore the square on the whole AB and the square on the segment BC are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC together with the square on the remaining segment AC. Q.E.D.

That route requires re-establishing that the parallelograms about the diameter are the squares on CB and AC. ## Proposition 2.8
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, four times the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments together with the square on the remaining segment is equal to the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. Produce AB in a straight line beyond B [P2], and on the produced part let BD be made equal to CB [1.3]. It is to be proved that four times the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on AC is equal to the square on AD.

**Step 2.** The straight line AD is cut at the point B. Therefore, by 2.4, the square on AD is equal to the squares on AB, BD together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, BD.

**Step 3.** Since BD is equal to CB, the square on BD is a square described on a straight line equal to CB, that is, it is the square on CB; and the rectangle contained by AB, BD, being the rectangle contained by AB and a straight line equal to CB, is the rectangle contained by AB, CB, a rectangle being that which is contained by the two straight lines about its right angle [D2.1]. Hence, from Step 2, the square on AD is equal to the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB.

**Step 4.** Again, the straight line AB is cut at C. Therefore, by 2.7, the squares on AB, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC.

**Step 5.** Let twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB be added to each of these equals. Then the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB are equal to four times the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC [CN2].

**Step 6.** But the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB were shown in Step 3 to be equal to the square on AD. Therefore, things equal to the same thing being equal to one another [CN1], the square on AD is equal to four times the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC.

**Step 7.** Therefore four times the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC, together with the square on the remaining segment AC, is equal to the square on AD, which is the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line. Q.E.D.

Being equal, each of them is half a right angle.

**Step 7.** In the same way, since CE = CB, the angle CEB is equal to the angle CBE [1.5], and the angle ECB is right, so each of the angles CEB and EBC is half a right angle [1.32, CN3]. Therefore the whole angle AEB, being made up of the halves AEC and CEB, is a right angle [CN2].

**Step 8.** The angle EBC is half a right angle; and the angle DBG is equal to the angle EBC, since they are vertical angles formed by the straight lines EG and AD crossing at B [1.15]. Therefore the angle DBG is half a right angle.

**Step 9.** The straight line CD falls upon the parallel straight lines CE and DG, so the alternate angles ECD and BDG are equal [1.29]. The angle ECD is right; therefore the angle BDG is right.

## Proposition 2.11
**Statement:** To cut a given straight line so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the square on the remaining segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line. On AB describe the square ABDC [1.46]; its four sides are equal and its angles are right [D1.22].

**Step 3.** Produce CA in a straight line through A to F [P2], and on the produced line cut off EF equal to EB [1.3].

**Step 4.** On AF describe the square AFGH [1.46]. Since the angle BAC is right and F lies on CA produced, the adjacent angle BAF is also right [1.13]; hence the side AH of the square AFGH, which stands at right angles to AF at A, lies along AB, so that H is a point of AB.

**Step 5.** Produce GH to meet CD at K [P2]. Then FCKG (call it FK) is a rectangle with sides CF and FG, and AHKC (call it AK) is a rectangle with sides AH and AC, common to FK and to the square AD.

**Step 6.** The straight line AC has been bisected at E, and the straight line AF has been added to it in a straight line. Therefore the rectangle contained by CF and FA together with the square on AE is equal to the square on EF [2.6].

**Step 7.** But EF is equal to EB (Step 3), so the square on EF is equal to the square on EB. Hence the rectangle CF·FA together with the square on AE is equal to the square on EB.

**Step 8.** Since the angle EAB, which is the angle CAB of the square, is right, in the right-angled triangle EAB the square on EB is equal to the squares on BA and AE together [1.47].

**Step 9.** Therefore the rectangle CF·FA together with the square on AE is equal to the squares on BA and AE together [CN1].

**Step 10.** Subtract the square on AE from each; the remainders are equal [CN3]. Therefore the rectangle CF·FA is equal to the square on AB.

**Step 11.** Now the rectangle CF·FA is the rectangle FK, for FG is equal to FA (sides of the square AFGH) and the angle at F is right, so that FK is contained by CF and FG [D2.1]. And the square on AB is the square AD. Therefore FK is equal to AD [CN1].

**Step 12.** From each subtract the rectangle AK, which is common to both; the remainders are equal [CN3]. Therefore the remainder FH, the square AFGH, is equal to the remainder HD, the rectangle HBDK.

**Step 13.** But HD is the rectangle contained by AB and BH, since BD is equal to AB (sides of the square ABDC) and the angle at B is right [D2.1]; and FH is the square on AH.

**Step 14.** Therefore the rectangle contained by AB and BH is equal to the square on AH [CN1]. Thus the given straight line AB has been cut at H so that the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BH is equal to the square on the remaining segment AH. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 2.12
**Statement:** In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the   perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be an obtuse-angled triangle having the angle BAC obtuse. Produce CA beyond A (P2), and from the point B draw BD perpendicular to CA produced (1.12), meeting it at D. Since BD is a perpendicular, the angles BDC and BDA are right (D1.10).

**Step 2.** The foot D lies on CA produced beyond A, that is, outside the triangle on the side of the obtuse angle. For if D coincided with A, the angle BAC would be right, whereas it is obtuse, i.e. greater than a right angle (D1.11); and if D lay on CA itself or on AC produced beyond C, then in the triangle BAD the angle BDA would be right and the angle BAD would be the obtuse angle BAC itself, so that two angles of the triangle BAD would together not be less than two right angles, contrary to 1.17. Hence D falls beyond A, CD is one straight line cut at the point A, and AD is the straight line cut off outside the triangle by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line CD has been cut at random at the point A, the square on DC is equal to the squares on CA, AD and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (2.4).

**Step 4.** Let the square on DB be added to each (CN2); therefore the squares on CD, DB are equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD.

**Step 5.** Since the angle BDC is right, the triangle BDC is right-angled, so the square on CB is equal to the squares on CD, DB (1.47); and likewise, since the angle BDA is right, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB (1.47).

**Step 6.** Therefore the square on CB, being equal to the squares on CD, DB (Step 5), is equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle CA, AD (Step 4, CN1); and since the squares on AD, DB are together equal to the square on AB (Step 5), the square on CB is equal to the squares on CA, AB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (CN1).

**Step 7.** Hence the square on CB, the side subtending the obtuse angle, is greater than the squares on CA, AB, the sides containing the obtuse angle, by twice the rectangle contained by CA, the side on which the perpendicular falls, and AD, the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.13
**Statement:** In acute-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the acute angle is less than the squares on the sides containing the acute angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the acute angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle.

Produce BC indefinitely in both directions (P2), and from the point A draw AD perpendicular to the straight line BC (1.12); then the angles ADB, ADC are right (D1.10).

**Step 2.** The foot D lies within BC. For suppose D fell on BC produced beyond B. Then angle ABC would be an exterior angle of triangle ABD, and so greater than the interior and opposite angle ADB (1.16), which is right; since all right angles are equal (P4), angle ABC would be greater than a right angle and hence not acute (D1.12), contrary to hypothesis. If D coincided with B, angle ABC would itself be a right angle (D1.10), again contrary to hypothesis. The same reasoning applied to the acute angle ACB shows that D neither falls beyond C nor coincides with C. Therefore D lies between B and C, so that the straight line BC is cut at the point D into the segments BD, DC.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line BC has been cut at D, the square on BC together with the square on BD is equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the square on DC (2.7).

**Step 4.** Let the square on AD be added to each; then the squares on BC, BD, AD are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the squares on DC, AD (CN2).

**Step 5.** Since the angle ADB is right, the square on AB is equal to the squares on BD, AD (1.47); and since the angle ADC is right, the square on AC is equal to the squares on DC, AD (1.47).

**Step 6.** Substituting these equalities into Step 4, the squares on BC, AB are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the square on AC (CN1).

**Step 7.** Subtracting twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD from each side, the square on AC is equal to the squares on BC, AB less twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD (CN3). That is, the square on AC, the side subtending the acute angle ABC, is less than the squares on the sides AB, BC containing that angle by twice the rectangle contained by BC, the side on which the perpendicular falls, and BD, the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.14
**Statement:** To construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given rectilineal figure. Draw a right angle [1.11], and in this right angle construct the parallelogram BD equal to the rectilineal figure A [1.45]; BD is thus a rectangular parallelogram with the right angle at E, contained by the two sides BE, ED [D2.1].

**Step 2.** If BE is equal to ED, then, since the opposite sides of the parallelogram BD are equal [1.34], BD is equilateral; and it is right-angled; therefore BD is a square [D1.22], and what was required has been done.

**Step 3.** If not, one of BE, ED is greater. Let BE be the greater. Produce BE in a straight line to F [P2], and cut off EF equal to ED [1.3].

**Step 4.** Bisect BF at the point G [1.10]. With centre G and distance GF describe a circle [P3]; since GB is equal to GF, the point B also lies on the circumference.

**Step 5.** From the point E draw EH at right angles to BF [1.11], and let it meet the circumference of the circle at H. Join GH [P1].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line BF has been cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at E, the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GF [2.5].

**Step 7.** But GF is equal to GH, both being straight lines drawn from the centre G to the circumference [D1.15]; therefore the square on GF is the square on GH, and so the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GH.

**Step 8.** Since the angle HEG is right, the square on GH is equal to the squares on HE, EG [1.47].

**Step 9.** Therefore the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the squares on HE, EG, each being equal to the square on GH [CN1].

**Step 10.** Let the square on EG be subtracted from each; then the remaining rectangle contained by BE, EF is equal to the square on EH [CN3].

**Step 11.** But EF is equal to ED; therefore the rectangle contained by BE, EF is the rectangle contained by BE, ED, which is the parallelogram BD [D2.1]. Therefore BD is equal to the square on EH.

**Step 12.** And BD is equal to the rectilineal figure A; therefore the rectilineal figure A is also equal to the square on EH [CN1].

**Step 13.** On EH describe the square [1.46]; this square is equal to the given rectilineal figure A. Therefore a square has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure A. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 3.1
**Statement:** To find the centre of a given circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle. Take any two points A, B on its circumference and join the straight line AB (P1).

**Step 2.** Bisect AB at the point D (1.10), so that AD = DB.

**Step 3.** From D draw DC at right angles to AB (1.11), C being the point in which this perpendicular meets the circumference; then the angles ADC, BDC are right (D1.10). Produce CD in a straight line beyond D to meet the circumference again at E (P2). Thus CE is a straight line through D, at right angles to AB, terminated at both ends by the circumference, with D lying between C and E.

**Step 4.** Bisect CE at the point F (1.10), so that CF = FE. I say that F is the centre of the circle ABC.

**Step 5.** For suppose it is not. The circle has a centre (D1.16); let G be the centre, G being a point other than F.

**Step 6.** G lies on neither of the straight lines AB, CE. For let XY be either of these two chords and M its point of bisection (M = D for AB, M = F for CE), so that XM = MY, and suppose G lies on XY. Since G is the centre, G lies within the circle (D1.15), hence between X and Y; and GX = GY, both being radii (D1.15). If G were not M, G would lie either between X and M or between M and Y; say between X and M. Then GX is a part of MX and MY is a part of GY, so GX < MX and MY < GY (CN5); but MX = MY; hence GX < GY, contrary to GX = GY. Therefore G = M. Applied to CE this gives G = F, contrary to Step 5; so G is not on CE. Applied to AB it would give G = D, and D lies on CE, which has just been excluded; so G is not on AB either.

**Step 7.** Join GA, GD, GB (P1). Since G is not on AB, ADG and BDG are triangles.

**Step 8.** In the triangles ADG, BDG: AD = DB (Step 2), DG is common, and the base GA equals the base GB, both being straight lines drawn from the centre G to the circumference (D1.15). Therefore the angle ADG, contained by AD, DG, equals the angle BDG, contained by BD, DG (1.8).

**Step 9.** Thus the straight line DG, set up on the straight line AB, makes the adjacent angles ADG, BDG equal to one another; therefore each of them is right (D1.10). In particular the angle GDB is right.

**Step 10.** Since D lies between C and E, the points C, E are on opposite sides of AB; and G, not lying on AB, is on one side of it. Let H be that one of the points C, E which lies on the same side of AB as G. The angle HDB is right: if H = C this is Step 3; if H = E, the angle EDB is vertically opposite to the angle CDA, the straight lines AB and CE cutting one another at D, so that the angle EDB equals the angle CDA (1.15), and the angle CDA is right (Step 3).

**Step 11.** The angles GDB, HDB being both right, the angle GDB equals the angle HDB (P4). But DG and DH are distinct straight lines drawn from D on the same side of AB (G not lying on CE, Step 6), so one of the angles GDB, HDB is a part of the other; hence a part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible (CN5).

**Step 12.** Therefore G is not the centre of the circle ABC. In the same way it is shown that no point other than F is the centre. Since the circle has a centre (D1.16), F is the centre of the given circle ABC; which was to be found.

Note on path: the right angle EDB in Step 10 is obtained from vertical angles (1.15) rather than from 1.13, since 1.15 gives the equality directly without a subtraction step.

## Proposition 3.2
**Statement:** If on the circumference of a circle two points be taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within the circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and let A and B be two points taken at random on its circumference. Join the straight line AB (P1). I say that AB falls within the circle.

**Step 2.** Suppose it does not. Then some point E of AB, lying between A and B, does not fall within the circle; so E lies either on the circumference or outside the circle.

**Step 3.** Take the centre D of the circle ABC (3.1), and join DA, DB, DE (P1).

**Step 4.** Since D is the centre, the straight lines DA and DB, falling upon the circumference from the centre, are equal to one another (D1.15). Therefore triangle DAB is isosceles, and the angles at its base are equal: angle DAB = angle DBA (1.5).

**Step 5.** Since E lies on AB between A and B, angle DAE is the same angle as angle DAB, and angle DBE is the same angle as angle DBA. Hence angle DAE = angle DBE.

**Step 6.** In triangle DAE, the side AE is produced to B; hence the exterior angle DEB is greater than the interior and opposite angle DAE (1.16).

**Step 7.** Combining Steps 5 and 6, angle DEB is greater than angle DBE.

**Step 8.** In triangle DEB, the greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19): angle DEB is subtended by DB, and angle DBE is subtended by DE. Therefore DB is greater than DE.

**Step 9.** Case (i): E lies on the circumference. Then DE, falling upon the circumference from the centre, is equal to DB (D1.15). This contradicts Step 8, in which DB is greater than DE.

**Step 10.** Case (ii): E lies outside the circle. Since D is within the circle and E is outside it, the straight line DE crosses the circumference at some point F lying between D and E. Then DF is equal to DB (D1.15); but DF is a part of DE, so DF is less than DE (CN5); hence DB is less than DE. This again contradicts Step 8.

**Step 11.** Both cases are impossible. Therefore no point of AB between A and B lies on or outside the circle, and so the straight line AB falls within the circle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.3
**Statement:** If in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and in it let a straight line CD through the centre bisect a straight line AB, not through the centre, at the point F. I say first that CD also cuts AB at right angles.

**Step 2.** Take the centre of the circle ABC [3.1], and let it be E; join EA and EB [P1]. Since AB does not pass through the centre, E does not lie on AB; hence E is distinct from F, and AFE, BFE are triangles.

**Step 3.** Since F bisects AB, AF is equal to FB; and FE is common. Therefore the two sides AF, FE are equal to the two sides BF, FE respectively.

**Step 4.** The base EA is equal to the base EB, since E is the centre and EA, EB are straight lines falling from the centre upon the circumference [D1.15].

**Step 5.** Therefore, the two triangles AFE, BFE having their two sides equal to two sides respectively and their bases equal, the angle AFE is equal to the angle BFE [1.8].

**Step 6.** But when a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right [D1.10]. Therefore each of the angles AFE, BFE is right, and CD, which passes through the centre and bisects AB not through the centre, also cuts it at right angles.

**Step 7.** Next, let CD cut AB at right angles at F. I say that it also bisects AB, that is, that AF is equal to FB.

**Step 8.** With the same construction (E the centre, EA and EB joined), since EA is equal to EB [D1.15], the triangle EAB is isosceles, and therefore the angle EAF is equal to the angle EBF, these being the angles at the base AB [1.5].

**Step 9.** The angle AFE is right and the angle BFE is right, by hypothesis; and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]. Therefore the angle AFE is equal to the angle BFE.

**Step 10.** Thus EAF, EBF are two triangles having two angles equal to two angles respectively, namely the angle EAF to the angle EBF and the angle AFE to the angle BFE, and one side equal to one side, namely EF, which is common to both and subtends one of the equal angles (the angle EAF in the one triangle and the angle EBF in the other). Therefore they have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides [1.26]; hence AF is equal to FB.

**Step 11.** Therefore CD, which passes through the centre and cuts AB not through the centre at right angles, also bisects it. Consequently, if in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.4
**Statement:** If in a circle two straight lines cut one another which are not through the centre, they do not bisect one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and in it let AC and BD be two straight lines, neither of which passes through the centre, cutting one another at the point E. Suppose, if possible, that they bisect one another, so that AE = EC and BE = ED.

**Step 2.** Find the centre of the circle ABCD [3.1] and let it be F. Since AC does not pass through the centre, the point E, which lies on AC, is not the centre; so E and F are distinct points. Join the straight line FE [P1].

**Step 3.** FE is a straight line through the centre F, and it bisects at E the straight line AC, which is not through the centre (AE = EC by Step 1). Therefore FE cuts AC at right angles [3.3]; in particular the angle FEA is a right angle.

**Step 4.** Likewise FE is a straight line through the centre which bisects at E the straight line BD, which is not through the centre (BE = ED by Step 1). Therefore FE cuts BD at right angles [3.3]; in particular the angle FEB is a right angle.

**Step 5.** Since the angles FEA and FEB are both right angles, they are equal to one another [P4].

**Step 6.** Now consider the position of these two angles. The straight line FE passes through E, a point of AC lying between A and C, and FE is a different straight line from AC (because F is not on AC); hence A and C lie on opposite sides of the straight line FE. Also, since BD does not pass through F, BD is a different straight line from FE, and the two have only the point E in common; so B, a point of BD distinct from E (as BE = ED and B is not D), does not lie on the straight line FE. Therefore B lies on the same side of FE as exactly one of the points A, C. Because the supposition AE = EC is symmetric in A and C, we may name the extremities of the first line so that B lies on the same side of FE as A.

**Step 7.** The straight lines AC and BD are two distinct straight lines which cut one another at E, so they have no point in common other than E; in particular B does not lie on AC, and hence the straight lines EA and EB, drawn from E on the same side of FE, are distinct. Consequently one of them falls within the angle contained by FE and the other: either EB falls within the angle FEA, so that the angle FEB is a part of the angle FEA, or EA falls within the angle FEB, so that the angle FEA is a part of the angle FEB.

**Step 8.** In either case one of the angles FEA, FEB is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part [CN5]; so the angles FEA and FEB are unequal. This contradicts Step 5, in which they were shown to be equal.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition of Step 1 is impossible, and AC, BD do not bisect one another. Hence, if in a circle two straight lines cut one another which are not through the centre, they do not bisect one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.5
**Statement:** If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.

**Step 1.** Let the circles ABC and CDG cut one another at the points B and C. Suppose, if possible, that the two circles have the same centre, and let that common centre be E.

**Step 2.** Join EC (P1). Since the circles ABC and CDG cut one another, they are two distinct circles whose circumferences do not coincide; hence there is a point F on the circumference of circle ABC which does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG.

**Step 3.** Join EF (P1). Since E, being the centre of circle CDG, lies within that circle, the straight line drawn from E through F and, if F falls within circle CDG, produced in a straight line beyond F (P2), passes out of circle CDG and so meets its circumference; let it meet the circumference of circle CDG at the point G, on the same side of E as F. Because F does not lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the points F and G are distinct. Thus E, F, G lie on one straight line with F and G on the same side of E, so that one of the straight lines EF, EG is a part of the other: if F lies within circle CDG, EF is a part of EG, and if F lies outside circle CDG, EG is a part of EF.

**Step 4.** Since E is the centre of circle ABC (D1.16), and the points C and F both lie on the circumference of circle ABC, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EF (D1.15).

**Step 5.** Since E is also the centre of circle CDG (D1.16), and the points C and G both lie on the circumference of circle CDG, the straight line EC is equal to the straight line EG (D1.15).

**Step 6.** Therefore EF is equal to EG, since each of them is equal to EC (CN1).

**Step 7.** But by Step 3 one of EF, EG is a part of the other, and the whole is greater than the part (CN5); so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible.

**Step 8.** Therefore E is not the centre of both circles ABC and CDG. Hence, if two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre. Q.E.D.
