## Proposition 3.31
**Statement:** In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, let BC be a diameter of it, and let E be its centre; since BC is a diameter, it passes through the centre E (D1.17). The semicircle BAC is the figure contained by the diameter BC and the circumference BAC cut off by it (D1.18). Take any point A on the circumference BAC and join BA, AC (P1). Then the angle BAC, contained by the straight lines joined from A to the extremities B, C of the diameter, is the angle in the semicircle BAC (D3.8).

**Step 2.** The straight line AC divides the circle into the two segments ABC and ADC, each contained by AC and a circumference (D3.6). Because the diameter BC bisects the circle (D1.17), the circumference ABC consists of the circumference AB together with the semicircle from B to C on the side remote from A; hence the segment ABC is greater than a semicircle (CN5). The circumference ADC is a part of the semicircle BAC; hence the segment ADC is less than a semicircle (CN5). Take any point D on the circumference ADC and join AD, DC (P1). Then ABC is an angle in the greater segment ABC, and ADC is an angle in the less segment ADC (D3.8).

**Step 3.** Join AE (P1), and produce BA beyond A to a point F (P2).

**Step 4.** Since E is the centre, BE = EA and EA = EC (D1.15). In triangle ABE the sides BE, EA are equal, so the angle ABE equals the angle BAE (1.5). In triangle AEC the sides EA, EC are equal, so the angle EAC equals the angle ECA (1.5).

**Step 5.** E lies on BC between B and C, so AE falls within the angle BAC, and the angle BAC is the sum of the angles BAE, EAC; moreover the angle ABE is the angle ABC and the angle ECA is the angle ACB. Adding the two equalities of Step 4 (CN2), the angle BAC equals the sum of the angles ABC, ACB.

**Step 6.** Since the side BA of triangle ABC is produced to F, the angle FAC is an exterior angle of that triangle and equals the sum of the two interior and opposite angles ABC, ACB (1.32). Therefore the angle BAC equals the angle FAC (CN1).

**Step 7.** The straight line CA, set up on the straight line BF, makes the adjacent angles BAC, CAF equal to one another; therefore each of them is right (D1.10). Thus the angle BAC in the semicircle BAC is right. (First part.)

**Step 8.** In triangle ABC the two angles ABC, BAC are together less than two right angles (1.17). The angle BAC is right (Step 7); therefore the angle ABC is less than a right angle. Since all angles in the same segment are equal to one another (3.21), every angle in the greater segment ABC is less than a right angle. (Second part.)

**Step 9.** The points A, B, C, D lie on the circumference, so ABCD is a quadrilateral in the circle, and its opposite angles ABC, ADC are together equal to two right angles (3.22). The angle ABC is less than a right angle (Step 8); therefore the angle ADC is greater than a right angle. Since all angles in the same segment are equal to one another (3.21), every angle in the less segment ADC is greater than a right angle. (Third part.)

**Step 10.** The angle of the greater segment ABC is the angle contained by the straight line AC and the circumference ABC (D3.7). The straight line BA, joining the points B, A of the circumference, falls within the circle (3.2), and so lies within the segment ABC; hence the rectilineal angle BAC is a part of the angle contained by AC and the circumference ABC. The whole is greater than the part (CN5), and the angle BAC is right (Step 7); therefore the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle. (Fourth part.)

**Step 11.** The angle of the less segment ADC is the angle contained by the straight line AC and the circumference ADC (D3.7). Since F lies on BA produced beyond A, F is on the side of AC remote from B, which is the side on which the circumference ADC lies; and the circumference ADC lies on the same side of BF as C. Hence the circumference ADC falls within the angle CAF, and the angle contained by AC and the circumference ADC is a part of the angle CAF. The whole is greater than the part (CN5), and the angle CAF is right (Step 7); therefore the angle of the less segment is less than a right angle. (Fifth part.)

Therefore in a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle. Q.E.D.

Path note: in Step 8 the same inequality follows from 1.32 applied to triangle ABC (three angles together equal to two right angles, one of them right); 1.17 is cited as the more direct statement.

## Proposition 3.32
**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact there be drawn across, in the circle, a straight line cutting the circle, the angles which it makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF touch the circle at the point B, and from B let the straight line BD be drawn across in the circle, cutting it, so that its other extremity D lies on the circumference. From B draw BA at right angles to EF [1.11] and produce it [P2] until it meets the circumference again at A. Because EF touches the circle at B and BA is drawn from the point of contact at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle lies on BA [3.19]. Thus BA passes through the centre and is terminated at both ends by the circumference, so BA is a diameter of the circle [D1.17], and each of the two segments cut off by BA is a semicircle [D1.18].

**Step 2.** First suppose that BD does not pass through the centre, so that D is distinct from A and lies on one side of the diameter BA. Name the extremities of the tangent so that F lies on the same side of BA as D and E on the other side; then BD falls within the angle ABF, so that the angle ABF is made up of the angles ABD and DBF. Take a point C at random on the circumference BD remote from A (the arc from B to D not containing A), and join AD, DC, CB [P1]. The angles which BD makes with the tangent are DBF and DBE. The segment alternate to the angle DBF is the segment BAD, and the angle in it is the angle BAD; the segment alternate to the angle DBE is the segment DCB, and the angle in it is the angle DCB [D3.8].

**Step 3.** The angle ADB is an angle in the semicircle on the diameter BA, because D is a point on the circumference of that semicircle and DA, DB are joined from D to the extremities A, B of its base [D1.18, D3.8]. Therefore the angle ADB is right [3.31].

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABD the three angles BAD, ABD, ADB are together equal to two right angles [1.32]. Since the angle ADB is a right angle, subtracting it from the two right angles leaves the angles BAD and ABD together equal to one right angle [CN3].

**Step 5.** The angle ABF is right by the construction of Step 1. Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], the angle ABF is equal to the angles BAD and ABD taken together.

**Step 6.** The angle ABF is made up of the angles ABD and DBF (Step 2). Subtracting the angle ABD from the angle ABF and from the sum of BAD and ABD, the remaining angle DBF is equal to the remaining angle BAD [CN3]. That is, the angle DBF which BD makes with the tangent is equal to the angle BAD in the alternate segment BAD.

**Step 7.** The points A, B, C, D all lie on the circumference, A and C being on opposite sides of BD, so ABCD is a quadrilateral in the circle. Therefore its opposite angles BAD and BCD are together equal to two right angles [3.22].

**Step 8.** The straight line BD stands on the straight line EF at B, so the adjacent angles DBF and DBE are together equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 9.** Hence the angles DBF and DBE taken together are equal to the angles BAD and BCD taken together, each pair being equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 10.** Of these, the angle DBF is equal to the angle BAD (Step 6). Subtracting these equals from the equal sums, the remaining angle DBE is equal to the remaining angle BCD [CN3]. That is, the angle DBE which BD makes with the tangent is equal to the angle DCB in the alternate segment DCB.

**Step 11.** It remains to consider the case in which BD passes through the centre. Then BD is a diameter [D1.17], and the straight line joined from the centre to the point of contact B lies along BD and is perpendicular to the tangent EF [3.18]; hence BD is perpendicular to EF, and each of the angles DBF and DBE is right [D1.10]. The two segments into which BD divides the circle are semicircles [D1.18], and the angle in each of them is right [3.31]. Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], each of the angles DBF and DBE is equal to the angle in the segment alternate to it.

**Step 12.** Therefore, in every case, the angles which the straight line BD drawn from the point of contact makes with the tangent EF are equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.33
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

Let AB be the given straight line and C the given rectilineal angle. It is required to describe on AB a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to C. The angle C is either acute, right, or obtuse; the three cases are treated in turn.

**Case I: the angle C is acute.**

**Step 1.** On the straight line AB and at the point A on it, construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23].

**Step 2.** From the point A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the angle BAD (being equal to the acute angle C) is less than the right angle DAK, and AB, AK lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AB falls within the angle DAK; hence the angle BAK is the excess of the right angle DAK over the angle BAD, and so the angle BAK is less than a right angle.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11], taking FG on the same side of AB as K.

**Step 4.** The straight line AB falls on the two straight lines AK and FG and makes with them the interior angles BAK and AFG on the same side; the angle BAK is less than a right angle (Step 2) and the angle AFG is right (Step 3), so together they are less than two right angles. Therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at the point G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 5.** Since AF is equal to FB (Step 3) and FG is common, the two sides AF, FG are equal to the two sides BF, FG respectively; and the angle AFG is equal to the angle BFG, both being right angles [P4]. Therefore the base AG is equal to the base BG [1.4].

**Step 6.** With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]. Since GB is equal to GA (Step 5), the point B lies on the circumference of this circle [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] until it meets the circumference again at the point E; then AE, passing through the centre G and terminated in both directions by the circumference, is a diameter of the circle [D1.17]. The figure contained by the straight line AB and the circumference AEB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6].

**Step 7.** The straight line AD was drawn from A at right angles to AK (Step 2), and the diameter AE lies along AK; thus AD is drawn from the extremity A of the diameter AE at right angles to that diameter. Therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 8.** Since AB falls within the angle DAK (Step 2), the ray AK, and hence the point E on it, lies on the opposite side of AB from D; so the segment AEB is the segment alternate to the angle DAB. Now AD touches the circle at A, and from the point of contact A the straight line AB has been drawn across in the circle, cutting it; therefore the angle DAB, which AB makes with the tangent AD, is equal to the angle in the alternate segment AEB, that is, to the angle AEB [3.32], which is the angle in the segment AEB [D3.8].

**Step 9.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 1); therefore the angle AEB is also equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on the given straight line AB the segment AEB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case II: the angle C is right.**

**Step 10.** Bisect AB at the point F [1.10], and with centre F and distance FA describe a circle [P3]. Since FB is equal to FA, the point B lies on the circumference [D1.15]. Thus AB passes through the centre F and is terminated in both directions by the circumference, so AB is a diameter [D1.17], and the figure contained by AB and the circumference cut off by it on either side is a semicircle [D1.18]; let E be any point on this circumference, and join AE, EB [P1].

**Step 11.** The angle AEB, being the angle in the semicircle AEB, is a right angle [3.31]. But the angle C is also a right angle, and all right angles are equal to one another [P4]; therefore the angle AEB is equal to the angle C. Hence on AB the semicircle AEB has been described admitting the angle AEB equal to the given angle C.

**Case III: the angle C is obtuse.**

**Step 12.** On AB at the point A construct the angle BAD equal to the angle C [1.23], and from A draw AK at right angles to AD [1.11], taking AK on the same side of AD as B. Since the right angle DAK is less than the obtuse angle DAB, and AK, AB lie on the same side of AD, the straight line AK falls within the angle DAB; hence the angle KAB is the excess of the angle DAB over the right angle DAK. Since the angle DAB, being a rectilineal angle, is less than two right angles, the angle KAB is less than a right angle.

**Step 13.** Bisect AB at F [1.10], and from F draw FG at right angles to AB [1.11] on the same side of AB as K. The straight line AB falls on AK and FG and makes the interior angles KAB (less than a right angle) and AFG (right) on the same side, together less than two right angles; therefore AK and FG, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at G. Join GB [P1].

**Step 14.** As in Step 5, AF is equal to FB, FG is common, and the right angles AFG, BFG are equal [P4]; therefore AG is equal to BG [1.4]. With centre G and distance GA describe a circle [P3]; since GB is equal to GA, B lies on its circumference [D1.15]. Produce AG beyond G [P2] to meet the circumference at E; then AE is a diameter [D1.17], lying along AK, and AD is drawn from its extremity A at right angles to it; therefore AD touches the circle at A [3.16, Porism].

**Step 15.** In this case AK falls within the angle DAB (Step 12), so K, and with it G and E, lie on the same side of AB as D; the segment alternate to the angle DAB is therefore the segment on the other side of AB. Let H be any point on the circumference on that other side of AB, and join AH, HB [P1]; then AHB is a segment of the circle on AB [D3.6] and the angle AHB is the angle in it [D3.8]. Since AD touches the circle at A and AB is drawn across in the circle from the point of contact, the angle DAB is equal to the angle AHB in the alternate segment AHB [3.32].

**Step 16.** But the angle DAB is equal to the angle C (Step 12); therefore the angle AHB is equal to the angle C [CN1]. Hence on AB the segment AHB of a circle has been described admitting the angle AHB equal to the given angle C.

**Step 17.** Therefore in every case, on the given straight line AB a segment of a circle has been described admitting an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle C. Q.E.F.

*Path note:* in Case II the most direct route is taken: the semicircle on AB is described at once and its angle is shown right by 3.31, so neither the construction of the angle BAD nor the tangent AD is needed there; the tangent-and-alternate-segment argument (3.16 Por., 3.32) is used only in the acute and obtuse cases, where it is indispensable.

## Proposition 3.34
**Statement:** From a given circle to cut off a segment admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle and D the given rectilineal angle. It is required to cut off from the circle ABC a segment admitting an angle equal to the angle D.

**Step 2.** Let a straight line EF be drawn touching the circle ABC, and let B be the point of contact, so that EF touches the circle ABC at the point B [3.17].

**Step 3.** On the straight line FB, and at the point B on it, construct the angle FBC equal to the given angle D [1.23], the side BC being drawn on that side of EF on which the circle ABC lies.

**Step 4.** Since EF touches the circle ABC at B, no straight line can be interposed into the space between EF and the circumference of the circle [3.16]. Hence BC, being a straight line through B distinct from EF and lying on the side of the circle, falls within the circle; therefore, being produced, it meets the circumference again. Let C be the point at which it meets the circumference. Thus BC has been drawn across in the circle from the point of contact B and cuts the circle, and it cuts off from the circle the segment BAC lying on the opposite side of BC from F.

**Step 6.** But the angle FBC was constructed equal to the angle D (Step 3). Therefore the angle in the segment BAC is also equal to the angle D [CN1].

## Proposition 3.35
**Statement:** If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and in it let the two straight lines AC and BD cut one another at the point E. We must show that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Take the centre F of the circle [3.1].

Hence the rectangle AE, EC is the square on AE, the rectangle DE, EB is the square on DE, and since AE = DE these squares are equal. So the two rectangles are equal, and the proposition holds in this case.

**Step 3.** Next, suppose that E is not the centre F. We first establish the following for either of the two given straight lines: if XY is one of them (X, Y being its extremities on the circumference) and E the point on it at which they cut, then the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. **Step 4.** Case (a): XY passes through the centre F. Therefore, XY being cut into equal segments at F and into unequal segments at E, the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on FE is equal to the square on the half, that is, on FX [2.5]. This is the required equation.

**Step 5.** Case (b): XY does not pass through F. From F draw FG perpendicular to XY [1.12], so that the angles at G are right [D1.10]. Since FG is a straight line through the centre which cuts the straight line XY, not through the centre, at right angles, it also bisects it [3.3]; therefore XG = GY.

**Step 6.** Suppose E does not coincide with G. Then XY is cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at E; therefore the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GX [2.5]. **Step 7.** In the triangle EGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on EG, GF are equal to the square on FE; and in the triangle XGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on GX, GF are equal to the square on FX [1.47]. **Step 8.** If instead E coincides with G, then XE = EY, so the rectangle XE, EY is the square on XE; and FE is the perpendicular FG, so in the right-angled triangle XEF the square on XE together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX [1.47]. Thus again the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX.

**Step 9.** Therefore in every case (Steps 4 to 8) the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. Applying it to the straight line BD: the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FB.

**Step 11.** Subtract the square on EF from each: the rectangle AE, EC is equal to the rectangle DE, EB [CN3].

## Proposition 3.36
**Statement:** If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two straight lines, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference will be equal to the square on the tangent.

**Step 1.** Let a point D be taken outside the circle ABC, and from D let the two straight lines DCA, DB fall on the circle; let DCA cut the circle (meeting the convex circumference first at C and the concave circumference at A) and let DB touch it at B. I say that the rectangle contained by AD, DC is equal to the square on DB. Two cases arise: DCA either passes through the centre or it does not.

**Step 2.** Case 1: let DCA pass through the centre, and let F be the centre of the circle ABC. Join FB (P1).

**Step 3.** Since DB touches the circle at B and FB is joined from the centre to the point of contact, FB is perpendicular to DB; therefore the angle FBD is right (3.18).

**Step 4.** Since F is the centre, FA is equal to FC (D1.15); hence the straight line AC is bisected at F, and the straight line CD is added to it in a straight line.

**Step 5.** Therefore the rectangle contained by AD, DC together with the square on FC is equal to the square on FD (2.6).

**Step 6.** But FC is equal to FB (D1.15); therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on FB is equal to the square on FD.

**Step 7.** Since the angle FBD is right, the square on FD is equal to the squares on FB, BD (1.47).

**Step 8.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on FB is equal to the squares on FB, BD (CN1).

**Step 9.** Let the square on FB be subtracted from each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC which remains is equal to the square on the tangent DB (CN3).

**Step 10.** Case 2: let DCA not pass through the centre of the circle ABC. Let the centre E be taken (3.1), and from E let EF be drawn perpendicular to AC (1.12); join EB, EC, ED (P1). Since D lies on the straight line AC produced, F, C, D lie in one straight line, and the angles EFC, EFD are right.

**Step 11.** Since DB touches the circle at B and EB is joined from the centre to the point of contact, the angle EBD is right (3.18).

**Step 12.** Since the straight line EF through the centre cuts the straight line AC not through the centre at right angles, it also bisects it; therefore AF is equal to FC (3.3).

**Step 13.** Since the straight line AC is bisected at F and CD is added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by AD, DC together with the square on FC is equal to the square on FD (2.6).

**Step 14.** Let the square on FE be added to each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the squares on CF, FE is equal to the squares on FD, FE (CN2).

**Step 15.** Since the angle EFC is right, the squares on CF, FE are equal to the square on CE (1.47); and since the angle EFD is right, the squares on FD, FE are equal to the square on ED (1.47).

**Step 16.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on CE is equal to the square on ED (CN1).

**Step 17.** But CE is equal to EB, since E is the centre (D1.15); therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on EB is equal to the square on ED.

**Step 18.** Since the angle EBD is right, the square on ED is equal to the squares on EB, BD (1.47).

**Step 19.** Therefore the rectangle AD, DC together with the square on EB is equal to the squares on EB, BD (CN1).

**Step 20.** Let the square on EB be subtracted from each; therefore the rectangle AD, DC which remains is equal to the square on the tangent DB (CN3).

**Step 21.** Therefore in either case, if a point be taken outside a circle and from it two straight lines fall on the circle, one cutting it and the other touching it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the cutting line and the part intercepted outside between the point and the convex circumference is equal to the square on the tangent. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.37
**Statement:** If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which falls on it will touch the circle.

**Step 1.** Let D be a point taken outside the circle ABC, and from D let the two straight lines DCA and DB fall on the circle; let DCA cut the circle (meeting the circumference at C and at A), and let DB fall on the circle at B; and let the rectangle contained by AD, DC be equal to the square on DB. I say that DB touches the circle ABC.

**Step 2.** From the point D draw the straight line DE touching the circle ABC [3.17]; let F be the centre of the circle ABC [3.1]; and join FE, FB, FD [P1].

**Step 3.** Since DE touches the circle ABC and FE is joined from the centre F to the point of contact E, FE is perpendicular to DE; therefore the angle FED is right [3.18].

**Step 4.** Since DE touches the circle ABC and DCA cuts it, the rectangle contained by AD, DC is equal to the square on DE [3.36].

**Step 5.** But the rectangle contained by AD, DC is also equal to the square on DB, by hypothesis. Therefore the square on DE is equal to the square on DB [CN1]; hence the straight line DE is equal to the straight line DB.

**Step 6.** Moreover FE is equal to FB, since both are drawn from the centre F to the circumference of the circle [D1.15].

**Step 7.** Therefore, in the two triangles DEF, DBF, the two sides DE, EF are equal to the two sides DB, BF respectively (Steps 5 and 6), and the base FD is common to both. Therefore the angle DEF is equal to the angle DBF [1.8].

**Step 8.** But the angle DEF is right (Step 3); therefore the angle DBF is also right.

**Step 9.** Produce BF beyond F to meet the circumference at G [P2]. Then BG, being drawn through the centre F and terminated in both directions by the circumference, is a diameter of the circle ABC [D1.17]. Hence DB is a straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter BG from its extremity B (Step 8).

**Step 10.** But the straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity touches the circle [3.16, Porism]. Therefore DB touches the circle ABC.

Therefore, if a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which falls on it will touch the circle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 4.1
**Statement:** Into a given circle to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line which is not greater than the diameter of the circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle and D the given straight line, not greater than the diameter of the circle ABC. Let the centre G of the circle ABC be found [3.1]. Take any point B on the circumference, join BG [P1], and produce BG in a straight line to meet the circumference again at C [P2]. Then BC is a diameter of the circle ABC, since it passes through the centre and is terminated in both directions by the circumference [D1.17].

**Step 2.** Since D is not greater than the diameter of the circle, D is either equal to BC or less than BC.

**Step 3.** Suppose first that BC is equal to D. Then BC is a straight line equal to D, and its extremities B and C lie on the circumference of the circle ABC [D1.17]. Therefore BC has been fitted into the circle ABC equal to D [D4.7], and what was required is done.

**Step 4.** Suppose next that BC is greater than D. From the greater straight line CB let CE be cut off equal to the less D [1.3], so that E lies on CB between C and B.

**Step 5.** With centre C and distance CE let the circle EAF be described [P3].

**Step 6.** The point E lies within the circle ABC, since it lies on the diameter CB between its extremities; whereas the point F, the extremity of the diameter of the circle EAF drawn through C on the side away from B, lies outside the circle ABC, since C is on the circumference of ABC and F lies beyond C on BC produced. Hence the circle EAF cuts the circle ABC; let A be a point in which they cut one another, and let CA be joined [P1].

**Step 7.** Since the point C is the centre of the circle EAF, and CA, CE are straight lines drawn from the centre to the circumference, CA is equal to CE [D1.15].

**Step 8.** But CE was made equal to D [Step 4]. Therefore CA is also equal to D [CN1].

**Step 9.** Now the extremity C of the straight line CA lies on the circumference of the circle ABC, being an extremity of the diameter BC [D1.17], and the extremity A lies on the circumference of the circle ABC, being a point in which the circles cut. Therefore the straight line CA has been fitted into the circle ABC [D4.7].

**Step 10.** Hence into the given circle ABC the straight line CA has been fitted equal to the given straight line D, which is not greater than the diameter of the circle. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 4.2
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a triangle equiangular with a given triangle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle and DEF the given triangle. It is required to inscribe in the circle ABC a triangle equiangular with the triangle DEF.

**Step 2.** Take any point A on the circumference of the circle ABC. Find the centre K of the circle ABC (3.1), join AK (P1), and produce AK in both directions (P2), so that the portion of it terminated by the circumference is a diameter of the circle having A as one extremity. Through the point A draw the straight line GH at right angles to AK (1.11).

**Step 3.** Since GH has been drawn at right angles to a diameter of the circle from its extremity A, the straight line GH touches the circle ABC at A (3.16, Porism), and the whole circle lies on one side of GH.

**Step 4.** On the straight line AH, and at the point A on it, construct the angle HAC equal to the angle DEF (1.23), the angle being placed on the side of GH on which the circle lies. The straight line drawn from A containing this angle is distinct from the tangent GH; and since no straight line can be interposed between the tangent and the circumference (3.16), this straight line falls within the circle. Let it be produced (P2) to meet the circumference again, and let C be the point in which it meets it.

**Step 5.** In the same way, on the straight line AG, and at the point A on it, construct the angle GAB equal to the angle DFE (1.23), on the same side of GH. The straight line so drawn likewise falls within the circle (3.16), and, produced (P2), meets the circumference again at a point B.

**Step 6.** Join BC (P1). Then ABC is a triangle, and since each of its angular points A, B, C lies on the circumference of the circle ABC, the triangle ABC is inscribed in the circle ABC (D4.3).

**Step 7.** Now the straight line GH touches the circle ABC at A, and from the point of contact A the straight line AC has been drawn across in the circle, cutting it. Therefore the angle HAC, which AC makes with the tangent AH, is equal to the angle in the alternate segment of the circle, that is, to the angle ABC standing on AC at the point B of the circumference (3.32).

**Step 8.** But the angle HAC was constructed equal to the angle DEF (Step 4). Therefore the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF (CN1).

**Step 9.** Again, since GH touches the circle ABC at A, and from A the straight line AB has been drawn across in the circle cutting it, the angle GAB is equal to the angle in the alternate segment, that is, to the angle ACB (3.32). But the angle GAB was constructed equal to the angle DFE (Step 5). Therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle DFE (CN1).

**Step 10.** The three angles BAC, ABC, ACB of the triangle ABC are together equal to two right angles, and the three angles EDF, DEF, DFE of the triangle DEF are together equal to two right angles (1.32); therefore the angles BAC, ABC, ACB together are equal to the angles EDF, DEF, DFE together (CN1). Of these, the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF and the angle ACB is equal to the angle DFE (Steps 8, 9); if these equals are subtracted from the equal wholes, the remaining angle BAC is equal to the remaining angle EDF (CN3).

**Step 11.** Therefore the triangle ABC has its angle ABC equal to the angle DEF, its angle ACB equal to the angle DFE, and its angle BAC equal to the angle EDF; that is, the triangle ABC is equiangular with the triangle DEF. And it has been inscribed in the given circle ABC (Step 6). Therefore in the given circle ABC the triangle ABC has been inscribed equiangular with the given triangle DEF; which was to be done.

**Statement:** In a given triangle to inscribe a circle.

## Proposition 4.9
**Statement:** About a given square to circumscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the given square. It is required to circumscribe a circle about the square ABCD.

**Step 2.** Join AC and BD (P1), and let them cut one another at the point E.

**Step 3.** Since ABCD is a square, it is both equilateral and right-angled (D1.22); therefore DA = AB = BC = CD, and each of the angles DAB, ABC, BCD, CDA is a right angle.

**Step 4.** All right angles are equal to one another (P4); therefore the angle DAB is equal to the angle CBA, the angle ABC is equal to the angle DCB, and the angle BCD is equal to the angle ADC.

**Step 5.** In the triangles DAB and CBA, the side DA is equal to the side CB (Step 3), the side AB is common, and the included angle DAB is equal to the included angle CBA (Step 4). Therefore the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend (1.4): the angle ABD, subtended by DA, is equal to the angle BAC, subtended by CB. Since E lies on BD and on AC, this is to say that the angle EBA is equal to the angle EAB.

**Step 6.** In the triangle EAB the angle EAB is equal to the angle EBA; therefore the sides which subtend the equal angles are equal (1.6): EB = EA.

**Step 7.** Similarly, in the triangles ABC and DCB, the side AB is equal to the side DC (Step 3), the side BC is common, and the included angle ABC is equal to the included angle DCB (Step 4). Therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle DBC (1.4), that is, the angle ECB is equal to the angle EBC. Hence in the triangle EBC the side EC is equal to the side EB (1.6).

**Step 8.** Similarly again, in the triangles BCD and ADC, the side BC is equal to the side AD (Step 3), the side CD is common, and the included angle BCD is equal to the included angle ADC (Step 4). Therefore the angle BDC is equal to the angle ACD (1.4), that is, the angle EDC is equal to the angle ECD. Hence in the triangle ECD the side ED is equal to the side EC (1.6).

**Step 9.** Now EA = EB (Step 6), EB = EC (Step 7), and EC = ED (Step 8); therefore, things equal to the same thing being equal to one another (CN1), the four straight lines EA, EB, EC, ED are all equal to one another.

**Step 10.** With centre E and distance EA let a circle be described (P3).

**Step 11.** A circle is a figure such that all straight lines falling upon its circumference from the centre are equal to one another (D1.15); since EB, EC, ED are each equal to the radius EA (Step 9), the points B, C, D also lie on the circumference of this circle. Therefore the circle passes through the points A, B, C, D.

**Step 12.** Thus the circumference of the circle passes through each angle of the square ABCD; therefore the circle is circumscribed about the square (D4.6). Accordingly a circle has been circumscribed about the given square ABCD. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 4.10
**Statement:** To construct an isosceles triangle having each of the angles at the base double of the remaining one.

**Step 5.** Since the rectangle AB, BC is equal to the square on AC, and AC is equal to BD, the rectangle AB, BC is equal to the square on BD [CN1].

From B the two straight lines BA, BD fall on the circle ACD: BA cuts the circle (meeting it at A and C), and BD falls on it (meeting it at D); and the rectangle contained by the whole BA and the segment BC outside the circle is equal to the square on BD. Therefore BD touches the circle ACD [3.37].

**Step 7.** Since BD touches the circle ACD at D, and from the point of contact D the straight line DC is drawn across in the circle cutting it, the angle BDC which DC makes with the tangent BD is equal to the angle DAC in the alternate segment [3.32].

**Step 9.** In the triangle ACD the side AC has been produced to B; therefore the exterior angle BCD is equal to the two interior and opposite angles CDA, DAC [1.32]. Since the angle BDA is also equal to the angles CDA, DAC (Step 8), the angle BDA is equal to the angle BCD [CN1].

**Step 10.** Since A is the centre of the circle BDE and B, D lie on its circumference, AB is equal to AD [D1.15]. Hence in the triangle ABD the angle ABD is equal to the angle ADB [1.5]. Therefore the angle DBA is also equal to the angle BCD [CN1], and so the three angles BDA, DBA, BCD are equal to one another.

**Step 11.** Since the angle DBC (which is the same angle as DBA, because C lies on BA) is equal to the angle BCD, in the triangle BCD the side BD subtending the angle BCD is equal to the side DC subtending the angle DBC [1.6].

**Step 12.** But BD is equal to CA by construction (Step 3); therefore CA is equal to CD [CN1]. Hence in the triangle ACD the angle CDA is equal to the angle DAC [1.5].

## Proposition 4.11
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given circle. It is required to inscribe in the circle ABCDE a pentagon that is both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 2.** Set out an isosceles triangle FGH having each of the angles at G and H double of the remaining angle at F [4.10].

**Step 3.** In the circle ABCDE inscribe a triangle ACD equiangular with the triangle FGH, the vertices being lettered so that the angle CAD is equal to the angle at F, the angle ACD to the angle at G, and the angle CDA to the angle at H [4.2]. The points A, C, D therefore lie on the circumference of the circle.

**Step 4.** Since the angle at G is double of the angle at F, and the angle ACD is equal to the angle at G while the angle CAD is equal to the angle at F, the angle ACD is double of the angle CAD. In the same way, since the angle at H is double of the angle at F, the angle CDA is double of the angle CAD.

**Step 5.** Bisect the angle ACD by the straight line CE, and the angle CDA by the straight line DB [1.9], and let these bisecting lines be produced to meet the circumference of the circle at E and B respectively [P2]. Since CE falls within the angle ACD, the point E lies on the circumference AD remote from C; since DB falls within the angle CDA, the point B lies on the circumference AC remote from D. Thus the five points A, B, C, D, E lie in this order on the circumference.

**Step 6.** Join AB, BC, DE, EA [P1].

**Step 7.** The angle ACD is double of the angle CAD (Step 4), and, having been bisected by CE, it is also double of each of the angles ACE, ECD; therefore each of the angles ACE, ECD is equal to the angle CAD. Likewise the angle CDA is double of the angle CAD and also double of each of the angles CDB, BDA; therefore each of the angles CDB, BDA is equal to the angle CAD. Hence the five angles DAC, ACE, ECD, CDB, BDA, being each equal to the angle CAD, are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 8.** These five angles are angles at the circumference of the one circle ABCDE, and the angle DAC stands upon the circumference DC, the angle ACE upon the circumference EA, the angle ECD upon the circumference DE, the angle CDB upon the circumference BC, and the angle BDA upon the circumference AB [D3.9]. Now equal angles at the circumference stand upon equal circumferences, the circle being taken together with itself as a pair of equal circles [3.26]. Therefore the five circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal to one another.

**Step 9.** Equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines [3.29]; therefore the five straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal to one another. Hence the pentagon ABCDE is equilateral.

**Step 10.** Next, since the circumference AB is equal to the circumference DE, let the circumference BCD be added to each; then the whole circumference ABCD is equal to the whole circumference EDCB [CN2]. In the same manner, since each of the circumferences ABCD, BCDE, CDEA, DEAB, EABC is made up of three of the five equal circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, these five circumferences are all equal to one another [CN2].

**Step 11.** The angle AED stands upon the circumference ABCD, the angle BAE upon the circumference BCDE, the angle ABC upon the circumference CDEA, the angle BCD upon the circumference DEAB, and the angle CDE upon the circumference EABC [D3.9]. But in a circle angles at the circumference which stand upon equal circumferences are equal to one another [3.27]. Therefore the angle BAE is equal to the angle AED, and each of the angles ABC, BCD, CDE is equal to each of the angles BAE, AED; that is, the five angles BAE, ABC, BCD, CDE, DEA are equal to one another. Hence the pentagon ABCDE is equiangular.

**Step 12.** Finally, each of the angular points A, B, C, D, E of the pentagon lies on the circumference of the circle ABCDE (Steps 3 and 5); therefore the pentagon ABCDE is inscribed in the circle [D4.3]. Thus in the given circle an equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABCDE has been inscribed, which was to be done.

## Proposition 4.16
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the given circle. Construct an equilateral triangle LMN (1.1). Since LM = LN, the angles at M and N are equal, and since ML = MN, the angles at L and N are equal (1.5); hence the three angles of the triangle LMN are equal to one another (CN1).

**Step 3.** The angle AKC at the circumference stands upon the arc AC, the angle CAK upon the arc CK, and the angle ACK upon the arc KA. Since these angles are equal, the arcs upon which they stand are equal (3.26): arc AC = arc CK = arc KA. These three arcs together make up the whole circumference of the circle.

**Step 4.** In the same circle inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABFGH having A as a vertex (4.11), its vertices lying in the order A, B, F, G, H round the circle, and let B be that vertex adjacent to A for which the arc AB proceeds from A along the circumference in the same direction as the arc AC. Since the chords AB, BF, FG, GH, HA are equal, the arcs between adjacent vertices which they cut off are equal (3.28): arc AB = arc BF = arc FG = arc GH = arc HA. These five arcs together make up the whole circumference.

**Step 5.** The arc AB is less than the arc AC. For otherwise each of the five equal arcs AB, BF, FG, GH, HA would be not less than AC, so that the five together would be not less than five arcs each equal to AC; but five arcs each equal to AC are greater than three such arcs (CN5), that is, greater than the whole circumference (Step 3); thus the five arcs AB, BF, FG, GH, HA would exceed the whole circumference, which is impossible, since they make up exactly that circumference. Therefore, the arcs AB and AC proceeding from A in the same direction, the point B lies on the arc AC, and the arc AC is made up of the arcs AB and BC.

**Step 6.** Bisect the arc BC at the point E (3.30), so that arc BE = arc EC. Then the arc AC is made up of the arc AB together with two arcs each equal to BE (CN2).

**Step 7.** Three arcs each equal to AC make up the whole circumference (Step 3), and five arcs each equal to AB make up the whole circumference (Step 4); therefore three arcs each equal to AC are equal to five arcs each equal to AB (CN1). By Step 6, three arcs each equal to AC are made up of three arcs each equal to AB together with six arcs each equal to BE (CN2). Hence three arcs each equal to AB together with six arcs each equal to BE are equal to five arcs each equal to AB; and, taking away three arcs each equal to AB from both, six arcs each equal to BE are equal to two arcs each equal to AB (CN3).

**Step 8.** Therefore three arcs each equal to BE are equal to the arc AB. For if three arcs each equal to BE were greater than AB, then six arcs each equal to BE, being made up of two such sets of three, would contain two arcs each equal to AB together with a surplus, and so would be greater than two arcs each equal to AB (CN5), contrary to Step 7; and if three arcs each equal to BE were less than AB, then in the same way two arcs each equal to AB would be greater than six arcs each equal to BE (CN5), again contrary to Step 7.

**Step 9.** Consequently the arc AC, being made up of AB and two arcs each equal to BE (Step 6), is equal to five arcs each equal to BE (CN2); and the whole circumference, being made up of five arcs each equal to AB (Step 4), is equal to fifteen arcs each equal to BE (CN2).

## Proposition 5.1
**Statement:** If a magnitude be the same multiple of a magnitude that a part subtracted is of a part subtracted, the remainder will also be the same multiple of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.

**Step 1.** Let the magnitude AB be the same multiple of the magnitude CD that AE, a part subtracted from AB, is of CF, a part subtracted from CD; and let the remainders be EB and FD. I say that the remainder EB is the same multiple of the remainder FD that the whole AB is of the whole CD.

**Step 2.** Since AB is a multiple of CD, AB is measured by CD [D5.2]; therefore AB can be divided into magnitudes AG, GH, ..., KB, each equal to CD, and their number is the number of times that AB is a multiple of CD.

**Step 3.** Likewise, since AE is a multiple of CF, AE is measured by CF [D5.2]; therefore AE can be divided into magnitudes AL, LM, ..., NE, each equal to CF. And since AB is the same multiple of CD that AE is of CF, the magnitudes AL, LM, ..., NE are as many in number as the magnitudes AG, GH, ..., KB.

**Step 4.** Since CF is a part of CD, the whole CD is greater than CF [CN5], and CD is made up of CF together with the remainder FD. Now each of AG, GH, ..., KB is equal to CD; therefore from each of them let a magnitude equal to CF be cut off, namely AP from AG, GQ from GH, ..., KR from KB. Then, since AG is equal to CD and AP is equal to CF, if the equals AP, CF be subtracted from the equals AG, CD, the remainder PG is equal to the remainder FD [CN3]. In the same way each of QH, ..., RB is equal to FD.

**Step 5.** Now each of AP, GQ, ..., KR is equal to CF, and each of AL, LM, ..., NE is equal to CF; therefore AP is equal to AL, GQ to LM, and so on, each to each [CN1]. And these magnitudes are equal in number (Step 3). Therefore, adding equals to equals, the sum of AP, GQ, ..., KR is equal to the sum of AL, LM, ..., NE [CN2]; that is, the sum of AP, GQ, ..., KR is equal to AE.

**Step 6.** But the whole AB is made up of the sum of AP, GQ, ..., KR together with the sum of PG, QH, ..., RB; and the whole AB is also made up of AE together with EB. If from the same AB there be subtracted the equals, namely the sum of AP, GQ, ..., KR on the one hand and AE on the other, the remainders are equal [CN3]; therefore the sum of PG, QH, ..., RB is equal to EB.

**Step 7.** Therefore EB is made up of the magnitudes PG, QH, ..., RB, each of which is equal to FD, and which are as many in number as AG, GH, ..., KB. Hence FD measures EB, so that EB is a multiple of FD [D5.2], and the number of times is the same as the number of times that AB is a multiple of CD.

**Step 8.** Therefore the remainder EB is the same multiple of the remainder FD that the whole AB is of the whole CD. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.2
**Statement:** If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and a fifth also be the same multiple of the second that a sixth is of the fourth, the sum of the first and fifth will also be the same multiple of the second that the sum of the third and sixth is of the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let the first magnitude AB be the same multiple of the second magnitude C that the third magnitude DE is of the fourth magnitude F, and let the fifth magnitude BG be the same multiple of C that the sixth magnitude EH is of F. Let AB and BG be placed together so that the sum of the first and fifth is the whole magnitude AG, and let DE and EH likewise be placed together so that the sum of the third and sixth is the whole magnitude DH. It is required to prove that AG is the same multiple of C that DH is of F.

**Step 2.** Since AB is a multiple of C, AB is measured by C (D5.2); that is, AB is made up of a certain number of magnitudes each equal to C, exactly and with nothing left over. Since DE is the same multiple of F that AB is of C, DE is measured by F (D5.2) and is made up of the same number of magnitudes each equal to F. Let this common number be m: AB is composed of m magnitudes each equal to C, and DE is composed of m magnitudes each equal to F.

**Step 3.** In the same way, since BG is the same multiple of C that EH is of F, BG is measured by C and EH by F (D5.2), the number of measuring magnitudes being the same in each. Let this common number be n: BG is composed of n magnitudes each equal to C, and EH is composed of n magnitudes each equal to F.

**Step 4.** The whole AG is composed of AB together with BG. The m magnitudes equal to C which make up AB, taken together with the n magnitudes equal to C which make up BG, therefore make up the whole AG exactly, with nothing left over. Hence AG is composed of m + n magnitudes each equal to C; that is, C measures AG, and AG is that multiple of C which is m + n times C (D5.2).

**Step 5.** Likewise the whole DH is composed of DE together with EH. The m magnitudes equal to F which make up DE, taken together with the n magnitudes equal to F which make up EH, make up the whole DH exactly, with nothing left over. Hence DH is composed of m + n magnitudes each equal to F; that is, F measures DH, and DH is that multiple of F which is m + n times F (D5.2).

**Step 6.** Therefore as many magnitudes as there are in AG equal to C, so many also are there in DH equal to F, the number being m + n in each case. Consequently, whatever multiple AG is of C, that same multiple is DH of F (D5.2).

**Step 7.** Therefore, if a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and a fifth also be the same multiple of the second that a sixth is of the fourth, the sum of the first and fifth is also the same multiple of the second that the sum of the third and sixth is of the fourth. Q.E.D.

Path note: the proof proceeds directly from the definition of a multiple (D5.2) by counting the measuring magnitudes; 5.1, which concerns subtraction of parts, is not required.

## Proposition 5.3
**Statement:** If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and if equimultiples be taken of the first and third, then also ex aequali the magnitudes taken will be equimultiples respectively, the one of the second and the other of the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let a first magnitude A be the same multiple of a second B that a third C is of a fourth D, and let equimultiples EF and GH be taken of A and C respectively. We must show that EF is the same multiple of B that GH is of D.

**Step 2.** Since EF is the same multiple of A that GH is of C, EF is measured by A and GH is measured by C, and as many times the one as the other (D5.2). Divide EF into the magnitudes EK, KF, each equal to A, and GH into the magnitudes GL, LH, each equal to C; then the number of the magnitudes EK, KF in EF is equal to the number of the magnitudes GL, LH in GH.

**Step 3.** Since A is the same multiple of B that C is of D, and EK is equal to A while GL is equal to C, EK is measured by B exactly as many times as GL is measured by D (D5.2); that is, EK is the same multiple of B that GL is of D.

**Step 4.** For the same reason KF is the same multiple of B that LH is of D.

**Step 5.** Thus a first magnitude EK is the same multiple of a second B that a third GL is of a fourth D, and a fifth KF is also the same multiple of B that a sixth LH is of D. Therefore the sum of the first and fifth, EK together with KF, that is EF, is the same multiple of B that the sum of the third and sixth, GL together with LH, that is GH, is of D (5.2).

**Step 6.** If EF and GH contain more than two parts each, the same reasoning applies: each further part of EF is the same multiple of B that the corresponding part of GH is of D (Step 3), and adding it to the sum already formed keeps the sum of the parts of EF the same multiple of B that the sum of the corresponding parts of GH is of D (5.2), until all the parts are exhausted. Therefore EF is the same multiple of B that GH is of D.

**Step 7.** Therefore, if a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and if equimultiples be taken of the first and third, then also ex aequali the magnitudes taken are equimultiples respectively, the one of the second and the other of the fourth. Q.E.D.

**Path note:** The only natural route is to split the equimultiples into parts equal to A and C and sum them with 5.2; no alternative preceding theorem serves.

## Proposition 5.4
**Statement:** If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third to a fourth, any equimultiples whatever of the first and third will also have the same ratio to any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth respectively, taken in corresponding order.

**Step 1.** Let a first magnitude A have to a second B the same ratio as a third C has to a fourth D; and let equimultiples E, F be taken of A, C respectively (E the same multiple of A that F is of C), and any other equimultiples G, H of B, D respectively (G the same multiple of B that H is of D). It is required to prove that, as E is to G, so is F to H.

**Step 2.** Take any equimultiples whatever K, L of E, F respectively, and any other equimultiples whatever M, N of G, H respectively.

**Step 3.** Since E is the same multiple of A that F is of C, and K, L are equimultiples of E, F, therefore ex aequali K is the same multiple of A that L is of C [5.3]. That is, K, L are equimultiples of A, C.

**Step 4.** For the same reason, since G is the same multiple of B that H is of D, and M, N are equimultiples of G, H, therefore M is the same multiple of B that N is of D [5.3]. That is, M, N are equimultiples of B, D.

**Step 5.** Now, since A is to B as C is to D, and K, L have been taken as equimultiples of A, C, while M, N have been taken as other equimultiples of B, D, therefore, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, if K is in excess of M, L is also in excess of N; if K is equal to M, L is equal to N; and if K is less than M, L is less than N [D5.5].

**Step 6.** But K, L are any equimultiples whatever of E, F, and M, N are any other equimultiples whatever of G, H. Hence whatever equimultiples be taken of E and F, and whatever equimultiples of G and H, the former alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the latter, taken in corresponding order.

**Step 7.** Therefore, by the definition of same ratio, as E is to G, so is F to H [D5.5]. That is, the equimultiples E, F of the first and third have the same ratio to the equimultiples G, H of the second and fourth respectively, taken in corresponding order. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.5
**Statement:** If a magnitude be the same multiple of a magnitude that a part subtracted is of a part subtracted, the remainder will also be the same multiple of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.

**Step 1.** Let the magnitude AB be the same multiple of the magnitude CD that the part AE, subtracted from AB, is of the part CF, subtracted from CD; let EB be the remainder of AB and FD the remainder of CD. Thus AB is made up of a certain number of magnitudes each equal to CD, and AE is made up of that same number of magnitudes each equal to CF [D5.2]. I say that the remainder EB is the same multiple of the remainder FD that the whole AB is of the whole CD.

**Step 2.** Let a magnitude GH be taken which is the same multiple of FD that AE is of CF, namely by adding FD to itself as many times as CF has been added to itself to make up AE [D5.2].

**Step 3.** Then the two magnitudes AE, GH are equimultiples, respectively, of the two magnitudes CF, FD. Therefore, whatever multiple AE is of CF, the sum of AE and GH is that same multiple of the sum of CF and FD [5.1]. But the sum of CF and FD is the whole CD. Therefore the sum of AE and GH is the same multiple of CD that AE is of CF.

**Step 4.** But, by hypothesis, AB is also the same multiple of CD that AE is of CF. Hence AB and the sum of AE and GH are each made up of the same number of magnitudes, every one of which is equal to CD [D5.2]. The magnitudes which make up the one are therefore severally equal to the magnitudes which make up the other [CN1], and, equals being added to equals, the wholes are equal [CN2]: that is, AB is equal to the sum of AE and GH.

**Step 5.** Now AB is also the sum of AE and EB, since EB is the remainder when AE is subtracted from AB. Therefore the sum of AE and EB is equal to the sum of AE and GH. Let the common magnitude AE be subtracted from each; then the remainder EB is equal to the remainder GH [CN3].

**Step 6.** But GH is the same multiple of FD that AE is of CF (Step 2), and EB is equal to GH; therefore EB is measured by FD the same number of times that GH is, that is, EB is the same multiple of FD that AE is of CF [D5.2].

**Step 7.** And AE is the same multiple of CF that AB is of CD (hypothesis). Therefore the remainder EB is the same multiple of the remainder FD that the whole AB is of the whole CD. Q.E.D.

Path note: the multiple of FD is constructed directly and 5.1 is applied to the pair (CF, FD), rather than taking a submultiple of EB and proving the resulting magnitude equal to CD; this route needs no division of a magnitude into equal parts and no uniqueness lemma for submultiples, so it is the most direct.

## Proposition 5.6
**Statement:** If two magnitudes be equimultiples of two magnitudes, and any magnitudes subtracted from them be equimultiples of the same, the remainders also are either equal to the same or equimultiples of them.

**Step 1.** Let AB, CD be equimultiples of E, F respectively, so that AB is the same multiple of E that CD is of F; and let AG, CH, subtracted from AB, CD respectively, be equimultiples of E, F, so that AG is the same multiple of E that CH is of F. I say that the remainders GB, HD are either equal to E, F respectively or are equimultiples of them.

**Step 2.** Since AB is a multiple of E, it is measured by E, that is, it is made up of a certain number of magnitudes each equal to E [D5.2]; and AG, being a multiple of E, is likewise made up of magnitudes each equal to E. Since AG is a part of AB, AG is less than AB [CN5], so AG is made up of fewer of these magnitudes than AB is; hence, when AG is taken away from AB, the remainder GB is made up of the magnitudes equal to E that remain [CN3]. Therefore GB is either equal to E (if only one remains) or a multiple of E (if more than one remain). We treat these two cases in turn.

**Step 3.** (Case 1) Let GB be equal to E. I say that HD is also equal to F. Take CK equal to F, placed on the side of C away from H, so that KC and CH together make up KH.

**Step 4.** Since AG is the same multiple of E that CH is of F, and GB is equal to E while CK is equal to F, the sum AB of AG and GB is the same multiple of E that the sum KH of CH and CK is of F [5.2].

**Step 5.** But, by hypothesis, AB is the same multiple of E that CD is of F. Therefore KH and CD are each the same multiple of F; each is equal to F taken the same number of times; hence KH is equal to CD [CN1].

**Step 6.** From the equals KH, CD subtract the common magnitude CH; the remainders KC, HD are equal [CN3].

**Step 7.** But KC is equal to F (Step 3). Therefore HD is also equal to F [CN1]. Thus, when GB is equal to E, HD is equal to F.

**Step 8.** (Case 2) Let GB be a multiple of E. I say that HD is the same multiple of F that GB is of E. Take CK, on the side of C away from H, the same multiple of F that GB is of E, so that KC and CH together make up KH.

**Step 9.** Since AG is the same multiple of E that CH is of F, and GB is the same multiple of E that CK is of F, the sum AB of AG and GB is the same multiple of E that the sum KH of CH and CK is of F [5.2].

**Step 10.** But AB is the same multiple of E that CD is of F. Therefore KH and CD are each the same multiple of F; each is equal to F taken the same number of times; hence KH is equal to CD [CN1].

**Step 11.** From the equals KH, CD subtract the common magnitude CH; the remainders KC, HD are equal [CN3].

**Step 12.** But KC is the same multiple of F that GB is of E (Step 8); and HD, being equal to KC, is measured by F the same number of times that KC is, so HD is the same multiple of F that GB is of E [D5.2].

**Step 13.** Therefore, in either case, the remainders GB, HD are either equal to E, F respectively (Case 1) or equimultiples of E, F (Case 2). Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.7
**Statement:** Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio, as also has the same to equal magnitudes.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be equal magnitudes, and let C be any other magnitude of the same kind. I say that A has to C the same ratio as B has to C, and also that C has to A the same ratio as C has to B.

**Step 2.** Let D, E be any equimultiples whatever of A, B respectively, and let F be any other multiple whatever of C (D5.2).

**Step 3.** Since D is the same multiple of A that E is of B, D is composed of as many magnitudes equal to A as E is composed of magnitudes equal to B (D5.2). But A is equal to B; hence each of the equal parts composing D is equal to the corresponding part composing E, and adding these equals to equals one by one, the wholes are equal: D = E (CN2).

**Step 4.** Since D = E, D and E stand in the same relation of size to F. If D exceeds F, then E, being equal to D, also exceeds F; if D is equal to F, then E is equal to F, since things equal to the same thing are equal to one another (CN1); and if D falls short of F, then E, being equal to D, also falls short of F.

**Step 5.** Now D, E are equimultiples of A, B taken at will, and F is any multiple whatever of C; and it has been shown that D and E alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of F. Therefore, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio (D5.5), A has to C the same ratio as B has to C.

**Step 6.** Again, with the same equimultiples D, E of A, B and the same multiple F of C: since D = E, if F exceeds D it also exceeds E; if F is equal to D it is also equal to E (CN1); and if F falls short of D it also falls short of E.

**Step 7.** Here F is any multiple whatever of C, while D, E are any equimultiples whatever of A, B; and F alike exceeds, is alike equal to, or alike falls short of D and E. Therefore, by D5.5, C has to A the same ratio as C has to B.

**Step 8.** Therefore equal magnitudes have to the same magnitude the same ratio, and the same magnitude has to equal magnitudes the same ratio. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.8
**Statement:** Of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has; and the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater.

**Step 1.** Let AB, C be unequal magnitudes, of which AB is the greater, and let D be another magnitude of the same kind, so that AB, C, D have ratios to one another. It is to be proved that AB has to D a greater ratio than C has to D, and that D has to C a greater ratio than D has to AB.

**Step 2.** Since AB is greater than C, let EB, a part of AB, be made equal to C; then the remainder AE is the excess by which AB exceeds C, and the whole AB is made up of AE, EB.

**Step 3.** AE and D are magnitudes having a ratio to one another; therefore AE, being multiplied, will at some time exceed D [D5.4]. Let AE be multiplied until the multiple taken is greater than D, and let FG be this multiple of AE. Let GH be the same multiple of EB, and K the same multiple of C, that FG is of AE.

**Step 4.** Since FG is the same multiple of AE that GH is of EB, the whole FH, made up of FG, GH, is the same multiple of the whole AB, made up of AE, EB, that FG is of AE [5.1]. But K is also that same multiple of C; therefore FH, K are equimultiples of AB, C.

**Step 5.** Since GH, K are the same multiple of EB, C respectively, GH is made up of as many magnitudes equal to EB as K is of magnitudes equal to C; and EB is equal to C. Therefore, equals being added to equals the same number of times, GH is equal to K [CN2].

**Step 6.** D and K are magnitudes having a ratio to one another; therefore D, being multiplied, will at some time exceed K [D5.4]. Let the multiples of D be taken in succession, D itself, then the double of D, then the triple of D, and so on, each being made up of the preceding multiple together with D, until a multiple of D is reached which is the first that is greater than K; let this multiple be N. Then N is greater than K.

**Step 7.** FH is greater than N. For, if N is D itself, then, since FG is greater than D and the whole FH is greater than its part FG [CN5], FH is greater than D, that is, than N. If N is not D itself, let M be the multiple of D immediately preceding N, so that N is made up of M and D together. Since N is the first multiple of D greater than K, M is not greater than K; and GH is equal to K [Step 5]; therefore GH is not less than M. Also FG is greater than D, so that FG exceeds D by some magnitude. Therefore FG, GH together contain D, M together and exceed them by that magnitude, so that the whole FH is greater than N, its part [CN5]. Hence in either case FH is greater than N.

**Step 8.** Now FH, K are equimultiples of AB, C [Step 4], and N is a multiple of D. The multiple FH of AB exceeds the multiple N of D [Step 7], but the multiple K of C does not exceed the same multiple N of D, since N is greater than K [Step 6]. Therefore AB has to D a greater ratio than C has to D [D5.7].

**Step 9.** Again, N, N are equimultiples of D, D, and K, FH are equimultiples of C, AB [Step 4]. The multiple N of D exceeds the multiple K of C [Step 6], but the same multiple N of D does not exceed the multiple FH of AB, since FH is greater than N [Step 7]. Therefore D has to C a greater ratio than D has to AB [D5.7].

**Step 10.** Therefore, of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has, and the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.9
**Statement:** Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal to one another; and magnitudes to which the same has the same ratio are equal.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be magnitudes which have the same ratio to a magnitude C, so that A : C = B : C. We show that A = B.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that A and B are unequal. Then one of them is the greater; let A be greater than B (the argument with B greater than A is identical with the letters interchanged).

**Step 3.** Since A is greater than B, by 5.8 (first part) the greater A has to C a greater ratio than the less B has to C; that is, A : C is greater than B : C.

**Step 4.** By D5.7, "A : C greater than B : C" means that there exist equimultiples mA, mB of A, B and an equimultiple nC of C such that mA exceeds nC while mB does not exceed nC.

**Step 5.** But by hypothesis A : C = B : C, so by D5.5, for every choice of equimultiples mA, mB of A, B and every equimultiple nC of C, the multiples mA and mB must alike exceed, alike equal, or alike fall short of nC. The equimultiples of Step 4 violate this, since mA exceeds nC while mB does not. This is a contradiction.

**Step 6.** Therefore A is not greater than B, and by the same argument B is not greater than A. Hence A = B. This proves the first part.

**Step 7.** Now let a magnitude C have the same ratio to A and to B, so that C : A = C : B. We show that A = B.

**Step 8.** Suppose, if possible, that A and B are unequal, and let A be greater than B (the other case is identical with the letters interchanged).

**Step 9.** Since A is greater than B, by 5.8 (second part) the same C has to the less B a greater ratio than it has to the greater A; that is, C : B is greater than C : A.

**Step 10.** By D5.7, "C : B greater than C : A" means that there exist an equimultiple mC of C and equimultiples nB, nA of B, A such that mC exceeds nB while mC does not exceed nA.

**Step 11.** But by hypothesis C : A = C : B, so by D5.5, for every equimultiple mC of C and every choice of equimultiples nA, nB of A, B, the multiple mC must alike exceed, alike equal, or alike fall short of nA and nB. The equimultiples of Step 10 violate this, since mC exceeds nB but does not exceed nA. This is a contradiction.

**Step 12.** Therefore A is not greater than B, and by the same argument B is not greater than A. Hence A = B. This proves the second part.

**Step 13.** Therefore magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal to one another, and magnitudes to which the same has the same ratio are equal. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.10
**Statement:** Of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less.

Let A and B be two magnitudes each having a ratio to the same magnitude C.

**Part I.** Let A have to C a greater ratio than B has to C. I say that A is greater than B.

**Step 1.** Since A has to C a greater ratio than B has to C, by D5.7 there exist equimultiples mA, mB of A and B, and a multiple nC of C, such that mA exceeds nC while mB does not exceed nC.

**Step 2.** A is not equal to B. For suppose A = B. Then by 5.7 (equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio), A has to C the same ratio as B has to C. But then, by D5.5, since mA and mB are equimultiples of A and B and nC is a multiple of C, from mA > nC it would follow that mB > nC. This contradicts Step 1, in which mB does not exceed nC. Hence A is not equal to B.

**Step 3.** A is not less than B. For suppose A < B. Then by 5.8 (of unequal magnitudes, the greater has to the same a greater ratio than the less has), B has to C a greater ratio than A has to C. But by hypothesis A has to C a greater ratio than B has to C; and by D5.7 the ratio A:C is then the greater of the two ratios A:C and B:C, so it cannot at the same time be the less of them. Hence A is not less than B.

**Step 4.** Since A is neither equal to B nor less than B, A is greater than B. This proves the first part.

**Part II.** Now let C have to B a greater ratio than C has to A. I say that B is less than A.

**Step 5.** Since C has to B a greater ratio than C has to A, by D5.7 there exist a multiple mC of C (the same multiple taken as antecedent in both ratios) and equimultiples nB, nA of B and A, such that mC exceeds nB while mC does not exceed nA.

**Step 6.** B is not equal to A. For suppose B = A. Then by 5.7 (the same has to equal magnitudes the same ratio), C has to B the same ratio as C has to A. But then, by D5.5, since mC is a multiple of C and nB, nA are equimultiples of B and A, from mC > nB it would follow that mC > nA. This contradicts Step 5. Hence B is not equal to A.

**Step 7.** B is not greater than A. For suppose B > A. Then by 5.8 (the same has to the less a greater ratio than it has to the greater), C has to A a greater ratio than C has to B. But by hypothesis C has to B a greater ratio than C has to A; and by D5.7 the ratio C:B is then the greater of the two ratios C:B and C:A, so it cannot at the same time be the less of them. Hence B is not greater than A.

**Step 8.** Since B is neither equal to A nor greater than A, B is less than A. This proves the second part.

Therefore, of magnitudes which have a ratio to the same, that which has a greater ratio is greater; and that to which the same has a greater ratio is less. Q.E.D.

Path note: the reductio through 5.7 and 5.8 is the route reached first, because 5.10 is the converse of 5.8 and 5.9 was proved by the same reductio pattern from 5.8; D5.5 and D5.7 are invoked to make the exclusion of the "equal" case explicit from the equimultiples.

## Proposition 5.11
**Statement:** Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another.

**Step 1.** Let A be to B as C is to D, and let C be to D as E is to F. It is required to prove that A is to B as E is to F.

**Step 2.** Take any equimultiples G, H, K of A, C, E respectively, and any other equimultiples L, M, N of B, D, F respectively (so that G, H, K are the same multiple of A, C, E, and L, M, N are the same multiple of B, D, F).

**Step 3.** Since A is to B as C is to D, and G, H are equimultiples of A, C, while L, M are equimultiples of B, D, it follows from the definition of same ratio [D5.5] that: if G exceeds L, then H exceeds M; if G is equal to L, then H is equal to M; and if G falls short of L, then H falls short of M.

**Step 4.** Again, since C is to D as E is to F, and H, K are equimultiples of C, E, while M, N are equimultiples of D, F, it follows from the same definition [D5.5] that: if H exceeds M, then K exceeds N; if H is equal to M, then K is equal to N; and if H falls short of M, then K falls short of N.

**Step 5.** Combining Steps 3 and 4: if G exceeds L, then H exceeds M, and therefore K exceeds N; if G is equal to L, then H is equal to M, and therefore K is equal to N; and if G falls short of L, then H falls short of M, and therefore K falls short of N.

**Step 6.** Now G, K are any equimultiples whatever of A, E, and L, N are any other equimultiples whatever of B, F, and by Step 5 the former equimultiples alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the latter equimultiples taken in corresponding order.

**Step 7.** Therefore, by the definition of same ratio [D5.5], A is to B as E is to F. Hence ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 5.12
**Statement:** If any number of magnitudes be proportional, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so will all the antecedents be to all the consequents.

**Step 1.** Let any number of magnitudes A, B, C, D, E, F be proportional, so that, as A is to B, so is C to D and E to F; that is, A, B, C, D, E, F have the same ratio taken two and two (D5.6). Let A, C, E be the antecedents and B, D, F the consequents. I say that, as A is to B, so are A, C, E together to B, D, F together.

**Step 2.** Of A, C, E take any equimultiples whatever G, H, K, so that G, H, K are the same multiple of A, C, E respectively; and of B, D, F take any other equimultiples whatever L, M, N, so that L, M, N are the same multiple of B, D, F respectively.

**Step 3.** Since A is to B as C is to D, and G, H have been taken as equimultiples of A, C, while L, M are equimultiples of B, D, it follows from the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio (D5.5) that, if G exceeds L, H also exceeds M; if G is equal to L, H is equal to M; and if G is less than L, H is less than M.

**Step 4.** In the same way, since A is to B as E is to F, and G, K are equimultiples of A, E, while L, N are equimultiples of B, F, by D5.5, if G exceeds L, K also exceeds N; if equal, equal; and if less, less.

**Step 5.** Therefore, if G exceeds L, then H exceeds M and K exceeds N, so that the sum G, H, K together exceeds the sum L, M, N together. If G is equal to L, then H is equal to M and K is equal to N, so that G, H, K together are equal to L, M, N together, since equals added to equals give equal wholes (CN2). And if G is less than L, then H is less than M and K is less than N, so that G, H, K together fall short of L, M, N together.

**Step 6.** Now G, H, K are the same multiple of A, C, E respectively; therefore G, H, K together is the same multiple of A, C, E together that G is of A (5.1). Similarly, L, M, N are the same multiple of B, D, F respectively; therefore L, M, N together is the same multiple of B, D, F together that L is of B (5.1).

**Step 7.** Thus G and the sum G, H, K are equimultiples of the first A and the third A, C, E together, while L and the sum L, M, N are equimultiples of the second B and the fourth B, D, F together; and G, H, K were any equimultiples whatever, as were L, M, N. By Step 5, the multiple G of A and the multiple G, H, K of A, C, E together alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the multiple L of B and the multiple L, M, N of B, D, F together respectively.

**Step 8.** Therefore, by the definition of the same ratio (D5.5), as A is to B, so are A, C, E together to B, D, F together. That is, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents. Q.E.D.
