## Proposition 8.23
**Statement:** If four numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be cube, the fourth will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four numbers in continued proportion, so that A : B = B : C = C : D, and let the first, A, be a cube; that is, A is contained by three equal numbers, A = a·a·a for some number a (D7.19). We must show that D is also a cube.

**Step 2.** Since A : B = B : C = C : D, the numbers B and C fall between A and D as two mean proportional numbers. Therefore, by 8.21, A and D are similar solid numbers.

**Step 3.** Since A and D are similar solid numbers, they have their sides proportional (D7.21). The sides of A are the three equal numbers a, a, a (Step 1); let p, q, r be the sides of D corresponding to them, so that D = p·q·r and a : p = a : q = a : r.

**Step 4.** Since a has the same ratio to each of p, q, r, the number a is the same multiple, or the same part, or the same parts of p that it is of q and of r (D7.20); hence p, q, r are equal to one another.

**Step 5.** Therefore D is contained by three equal numbers, D = p·p·p, and so D is a cube (D7.19). Hence, if four numbers be in continued proportion and the first be cube, the fourth is also cube. Q.E.D.

Path note: the most direct route is through 8.21 (two mean proportionals between A and D make them similar solid numbers), with the cube property transferred through the definitions of cube and of similar solid numbers; an alternative route through the least numbers in the ratio (8.2, 8.3, 7.14, 7.20, 7.21, 8.15) is longer and was not taken.

## Proposition 8.24
**Statement:** If two numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and the first be square, the second will also be square.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be two numbers which have to one another the ratio which a square number C has to a square number D, so that A : B = C : D, and let A be a square number. I say that B is also a square number.

**Step 2.** Since C and D are square numbers, between C and D there falls one mean proportional number [8.11]. Let it be E, so that C, E, D are three numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 3.** Since A : B = C : D, and between C and D there falls one number E in continued proportion with them, therefore between A and B, which have the same ratio as C and D, there also falls one number in continued proportion with them [8.8]. Let it be F, so that A, F, B are three numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 4.** Now A, F, B are three numbers in continued proportion, and the first, A, is square by hypothesis. Therefore the third, B, is also square [8.22].

**Step 5.** Therefore, if two numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and the first be square, the second will also be square. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 8.25
**Statement:** If two numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number, and the first be cube, the second will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be two numbers such that A has to B the ratio which a cube number C has to a cube number D, and let A be a cube number. I say that B is also a cube number.

**Step 2.** Since C and D are cube numbers, between the two cube numbers C and D there fall two mean proportional numbers [8.12]. Let them be G and H, so that C, G, H, D are in continued proportion.

**Step 3.** Since two numbers G, H fall between C and D in continued proportion, and A, B have the same ratio as C, D (for A : B = C : D by hypothesis), it follows that as many numbers fall in continued proportion between A and B as fall between C and D [8.8]. Therefore two numbers fall between A and B in continued proportion. Let them be E and F, so that A, E, F, B are four numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 4.** Now A, E, F, B are four numbers in continued proportion, and the first, A, is a cube number. Therefore the fourth, B, is also a cube number [8.23].

**Step 5.** Therefore, if two numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number, and the first be cube, the second will also be cube. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 8.26
**Statement:** Similar plane numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be similar plane numbers. It is required to prove that A has to B the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** Since A and B are similar plane numbers, one mean proportional number falls between them [8.18]. Let C be that mean proportional; then A is to C as C is to B, so that A, C, B are three numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 3.** In the ratio of A to C, take three numbers D, E, F in continued proportion, the least that are in that ratio [8.2]. Then D is to E as E is to F, and each of these ratios is the same as the ratio of A to C.

**Step 4.** Since D, E, F are three numbers in continued proportion and are the least of those which have the same ratio with them, their extremes D and F are square numbers [8.2, Porism].

**Step 5.** Now A is to C as D is to E (Step 3); and C is to B as A is to C (Step 2), which is the same as E is to F (Step 3); hence C is to B as E is to F. Thus the numbers A, C, B and the numbers D, E, F, equal to them in multitude, taken two and two are in the same ratio.

**Step 6.** Therefore, ex aequali, A is to B as D is to F [7.14].

**Step 7.** But D and F are square numbers (Step 4). Therefore A has to B the ratio which the square number D has to the square number F; that is, similar plane numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* at Step 3 the least numbers D, E, F could equally be obtained by 7.33 applied to A, C, B (the least numbers having the same ratio with A, C, B), which are then in continued proportion because A, C, B are; 8.2 is chosen because it yields the three least numbers in continued proportion directly and its porism supplies their squareness, making it the more direct route.

## Proposition 8.27
**Statement:** Similar solid numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be similar solid numbers. We must show that A has to B the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.

**Step 2.** Since A and B are similar solid numbers, two mean proportional numbers fall between them (8.19). Let these be C and D, so that A, C, D, B are four numbers in continued proportion: A : C = C : D = D : B.

**Step 3.** Take E, F the least numbers of those which have the same ratio with A, C (7.33). Then E : F = A : C, and the ratio A : C is now given in least numbers E, F.

**Step 4.** With the ratio E : F given in least numbers, construct four numbers K, L, M, N in continued proportion, the least that are in the ratio E : F (8.2); thus K : L = L : M = M : N = E : F. In the construction of 8.2 the first of the four numbers is E multiplied by E and again by E (K = E·E·E), and the last is F multiplied by F and again by F (N = F·F·F).

**Step 5.** Hence each of K and N is contained by three equal numbers, so K and N are cube numbers (D7.19). This is precisely the Porism to 8.2: when four numbers in continued proportion are the least of those which have the same ratio with them, the extremes are cubes.

**Step 6.** From Steps 2, 3 and 4, K : L = E : F = A : C, L : M = E : F = C : D, and M : N = E : F = D : B. Thus K, L, M, N and A, C, D, B, being equal in multitude and taken two and two, are in the same ratio.

**Step 7.** Therefore, ex aequali, K : N = A : B (7.14).

**Step 8.** But K and N are cube numbers (Step 5). Therefore A has to B the ratio which the cube number K has to the cube number N. Q.E.D.

Path note: the least four numbers in continued proportion could also be obtained by applying 7.33 directly to A, C, D, B; I reduced only the ratio A : C by 7.33 and then built the four terms by 8.2, because the construction in 8.2 exhibits the extremes as E·E·E and F·F·F, making their cube form explicit.

## Proposition 9.1
**Statement:** If two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product will be square.

**Step 1.** Let A, B be two similar plane numbers, and let A by multiplying B make C. I say that C is square.

**Step 2.** Let A by multiplying itself make D. Then D is a square number, being equal multiplied by equal [D7.18].

**Step 3.** Since A by multiplying itself has made D, and by multiplying B has made C, therefore, as A is to B, so is D to C [7.17].

**Step 4.** Since A, B are similar plane numbers, one mean proportional number falls between A and B [8.18].

**Step 5.** Since as A is to B, so is D to C, and one mean proportional number falls between A and B, therefore one mean proportional number also falls between D and C [8.8].

**Step 6.** Let E be that mean proportional; then D, E, C are three numbers in continued proportion, and the first, D, is square. Therefore the third, C, is also square [8.22].

**Step 7.** Therefore, if two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product is square. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.2
**Statement:** If two numbers by multiplying one another make a square number, they are similar plane numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be two numbers, and let A by multiplying B make the square number C. I say that A and B are similar plane numbers.

**Step 2.** Let A by multiplying itself make D. Then D is a square number, being equal multiplied by equal [D7.18].

**Step 3.** Since the number A by multiplying the two numbers A and B has made D and C respectively, the numbers so produced have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied: as A is to B, so is D to C [7.17].

**Step 4.** Now D and C are square numbers. Each of them is a plane number, having been produced by two numbers multiplying one another [D7.16], and each is contained by two equal sides [D7.18]: D by A and A, and C by some number E and E, since C is square. The sides are therefore proportional, for as A is to A, so is E to E, each being the ratio of a number to itself. Hence D and C are similar plane numbers [D7.21].

**Step 5.** Since D and C are similar plane numbers, between D and C there falls one mean proportional number [8.18].

**Step 6.** But as D is to C, so is A to B (Step 3). Now when between two numbers there falls one number in continued proportion with them, one number also falls in continued proportion between any two numbers which have the same ratio as they [8.8]. Therefore between A and B there also falls one mean proportional number.

**Step 7.** But if one mean proportional number falls between two numbers, the numbers are similar plane numbers [8.20]. Therefore A and B are similar plane numbers.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two numbers by multiplying one another make a square number, they are similar plane numbers. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.3
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying itself make some number, the product will be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A be a cube number, and let A by multiplying itself make the number B. I say that B is cube.

**Step 2.** Since A is cube, it is a number contained by three equal numbers, being equal multiplied by equal and again by equal [D7.19]. Let C be the side of A: then C by multiplying itself makes some number D, and C by multiplying D makes A.

**Step 3.** Since C by multiplying itself has made D, D is C added to itself as many times as there are units in C [D7.15]; therefore C measures D according to the units in C. But the unit also measures C according to the units in C. Hence the unit is the same part of C that C is of D, and therefore, as the unit is to C, so is C to D [D7.20].

**Step 4.** Again, since C by multiplying D has made A, A is D added to itself as many times as there are units in C [D7.15]; therefore D measures A according to the units in C. But the unit measures C according to the units in C. Hence the unit is the same part of C that D is of A, and therefore, as the unit is to C, so is D to A [D7.20].

**Step 5.** By Steps 3 and 4, as the unit is to C, so is C to D, and so is D to A. Therefore the unit, C, D, A are in continued proportion; that is, between the two numbers, the unit and A, there fall two numbers, C and D, in continued proportion with them.

**Step 6.** Since A by multiplying itself has made B, B is A added to itself as many times as there are units in A [D7.15]; therefore A measures B according to the units in A. But the unit measures A according to the units in A. Hence the unit is the same part of A that A is of B, and therefore, as the unit is to A, so is A to B [D7.20].

**Step 7.** Thus A and B are two numbers having the same ratio as the unit and A (Step 6), and between the unit and A there fall two numbers in continued proportion with them (Step 5). Therefore between A and B there also fall two numbers in continued proportion [8.8]. Let them be G and H, so that A, G, H, B are four numbers in continued proportion.

**Step 8.** Now A, G, H, B are four numbers in continued proportion, and the first of them, A, is cube (Step 1). Therefore the fourth, B, is also cube [8.23].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if a cube number by multiplying itself make some number, the product is cube. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the route through the unit and 8.8 is the most direct and is the one taken. An equivalent but longer route avoids the unit by applying 7.17 to A multiplying C, D and A (obtaining A : G = G : H = H : B from C : D = D : A) before invoking 8.23; it is not used.

## Proposition 9.4
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product will be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A be a cube number, let B be a cube number, and let A by multiplying B make C. I say that C is cube.

**Step 2.** Let A by multiplying itself make D. Since A is a cube number and, by multiplying itself, has made D, the product D is cube. [9.3]

**Step 3.** Since the one number A, by multiplying the two numbers A and B, has made D and C respectively, the numbers so produced have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied; therefore, as A is to B, so is D to C. [7.17]

**Step 4.** Now A and B are both cube numbers; therefore the ratio of A to B is the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number. And D has to C the same ratio that A has to B (Step 3); therefore D and C have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.

**Step 5.** But the first of them, D, is cube (Step 2). Therefore the second, C, is also cube. [8.25]

**Step 6.** Therefore, if a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product will be cube. Q.E.D.

**Path note.** An equivalent but longer route exists: since A and B are cubes, each is contained by three equal numbers (D7.19), so their sides are proportional and they are similar solid numbers (D7.17, D7.21); hence two mean proportional numbers fall between A and B (8.19), hence also between D and C, which have the same ratio (8.8); and since D is cube, C is cube (8.23). The route through 8.25 was chosen as the most direct: once A : B = D : C is established, 8.25 is precisely the tool that converts "same ratio as a cube to a cube, first term cube" into "second term cube", whereas the longer route reconstructs the proof of 8.25 in place.

## Proposition 9.5
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A be a cube number, and let A by multiplying the number B make C, and let C be a cube number. I say that B is also a cube number.

**Step 2.** Let A by multiplying itself make D. Since A is a cube number and by multiplying itself has made D, D is a cube number [9.3].

**Step 3.** Since the number A by multiplying the two numbers A and B has made D and C respectively, the products have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied; therefore, as D is to C, so is A to B [7.17].

**Step 4.** Now D and C are both cube numbers, so each is contained by three equal numbers [D7.19]; hence the sides of D are proportional to the sides of C, and D, C are similar solid numbers [D7.21].

**Step 5.** Between two similar solid numbers there fall two mean proportional numbers; therefore two mean proportional numbers fall between D and C [8.19].

**Step 6.** But as D is to C, so is A to B (Step 3); and when numbers fall in continued proportion between two numbers, just as many fall in continued proportion between numbers having the same ratio as they. Therefore two mean proportional numbers also fall between A and B [8.8].

**Step 7.** Thus A, the two mean proportional numbers, and B are four numbers in continued proportion, and the first of them, A, is cube; therefore the fourth, B, is also cube [8.23].

**Step 8.** Therefore, if a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number is also cube. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.6
**Statement:** If a number by multiplying itself make a cube number, it will itself also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let the number A by multiplying itself make the cube number B. I say that A is also cube.

**Step 2.** Let B by multiplying A make C.

**Step 3.** Since A by multiplying itself has made B, and B by multiplying A has made C, the number C is A multiplied by A and again by A; that is, C is contained by the three equal numbers A, A, A. Therefore C is cube [D7.19].

**Step 4.** Thus the cube number B, by multiplying the number A, has made the cube number C. But if a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number is also cube [9.5]. Therefore A is cube.

**Step 5.** Therefore, if a number by multiplying itself make a cube number, it will itself also be cube. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.7
**Statement:** If a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product will be solid.

**Step 1.** Let A be a composite number, and let A by multiplying any number B make C. I say that C is solid.

**Step 2.** Since A is composite, it is measured by some number [D7.13]. Let D be a number measuring A, and let E be the number having as many units as the number of times D measures A.

**Step 3.** Since D measures A according to the units in E, A is produced by adding D to itself as many times as there are units in E; therefore E by multiplying D has made A [D7.15].

**Step 4.** Now A by multiplying B has made C, and A is itself the product of D and E; therefore the product of D and E by multiplying B has made C. Thus the three numbers D, E, B, having multiplied one another, have made C.

**Step 5.** Therefore C is a solid number, and its sides are D, E, B [D7.17]. Hence, if a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product is solid. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.8
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit will be square, as will also those which successively leave out one; the fourth will be cube, as will also all those which leave out two; and the seventh will be at once cube and square, as will also those which leave out five.

**Step 1.** Let the unit and the numbers A, B, C, D, E, F (and as many more, G, H, K, L, ..., as we please) be in continued proportion beginning from the unit, so that unit : A = A : B = B : C = C : D = D : E = E : F = ... . Thus A is the second from the unit, B the third, C the fourth, D the fifth, E the sixth, and F the seventh.

**Step 2.** Since unit : A = A : B, by D7.20 the unit is the same part of A that A is of B; that is, the unit measures A the same number of times that A measures B. But the unit measures A according to the units in A. Therefore A measures B according to the units in A.

**Step 3.** Hence B is made by adding A to itself as many times as there are units in A; that is, A by multiplying itself has made B (D7.15). Therefore B is equal multiplied by equal, and so B is square (D7.18). Thus the third from the unit is square.

**Step 4.** Now B, C, D are three numbers in continued proportion, and the first of them, B, is square; therefore the third, D, is also square (8.22). Again D, E, F are three numbers in continued proportion and D is square; therefore F is also square (8.22). Proceeding in the same way with each successive triple (F, G, H), (H, K, L), ..., all those numbers which successively leave out one, namely the fifth, seventh, ninth, ... from the unit, are square.

**Step 5.** Next, since unit : A = B : C (both being ratios of the same continued proportion), by D7.20 the unit measures A the same number of times that B measures C. But the unit measures A according to the units in A; therefore B measures C according to the units in A, so that A by multiplying B has made C (D7.15).

**Step 6.** But A by multiplying itself made B (Step 3), and A by multiplying B has made C (Step 5). Therefore C is A multiplied by A and again by A, that is, C is contained by the three equal numbers A, A, A; hence C is cube (D7.19). Thus the fourth from the unit is cube.

**Step 7.** Now C, D, E, F are four numbers in continued proportion, and the first of them, C, is cube; therefore the fourth of them, F, is also cube (8.23). Again F, G, H, K are four numbers in continued proportion and F is cube; therefore K is cube (8.23). Proceeding in the same way with each successive quadruple, all those numbers which leave out two, namely the seventh, tenth, thirteenth, ... from the unit, are cube.

**Step 8.** The seventh from the unit, F, has been shown to be square (Step 4) and also to be cube (Step 7); therefore F is at once cube and square.

**Step 9.** Those numbers which leave out five after F are the thirteenth, nineteenth, ... from the unit. Each of these is reached from the third by successively leaving out one (its place from the unit is odd), so it is square by Step 4; and each is reached from the fourth by successively leaving out two (its place exceeds the fourth by a multiple of three), so it is cube by Step 7. Therefore each of them is at once cube and square.

**Step 10.** Therefore, if as many numbers as we please beginning from a unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit is square, as are those which successively leave out one; the fourth is cube, as are all those which leave out two; and the seventh is at once cube and square, as are those which leave out five. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.9
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest will also be square.

**Step 1.** Let there be as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, E, F, beginning from an unit and in continued proportion, so that the unit is to A as A is to B, as B is to C, as C is to D, as D is to E, as E is to F; and let A, the number after the unit, be square. I say that all the rest, B, C, D, E, F, are also square.

**Step 2.** Since the numbers A, B, C, D, E, F beginning from the unit are in continued proportion, the third from the unit, B, is square, and so also are those which successively leave out one, namely D, the fifth from the unit, and F, the seventh [9.8]. Thus every number occupying an odd place after the unit is square.

**Step 3.** It remains to prove that C, E, and generally every number occupying an even place after the unit, are also square. Since the unit, A, B, C are in continued proportion, A is to B as B is to C; therefore the three numbers A, B, C are in continued proportion, and A, the first of them, is square by hypothesis; therefore C, the third of them, is also square [8.22].

**Step 4.** Again, since B is to C as C is to D, and C is to D as D is to E, the three numbers C, D, E are in continued proportion, and C, the first of them, has been proved square in Step 3; therefore E, the third of them, is also square [8.22].

**Step 5.** Proceeding in the same way, any number of the sequence occupying an even place after the unit is the third term of a continued proportion of three numbers whose first term is the number two places before it, which itself occupies an even place. Since A, the number in the second place, is square, and the property of being square is carried forward two places at a time by 8.22, every number occupying an even place after the unit is square. Together with Step 2, which covers every number occupying an odd place after the unit, this shows that all the numbers B, C, D, E, F following A are square.

**Step 6.** Therefore, if as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest will also be square. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.10
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one.

**Step 1.** Let as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, E, F, ..., beginning from an unit, be in continued proportion, so that as the unit is to A, so is A to B, B to C, C to D, D to E, E to F, and so on; and let A, the number after the unit, not be square. I say that no number of the series is square except B, the third from the unit, and D, F, ..., the numbers which successively leave out one after it; that is, A, C, E, ... are not square.

**Step 2.** Since the numbers beginning from the unit are in continued proportion, the third from the unit, B, is square, and so are those which successively leave out one, namely D, F, ... [9.8]. It remains to show that A, C, E, ... are not square.

**Step 3.** A is not square, by hypothesis.

**Step 4.** Suppose, if possible, that C is square. B is also square [Step 2]; therefore C has to B the ratio which a square number, C, has to a square number, B.

**Step 5.** Since as A is to B, so is B to C, inversely, as B is to A, so is C to B [D7.20]. Therefore B has to A the ratio which the square number C has to the square number B; that is, B and A have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 6.** But the first of them, B, is square [Step 2]; therefore the second, A, is also square [8.24]. This is contrary to the hypothesis [Step 3]. Therefore C is not square.

**Step 7.** Next suppose, if possible, that E is square. D is square [Step 2]; therefore E has to D the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Since as C is to D, so is D to E, inversely, as D is to C, so is E to D [D7.20]; therefore D has to C the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and D, the first, is square; therefore C is also square [8.24], which is contrary to Step 6. Therefore E is not square.

**Step 8.** The same argument applies to every subsequent number of the series which is neither the third from the unit nor one of those which leave out one. For let G be any such number; the number immediately before it, F, is square [Step 2], and the number two places before it, E, is of the same class as G. If G were square, then, since as E is to F, so is F to G, inversely F would be to E as G is to F [D7.20], so that F and E would have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and F being square, E would also be square [8.24]. Thus if any number of this class were square, the number two places before it would be square, and, repeating the argument, ultimately A would be square, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore none of A, C, E, G, ... is square.

**Step 9.** Therefore, if as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.11
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A be the unit, and let B, C, D, ..., K, L be as many numbers as we please, beginning from the unit A and in continued proportion, so that, as the unit A is to B, so is B to C, so is C to D, and so on, until, as K is to L. Thus the ratio of any term of the series to the term next after it is the same ratio as that of any other term to the term next after it [D7.20]. Let M and N be any two of the numbers B, C, ..., L, M standing earlier in the series than N. I say that M measures N according to some one of the numbers B, C, ..., L.

**Step 2.** First let Q be any one of the numbers C, D, ..., L, that is, any term of the series other than B, and let P be the term standing immediately before Q, so that P is one of B, C, ..., K. Then, as the unit A is to B, so is P to Q (Step 1). Now the unit A measures the number B, since B is a multitude composed of units [D7.2]; and since, as A is to B, so is P to Q, the unit A is the same part of B that P is of Q [D7.20]; that is, the unit A measures B the same number of times that P measures Q.

**Step 3.** Since, then, the unit A measures the number B, and the number P measures the number Q the same number of times, therefore, alternately, the unit A measures P the same number of times that B measures Q [7.15]. But the unit A measures P according to the units in P [D7.2]. Therefore B measures Q according to the units in P, that is, B measures Q according to the number P, the term standing immediately before Q. This holds for every term Q of the series after B.

**Step 4.** Now return to the two numbers M and N. Let Q be that term of the series which stands as many places after B as N stands after M. Since N stands at least one place after M, Q stands at least one place after B, so that Q is not B; and since M stands at least one place after the unit A, N stands fewer places after M than after A, so that Q stands not later than N. Hence Q is one of the numbers C, D, ..., L, and Q has a term P standing immediately before it, P being one of B, C, ..., K.

**Step 5.** Consider the row of numbers B, C, ..., Q (from B up to Q inclusive) and the row of numbers from M up to N inclusive. By the choice of Q (Step 4) these two rows are equal in multitude. Moreover, taken two and two they are in the same ratio: as B is to C, so is M to the term next after M; as C is to D, so is that term to the term next after it; and so on, until, as P is to Q, so is the term before N to N; for each of these is the ratio of a term of the series to the term next after it, and all such ratios are the same (Step 1). Therefore, ex aequali, as B is to Q, so is M to N [7.14]. (When N is the term next after M, the rows are B, C and M, N, and this proportion is simply the given proportion, Q being C and P being B.)

**Step 6.** By Step 3, B measures Q according to P; thus B is a part of Q. Since, as B is to Q, so is M to N (Step 5), M is the same part of N that B is of Q [D7.20]; that is, M measures N the same number of times that B measures Q. Therefore M measures N according to the number P.

**Step 7.** Since M measures N, M is a part of N, the less of the greater [D7.3]; so M is the less and N the greater of the two numbers. And P is one of the numbers B, C, ..., K, which have place among the proportional numbers (Step 4). Therefore the less number M measures the greater number N according to P, some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers. Since M and N were any two of the numbers B, C, ..., L, the same holds for every pair of them. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the proportion needed for M and N could be obtained in a single stroke as A : P = M : N by applying ex aequali to the rows A, B, ..., P and M, ..., N, which would dispense with 7.15. That route was not taken because 7.14 is enunciated for numbers, whereas the unit is not a number; the alternation required when a unit is one of the terms is supplied separately by 7.15. The proof therefore first settles, by 7.15, that B measures every later term according to the term before it, and then extends this to any pair by ex aequali among numbers only.

## Proposition 9.12
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

**Step 1.** Let as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, beginning from the unit be in continued proportion, so that the unit is to A as A is to B, as B is to C, and as C is to D; let D be the last, and let D be measured by any prime number E. I say that E also measures A, the number next to the unit.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that E does not measure A. Now E is prime, and any prime number is prime to any number which it does not measure [7.29]; therefore E and A are prime to one another.

**Step 3.** Since A is the least of the numbers A, B, C, D and the numbers are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, A measures each greater term according to one of the numbers of the sequence [9.11], and by the Porism to 9.11 that number occupies, reckoned from the term standing immediately before the measured term, the same (first) place that A occupies reckoned from the unit; that is, A measures each later term according to the term immediately preceding it. Hence A multiplied by C makes D, A multiplied by B makes C, and A multiplied by A makes B.

**Step 4.** (Descent step.) Let T be any term of the sequence other than A, let S be the term immediately before T, and suppose E measures T; let E measure T according to F, so that E multiplied by F makes T. By Step 3, A multiplied by S also makes T. Therefore the product of A and S is equal to the product of E and F, and consequently, as A is to E, so is F to S [7.19].

**Step 5.** Since A and E are prime to one another (Step 2), they are the least of those numbers which have the same ratio with them [7.21]; and the least numbers of those which have the same ratio measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent [7.20]. In the proportion A : E = F : S, the consequent E therefore measures the consequent S. Thus, whenever E measures a term T other than A, E also measures the term S immediately before T.

**Step 6.** By hypothesis E measures D. Applying Step 5 with T = D, S = C: E measures C. Applying Step 5 with T = C, S = B: E measures B. Applying Step 5 with T = B, S = A: E measures A. (If the sequence had more terms, the same descent step would be applied once for each term, passing from the last term down to A.)

**Step 7.** But by the supposition of Step 2, E does not measure A: which is impossible. Therefore the supposition is false, and E measures A.

**Step 8.** Since E was any prime number measuring D, the same argument shows that by however many prime numbers the last number D is measured, the number A next to the unit is also measured by the same. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.13
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let the unit, A, B, C, D be as many numbers as we please beginning from the unit and in continued proportion, so that, as the unit is to A, so is A to B, B to C, and C to D; and let A, the number after the unit, be prime. I say that D, the greatest, is not measured by any number other than the unit, A, B, C, D. For suppose, if possible, that D is measured by a number E which is not the unit and is not the same with any of A, B, C, D.

**Step 2.** Since, as the unit is to A, so is C to D, the unit is the same part of A that C is of D [D7.20]. Now the unit measures A according to the units in A, A being a multitude composed of units [D7.2]; therefore C measures D according to the units in A, that is, D is C added to itself as many times as there are units in A; thus A by multiplying C makes D [D7.15]. In the same way, since, as the unit is to A, so is B to C, A by multiplying B makes C; and since, as the unit is to A, so is A to B, A by multiplying itself makes B. Consequently A measures B, B measures C, and C measures D [D7.15].

**Step 3.** I show first that every number, other than the unit, which measures D is measured by A. Let X be any such number. X is either prime or composite [D7.11, D7.13]. If X is prime, let P be X itself; if X is composite, let P be a prime number which measures X [7.31]. In either case the prime number P measures X, and X measures D; therefore P measures D. Now the unit, A, B, C, D are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and P is a prime number measuring the last of them; therefore P also measures A, the number next to the unit [9.12]. But A is prime, so that it is measured by the unit alone [D7.11]; and P, being a prime number, is not the unit; hence P is the same with A. Therefore A measures X.

**Step 4.** By Step 3, A measures E; and since E is not the same with A, A is a part of E, the less of the greater [D7.3].

**Step 5.** Since E measures D, let E measure D according to the units in F, so that D is E added to itself as many times as there are units in F; thus F by multiplying E makes D [D7.15], and hence also E by multiplying F makes D [7.16]. F is not the unit, for otherwise D would be E itself, whereas E is not the same with D.

**Step 6.** F is not the same with any of A, B, C. For, if F were one of them, then, since E by multiplying F makes D, F would measure D according to the units in E [D7.15]; but F, having a place among the proportional numbers before D, measures D according to some one of the numbers which have a place among the proportional numbers [9.11]; and the number according to which F measures D is one only; hence E would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, C, D, contrary to hypothesis. Therefore F is a number which is not the same with any of the unit, A, B, C.

**Step 7.** Since A by multiplying C makes D (Step 2) and E by multiplying F makes D (Step 5), the product of A, C is equal to the product of E, F; therefore, as A is to E, so is F to C [7.19]. But A is a part of E (Step 4); therefore F is the same part of C [D7.20], so that F measures C. Let F measure C according to the units in G; then G by multiplying F makes C [D7.15], and F by multiplying G makes C [7.16].

**Step 8.** G is not the unit, for otherwise C would be F itself, whereas F is not the same with C (Step 6). Nor is G the same with A or with B: for, if it were, then, since F by multiplying G makes C, G would measure C according to the units in F [D7.15]; but the unit, A, B, C are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and G, having a place among these proportional numbers before C, measures C according to some one of the numbers which have a place among them [9.11]; hence F would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, C, contrary to Step 6. Therefore G is a number not the same with any of the unit, A, B. Moreover, F measures C and C measures D (Step 2), so that F measures D; therefore A measures F (Step 3), and, F not being the same with A, A is a part of F [D7.3].

**Step 9.** Since A by multiplying B makes C (Step 2) and F by multiplying G makes C (Step 7), the product of A, B is equal to the product of F, G; therefore, as A is to F, so is G to B [7.19]. But A is a part of F (Step 8); therefore G is the same part of B [D7.20], so that G measures B. Let G measure B according to the units in H; then H by multiplying G makes B [D7.15], and G by multiplying H makes B [7.16].

**Step 10.** H is not the unit, for otherwise B would be G itself, whereas G is not the same with B (Step 8). Nor is H the same with A: for, if it were, then, since G by multiplying H makes B, H, that is A, would measure B according to the units in G [D7.15]; but the unit, A, B are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and A measures B according to some one of the numbers which have a place among these proportional numbers [9.11]; hence G would be the same with one of the unit, A, B, contrary to Step 8. Therefore H is a number which is neither the unit nor A. Moreover, G measures B, B measures C, and C measures D (Step 2), so that G measures D; therefore A measures G (Step 3), and, G not being the same with A, A is a part of G [D7.3].

**Step 11.** Since A by multiplying itself makes B (Step 2) and G by multiplying H makes B (Step 9), the product of A, A is equal to the product of G, H; therefore, as A is to G, so is H to A [7.19]. But A is a part of G (Step 10); therefore H is the same part of A [D7.20], so that H measures A. Thus the prime number A is measured by a number H which is neither the unit nor A itself (Step 10); but a prime number is measured by the unit alone [D7.11]: which is impossible.

**Step 12.** Therefore no such number E exists, and D, the greatest, is not measured by any number except those which have a place among the proportional numbers. If the continued proportion beginning from the unit has more terms, the same descent applies: a supposed measurer of the greatest term which is not among the proportional numbers yields, as in Steps 5 to 7, a measurer of the term before it which again is not among the proportional numbers, and so on until the number next to the unit is reached, where the argument of Step 11 gives the same impossibility. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.14
**Statement:** If a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it.

**Step 1.** Let A be the least number that is measured by the prime numbers B, C, D. I say that A is not measured by any other prime number except B, C, D.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let A be measured by a prime number E which is not the same as any one of B, C, D.

**Step 3.** Since E measures A, let E measure A according to F, so that E multiplied by F makes A (D7.15).

**Step 4.** Now B measures A, and A is the number made by E and F multiplying one another. But if two numbers by multiplying one another make some number, and any prime number measure the product, it also measures one of the original numbers (7.30). Since B is prime and measures A, B measures one of E, F.

**Step 5.** But B does not measure E. For E is prime, and is therefore measured by an unit alone (D7.11); B, being prime, is a number and not an unit, and by hypothesis B is not the same as E; therefore B cannot measure E.

**Step 6.** Therefore B measures F. In the same way, since C and D are prime numbers each measuring A, and neither of them is the same as E, each of C, D measures one of E, F (7.30) but does not measure E (D7.11); therefore each of C, D measures F. Thus F is measured by B, C, D.

**Step 7.** Now, since E multiplied by F makes A, F multiplied by E also makes A (7.16); therefore F measures A according to E, so that F is a part of A (D7.3). And E, being prime, is not an unit, so that A is made up of F taken more than once; therefore F is less than A (CN5).

**Step 8.** Thus F, which is less than A, is measured by the prime numbers B, C, D. But A was by hypothesis the least number measured by B, C, D; which is impossible.

**Step 9.** Therefore no prime number other than B, C, D measures A. Hence, if a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.15
**Statement:** If three numbers in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, any two whatever added together will be prime to the remaining number.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three numbers in continued proportion, so that A : B = B : C, and let them be the least of those which have the same ratio with them. It is required to show that A + B is prime to C, that B + C is prime to A, and that A + C is prime to B.

**Step 2.** Take DE, EF, the least numbers of those which have the same ratio as A, B [7.33]. Represent DE and EF, as usual in the arithmetical books, by straight lines placed end to end on one straight line DF, so that DF is cut at E and DF is the sum of DE and EF.

**Step 3.** By the construction of 8.2, the three numbers DE·DE, DE·EF, EF·EF are in continued proportion, each has to the next the ratio DE : EF, and they are the least of those which have that ratio [8.2]. Now A, B, C are likewise three numbers in continued proportion whose ratio A : B is the ratio DE : EF, and they too are the least of those having that ratio. Two sets each of which is the least having the same ratio can neither be less than the other; therefore A = DE·DE, B = DE·EF and C = EF·EF.

**Step 4.** Since DE, EF are the least of those which have the same ratio with them, DE and EF are prime to one another [7.22].

**Step 5.** Since DE, EF are prime to one another, their sum DF is prime to each of the numbers DE, EF [7.28, first part].

**Step 6.** (A + B is prime to C.) DF is prime to EF (Step 5) and DE is prime to EF (Step 4); hence the two numbers DF, DE are both prime to EF, so their product DF·DE is prime to EF [7.24]. Since DF·DE and EF are prime to one another, the product of EF into itself, EF·EF, is prime to DF·DE [7.25].

**Step 7.** Because DF is cut at E, the rectangle contained by DF, DE is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EF together with the square on DE [2.3]; in numbers, DF·DE = DE·DE + DE·EF = A + B. Also EF·EF = C. Therefore, by Step 6, A + B is prime to C.

**Step 8.** (B + C is prime to A.) DF is prime to DE (Step 5) and EF is prime to DE (Step 4); hence the product DF·EF is prime to DE [7.24], and consequently DE·DE is prime to DF·EF [7.25].

**Step 9.** By 2.3 again, the rectangle contained by DF, EF equals the rectangle contained by DE, EF together with the square on EF, so DF·EF = DE·EF + EF·EF = B + C; and DE·DE = A. Therefore, by Step 8, B + C is prime to A.

**Step 10.** (A + C is prime to B.) DF is prime to DE and DF is prime to EF (Step 5); hence the two numbers DE, EF are both prime to DF, so their product DE·EF is prime to DF [7.24]. Since DF and DE·EF are prime to one another, the product of DF into itself, DF·DF, is prime to DE·EF [7.25].

**Step 11.** Because DF is cut at E, the square on DF is equal to the squares on DE, EF together with twice the rectangle contained by DE, EF [2.4]; in numbers, DF·DF = DE·DE + EF·EF + 2·(DE·EF) = A + C + 2B, while DE·EF = B. Therefore A + C + 2B is prime to B.

**Step 12.** The number A + C + 2B is the sum of the two numbers (A + C + B) and B, and this sum is prime to one of them, namely B; therefore A + C + B is prime to B [7.28, second part]. Again, A + C + B is the sum of the two numbers (A + C) and B, and this sum is prime to B; therefore A + C is prime to B [7.28, second part].

**Step 13.** Thus A + B is prime to C, B + C is prime to A, and A + C is prime to B; that is, any two of the three numbers added together are prime to the remaining one. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.16
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second.

**Step 1.** Let A, B be two numbers prime to one another. I say that B is not to any other number as A is to B.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let there be some number C such that, as A is to B, so is B to C.

**Step 3.** Since A, B are prime to one another, they are the least of those numbers which have the same ratio with them [7.21].

**Step 4.** Now the least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the greater the greater and the less the less, that is, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent [7.20]. Since A, B are the least numbers in the ratio of A to B, and B, C have that same ratio (Step 2), it follows that A measures B and B measures C, the same number of times.

**Step 5.** But A also measures itself. Therefore A measures both A and B, so that A is a common measure of A and B.

**Step 6.** Now A is a number, that is, a multitude composed of units, and hence is not a unit [D7.2]. Thus A, B are measured as a common measure by a number other than the unit. But A, B are prime to one another, that is, they are measured by an unit alone as a common measure [D7.12]. This is absurd.

**Step 7.** Therefore there is no number C such that, as A is to B, so is B to C. Hence, if two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.17
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the last will not be to any other number as the first to the second.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, so that A : B = B : C = C : D, and let the extremes A, D be prime to one another. I say that D is not to any other number as A is to B.

**Step 2.** For, if possible, let A : B = D : E, where E is some number.

**Step 3.** Since the four numbers A, B, D, E are proportional, they are also proportional alternately [7.13]; therefore A : D = B : E.

**Step 4.** Since A, D are prime to one another, they are the least of the numbers which have the same ratio with them [7.21].

**Step 5.** The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent [7.20]. Since A : D = B : E and A, D are the least numbers in that ratio, A measures B.

**Step 6.** Since A measures B, A is a part of B [D7.3]. And A : B = B : C; but numbers are proportional when the first is the same part of the second that the third is of the fourth [D7.20]; therefore B is the same part of C that A is of B, so that B measures C [D7.3].

**Step 7.** Since A measures B and B measures C, A also measures C.

**Step 8.** Again, since B : C = C : D and B measures C, by the same reasoning as in Step 6, C measures D [D7.3, D7.20]. And A measures C; therefore A also measures D. In the same manner, however many the numbers in the continued proportion, A measures each of them in turn, and therefore measures the last, D.

**Step 9.** But A also measures itself. Therefore A, which is a number and not an unit [D7.2], measures both A and D, so that A, D have a number as a common measure. But A, D are prime to one another, that is, they are measured by an unit alone as a common measure [D7.12]: which is absurd.

**Step 10.** Therefore D is not to any other number as A is to B. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.18
**Statement:** Given two numbers, to investigate whether it is possible to find a third proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let A, B be the two given numbers. A third proportional to A, B is a number D such that, as A is to B, so is B to D. It is required to investigate whether such a number D can be found.

**Step 2.** The numbers A, B are either prime to one another or they are not.

**Step 3.** First, let A, B be prime to one another. Then by 9.16, B is not to any other number as A is to B; that is, there is no number D such that A : B = B : D. Hence, when A, B are prime to one another, it is impossible to find a third proportional to them.

**Step 4.** Next, let A, B not be prime to one another. Let B by multiplying itself make C [D7.15], so that B × B = C. Then A either measures C or does not measure it.

**Step 5.** First, let A measure C, and let A measure C according to the units in D, so that A by multiplying D makes C [D7.15]: A × D = C. But B × B = C also. Therefore A × D = B × B [CN1].

**Step 6.** Now A, B, B, D are four numbers, and the product of the first and fourth, A × D, is equal to the product of the second and third, B × B. Therefore by 7.19 (second part), the four numbers are proportional: as A is to B, so is B to D. Hence D is a third proportional to A, B, and in this case it is possible to find one.

**Step 7.** Next, let A not measure C. I say that in this case it is impossible to find a third proportional to A, B. For, if possible, let D be a third proportional, so that as A is to B, so is B to D.

**Step 8.** Then, since the four numbers A, B, B, D are proportional, by 7.19 (first part) the product of the first and fourth is equal to the product of the second and third: A × D = B × B. But B × B = C; therefore A × D = C [CN1].

**Step 9.** But A × D = C means that A, added to itself as many times as there are units in D, makes C [D7.15]; that is, A measures C according to the units in D. This is contrary to the hypothesis that A does not measure C. Therefore no such D exists, and it is impossible to find a third proportional to A, B.

**Step 10.** Summing up: if A, B are prime to one another, no third proportional exists; if A, B are not prime to one another, let B multiplied by itself make C; then a third proportional exists if A measures C (namely the number D according to which A measures C), and does not exist if A does not measure C. This is the required investigation.

## Proposition 9.19
**Statement:** Given three numbers, to investigate when it is possible to find a fourth proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the three given numbers. A fourth proportional to them is a number X such that, as A is to B, so is C to X. We investigate when such a number X exists.

**Step 2.** First, suppose that A, B, C are in continued proportion (as A is to B, so is B to C) and that the extremes A, C are prime to one another. Then by 9.17 the last number C is not to any other number as the first A is to the second B. Hence no number X satisfies A : B = C : X, and in this case it is impossible to find a fourth proportional.

**Step 3.** In every other case (either A, B, C are not in continued proportion, or the extremes A, C are not prime to one another) proceed as follows. Let B by multiplying C make D (D7.15). Then either A measures D or A does not measure D.

**Step 4.** Suppose A measures D, and let A measure D according to the units in E; that is, A by multiplying E makes D (D7.15). Then A × E = D and B × C = D, so A × E = B × C (CN1).

**Step 5.** Since the product of the first A and the fourth E is equal to the product of the second B and the third C, by 7.19 the four numbers A, B, C, E are proportional: as A is to B, so is C to E. Therefore E is a fourth proportional to A, B, C, and in this case it is possible to find one.

**Step 6.** Now suppose A does not measure D. I say that it is then impossible to find a fourth proportional. For, if possible, let E be a fourth proportional, so that as A is to B, so is C to E.

**Step 7.** Since A, B, C, E are four proportional numbers, by 7.19 the product of the first and fourth, A × E, is equal to the product of the second and third, B × C. But B × C = D; therefore A × E = D (CN1).

**Step 8.** But A × E is A added to itself as many times as there are units in E (D7.15); hence A measures A × E, that is, A measures D. This contradicts the hypothesis that A does not measure D. Therefore, when A does not measure D, no fourth proportional exists.

**Step 9.** Conclusion. Given three numbers A, B, C: if A, B, C are in continued proportion with extremes prime to one another, a fourth proportional cannot be found (Step 2). Otherwise, form the product D = B × C; a fourth proportional exists precisely when A measures D, and in that case the number E according to which A measures D is the fourth proportional (Steps 4–5), while if A does not measure D no fourth proportional exists (Steps 6–8). Thus a fourth proportional to A, B, C can be found if and only if A measures the product of B and C.

## Proposition 9.20
**Statement:** Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the assigned prime numbers (the argument is the same for any assigned multitude, three being taken as representative). I say that there are more prime numbers than A, B, C.

**Step 2.** Take the least number DE which A, B, C measure [7.36], so that each of A, B, C measures DE; and to DE add the unit DF, so that EF is a number made up of DE together with the unit DF. (Any number measured by A, B, C, for instance their product, would serve here; the least such number is chosen because 7.36 supplies it in a single step.)

**Step 3.** EF either is prime or is measured by some prime number [7.32]. (7.32 is invoked rather than 7.31 because it yields exactly the alternative required, without first establishing that EF is composite.)

**Step 4.** First, let EF be prime. Then EF is not the same as any of A, B, C. For each of A, B, C measures DE, and a number which measures another is the less of the two, a part of it, or else equal to it [D7.3]; hence none of A, B, C is greater than DE. But EF is greater than DE, since DE is a part of EF [CN5]. Therefore EF is greater than each of A, B, C, and so is a prime number different from all of them. Thus the prime numbers A, B, C, EF have been found, more in multitude than the assigned A, B, C.

**Step 5.** Next, let EF not be prime. Then, by Step 3, EF is measured by some prime number G. I say that G is not the same as any of A, B, C.

**Step 6.** For, if possible, let G be the same as one of A, B, C. Since each of A, B, C measures DE (Step 2), G measures DE. But G also measures EF. Now EF is made up of parts each equal to G, and DE, which is a part of EF, is likewise made up of parts each equal to G; therefore the remainder DF, which is what is left of EF when DE is taken away, is also made up of parts each equal to G. That is, G measures DF.

**Step 7.** But DF is a unit. Since G measures DF, DF is not less than G [D7.3]. Yet G, being a number, is a multitude composed of units [D7.2], and so is greater than a single unit, the unit being a part of it [CN5]; that is, DF is less than G. Thus DF would be at once not less than G and less than G, which is absurd. Therefore G is not the same as any of A, B, C.

**Step 8.** And G is prime (Step 5). Therefore the prime numbers A, B, C, G have been found, more in multitude than the assigned A, B, C.

**Step 9.** Hence in either case a prime number has been found which is different from every one of A, B, C. Since the assigned multitude A, B, C was arbitrary, prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.21
**Statement:** If as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even.

**Step 1.** Let as many even numbers as we please, AB, BC, CD, DE, be added together, and let the whole be AE. I say that AE is even.

**Step 2.** Since AB is even, it is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]; let AB be divided into the two equal parts AG, GB, so that AG is equal to GB. For the same reason each of BC, CD, DE is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]; let BC be divided into the equal parts BH, HC, CD into the equal parts CK, KD, and DE into the equal parts DL, LE.

**Step 3.** Let the number F be made up of AG, BH, CK, DL added together, and let the number G' be made up of GB, HC, KD, LE added together. Since AG is equal to GB, BH to HC, CK to KD, and DL to LE, and if equals be added to equals the wholes are equal [CN2], therefore F is equal to G'.

**Step 4.** But F and G' added together make up AG, GB, BH, HC, CK, KD, DL, LE all together, that is, AB, BC, CD, DE together, which is the whole AE. Therefore AE is divided into the two equal parts F, G'.

**Step 5.** Therefore AE is divisible into two equal parts; and a number which is divisible into two equal parts is even [D7.6]. Therefore AE is even.

**Step 6.** Therefore, if as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.22
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole will be even.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC, CD, DE be as many odd numbers as we please, even in multitude, added together so that the whole is AE. I say that AE is even.

**Step 2.** Since each of AB, BC, CD, DE is odd, each differs by a unit from an even number [D7.7]; hence, if a unit be subtracted from each of AB, BC, CD, DE, each of the remainders will be even.

**Step 3.** Therefore the sum of all the remainders, being a sum of even numbers, is even [9.21].

**Step 4.** The units subtracted are as many as the odd numbers AB, BC, CD, DE, and the multitude of these odd numbers is even by hypothesis; therefore the units subtracted are even in multitude, that is, taken together they compose an even number.

**Step 5.** Now the whole AE is made up of the sum of the remainders together with the units subtracted. Thus AE is the sum of two even numbers, namely the sum of the remainders (Step 3) and the number composed of the units (Step 4); therefore AE is even [9.21].

**Step 6.** Therefore, if as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole is even. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.23
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be odd, the whole will also be odd.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC, CD be as many odd numbers as we please, their multitude being odd, and let them be added together so as to make up the whole AD. I say that AD is odd.

**Step 2.** If the multitude is a single number, the whole AD is that odd number itself and the statement holds at once. Suppose then that the multitude is greater than one, so that there is a last number CD with numbers AB, BC before it.

**Step 3.** Since CD is odd, it differs by a unit from an even number [D7.7]. Let the unit DE be subtracted from CD; then the remainder CE is even [D7.7].

**Step 4.** The multitude of the numbers AB, BC, CD is odd, and the multitude of the numbers AB, BC falls short of it by a unit (the number CD having been set aside); therefore the multitude of AB, BC is even [D7.7].

**Step 5.** Thus AB, BC are odd numbers whose multitude is even; therefore their sum AC is even [9.22].

**Step 6.** Since AC is even and CE is even, the whole AE, made up of the even numbers AC and CE, is even [9.21].

**Step 7.** But AD exceeds AE by the unit DE. Therefore AD differs by a unit from the even number AE, and so AD is odd [D7.7].

**Step 8.** Therefore, if as many odd numbers as we please be added together and their multitude be odd, the whole is also odd. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.24
**Statement:** If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

Let AB be an even number, and from it let the even number BC, which is less than AB, be subtracted. I say that the remainder AC is even.

**Step 1.** Since AB is even, it is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]. Let D be one of these two equal parts, so that AB is twice D. Then D measures AB, namely twice; hence D is a part of AB, the half of AB [D7.3].

**Step 2.** For the same reason, since BC is even, it is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]. Let E be one of these two equal parts, so that BC is twice E. Then E measures BC twice; hence E is a part of BC, the half of BC [D7.3].

**Step 3.** Therefore D is the same part of AB, namely the half, that E is of BC. Moreover E is less than D: for BC is twice E and AB is twice D, and if E were equal to or greater than D, then twice E would be equal to or greater than twice D, that is, BC would be equal to or greater than AB, contrary to the hypothesis that BC is subtracted from AB. Hence E can be subtracted from D, leaving a remainder.

**Step 4.** Now D is that part of AB which E, subtracted from D, is of BC, subtracted from AB. Therefore the remainder of D after E is subtracted is the same part of the remainder AC that the whole D is of the whole AB [7.7]. But D is the half of AB; therefore the remainder of D after E is subtracted is the half of AC, that is, AC is twice this remainder.

**Step 5.** Therefore AC is divisible into two equal parts, each equal to the remainder of D after E is subtracted; hence AC is even [D7.6].

Therefore, if from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.30
**Statement:** If an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it.

**Step 1.** Let A be an odd number and B an even number, and let A measure B. Since A measures B, let it measure B according to C; that is, A added to itself as many times as there are units in C makes B, so that A by multiplying C makes B (D7.15).

**Step 5.** Now B is A added to itself as many times as there are units in C (Step 1, D7.15). But the units in C are the units in D together with the units in D again (Step 4). Therefore B is A added to itself as many times as there are units in D, together with A added to itself as many times as there are units in D again; and each of these two sums is E (Step 4, D7.15). Therefore B is made up of E and E.

**Step 6.** Thus B is divided into two equal parts E, E; therefore E is the half of B (D7.6). And since A added to itself as many times as there are units in D makes E, A measures E according to D (D7.15). Therefore A measures E, the half of B.

Therefore, if an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.31
**Statement:** If an odd number be prime to any number, it will also be prime to the double of it.

**Step 1.** Let A be an odd number, let A be prime to any number B, and let C be double of B, so that C is made up of B and B. I say that A is also prime to C.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that A and C are not prime to one another. Then A and C are not measured by an unit alone as a common measure [D7.12], so some number D (other than an unit) measures both A and C.

**Step 3.** I say that D is odd. For, since D measures A, A is a multiple of D [D7.5], that is, A is made up of D taken some number of times, so A is the sum of numbers each equal to D. If D were even, A would be a sum of even numbers (or D itself, if taken once), and therefore A would be even [9.21], that is, divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]. But A is odd, that is, not divisible into two equal parts [D7.7]; which is impossible. Therefore D is not even, so D is odd.

**Step 4.** Now C, being made up of the two equal parts B and B, is divisible into two equal parts, and so C is even [D7.6], and the half of C is B.

**Step 5.** Since the odd number D measures the even number C, D also measures the half of C [9.30]; that is, D measures B.

**Step 6.** But D also measures A. Therefore the number D, which is not an unit, measures both A and B, so A and B are not measured by an unit alone as a common measure; hence A and B are not prime to one another [D7.12]. But by hypothesis A is prime to B; which is absurd.

**Step 7.** Therefore A and C are not measured by any number other than an unit as a common measure, so A and C are prime to one another [D7.12]. Hence, if an odd number be prime to any number, it is also prime to the double of it. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.32
**Statement:** Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

**Step 1.** Let A be the dyad, and let B, C, D be as many numbers as we please continually doubled beginning from A, so that B is double of A, C is double of B, and D is double of C. A number is even-times even only when it is even-times even and is not even-times odd. It suffices to prove that D, the last of the numbers, is even-times even only, since the same argument applied to the sequence cut short at B or at C proves the same for B or C.

**Step 2.** Each of A, B, C, D is even. A, the dyad, is a multitude composed of two units [D7.2], so it is divisible into two equal parts, an unit and an unit; hence A is even [D7.6]. B, being double of A, is A together with A, and so is divisible into the two equal parts A and A; hence B is even [D7.6]. In the same way C, being B together with B, and D, being C together with C, are each divisible into two equal parts, so C and D are even [D7.6].

**Step 3.** D is even-times even. Since D is double of C, D is C taken twice, that is, C measures D according to the units in the dyad A. Now C is even and A is even (Step 2); therefore D is measured by an even number according to an even number, so D is even-times even [D7.8].

**Step 4.** Let an unit U be set out. Since A is double of U, B double of A, C double of B, and D double of C, the unit U is the half of A, A is the half of B, B is the half of C, and C is the half of D; thus each term is the same part, namely the half, of the term following it [D7.3]. Numbers are proportional when the first is the same part of the second that the third is of the fourth [D7.20]; therefore U is to A as A is to B, as B is to C, as C is to D. Hence U, A, B, C, D are numbers beginning from an unit in continued proportion, and D is the greatest of them.

**Step 5.** A, the number next after the unit, is prime. For any number other than A which measures A is a part of A, the less of the greater [D7.3], and so is less than the dyad; but every number is a multitude composed of units [D7.2], so that no number is less than the dyad. Hence no number other than A itself measures A, and A is measured by an unit alone; therefore A is prime [D7.11].

**Step 6.** By Steps 4 and 5 the numbers U, A, B, C, D beginning from an unit are in continued proportion and the number A after the unit is prime. Therefore D, the greatest of them, is not measured by any number except those which have a place among the proportional numbers, namely A, B, C, and D itself [9.13].

**Step 7.** D is not even-times odd. For suppose, if possible, that D is even-times odd, that is, that D is measured by some even number E according to some odd number F [D7.9]. Then D is E added to itself as many times as there are units in F, that is, F by multiplying E makes D [D7.15]. But if two numbers by multiplying one another make certain numbers, the numbers so produced are equal to one another [7.16]; hence E by multiplying F also makes D, that is, D is F added to itself as many times as there are units in E [D7.15], so that F measures D according to E. Thus F is a number which measures D, and so by Step 6 F is one of the numbers A, B, C, D. But each of A, B, C, D is even (Step 2), being divisible into two equal parts, whereas F is odd and so is not divisible into two equal parts [D7.7]; this is impossible. Therefore D is not even-times odd.

**Step 8.** D is even-times even (Step 3) and is not even-times odd (Step 7); therefore D is even-times even only. Applying the same argument to the sequence U, A, B (in which B is the greatest) and to the sequence U, A, B, C (in which C is the greatest), each of B and C is likewise even-times even only. Therefore each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.33
**Statement:** If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.

**Step 1.** Let A be a number whose half is odd, and let E be that half; so A = E + E, and E is odd. We must show that A is even-times odd, and that A is not even-times even.

**Step 2.** The dyad is an even number, for it is divisible into two equal parts, namely its two units [D7.6].

**Step 3.** Since A = E + E, A is E added to itself twice, that is, as many times as there are units in the dyad; hence E multiplied by the dyad makes A [D7.15]. Therefore the dyad multiplied by E also makes A [7.16]; that is, A is the dyad added to itself as many times as there are units in E, so that the dyad measures A according to the units in E [D7.15].

**Step 4.** Thus A is measured by an even number, the dyad (Step 2), according to an odd number, E (Step 1). Therefore A is even-times odd [D7.9].

**Step 5.** I say next that A is not also even-times even. For suppose, if possible, that it is. Then A is measured by some even number B according to some even number C [D7.8]; that is, A is the number made by adding B to itself as many times as there are units in C, namely B multiplied by C [D7.15].

**Step 6.** Since C is even, it is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6]; let F be its half, so that C = F + F. To add B to itself C times is to add B to itself F times and then F times again. Hence, if G is the number made by adding B to itself F times, that is, B multiplied by F [D7.15], we have A = G + G.

**Step 7.** But also A = E + E (Step 1). Therefore G = E. For if G were greater than E, exceeding it by some number K, then G + G would be E + E together with K + K, that is, A together with K + K; so A, which is G + G, would be equal to a number of which A is a part, whereas the whole is greater than the part [CN5], which is impossible. In the same way G cannot be less than E. Hence G = E.

**Step 8.** Therefore E, being equal to G, is B added to itself as many times as there are units in F (Step 6). Since B is even, E is either B itself (if F is an unit) or a sum of even numbers each equal to B; in either case E is even [9.21].

**Step 9.** But E is odd (Step 1). Thus E is at once divisible into two equal parts, being even [D7.6], and not so divisible, being odd [D7.7], which is absurd. Therefore A is not even-times even.

**Step 10.** Hence A is even-times odd (Step 4) and is not even-times even (Step 9); that is, A is even-times odd only. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 9.34
**Statement:** If a number neither be one of those which are continually doubled from a dyad, nor have its half odd, it is both even-times even and even-times odd.

**Step 1.** Let A be a number which is neither one of those continually doubled from a dyad nor has its half odd; I say that A is both even-times even and even-times odd. Since the hypothesis speaks of the half of A and of its being odd or not, A is divisible into two equal parts, that is, A is even [D7.6], and its half B is a number [D7.2], the distinction of odd and even applying to numbers and not to the unit. Thus A = B + B.

**Step 2.** By hypothesis B is not odd. Now an odd number is one which is not divisible into two equal parts [D7.7]; hence B, not being odd, is divisible into two equal parts, that is, B is even [D7.6].

**Step 3.** Since A = B + B, B added to itself as many times as there are units in the dyad makes A; that is, B measures A according to the dyad [D7.3, D7.15]. The dyad is even, being divisible into two equal parts, each a unit [D7.6], and B is even (Step 2). Therefore A is measured by an even number according to an even number, so that A is even-times even [D7.8].

**Step 4.** I say next that A is also even-times odd. Bisect A into B, B; since B is even (Step 2), bisect B into C, C; if C is even, bisect C likewise; and continue in this way. At each stage the number reached is either odd [D7.7], in which case it cannot be bisected into two equal parts and the process ends; or even [D7.6], in which case either its two equal parts are units, so that it is the dyad and the process ends (a unit not being a number [D7.2]), or its two equal parts are numbers and we bisect again.

**Step 5.** The process cannot go on without end. For each half is less than its whole [CN5], so the numbers A, B, C, ... obtained by the successive bisections continually decrease; and since A is a finite multitude of units [D7.2], there cannot be a series of numbers, each less than the one before, going on without limit: which is impossible in numbers. Hence the bisection comes to an end, either at the dyad or at an odd number.

**Step 6.** It does not end at the dyad. For suppose the last number reached were the dyad. Each number of the series is the sum of two equal parts, each of which is the next number of the series; that is, each is the double of the next. Hence, starting from the dyad and doubling continually, we obtain in turn all the numbers of the series taken backwards, ending with A. Thus A would be one of those continually doubled from a dyad, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore the process ends at an odd number; let it be D.

**Step 7.** D measures A. For D measures the number before it in the series (which is D + D), that number measures the one before it, and so on up to B, which measures A (Step 3); and a number which measures a number that measures a third number measures the third also [D7.3]. Moreover D is less than A, since A is even and D is odd; hence D measures A according to the units in some number E, that is, D added to itself as many times as there are units in E makes A, so that E multiplied by D makes A [D7.15].

**Step 8.** E is even. For, if E were odd, then, D being odd and E odd, E by multiplying D would make an odd product [9.29]; but that product is A, which is even (Step 1); and a number cannot be both even and odd, since an odd number is precisely one which is not divisible into two equal parts [D7.6, D7.7]. Hence E is not odd, and therefore E is even [D7.7, D7.6].

**Step 9.** Since E multiplied by D makes A, D multiplied by E also makes A [7.16]; that is, E added to itself as many times as there are units in D makes A, so that E measures A according to the units in D [D7.15, D7.3]. Thus A is measured by an even number E according to an odd number D; therefore A is even-times odd [D7.9].

**Step 10.** Therefore A is both even-times even (Step 3) and even-times odd (Step 9). Q.E.D.

Path note: the multiplicity E could alternatively be identified directly as the dyad doubled once for each bisection beyond the first, which is even by construction; the route through 9.29 was chosen as more direct, since it avoids counting the bisections.
