## Proposition 10.44
**Statement:** A second bimedial straight line is divided at one point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a second bimedial straight line divided at C, so that AC, CB are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle [10.38]. Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at a point D, different from C, so that AD, DB are likewise medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle, and that this division is not the same as the division at C; that is, AC is not equal to DB (and hence AD is not equal to CB either, the remainders of AB being unequal [CN3]).

**Step 2.** Since AC, CB are commensurable in square only, AC is incommensurable in length with CB [D10.1.2]; therefore AC is not equal to CB, for equal straight lines measure one another and so are commensurable [D10.1.1]. For the same reason AD is not equal to DB.

**Step 3.** Let a rational straight line EF be set out [D10.1.3], and to EF let there be applied, at right angles, the rectangle EK equal to the square on AB [1.45]; let EN be its other side, so that EK is the rectangle contained by EF, EN.

**Step 4.** Since AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]; so the squares on AC, CB are less than the square on AB, that is, than EK [CN5]. Let a rectangle EG equal to the squares on AC, CB be applied to EF [1.45], with its breadth EH placed along EN from E. Since EG is less than EK and both stand on EF, EH is less than EN (otherwise EK would be a part of EG or coincide with it, and EG would not be less [CN4, CN5]); so H lies between E and N. Let HK be the remaining rectangle, contained by EF, HN. Then HK, the excess of EK over EG, is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4, CN3].

**Step 5.** In the same way, since AB is cut at D, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4]. Let EL, equal to the squares on AD, DB, be applied to EF with breadth EM along EN [1.45]; as before M lies between E and N, and the remaining rectangle MK, contained by EF, MN, is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4, CN3].

**Step 6.** Since AC is medial, the square on AC is a medial area, being equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.21]. Since AC, CB are commensurable in square, the square on AC is commensurable with the square on CB [D10.1.2]; therefore the squares on AC, CB together are commensurable with the square on AC [10.15]. But an area commensurable with a medial area is medial [10.23, Porism]; therefore EG, which is equal to the squares on AC, CB, is a medial area, equal to the square on a medial straight line.

**Step 7.** EG is applied to the rational straight line EF and produces EH as breadth; therefore EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 8.** The rectangle AC, CB is medial by hypothesis. Twice the rectangle AC, CB has to the rectangle AC, CB the ratio of 2 to 1, which is the ratio of a number to a number; therefore they are commensurable [10.6], and twice the rectangle AC, CB, that is HK, is medial [10.23, Porism]. HK is applied to EF and produces HN as breadth; therefore HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 9.** The square on AC and the rectangle AC, CB are parallelograms under the same height AC standing on the bases AC, CB; therefore as AC is to CB, so is the square on AC to the rectangle AC, CB [6.1]. But AC is incommensurable in length with CB (Step 2); therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB [10.11].

**Step 10.** The squares on AC, CB are commensurable with the square on AC (Step 6), and the square on AC is incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB; therefore the squares on AC, CB are incommensurable with the rectangle AC, CB [10.13]. Again, twice the rectangle AC, CB is commensurable with the rectangle AC, CB (Step 8); therefore the squares on AC, CB are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC, CB [10.13]; that is, EG is incommensurable with HK.

**Step 11.** EG, HK are parallelograms under the same height EF standing on the bases EH, HN; therefore as EG is to HK, so is EH to HN [6.1]; and EG is incommensurable with HK; therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 12.** EH is rational, that is, commensurable with EF either in length or in square only [D10.1.3]; and it is incommensurable in length with EF (Step 7); therefore it is commensurable in square with EF, so that the square on EH is commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]. Likewise the square on HN is commensurable with the square on EF. Therefore the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HN [10.12], and EH, HN are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Being also incommensurable in length (Step 11), EH, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EN, their sum, is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms at H [10.36].

**Step 13.** Further, EH is greater than HN. For AC, CB are unequal (Step 2); let AC be the greater, and from AC let a straight line equal to CB be cut off [1.3]. AC is then a straight line cut into a segment equal to CB and a remaining segment; therefore the square on AC together with the square on CB is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on the remaining segment [2.7]. Hence the squares on AC, CB are greater than twice the rectangle AC, CB [CN5]; that is, EG is greater than HK. Both rectangles stand on EF; therefore EH is greater than HN (otherwise EG would be a part of HK or coincide with it, and would not be greater [CN4, CN5]). If CB is the greater, the same argument with CB in place of AC gives the same conclusion.

**Step 14.** AD, DB are also medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a medial rectangle, and EL is equal to the squares on AD, DB while MK is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB (Step 5). Therefore, repeating Steps 6 to 13 with AD, DB, EL, MK, EM, MN in place of AC, CB, EG, HK, EH, HN: EM and MN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so that EN is a binomial straight line divided into its terms also at M [10.36]; and EM is greater than MN.

**Step 15.** I say that H coincides with M. For if not, EH is not equal to EM. Nor is EH equal to MN: for then HN, the remainder of EN after EH, would be equal to EM, the remainder after MN [CN3]; and we should have EM equal to HN, HN less than EH (Step 13), EH equal to MN, and MN less than EM (Step 14), so that EM would be less than itself, which is absurd. Thus the terms EH, HN of the one division would be different from the terms EM, MN of the other, and the binomial straight line EN would be divided into its terms at two different points; but a binomial straight line is divided into its terms at one point only [10.42]. Therefore H coincides with M, EH is equal to EM, and the rectangles EG, EL contained by EF, EH and by EF, EM coincide and are equal [CN4]; that is, the squares on AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 16.** Likewise HN coincides with MN, so that HK coincides with MK and they are equal [CN4]; therefore twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN1], and the rectangle AC, CB is equal to the rectangle AD, DB, being their halves.

**Step 17.** Let AB be bisected at O [1.10]. Since AC is not equal to CB (Step 2), C is not the point O; so AB is cut into equal segments at O and into unequal segments at C, and therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on OC is equal to the square on AO [2.5]. Likewise, since AD is not equal to DB, D is not O, and the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on OD is equal to the square on AO [2.5].

**Step 18.** Therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on OC is equal to the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on OD [CN1]; and the rectangles are equal (Step 16); therefore the square on OC is equal to the square on OD [CN3]. Hence OC is equal to OD; for if one of them were greater, the square on the other would be a part of the square on it, and the squares would be unequal [CN5].

**Step 19.** Now C, D are points of AB equidistant from O. They do not lie on the same side of O: for C, D being different points, one of OC, OD would then be a part of the other and less than it [CN5], whereas OC is equal to OD. Therefore they lie on opposite sides of O. If C lies towards B and D towards A, then AC is the sum of AO, OC and DB is the sum of DO, OB; and AO is equal to OB, OC to OD; therefore AC is equal to DB [CN2]. If instead C lies towards A and D towards B, then in the same way CB is equal to AD [CN2], and AC, DB, the remainders of AB, are equal [CN3]. In either case AC is equal to DB.

**Step 20.** But AC was supposed not equal to DB (Step 1): which is absurd. Therefore AB cannot be divided at a second point D into medial straight lines commensurable in square only containing a medial rectangle otherwise than as it is divided at C. Therefore a second bimedial straight line is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

*Path note:* the proof reduces the question to the uniqueness of the division of the binomial EN [10.42]; the identity of the two divisions (EH = EM) is then carried back to AB through 2.4 and 2.5, which is more direct than first proving an inequality between the squares on AC, CB and on AD, DB.

## Proposition 10.45
**Statement:** A major straight line is divided at one and the same point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a major straight line, divided at C into the two straight lines AC, CB from which it is compounded; that is (10.39), AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is rational, and the rectangle AC·CB is medial. Throughout, an area is called rational when it is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.4).

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D, different from C, into straight lines AD, DB having the same properties: AD and DB incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB rational, and the rectangle AD·DB medial; and let the division at D be different from the division at C. Then AC is not equal to DB: for if AC = DB, then AD = CB (CN3), so that AD, DB would be the very same two straight lines CB, AC, and AB would be divided at D in the same way as at C, which is not a different division.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at E (1.10). The point C is not E: for if C were E, then AC = CB, the squares on AC, CB would be equal and therefore measured by the same measure, that is, commensurable (D10.1.1), so that AC, CB would be commensurable in square (D10.1.2), contrary to Step 1. In the same way, D is not E. Hence AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at C, and again into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D.

**Step 4.** Therefore, by 2.5, the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on EC is equal to the square on AE, and the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on ED is equal to the square on AE. Hence (CN1) the rectangle AC·CB together with the square on EC is equal to the rectangle AD·DB together with the square on ED.

**Step 5.** EC is not equal to ED. For suppose EC = ED. Since C and D are different points at the same distance from E, they lie on opposite sides of E. If D lies between A and E and C between E and B, then AC = AE + EC and DB = EB + ED, and since AE = EB and EC = ED, AC = DB (CN2). If instead C lies between A and E and D between E and B, then CB = CE + EB = DE + EA = AD (CN2), whence AC = DB (CN3). Either case contradicts Step 2. Therefore EC and ED are unequal; and since the hypotheses concerning C and D are alike, let the lettering be so chosen that EC is greater than ED.

**Step 6.** Since EC > ED, the square on EC is greater than the square on ED. But by Step 4 the rectangle AC·CB together with the greater square (on EC) equals the rectangle AD·DB together with the less square (on ED). Therefore the rectangle AC·CB is less than the rectangle AD·DB, and consequently twice the rectangle AC·CB is less than twice the rectangle AD·DB. Let K be the excess of twice the rectangle AD·DB over twice the rectangle AC·CB, so that twice AD·DB = twice AC·CB + K.

**Step 7.** By 2.4, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB; and also the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD·DB. Hence (CN1) the squares on AC, CB together with twice AC·CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice AD·DB, that is, to the squares on AD, DB together with twice AC·CB and K. Taking away twice the rectangle AC·CB from each (CN3), the squares on AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with K.

**Step 8.** K is rational. For the sum of the squares on AC, CB and the sum of the squares on AD, DB are both rational, that is, each is commensurable with the rational square set out (D10.1.4); therefore they are commensurable with one another (10.12). Now the whole, the sum of the squares on AC, CB, is made up of the sum of the squares on AD, DB and K (Step 7), and the whole is commensurable with the former part; therefore the parts, namely the sum of the squares on AD, DB and K, are commensurable with one another (10.15). Thus K is commensurable with the sum of the squares on AD, DB, which is commensurable with the rational square set out; therefore K is commensurable with the rational square set out (10.12), that is, K is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 9.** Twice the rectangle AD·DB and twice the rectangle AC·CB are medial. For the rectangle AD·DB is medial (Step 2), and twice the rectangle AD·DB has to the rectangle AD·DB the ratio which the number 2 has to the unit, a ratio of a number to a number; therefore twice AD·DB is commensurable with AD·DB (10.6); and an area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23, Porism). Hence twice the rectangle AD·DB is medial; and in the same way twice the rectangle AC·CB is medial.

**Step 10.** By Step 6, twice the rectangle AD·DB is equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB together with K; that is, the medial area twice AD·DB exceeds the medial area twice AC·CB by the rational area K. But a medial area does not exceed a medial area by a rational area (10.26). This is impossible.

**Step 11.** Therefore AB cannot be divided at any point D other than C into two straight lines incommensurable in square whose squares have a rational sum and which contain a medial rectangle. Hence a major straight line is divided at one and the same point only. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 10.46
**Statement:** The side of a rational plus a medial area is divided at one point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of a rational plus a medial area, divided at C, so that AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, and twice the rectangle AC, CB is rational [10.40]. Let R denote the square on the rational straight line set out, so that an area is rational precisely when it is commensurable with R [D10.1.4]. I say that AB is not divided at any other point into two straight lines having these properties.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D, so that AD, DB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB is medial, and twice the rectangle AD, DB is rational. "Another point" means a division different from that at C: D is not the same point as C, and moreover AC is not the same as DB. For if AC = DB, then, AB being the same whole in both divisions, the remainders CB and AD would be equal [CN3], and AB would be divided at D into the very same two straight lines as at C, merely interchanged; that is the same division, not a different one.

**Step 3.** Bisect AB at E [1.10]. Neither C nor D coincides with E. For if C were the point E, then AC = CB, so the squares on AC, CB would be equal and therefore measured by one and the same area (namely either of them); thus AC, CB would be commensurable in square [D10.1.2], contrary to hypothesis. In the same way D is not the point E.

**Step 4.** Further, C and D are not equidistant from E, that is, EC is not equal to ED. For suppose EC = ED. Since C is not the same point as D, the points C and D lie on opposite sides of E. If C lies between A and E and D between E and B, then AC is the remainder of AE after EC, and DB is the remainder of EB after ED; since AE = EB and EC = ED, it follows that AC = DB [CN3]. If instead C lies between E and B and D between A and E, then in the same way CB = AD, whence, subtracting these equals from the whole AB, AC = DB [CN3]. In either case AC = DB, which was excluded in Step 2. Therefore EC is not equal to ED.

**Step 5.** Since AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at C, the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on EC is equal to the square on EB [2.5]. Similarly, since AB is cut into equal segments at E and into unequal segments at D, the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on ED is equal to the square on EB [2.5]. Therefore the rectangle AC, CB together with the square on EC is equal to the rectangle AD, DB together with the square on ED [CN1].

**Step 6.** Since EC is not equal to ED, the squares on EC, ED are unequal, the square on the less being equal to a part of the square on the greater [CN5]. Hence the rectangle AC, CB is not equal to the rectangle AD, DB; for otherwise, subtracting these equal rectangles from the equals of Step 5, the square on EC would be equal to the square on ED [CN3], which is not so. Consequently twice the rectangle AC, CB is not equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB. Since C and D satisfy exactly the same hypotheses, we may take twice the rectangle AC, CB to be the greater (otherwise interchange the roles of C and D). Let K be the area by which it exceeds, so that twice the rectangle AC, CB is equal to twice the rectangle AD, DB together with K.

**Step 7.** Since AB is cut at C, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB [2.4]; and since AB is cut at D, the square on AB is also equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [2.4]. Therefore the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 8.** Replacing twice the rectangle AC, CB by its equal from Step 6, the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB and K are equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD, DB. Subtracting twice the rectangle AD, DB from both [CN3], the squares on AD, DB are equal to the squares on AC, CB together with K. That is, the sum of the squares on AD, DB exceeds the sum of the squares on AC, CB by the area K.

**Step 9.** The area K is rational. For twice the rectangle AC, CB and twice the rectangle AD, DB are both rational, so each is commensurable with R [D10.1.4]; being commensurable with the same area, they are commensurable with one another [10.12]. Now twice the rectangle AC, CB is the whole made up of the two parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB and K, and this whole is commensurable with one of the parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB; therefore the two parts, twice the rectangle AD, DB and K, are commensurable with one another [10.15]. Thus K is commensurable with twice the rectangle AD, DB, which is commensurable with R; hence K is commensurable with R [10.12], that is, K is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** But the sum of the squares on AD, DB is a medial area, and the sum of the squares on AC, CB is a medial area (Steps 1 and 2). Therefore, by Step 8, a medial area exceeds a medial area by the rational area K, which is impossible [10.26].

**Step 11.** Therefore the supposition of Step 2 is false: AB cannot be divided at any point other than C into two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial and twice the rectangle contained by them rational. Hence the side of a rational plus a medial area is divided at one point only. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 10.47
**Statement:** The side of the sum of two medial areas is divided at one point only.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the side of the sum of two medial areas, divided at C, so that AC, CB are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is medial, the rectangle AC·CB is medial, and the rectangle AC·CB is incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AC, CB [10.41]. Suppose, if possible, that AB is also divided at another point D fulfilling the same conditions — AD, DB incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on AD, DB medial, the rectangle AD·DB medial and incommensurable with the sum of the squares on AD, DB — and that the division at D is not the same as that at C; that is, AD is not equal to CB (for if AD = CB, then DB = AC as well, and AB would be divided at D into the very same two segments as at C, which, exactly as in 10.42, is not a different division).

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line EF. To EF apply, in a right angle, the rectangle EG equal to the squares on AC, CB, its breadth being EH; and to the same EF (that is, to its equal HG), continuing along the same breadth, apply the rectangle HK equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB, its breadth being HN [1.44, 1.45]. Since the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB [2.4], the whole rectangle EK, contained by EF and EN, is equal to the square on AB [CN2].

**Step 3.** Again, to EF apply the rectangle EL equal to the squares on AD, DB, its breadth being EM [1.44, 1.45]. Since the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB together with twice the rectangle AD·DB [2.4], the squares on AD, DB are less than the square on AB [CN5]; so EL is less than EK, M falls between E and N, and the remainder LK, contained by ML (equal to EF) and MN, is equal to twice the rectangle AD·DB [CN3].

**Step 4.** EG is equal to the sum of the squares on AC, CB, which is medial; so EG is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF, and therefore its breadth EH is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22]. Again, twice the rectangle AC·CB is measured by the rectangle AC·CB, so the two are commensurable [D10.1.1]; and AC·CB is medial; therefore twice AC·CB is medial [10.23, Porism]. Thus HK is a medial area applied to the rational straight line EF, so that HN is rational and incommensurable in length with EF [10.22].

**Step 5.** The sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with the rectangle AC·CB, and AC·CB is commensurable with twice AC·CB (Step 4); therefore the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC·CB [10.13], that is, EG is incommensurable with HK. But EG, HK are parallelograms under the same height, so EG : HK = EH : HN [6.1]; therefore EH is incommensurable in length with HN [10.11].

**Step 6.** EH and HN are each rational, that is, each is commensurable with EF at least in square [D10.1.3], so that the square on EH and the square on HN are each commensurable with the square on EF [D10.1.2]; hence the square on EH is commensurable with the square on HN [10.12], that is, EH, HN are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Together with Step 5, EH, HN are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EN is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms EH, HN at the point H [10.36].

## Proposition 10.48
**Statement:** To find the first binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let a rational straight line D be set out. Throughout, a straight line is called rational when it is commensurable with D, whether in length and in square or in square only (D10.1.3).

**Step 2.** By 10.29, let two rational straight lines A, B be found which are commensurable in square only, A being the greater, and such that the square on A is greater than the square on B by the square on a straight line C commensurable in length with A.

**Step 3.** Let EF be a straight line commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 4.** To the three given straight lines A, B, EF let a fourth proportional be found (6.12), and let it be FG, placed in a straight line with EF on the far side of F, so that as A is to B, so is EF to FG. Let EG be the whole straight line made up of EF and FG.

**Step 5.** Since A is greater than B, and as A is to B, so is EF to FG, therefore EF is greater than FG (5.14).

**Step 6.** Since A, B are commensurable in square only, A is incommensurable in length with B. And the four straight lines A, B, EF, FG are proportional; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG (10.11).

**Step 7.** Since as A is to B, so is EF to FG, the squares on them, being similar figures similarly described on four proportional straight lines, are also proportional: as the square on A is to the square on B, so is the square on EF to the square on FG (6.22). But A, B are commensurable in square, so the squares on A, B are measured by the same area (D10.1.2), that is, the square on A is commensurable with the square on B (D10.1.1). Therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG (10.11); that is, EF, FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 8.** Since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the ratio which a number has to a number; hence the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (10.6). But the square on FG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 7). Therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D (10.12), so that FG is commensurable in square with D (D10.1.2); therefore FG is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 9.** Therefore EF, FG are rational straight lines (Steps 3, 8) commensurable in square (Step 7) but incommensurable in length (Step 6), that is, commensurable in square only. Therefore EG, the sum of EF and FG, is a binomial straight line (10.36), whose terms are EF and FG, and of which EF is the greater term (Step 5).

**Step 10.** Since the four straight lines A, B, EF, FG are proportional, and the square on the first, A, is greater than the square on the second, B, by the square on C, which is commensurable in length with A (Step 2), therefore the square on the third, EF, is also greater than the square on the fourth, FG, by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EF (10.14).

**Step 11.** Thus EG is a binomial divided into its terms EF, FG at F; the square on the greater term EF is greater than the square on the lesser term FG by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with EF (Step 10); and the greater term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 3). Therefore EG is a first binomial straight line (D10.2.1). Therefore the first binomial straight line EG has been found, which it was required to do.

Path note: the required pair of rational lines with the square-difference property is already supplied by 10.29; the most direct route is therefore to transfer that pair to a line commensurable in length with D by a fourth proportional, 10.14 carrying the square-difference property across the proportion and 10.11 carrying commensurability, rather than rebuilding the pair from a fresh choice of numbers.

## Proposition 10.49
**Statement:** To find the second binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let D be the rational straight line set out (D10.1.3). Take two numbers AC, CB whose sum AB has to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to CA such a ratio: namely, let AB be the number 9, BC the number 4, and CA the number 5, so that AB is the sum of AC and CB. Since 9 is 3 multiplied by 3 and 4 is 2 multiplied by 2, AB and BC are square numbers (D7.18); therefore AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. But AB has not to CA the ratio which a square number has to a square number: for if it had, then, AB being square, CA would also be square (8.24); but 5 is not a square number, since 2 by 2 makes 4 and 3 by 3 makes 9, and no number multiplied by itself makes 5.

**Step 2.** Let EF be a straight line commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 3.** Produce EF to G (P2) so that, as the number CA is to the number AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG; this is possible by the Porism to 10.6 (a straight line X is found such that EF is to X as CA is to AB, and FG is taken as a mean proportional between EF and X, so that EF is to X as the square on EF is to the square on FG). Thus EG is one straight line divided at F.

**Step 4.** Since the square on EF has to the square on FG the ratio which the number CA has to the number AB, the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6); that is, EF and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 5.** Since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (10.6). But the square on FG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 4). Therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D (10.12), so that FG is commensurable in square with D and is therefore rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 6.** Since CA has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1), and the square on EF has to the square on FG the same ratio as CA has to AB (Step 3), neither has the square on EF to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 7.** Accordingly EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 2, 4, 5, 6). Therefore EG, which is made up of them, is a binomial straight line, and EF, FG are its terms (10.36).

**Step 8.** Since, as CA is to AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG, inversely, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (5.7 Porism). Now AB, being 9, is greater than CA, being 5. Take the same equimultiples of all four magnitudes, say the doubles: since AB is greater than CA, the double of AB exceeds the double of CA; hence, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, the double of the square on FG exceeds the double of the square on EF (D5.5). Therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on EF, and consequently FG is greater than EF; so FG is the greater and EF the lesser of the two terms.

**Step 9.** On FG describe a semicircle FKG, and, since EF is less than FG, fit into it the straight line FK equal to EF (4.1); join KG (P1). The angle FKG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FK, KG (1.47), that is, to the squares on EF, KG. Let H denote KG. Thus the square on FG is greater than the square on EF by the square on H.

**Step 10.** Since, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (Step 8), and AB exceeds CA by CB, while the square on FG exceeds the square on EF by the square on H (Step 9), convertendo, as AB is to BC, so is the square on FG to the square on H (5.19 Porism).

**Step 11.** But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1). Therefore the square on FG has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and hence FG is commensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 12.** Therefore EG is a binomial straight line divided into its terms EF, FG (Step 7); the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term EF by the square on H, a straight line commensurable in length with FG (Steps 9, 11); and the lesser term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 2). Therefore EG is a second binomial straight line (D10.2.2). Thus the second binomial straight line EG has been found. Q.E.F.

**Path note.** The numbers were fixed explicitly (9, 4, 5) rather than by appeal to the unnumbered lemma after 10.28, and H was constructed by the semicircle method (the unnumbered lemma before 10.14) rather than cited, since lemmas carry no proposition numbers.

## Proposition 10.50
**Statement:** To find the third binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Set out two numbers AC, CB such that their sum AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** Set out a further number D which is not square and has not to either of the numbers BA, AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line E (D10.1.3), and find a straight line FG such that, as the number D is to the number AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG (10.6, Porism).

**Step 4.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG), the square on E has to the square on FG the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6). Hence E and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2), and, E being rational, FG is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 5.** Since D has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on E to the square on FG; therefore E is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 6.** Produce FG beyond G (P2), and cut off from the produced part a straight line GH such that, as the number BA is to the number AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH (10.6 Porism, 1.3). Thus FG, GH lie in a straight line, and FH is their sum.

**Step 7.** Since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that FG, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). But BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 8.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG) and AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), ex aequali D : AC = (sq. on E) : (sq. on GH) (5.22). Therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that E, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2) and GH is rational (D10.1.3); and, since D has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, E is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 9.** Accordingly FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 4, 7, 8); therefore the whole FH is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms FG, GH at the point G (10.36).

**Step 10.** Since AB is the sum of AC and CB, AB is greater than AC (CN5); and since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is greater than the square on GH (5.14). Consequently FG is greater than GH (for otherwise the square on FG would not exceed the square on GH), and FG is the greater term of the binomial.

**Step 11.** Bisect FG at M (1.10), and with centre M and distance MF describe the semicircle FLG on FG (P3). Since GH is less than the diameter FG, fit into the semicircle a straight line FL equal to GH (4.1), and join LG (P1). The angle FLG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FL, LG together (1.47). Denote LG by K; then the square on FG is equal to the squares on GH, K together, that is, the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 12.** Now AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), where AB is composed of AC, CB and the square on FG is composed of the squares on GH, K. Therefore, convertendo, AB : CB = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on K) (5.19, Porism).

**Step 13.** But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and FG is commensurable in length with K (10.9). Thus the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term GH by the square on a straight line K commensurable in length with the greater term FG.

**Step 14.** Moreover, neither of the terms FG, GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line E set out (Steps 5, 8). Therefore FH is a third binomial straight line (D10.2.3); and it has been found. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 10.51
**Statement:** To find the fourth binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let two numbers AC, CB be set out such that their sum AB has neither to BC nor to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. (Construction: the numbers are chosen so that both AB : BC and AB : AC fail to be ratios of square numbers.)

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line D, and let EF be commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational, being commensurable with the rational straight line set out [D10.1.3].

**Step 3.** Let it be contrived that, as the number BA is to the number AC, so is the square on EF to the square on FG [10.6, Porism: given the two numbers BA, AC and the straight line EF, a straight line FG is constructed so that EF² : FG² = BA : AC].

**Step 4.** Since the square on EF has to the square on FG the ratio which the number BA has to the number AC, the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6]. Moreover, since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9], so that the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D [10.6]; hence the square on FG, being commensurable with the square on EF, is commensurable with the square on D [10.12]. Thus FG is commensurable in square with the rational straight line D, and therefore FG is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 5.** Since BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on EF to the square on FG; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG [10.9]. But their squares are commensurable (Step 4), so EF, FG are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. Therefore EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and hence the whole EG (EF together with FG) is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms EF, FG [10.36].

**Step 6.** Since AB is greater than its part AC [CN5], and as AB is to AC so is the square on EF to the square on FG, the square on EF is greater than the square on FG [5.14]; hence EF is greater than FG (for if FG were not less than EF, the square on FG would not be less than the square on EF), so EF is the greater term. Let the square on EF be greater than the square on FG by the square on H [10.13, Lemma: to find a straight line the square on which equals the difference of two given squares], so that the square on H together with the square on FG equals the square on EF.

**Step 7.** Since, as BA is to AC, so is the square on EF to the square on FG, therefore, convertendo, as AB is to CB, so is the square on EF to the excess of the square on EF over the square on FG, that is, to the square on H [5.19, Porism].

**Step 8.** But AB has not to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on EF to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 9.** Therefore EG is a binomial straight line whose terms EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; the square on the greater term EF is greater than the square on the lesser term FG by the square on H, a straight line incommensurable in length with EF (Step 8); and the greater term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 2). Therefore EG is a fourth binomial straight line [D10.2.4]; and it has been found. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 10.52
**Statement:** To find the fifth binomial straight line.

But the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (Step 2); therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D [10.12], that is, FG is commensurable in square with D [D10.1.2]; therefore FG is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 5.** Since CA has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on EF to the square on FG (for if the square on EF had to the square on FG the ratio of a square number to a square number, CA would have that same ratio to AB [5.11]); therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG [10.9].

**Step 6.** Therefore EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; hence the whole EG is irrational and is a binomial straight line [10.36], whose terms are EF and FG.

**Step 7.** Now AB, being composed of AC and CB, is greater than CA [CN5]. And, as CA is to AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG; since the first falls short of the second, the third falls short of the fourth [D5.5]; therefore the square on EF is less than the square on FG. Hence FG is greater than EF (for if FG were equal to or less than EF, the square on FG would be equal to or less than the square on EF); thus FG is the greater term and EF the lesser term of the binomial EG.

**Step 10.** But AB has not to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on H (for otherwise AB would have to CB that same ratio [5.11]); therefore FG is incommensurable in length with H [10.9].

**Step 11.** Therefore EG is a binomial straight line whose terms FG (the greater) and EF (the lesser) are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, in which the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term EF by the square on the straight line H incommensurable in length with the greater term FG [D10.2.4], and in which the lesser term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out. Therefore EG is a fifth binomial straight line [D10.2.5]; and it has been found. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 10.53
**Statement:** To find the sixth binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let two numbers AC, CB be set out, and let AB be their sum, such that AB has neither to AC nor to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and let D be another number which has neither to BA nor to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Let a rational straight line E be set out; E is the assigned rational straight line of D10.1.3.

**Step 2.** By the porism to 10.6, let a straight line FG be made such that, as the number D is to the number AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG. Since the square on E has to the square on FG the ratio which the number D has to the number AB, the square on E is commensurable with the square on FG [10.6]; that is, FG is commensurable in square with E [D10.1.2]. And E is rational; therefore FG is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 3.** Since D has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and as D is to AB so is the square on E to the square on FG, neither has the square on E to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore E is incommensurable in length with FG [10.9].

**Step 4.** Again, by the porism to 10.6, let a straight line be made such that, as the number BA is to the number AC, so is the square on FG to the square on that straight line. Produce FG beyond G [P2] and cut off GH equal to the straight line so made [1.3]; then F, G, H lie in one straight line, and as BA is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH.

**Step 5.** Since, as D is to AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG, and, as AB is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as D is to AC, so is the square on E to the square on GH [5.22]. Hence the square on E is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6], so that GH is commensurable in square with E [D10.1.2], and therefore GH is rational [D10.1.3]. But D has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on E to the square on GH that ratio, and E is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9].

**Step 6.** Since, as BA is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH [10.6], so that FG, GH are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on GH that ratio, and FG is incommensurable in length with GH [10.9]. Therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and the whole FH is a binomial straight line [10.36], its terms being FG and GH.

**Step 7.** Since AC is a part of AB, AB is greater than AC [CN5]. And as AB is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH; therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH [5.14], so that FG is greater than GH, and FG is the greater term of the binomial FH.

**Step 8.** Produce FH beyond H [P2] and cut off GN equal to FG [1.3]. Since GH is less than FG, that is, than GN, the point H falls between G and N. Thus the straight line FN is cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at H, and GH is the straight line between the points of section; therefore the rectangle contained by FH, HN together with the square on GH is equal to the square on FG [2.5]. Let K be the side of the square equal to the rectangle contained by FH, HN [2.14]. Then the square on GH together with the square on K is equal to the square on FG; that is, the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 9.** Since, as AB is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, where AB is the sum of CB and AC, and the square on FG is the sum of the square on K and the square on GH, therefore, convertendo, as AB is to CB, so is the square on FG to the square on K [5.19]. But AB has not to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on FG to the square on K that ratio, and FG is incommensurable in length with K [10.9]. Therefore the square on FG, the greater term, is greater than the square on GH, the lesser term, by the square on a straight line K incommensurable in length with FG.

**Step 10.** Thus FH is a binomial straight line divided into its terms FG, GH; the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term GH by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with FG [D10.2.4]; and neither term is commensurable in length with the rational straight line E set out, since E is incommensurable in length with FG (Step 3) and with GH (Step 5). Therefore FH is a sixth binomial straight line [D10.2.6]. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 10.54
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line which is called binomial.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line which is called binomial.

**Setting.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the first binomial AD, the angle at A being right, so that AC is the rectangle contained by AB, AD (D2.1); AB is the rational straight line set out with respect to which AD is a first binomial. I say that the side of AC (the straight line on which a square equal to AC is described) is a binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Since AD is a first binomial it is a binomial straight line; let it be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. By 10.36 the terms AE, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so that AE is incommensurable in length with ED. By D10.2.1 the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and AE is commensurable in length with AB.

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F (1.10). Since EF = FD, the square on ED is equal to the squares on EF, FD together with twice the rectangle EF·FD (2.4), that is, to four times the square on EF. Hence the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED.

**Step 3.** Since ED is less than AE, EF (the half of ED) is less than the half of AE, so the square on EF is not greater than the square on the half of AE. Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure (6.28): let it be the rectangle AG·GE, deficient by the square on GE, so that AG·GE = sq(EF), the fourth part of sq(ED).

**Step 4.** AE, ED are two unequal straight lines; the square on the greater AE exceeds the square on the less ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE (Step 1); and to AE there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on ED and deficient by a square, dividing AE at G. Therefore AG, GE are commensurable in length (10.17).

**Step 5.** Since AG, GE are commensurable, the whole AE is commensurable in length with each of AG, GE (10.15). But AE is commensurable in length with AB (Step 1). Therefore each of AG, GE is commensurable in length with AB (10.12), and hence AG, GE are rational straight lines (D10.1.3).

**Step 6.** AE is commensurable in length with AB, while AE is incommensurable in length with ED (Step 1); therefore ED is incommensurable in length with AB (10.13). Again, ED is double of EF, so ED : EF = 2 : 1, the ratio which a number has to a number; hence ED, EF are commensurable in length (10.6). Therefore EF is incommensurable in length with AB (10.13).

**Step 7.** EF is rational. For sq(ED) : sq(EF) = 4 : 1 (Step 2), a ratio of a number to a number, so sq(ED), sq(EF) are commensurable (10.6). And ED, being rational, is commensurable in square with AB (D10.1.3), so sq(ED) is commensurable with sq(AB) (D10.1.2). Hence sq(EF) is commensurable with sq(AB) (10.12); thus EF is commensurable in square with AB (D10.1.2) and so rational (D10.1.3). Since EF is incommensurable in length with AB (Step 6), AB, EF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 8.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L (1.31). Then AC is divided into the rectangles AH, GK, EL, FC, contained by AB and AG, GE, EF, FD respectively, and AC is equal to AH, GK, EL, FC together (2.1). Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on equal bases in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC (1.36).

**Step 9.** AH is contained by the rational straight lines AB, AG, which are commensurable in length (Step 5); therefore AH is rational (10.19). Likewise GK, contained by AB, GE, is rational (10.19). Being rational, AH and GK are each commensurable with the square on AB (D10.1.4).

**Step 10.** EL is contained by the rational straight lines AB, EF, which are commensurable in square only (Step 7); therefore EL is irrational, namely a medial area (10.21), that is, EL is incommensurable with the square on AB (D10.1.4).

**Step 11.** AH, GK are parallelograms under the same height AB; therefore AH : GK = AG : GE (6.1). But AG is commensurable in length with GE (Step 4); therefore AH is commensurable with GK (10.11).

**Step 12.** Since AG·GE = sq(EF) (Step 3), the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE (6.17). Also, the parallelograms being under the same height AB, AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE (6.1). Therefore AH : EL = EL : GK (5.11).

**Step 13.** Construct a square equal to AH (2.14) and let MN be equal to its side, so that sq(MN) = AH. To the three straight lines AG, EF, MN find a fourth proportional NO (6.12), so that AG : EF = MN : NO, and let NO be placed in a straight line with MN, so that MO is a straight line cut at N.

**Step 14.** The square on MN and the rectangle MN·NO are parallelograms under the same height MN; hence sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = MN : NO (6.1). But MN : NO = AG : EF (Step 13) and AG : EF = AH : EL (Step 12); therefore sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL (5.11). Since sq(MN) = AH, sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = AH : rect(MN, NO) (5.7); hence AH : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL (5.11). Therefore rect(MN, NO) = EL (5.9).

**Step 15.** The rectangle MN·NO and the square on NO are parallelograms under the same height NO; hence rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = MN : NO (6.1). But MN : NO = AG : EF = EF : GE = EL : GK (Steps 12, 13); therefore rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = EL : GK (5.11). Since rect(MN, NO) = EL (Step 14), rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = EL : sq(NO) (5.7); hence EL : sq(NO) = EL : GK (5.11). Therefore sq(NO) = GK (5.9).

**Step 16.** Since the straight line MO is cut at N, the square on MO is equal to the squares on MN, NO together with twice the rectangle MN·NO (2.4). Now sq(MN) = AH, sq(NO) = GK and rect(MN, NO) = EL (Steps 13, 14, 15); therefore sq(MO) is equal to AH, GK, EL, EL together (CN2). But AC is equal to AH, GK, EL, FC together, and FC = EL (Step 8); therefore AC is also equal to AH, GK, EL, EL together (CN2). Hence sq(MO) = AC (CN1), and MO is the side of the area AC (D10.1.4).

**Step 17.** It remains to show that MO is binomial. sq(MN) = AH and sq(NO) = GK are rational areas (Step 9), hence each is commensurable with sq(AB) (D10.1.4); therefore MN and NO are each commensurable in square with AB (D10.1.2), and so MN, NO are rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 18.** sq(MN) = AH is commensurable with GK = sq(NO) (Step 11); therefore MN, NO are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 19.** sq(MN) is commensurable with sq(AB) (Step 17), while rect(MN, NO) = EL is incommensurable with sq(AB) (Step 10); therefore sq(MN) is incommensurable with rect(MN, NO) (10.13). But sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = MN : NO (Step 14); therefore MN is incommensurable in length with NO (10.11).

**Step 20.** Thus MN, NO are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 17, 18, 19); therefore the whole MO is irrational, namely a binomial straight line (10.36). And MO is the side of AC (Step 16). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the side of the area is the irrational straight line called binomial. Q.E.D.

Path note: NO is constructed as a fourth proportional (6.12) so that rect(MN, NO) = EL and sq(NO) = GK follow directly from 5.9; this is chosen over constructing both squares by 2.14 and then needing an auxiliary argument that two mean proportionals between the same two areas are equal.

## Proposition 10.55
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line which is called a first bimedial.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line which is called a first bimedial.

Notation: sq(X) denotes the square on X; rect(X, Y) denotes the rectangle contained by X, Y.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the second binomial AD, so that AC is the rectangle with adjacent sides AB, AD. Let AD be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. Since AD is a binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a second binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and the lesser term ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB [D10.2.1, D10.2.2].

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is cut at F, sq(ED) is equal to sq(EF), sq(FD) together with twice rect(EF, FD) [2.4]; and EF = FD, so sq(ED) is four times sq(EF), i.e. sq(EF) is the fourth part of sq(ED).

**Step 3.** Since AE is greater than ED, EF (the half of ED) is less than the half of AE, so that sq(EF) is less than the square on the half of AE. Therefore to AE there can be applied a parallelogram equal to sq(EF) and deficient by a square figure [6.28]. Let it be applied, cutting AE at G, the deficient square being described on GE; the applied parallelogram, having sides AG and GE, is rect(AG, GE), and thus rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF).

**Step 4.** Now sq(AE), the square on the greater of the two unequal straight lines AE, ED, exceeds sq(ED) by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and to AE has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of sq(ED) [Step 2] and deficient by a square figure, dividing AE into AG, GE; therefore AG and GE are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 5.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L [1.31]. Then AH, GK, EL, FC are rectangles, and the whole AC is made up of AH, GK, EL, FC. Their sides GH, EK, DC are each equal to AB [1.34], so AH = rect(AB, AG), GK = rect(AB, GE), EL = rect(AB, EF), FC = rect(AB, FD). Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on equal bases and are in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 6.** Since rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF), the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE [6.17]. Also AH, EL, GK are parallelograms under the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE [6.1].

**Step 7.** Let MN be the side of a square equal to AH [2.14], and to the three straight lines AG, EF, MN let NO be a fourth proportional, so that AG : EF = MN : NO [6.12]; and let NO be placed in a straight line with MN, so that MO is the straight line made up of MN and NO.

**Step 8.** The square on MN and the rectangle MN, NO are parallelograms under the same height MN on the bases MN, NO; therefore sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = MN : NO [6.1]. But MN : NO = AG : EF [Step 7] and AG : EF = AH : EL [Step 6]; therefore sq(MN) : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL [5.11]. And sq(MN) = AH, so AH : rect(MN, NO) = AH : EL [5.7]; therefore rect(MN, NO) = EL [5.9].

**Step 9.** Likewise the rectangle MN, NO and the square on NO are parallelograms under the same height NO on the bases MN, NO; therefore rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = MN : NO [6.1]. But MN : NO = AG : EF = EF : GE = EL : GK [Steps 6, 7]; therefore rect(MN, NO) : sq(NO) = EL : GK [5.11]. And rect(MN, NO) = EL [Step 8], so EL : sq(NO) = EL : GK [5.7]; therefore sq(NO) = GK [5.9].

**Step 10.** Since MO is cut at N, sq(MO) is equal to sq(MN), sq(NO) together with twice rect(MN, NO) [2.4]. But sq(MN) = AH, sq(NO) = GK, and twice rect(MN, NO) equals EL together with FC [Steps 5, 8, 9]; so sq(MO) equals AH, GK, EL, FC together [CN2], that is, the whole AC [CN1]. Therefore MO is the "side" of the area AC [D10.1.4].

It remains to show that MO is a first bimedial.

**Step 11.** Since AG, GE are commensurable in length [Step 4], the whole AE is commensurable in length with each of AG, GE [10.15].

**Step 12.** Since AE, ED are commensurable in square only, AE is incommensurable in length with ED; but ED is commensurable in length with AB; therefore AE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. And each of AG, GE is commensurable in length with AE [Step 11]; therefore each of AG, GE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13].

**Step 13.** Since AG is commensurable in length with AE, sq(AG) has to sq(AE) the ratio which a square number has to a square number [10.9]; hence sq(AG), sq(AE) are commensurable [10.6]. And AE, being rational, is commensurable with AB in square, i.e. sq(AE), sq(AB) are commensurable [D10.1.3, D10.1.2]; therefore sq(AG), sq(AB) are commensurable [10.12], so that AG is commensurable in square with AB [D10.1.2] and hence rational [D10.1.3]. But AG is incommensurable in length with AB [Step 12]; hence AB, AG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. In the same way AB, GE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 14.** Therefore AH = rect(AB, AG) and GK = rect(AB, GE) are each contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only, so each is irrational and the side of the square equal to each is medial [10.21]. Since sq(MN) = AH and sq(NO) = GK, MN and NO are medial straight lines.

**Step 15.** AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1], and AG is commensurable with GE [Step 4]; therefore AH is commensurable with GK [10.11], that is, sq(MN) is commensurable with sq(NO); hence MN, NO are commensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 16.** Since ED is double of EF, EF measures ED, so ED and EF are commensurable [D10.1.1]; and ED is commensurable in length with AB; therefore EF is commensurable in length with AB [10.12]. But AG is incommensurable in length with AB [Step 12]; therefore AG is incommensurable in length with EF [10.13]. And AG : EF = MN : NO [Step 7]; therefore MN is incommensurable in length with NO [10.11]. Hence MN, NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only.

**Step 17.** The rectangle MN, NO is equal to EL [Step 8], which is rect(AB, EF) [Step 5]. Now AB is rational, and EF, being commensurable in length with AB [Step 16], is rational [D10.1.3]; therefore rect(AB, EF) is rational [10.19], and so rect(MN, NO) is rational.

**Step 18.** Thus MN, NO are medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a rational rectangle; therefore the whole MO is irrational, namely the straight line called a first bimedial [10.37]. And MO is the side of the area AC [Step 10]. Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the second binomial, the side of the area is the irrational straight line called a first bimedial. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 10.56
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the third binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called a second bimedial.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the third binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called a second bimedial.

Let the area AC (the rectangle ABCD, AB and AD being adjacent sides at the right angle A) be contained by the rational straight line AB and the third binomial AD, and let AD be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. I say that the "side" of AC is a second bimedial straight line.

**Step 1.** Since AD is a third binomial, it is a binomial, so its terms AE, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; further, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and neither AE nor ED is commensurable in length with AB [D10.2.3]. Hence AE is incommensurable in length with ED; and, since AE, ED are rational, each is commensurable in square with AB, so that each of AE², ED² is commensurable with AB² [D10.1.3, D10.1.2].

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10], so that EF = FD. Since ED is cut at F, ED² = EF² + FD² + 2·EF·FD [2.4] = 4·EF²; so EF² is the fourth part of ED². Also ED, being double of EF, is measured by EF; hence ED is commensurable in length with EF [D10.1.1].

**Step 3.** Since AE is greater than ED, the half of AE is greater than EF, the half of ED, and so the square on the half of AE is greater than EF². Therefore to AE a parallelogram equal to EF² and deficient by a square figure can be applied [6.28]; let it be applied, dividing AE at G, so that the applied parallelogram is the rectangle AG·GE (deficient by the square on GE) and AG·GE = EF².

**Step 4.** AE² exceeds ED² by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and to AE has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of ED², namely EF², deficient by a square figure; therefore it divides AE into parts AG, GE which are commensurable in length [10.17].

**Step 5.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L [1.31]. Thus AC is divided into the rectangles AH, GK, EL, FC, all lying between the parallels AD, BC, and in them the sides GH, EK, FL opposite to AB are each equal to AB [1.34]; hence AH is the rectangle contained by AB, AG; GK the rectangle contained by AB, GE; EL the rectangle contained by AB, EF; and FC the rectangle contained by AB, FD. Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC, being on equal bases and in the same parallels, are equal [1.36].

**Step 6.** Since AG·GE = EF², the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE [6.17]. And since AH, EL, GK are parallelograms under the same height AB, AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE [6.1]. Therefore AH : EL = EL : GK [5.11].

**Step 7.** Construct a square equal to the rectangle AH [2.14] and let MN be its side, so that MN² = AH. Produce MN beyond N [P2] and cut off NO equal to the fourth proportional to the three straight lines AG, EF, MN [6.12, 1.3]; then MN, NO lie in one straight line MO, and AG : EF = MN : NO.

**Step 8.** The square MN² and the rectangle MN·NO are under the same height MN; hence MN² : MN·NO = MN : NO [6.1]. But MN : NO = AG : EF (Step 7) and AG : EF = AH : EL (Step 6), while AH = MN²; therefore MN² : MN·NO = MN² : EL [5.11], and so MN·NO = EL [5.9].

**Step 9.** Likewise MN·NO : NO² = MN : NO [6.1], and MN : NO = AG : EF = EF : GE = EL : GK (Steps 6, 7) [5.11]. Since MN·NO = EL, this gives EL : NO² = EL : GK; therefore NO² = GK [5.9].

**Step 10.** Since MO is cut at N, MO² = MN² + NO² + 2·MN·NO [2.4]. Here MN² = AH, NO² = GK, and MN·NO = EL = FC (Steps 5, 8) [CN1]; so, adding these equals, MO² = AH + GK + EL + FC = AC [CN2]. Hence MO is the "side" of the area AC, that is, the straight line on which the square is equal to AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 11.** Since AG, GE are commensurable in length (Step 4), the whole AE is commensurable in length with each of AG, GE [10.15]. But AE is incommensurable in length with AB (Step 1); therefore each of AG, GE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13].

**Step 12.** Moreover AG, GE are rational. Thus AB, EF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore the rectangle EL contained by AB, EF is medial [10.21]. But EL = MN·NO (Step 8); therefore the rectangle contained by MN, NO is medial.

And MO is the "side" of AC (Step 10). Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AB and the third binomial AD is the irrational straight line called a second bimedial. ## Proposition 10.57
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called major.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fourth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called major.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial AD [D2.1], and let AD be divided into its terms at E, AE being the greater term. Since AD is a binomial, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a fourth binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, and the greater term AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB set out [D10.2.4].

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is made up of the equal segments EF, FD, the square on ED is equal to the squares on EF, FD together with twice the rectangle EF, FD [2.4], that is, to four times the square on EF. Hence the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED.

**Step 3.** Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure [6.28]; let it be the rectangle contained by AG, GE, so that rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF). (This is possible: AE, being the greater term, exceeds ED, so EF, the half of ED, is less than the half of AE, and the square on EF is less than the square on the half of AE.)

**Step 4.** AE, ED are two unequal straight lines, AE the greater; the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE (Step 1); and to AE there has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, ED (Step 2), and deficient by a square figure (Step 3). Therefore it divides AE into parts AG, GE which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 5.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB [1.31], meeting BC at H, K, L. Then AH, GK, EL, FC are the rectangles contained by AB and AG, GE, EF, FD respectively, AK is the rectangle contained by AB, AE [D2.1], and the whole area AC is made up of AH, GK, EL, FC.

**Step 6.** Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on the equal bases EF, FD and are in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 7.** AK is contained by AB and AE, which are rational straight lines commensurable in length (Step 1). Therefore AK is rational [10.19]. And AK is the sum of AH and GK.

**Step 8.** AE, ED are commensurable in square only, so AE is incommensurable in length with ED; but AE is commensurable in length with AB; therefore ED is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. Again, EF measures ED, ED being twice EF, so EF is commensurable in length with ED [D10.1.1]; and ED is incommensurable in length with AB; therefore EF is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13].

**Step 9.** The square on ED is four times the square on EF (Step 2), so the square on EF has to the square on ED the ratio which a number has to a number, and is commensurable with it [10.6]. ED is rational, so the square on ED is commensurable with the square on AB [D10.1.3, D10.1.2]. Therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on AB [10.12], that is, EF is commensurable in square with AB and is rational [D10.1.3]. Thus AB, EF are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Step 8), and the rectangle contained by them, EL, is medial [10.21].

**Step 10.** AH and GK have the same height AB, so AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1]. But AG is incommensurable in length with GE (Step 4); therefore AH is incommensurable with GK [10.11].

**Step 11.** Likewise the square on AG and the rectangle AG, GE have the same height AG, so sq(AG) : rect(AG, GE) = AG : GE [6.1]; and rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF) (Step 3), so AG : GE = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.7]. Hence, by Step 10, AH : GK = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.11].

**Step 12.** Construct a square equal to AH and let SN be its side, and construct a square equal to GK [2.14]; produce SN to Q [P2] and cut off NQ equal to the side of the latter square [1.3]. Then sq(SN) = AH and sq(NQ) = GK, so sq(SN) : sq(NQ) = AH : GK [5.7] = sq(AG) : sq(EF) [5.11]. The squares are similar figures similarly described on SN, NQ, AG, EF; therefore SN : NQ = AG : EF [6.22].

**Step 13.** The square on SN and the rectangle SN, NQ have the same height SN, so sq(SN) : rect(SN, NQ) = SN : NQ [6.1]; and AH, EL have the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF [6.1]. Since SN : NQ = AG : EF (Step 12), sq(SN) : rect(SN, NQ) = AH : EL [5.11]. But sq(SN) = AH, so AH : rect(SN, NQ) = AH : EL [5.7]; therefore rect(SN, NQ) = EL [5.9], and hence also rect(SN, NQ) = FC (Step 6).

**Step 14.** The straight line SQ is divided at N, so the square on SQ is equal to the squares on SN, NQ together with twice the rectangle SN, NQ [2.4]; and these are equal respectively to AH, GK, EL, FC, so that the square on SQ is equal to AH + GK + EL + FC [CN2], which is the whole area AC (Step 5). Therefore SQ is the "side" of AC, namely the straight line on which is described a square equal to the area AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 15.** Now the squares on SN, NQ are AH, GK, which are incommensurable with one another (Step 10); therefore SN, NQ are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2]. The sum of the squares on SN, NQ is AH + GK, that is AK, which is rational (Step 7). And the rectangle contained by SN, NQ is EL, which is medial (Step 9).

**Step 16.** Therefore SN, NQ are two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial; hence the whole SQ made up of them is irrational and is the straight line called major [10.39]. Thus the "side" of the area AC, contained by the rational straight line AB and the fourth binomial AD, is the irrational straight line called major. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 10.58
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the fifth binomial AD, divided into its terms at E, so that AE is the greater term. Since AD is a binomial divided into its terms, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [10.36]; and since AD is a fifth binomial, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AE, while the lesser term ED is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB [D10.2.4, D10.2.5]. It is required to prove that the "side" of AC is the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 2.** Bisect ED at F [1.10]. Since ED is bisected at F, the square on ED is four times the square on EF [2.4], so the square on EF is the fourth part of the square on ED. Apply to AE a parallelogram equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure [6.28] (this is possible, since EF, being half of ED, is less than half of AE), and let it be the rectangle contained by AG, GE; thus rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF). Now AE, ED are two unequal straight lines, the square on the greater AE exceeds the square on the less ED by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AE, and to AE has been applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on ED and deficient by a square figure; therefore it divides AE into parts AG, GE which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 3.** Through G, E, F draw GH, EK, FL parallel to AB, meeting BC at H, K, L [1.31]. Then AC is divided into the rectangles AH, GK, EL, FC, contained by AB together with AG, GE, EF, FD respectively; AK is the rectangle contained by AB, AE, and EC is the rectangle contained by AB, ED. Since EF = FD, the parallelograms EL, FC stand on equal bases and lie in the same parallels AD, BC; therefore EL = FC [1.36].

**Step 4.** Construct a square equal to AH and let MN be one of its sides; construct a square equal to GK [2.14]; produce MN to O [P2] and cut off NO equal to a side of the second square [1.3]. On MO describe the square SQ [1.46]. Since MO is cut at N, the square on MO is equal to the squares on MN, NO together with twice the rectangle contained by MN, NO [2.4]; accordingly SQ is made up of the square SN on MN, the square NQ on NO, and two rectangles MR, OP, each contained by straight lines equal to MN, NO, so that MR = OP and SQ = SN + NQ + MR + OP. Moreover SN = AH and NQ = GK.

**Step 5.** Since rect(AG, GE) = sq(EF), the three straight lines AG, EF, GE are proportional: AG : EF = EF : GE [6.17]. But the rectangles AH, EL, GK are under the same height AB, so AH : EL = AG : EF and EL : GK = EF : GE [6.1]. Therefore AH : EL = EL : GK [5.11]; that is, EL is a mean proportional between AH and GK.

**Step 6.** Again, SN and MR are under the same height MN with bases MN, NO, and MR and NQ are under the same height NO with bases MN, NO; therefore SN : MR = MN : NO and MR : NQ = MN : NO [6.1], whence SN : MR = MR : NQ [5.11]. Since SN = AH and NQ = GK, AH : MR = SN : MR and MR : NQ = MR : GK [5.7]; therefore AH : MR = MR : GK [5.11]; that is, MR is also a mean proportional between AH and GK.

**Step 7.** EL = MR. For suppose EL > MR. Then AH has to the less, MR, a greater ratio than to the greater, EL [5.8]. But AH : MR = MR : GK and AH : EL = EL : GK, so MR has to GK a greater ratio than EL has to GK [5.13]; therefore MR > EL [5.10], which contradicts the supposition. In the same way EL is not less than MR. Therefore EL = MR; and since FC = EL and OP = MR, also FC = OP [CN1].

**Step 8.** Therefore SQ = SN + NQ + MR + OP = AH + GK + EL + FC = AC [CN2]. Thus the square on MO is equal to the area AC, and MO is the "side" of AC [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** Since the rectangles AH, GK are under the same height AB, AH : GK = AG : GE [6.1]. But AG is incommensurable in length with GE (Step 2); therefore AH is incommensurable with GK [10.11]. Now AH is the square on MN and GK is the square on NO; hence the square on MN is incommensurable with the square on NO, and MN, NO are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 10.** The sum of the squares on MN, NO is SN + NQ = AH + GK = AK [CN2], the rectangle contained by AB, AE. Now ED is commensurable in length with AB, while ED is incommensurable in length with AE (Step 1); therefore AE is incommensurable in length with AB [10.13]. But AB and AE are both rational, so each is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.3], and hence the squares on AB, AE are commensurable with one another [10.12]; thus AB, AE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only [D10.1.2]. Therefore the rectangle AK contained by them is medial [10.21]; that is, the sum of the squares on MN, NO is medial.

**Step 11.** The rectangle contained by MN, NO is MR, which is equal to EL (Step 7). Since AB, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in length (Step 1), the rectangle EC contained by them is rational [10.19]. But EC = EL + FC = twice EL, so EL measures EC and is commensurable with it [D10.1.1]; and EC, being rational, is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line [D10.1.4]; therefore EL is commensurable with that square [10.12] and is rational [D10.1.4]. Hence the rectangle contained by MN, NO is rational.

**Step 12.** Therefore MN, NO are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 9) which make the sum of the squares on them medial (Step 10) but the rectangle contained by them rational (Step 11); so the whole MO, made up of them, is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area [10.40]. But MO is the "side" of AC (Step 8). Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and the fifth binomial, the "side" of the area is the irrational straight line called the side of a rational plus a medial area. Q.E.D.

Path note: the square on MO is decomposed at once by 2.4 into the squares on MN, NO and the two equal rectangles MN·NO; the alternative of constructing the two squares SN, NQ separately and placing them about a common diameter (which would require 6.26 and 1.43 to identify the complements) reaches the same figure by a longer route.
