## Proposition 11.34
**Statement:** In equal parallelepipedal solids the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those parallelepipedal solids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be parallelepipedal solids. Let the base of AB be the parallelogram EH, with vertices E, A, H, L in order, let its sides standing up be EF, AG, HK, LB, and let the face opposite the base be the parallelogram FK (vertices F, G, K, B). Let the base of CD be the parallelogram NQ, with vertices N, C, Q, P in order, let its sides standing up be NO, CM, QR, PD, and let the face opposite the base be the parallelogram OR (vertices O, M, R, D). The height of each solid is the perpendicular drawn from the face opposite the base to the plane of the base [D6.4]. We must prove: (I) if the solid AB is equal to the solid CD, then the base EH is to the base NQ as the height of CD is to the height of AB; and (II) if the base EH is to the base NQ as the height of CD is to the height of AB, then the solid AB is equal to the solid CD.

**Step 2.** Case 1: let the sides which stand up be at right angles to the bases. Since AG is at right angles to the plane of the base EH, AG is the height of AB; likewise CM is the height of CD [D6.4]. So in this case we must prove (I) AB = CD implies EH : NQ = CM : AG, and (II) EH : NQ = CM : AG implies AB = CD.

**Step 3.** First let AG = CM. Then AB and CD are of the same height, so that AB : CD = EH : NQ [11.32].

**Step 4.** (I) Let AB = CD. Then AB : CD is the ratio of a magnitude to an equal magnitude, and so is CM : AG. Any two such ratios are the same: whatever equimultiples are taken, the multiple of the antecedent exceeds, equals or falls short of the multiple of the consequent according as the first multiplier exceeds, equals or falls short of the second, alike in both ratios [D5.5]. Hence AB : CD = CM : AG, and therefore EH : NQ = CM : AG [Step 3, 5.11].

**Step 5.** (II) Let EH : NQ = CM : AG. Then AB : CD = CM : AG [Step 3, 5.11]. But CM : AG is the ratio of a magnitude to an equal magnitude, and so is CD : CD; hence CM : AG = CD : CD [D5.5], and AB : CD = CD : CD [5.11]. Therefore AB = CD [5.9].

**Step 6.** Next let AG and CM be unequal, and first let CM be the greater. From CM cut off CT equal to AG [1.3]. In the plane of the face NCMO draw TU through T parallel to CN, meeting NO at U, and in the plane of the face CQRM draw TW through T parallel to CQ, meeting QR at W [1.31]. The straight lines TU, TW meeting at T are parallel to the straight lines CN, CQ meeting at C and are not in the plane of NQ; hence the plane through TU, TW is parallel to the plane of NQ [11.15]. Let this plane meet PD at V. It cuts off from CD the solid CV, contained by the base NQ, the plane TV parallel to it, and portions of the four side faces of CD, of which the opposite ones are parallel; so CV is a parallelepipedal solid on the base NQ. Its sides standing up CT, NU, QW, PV, being parts of CM, NO, QR, PD, are at right angles to NQ; therefore the height of CV is CT, which is equal to AG [D6.4].

**Step 7.** The solids AB and CV are thus of the same height; therefore AB : CV = EH : NQ [11.32].

**Step 8.** Now regard the parallelogram MQ (the face CQRM) as the base of the solid CD, and the parallelogram TQ (the face CQWT, which lies in the same plane) as the base of the solid CV. The faces opposite these bases, PNOD of CD and PNUV of CV, lie in one plane, which is parallel to the plane of CQRM; hence with respect to these bases the solids CD, CV are of the same height, and CD : CV = MQ : TQ [11.32].

**Step 9.** The parallelograms MQ, TQ have their bases CM, CT on the same straight line and lie between the same parallels CM, QR; they are therefore under the same height, and MQ : TQ = CM : CT [6.1]. Hence CD : CV = CM : CT [5.11]. And since CT = AG, CM : CT = CM : AG [5.7]; therefore CD : CV = CM : AG [5.11].

**Step 10.** (I) Let AB = CD. Then AB : CV = CD : CV [5.7]. But AB : CV = EH : NQ [Step 7] and CD : CV = CM : AG [Step 9]. Therefore EH : NQ = CM : AG [5.11].

**Step 11.** (II) Let EH : NQ = CM : AG. Since AB : CV = EH : NQ [Step 7] and CD : CV = CM : AG [Step 9], we have AB : CV = CD : CV [5.11]. Therefore AB = CD [5.9].

**Step 12.** If instead AG is greater than CM, the same construction is made on AG (a part of AG equal to CM is cut off, and through its extremity a plane parallel to EH is drawn), and the reasoning of Steps 6-11 with the two solids interchanged shows: (I) if AB = CD, then NQ : EH = AG : CM, whence, inversely, EH : NQ = CM : AG [5.7 Por.]; (II) if EH : NQ = CM : AG, then inversely NQ : EH = AG : CM [5.7 Por.], whence CD = AB. Thus both parts of the proposition hold whenever the sides which stand up are at right angles to the bases.

**Step 13.** Case 2: let the sides which stand up not be at right angles to the bases. From F, G, K, B draw FS, GX, KY, BZ perpendicular to the plane of EH, meeting it at S, X, Y, Z; and from O, M, R, D draw OS', MX', RY', DZ' perpendicular to the plane of NQ, meeting it at S', X', Y', Z' [11.11].

**Step 14.** Complete the solid FY. Since FS, GX, KY, BZ are at right angles to the same plane, they are parallel to one another [11.6]. FK is a parallelogram [11.24], so that FG is parallel to BK and GK to FB. Hence FG, FS meeting at F are parallel to BK, BZ meeting at B, and GK, GX meeting at G are parallel to FB, FS meeting at F, the pairs not being in one plane; so the plane through FG, FS is parallel to the plane through BK, BZ, and the plane through GK, GX is parallel to the plane through FB, FS [11.15]. Also the plane of EH, which contains S, X, Y, Z, is parallel to the plane of FK, these being opposite faces of the parallelepipedal solid AB. In the same way the solid OY' is completed: a parallelepipedal solid having OR as one face, its opposite face S'Y' in the plane of NQ, and its sides OS', MX', RY', DZ' at right angles to S'Y'.

Therefore AB = FY, whether the extremities of the sides standing up are on the same straight lines or not [11.29, 11.30]. In the same way CD = OY' [11.29, 11.30].

**Step 16.** EH and FK are opposite faces of AB, and SY and FK are opposite faces of FY; hence EH = FK and SY = FK [11.24], so that EH = SY [CN1]. In the same way NQ = OR and S'Y' = OR [11.24], so that NQ = S'Y' [CN1].

## Proposition 11.35
**Statement:** If there be two equal plane angles, and on their vertices there be set up elevated straight lines containing equal angles with the original straight lines respectively, if on the elevated straight lines points be taken at random and perpendiculars be drawn from them to the planes in which the original angles are, and if from the points so arising in the planes straight lines be joined to the vertices of the original angles, they will contain, with the elevated straight lines, equal angles.

**Step 1.** Let BAC, EDF be two equal rectilineal angles, and from the vertices A, D let the elevated straight lines AG, DM be set up, containing with the original straight lines equal angles respectively, so that the angle GAB is equal to the angle MDE and the angle GAC is equal to the angle MDF. Let G, M be points taken at random on AG, DM; from G let GL be drawn perpendicular to the plane through BA, AC, and from M let MN be drawn perpendicular to the plane through ED, DF [11.11], meeting the planes at L, N; and let LA, ND be joined [P1]. I say that the angle GAL is equal to the angle MDN.

**Step 2.** From AG let AH be cut off equal to DM [1.3]. The triangle AGL lies in one plane [11.2]; in that plane, through the point H, let HK be drawn parallel to GL [1.31]. Now HK is not parallel to AL; for otherwise GL and AL, being each parallel to HK, would be parallel to one another [1.30], whereas they meet at L. Therefore HK and AL, being in one plane and not parallel, meet when produced [D1.23]; let them meet at K. Thus K lies on the straight line AL, and, since H lies on AG, the angle HAK is the angle GAL.

**Step 3.** Since GL is at right angles to the plane through BA, AC, and HK is parallel to GL, HK is also at right angles to the plane through BA, AC [11.8]; hence HK makes right angles with every straight line in that plane which meets it [D11.3].

**Step 4.** In the plane through BA, AC let KC be drawn from K perpendicular to AC and KB perpendicular to AB [1.12], C and B being the feet of these perpendiculars on AC and AB; likewise in the plane through ED, DF let NF, NE be drawn from N perpendicular to DF, DE [1.12]. Let HC, HB, BC, MF, ME, EF be joined [P1]. Since KA, KC, KB lie in the plane through BA, AC and meet HK, the angles HKA, HKC, HKB are right [D11.3]; and since MN is at right angles to the plane through ED, DF, the angles MND, MNF, MNE are likewise right [D11.3].

**Step 5.** Since the angle HKA is right, the square on HA is equal to the squares on HK, KA [1.47]; and since the angle KCA is right, the square on KA is equal to the squares on KC, CA [1.47]. Adding the square on HK to each side of the latter equality, the squares on HK, KA are equal to the squares on HK, KC, CA [CN2]; therefore the square on HA is equal to the squares on HK, KC, CA [CN1]. Again, since the angle HKC is right, the square on HC is equal to the squares on HK, KC [1.47]; adding the square on CA, the squares on HC, CA are equal to the squares on HK, KC, CA [CN2]. Therefore the square on HA is equal to the squares on HC, CA [CN1]; hence the angle HCA is right [1.48]. In the same way, since the square on MD is equal to the squares on MN, ND, the square on ND to the squares on NF, FD, and the square on MF to the squares on MN, NF [1.47], the square on MD is equal to the squares on MF, FD [CN2, CN1], so that the angle MFD is right [1.48]. By the same argument the angles HBA, MED are also right.

**Step 6.** Since the angles HCA, MFD are right, they are equal to one another [P4]. And the angle HAC, which is the angle GAC, is equal to the angle MDF by hypothesis; and the side AH is equal to the side DM, each subtending one of the equal right angles. Therefore the triangles HAC, MDF have two angles equal to two angles respectively and one side equal to one side; hence AC is equal to DF and HC to MF [1.26]. Similarly, since the angles HBA, MED are right and therefore equal [P4], the angle HAB is equal to the angle MDE by hypothesis, and AH is equal to DM, the triangles HAB, MDE give AB equal to DE and HB equal to ME [1.26].

**Step 7.** Since AC is equal to DF and AB to DE, the two sides CA, AB are equal to the two sides FD, DE respectively; and the angle CAB is equal to the angle FDE by hypothesis. Therefore the base BC is equal to the base EF, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles: the angle ACB is equal to the angle DFE, and the angle ABC to the angle DEF [1.4].

**Step 8.** The angle ACK is right, being the angle of the perpendicular KC to AC, and the angle DFN is right; therefore they are equal [P4]. Subtracting from them the equal angles ACB, DFE, the remaining angle BCK is equal to the remaining angle EFN [CN3]. In the same way the right angles ABK, DEN are equal [P4], and subtracting the equal angles ABC, DEF, the remaining angle CBK is equal to the remaining angle FEN [CN3].

**Step 9.** Therefore the triangles BCK, EFN have two angles equal to two angles respectively and the side BC, adjoining the equal angles, equal to the side EF; hence CK is equal to FN and BK to EN [1.26].

**Step 10.** Since AC is equal to DF and CK to FN, the two sides AC, CK are equal to the two sides DF, FN respectively, and the angle ACK is equal to the angle DFN, both being right [P4]; therefore the base AK is equal to the base DN [1.4].

**Step 11.** Since AH is equal to DM, the square on AH is equal to the square on DM. But the angle AKH is right, so the square on AH is equal to the squares on AK, KH [1.47]; and the angle DNM is right, so the square on DM is equal to the squares on DN, NM [1.47]. Therefore the squares on AK, KH are equal to the squares on DN, NM [CN1]. Of these the square on AK is equal to the square on DN, since AK is equal to DN; therefore the remaining square on KH is equal to the remaining square on NM [CN3], so that KH is equal to NM.

**Step 12.** Thus in the triangles HAK, MDN the two sides HA, AK are equal to the two sides MD, DN respectively, and the base HK is equal to the base MN; therefore the angle HAK is equal to the angle MDN [1.8].

**Step 13.** But the angle HAK is the angle GAL, since H lies on AG and K lies on AL (Step 2). Therefore the angle GAL is equal to the angle MDN, which was to be proved.

*Path note:* the congruence route (cutting off AH = DM and using 1.26, 1.4, 1.8) was chosen over a proportional route through Book 6 (6.4, 6.6, 6.7) because it reaches the equal angles directly without ratios; the existence of K on AL is justified by 11.2, 1.30 and D1.23 rather than read from a figure.

## Proposition 11.36
**Statement:** If three straight lines be proportional, the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three is equal to the parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equilateral, but equiangular with the aforesaid solid.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be three straight lines in proportion, so that A : B = B : C. Let a solid angle be set out at the point E, contained by the three plane angles DEG, GEF, FED, and let each of the straight lines ED, EF, EG be made equal to the mean B [1.3]. Let the parallelepipedal solid EK be completed, having ED, EF, EG as its three edges meeting at E. Since its three edges at E are each equal to the mean B, EK is the parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equilateral.

**Step 2.** Let LM be set out equal to A [1.3], and on the straight line LM, at the point L on it, let a solid angle be constructed equal to the solid angle at E [11.26], namely the angle contained by the plane angles NLO, OLM, MLN, so that the angle NLO is equal to the angle DEG, the angle OLM to the angle GEF, and the angle MLN to the angle FED. Let LO be made equal to B and LN equal to C [1.3], and let the parallelepipedal solid LH be completed, having LM, LN, LO as its three edges meeting at L.

**Step 3.** The solid LH is the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three straight lines A, B, C, since its edges at L are LM = A, LO = B, LN = C; and the solid EK is equiangular with it, since by construction the solid angle at E is equal to the solid angle at L. It remains to prove that the solid LH is equal to the solid EK.

**Step 4.** Since A : B = B : C, while LM = A, EF = B, ED = B and LN = C, and equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude and the same magnitude has the same ratio to equal magnitudes [5.7], we have LM : EF = A : B and ED : LN = B : C; therefore LM : EF = ED : LN [5.11].

**Step 5.** Consider the parallelogram MN, contained by LM, LN about the angle MLN, and the parallelogram DF, contained by ED, EF about the angle DEF. The angle MLN is equal to the angle DEF (Step 2), so the two parallelograms are equiangular; and by Step 4 the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional, namely LM : EF = DE : LN. But equiangular parallelograms in which the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional are equal [6.14]; therefore the parallelogram MN is equal to the parallelogram DF.

**Step 6.** Now there are two equal plane angles, DEF and NLM, and on their vertices E and L there are set up the elevated straight lines EG and LO, which are equal to one another, each being equal to B [CN1], and which contain equal angles with the original straight lines respectively: the angle GED is equal to the angle OLN and the angle GEF is equal to the angle OLM (Step 2). Therefore the perpendiculars drawn from G and O to the planes through DEF and NLM are equal to one another [11.35, Porism].

**Step 7.** The perpendicular from G to the plane of DEF is the height of the solid EK standing on the base DF, and the perpendicular from O to the plane of NLM is the height of the solid LH standing on the base MN; hence the solids EK and LH are of the same height.

**Step 8.** Thus the parallelepipedal solids LH and EK are on equal bases MN, DF (Step 5) and of the same height (Step 7). But parallelepipedal solids which are on equal bases and of the same height are equal to one another [11.31]; therefore the solid LH is equal to the solid EK.

**Step 9.** And LH is the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three proportional straight lines A, B, C, while EK is the parallelepipedal solid on the mean B which is equilateral but equiangular with LH. Therefore, if three straight lines be proportional, the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three is equal to the parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equilateral, but equiangular with the aforesaid solid. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 11.37
**Statement:** If four straight lines be proportional, the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described will also be proportional; and, if the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described be proportional, the straight lines will themselves also be proportional.

**Step 1.** Let AB, CD, EF, GH be four straight lines, and let KA, LC, ME, NG be parallelepipedal solids described on AB, CD, EF, GH respectively, similar and similarly situated to one another, so that AB, CD, EF, GH are corresponding sides of the four solids. First let AB : CD = EF : GH; I say that KA : LC = ME : NG.

**Step 2.** Since the solid KA is similar to the solid LC, and AB, CD are corresponding sides, KA has to LC the ratio triplicate of that which AB has to CD [11.33]. For the same reason ME has to NG the ratio triplicate of that which EF has to GH [11.33].

**Step 3.** Let X be a third proportional to AB, CD, so that AB : CD = CD : X, and let Y be a third proportional to CD, X, so that CD : X = X : Y [6.11]. Then AB, CD, X, Y are four straight lines continuously proportional, and therefore AB has to Y the ratio triplicate of that which AB has to CD [D5.10]. Hence, by Step 2, KA : LC = AB : Y.

**Step 4.** In the same way let Z be a third proportional to EF, GH and W a third proportional to GH, Z [6.11], so that EF : GH = GH : Z = Z : W. Then EF has to W the ratio triplicate of that which EF has to GH [D5.10], and hence, by Step 2, ME : NG = EF : W.

**Step 5.** Since AB : CD = EF : GH by hypothesis, while CD : X = AB : CD and GH : Z = EF : GH, it follows that CD : X = GH : Z [5.11]; and since X : Y = CD : X and Z : W = GH : Z, it follows likewise that X : Y = Z : W [5.11].

**Step 6.** Thus there are two sets of magnitudes, AB, CD, X, Y and EF, GH, Z, W, equal in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio; therefore, ex aequali, AB : Y = EF : W [5.22].

**Step 7.** But KA : LC = AB : Y (Step 3) and ME : NG = EF : W (Step 4); therefore KA : LC = ME : NG [5.11]. This proves the first part.

**Step 8.** Next let KA : LC = ME : NG; I say that AB : CD = EF : GH. Let O be a fourth proportional to the three straight lines AB, CD, EF, so that AB : CD = EF : O [6.12].

**Step 9.** On O describe the parallelepipedal solid PO similar and similarly situated to the solid ME, the side O corresponding to EF [11.27].

**Step 10.** Then KA, LC, ME, PO are similar and similarly described parallelepipedal solids on the straight lines AB, CD, EF, O, and AB : CD = EF : O; therefore, by the first part (Steps 2 to 7), KA : LC = ME : PO.

**Step 11.** But KA : LC = ME : NG by hypothesis; therefore ME : NG = ME : PO [5.11]. Thus the same solid ME has the same ratio to NG and to PO; therefore NG = PO [5.9].

**Step 12.** The faces of NG are similar to the corresponding faces of ME, and the faces of PO are similar to the same faces of ME; therefore the faces of NG are similar to the corresponding faces of PO [6.21]. Hence NG and PO are contained by similar planes equal in multitude, so they are similar solids [D11.9], and GH, O are corresponding sides of them, each corresponding to EF. Therefore NG has to PO the ratio triplicate of that which GH has to O [11.33].

**Step 13.** Let S be a third proportional to GH, O and T a third proportional to O, S [6.11], so that GH : O = O : S = S : T. Then GH has to T the ratio triplicate of that which GH has to O [D5.10]; hence, by Step 12, NG : PO = GH : T.

**Step 14.** Since NG = PO (Step 11), NG : PO = PO : PO [5.7]. Further, PO : PO = T : T; for if any equimultiples be taken of PO and of T according to one number, and any equimultiples of PO and of T according to another number, the former alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the latter [D5.5]. Therefore GH : T = NG : PO = PO : PO = T : T, so that GH : T = T : T [5.11]. Thus GH and T have the same ratio to T; therefore GH = T [5.9].

**Step 15.** Now GH is not greater than O. For if GH were greater than O, then, since GH : O = O : S and GH is greater than O, O would be greater than S; and since O : S = S : T and O is greater than S, S would be greater than T [5.14]; so that GH would be greater than O, O greater than S, and S greater than T, whence GH would be greater than T, which contradicts Step 14. Nor is GH less than O; for then in the same way O would be less than S and S less than T [5.14], so that GH would be less than T, again contradicting Step 14. Therefore GH = O.

**Step 16.** Since O = GH, EF : O = EF : GH [5.7]; and AB : CD = EF : O (Step 8); therefore AB : CD = EF : GH [5.11]. This proves the second part. Therefore, if four straight lines are proportional, the similar and similarly described parallelepipedal solids on them are proportional; and if the solids are proportional, the straight lines are proportional. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 11.38
**Statement:** If the sides of the opposite planes of a cube be bisected, and planes be carried through the points of section, the common section of the planes and the diameter of the cube bisect one another.

**Step 1.** Let the cube have the opposite faces ABCD and EFGH, with the four edges AE, BF, CG, DH joining corresponding vertices, so that its remaining faces are ABFE, BCGF, CDHG, DAEH. All six faces are equal squares [D11.25]; hence all the edges of the cube are equal, and in every face the opposite sides are equal and parallel. Let the sides of the face ABCD be bisected at K, L, M, N (K on AB, L on BC, M on CD, N on DA), and the sides of the opposite face EFGH at O, P, Q, R (O on EF, P on FG, Q on GH, R on HE). Through the points K, M, Q, O let the plane α be carried, and through L, N, R, P the plane β. Join AC and EG, and join AG, a diameter of the cube. I say that the common section of the planes α, β and the diameter AG bisect one another.

**Step 2.** The plane α and the plane of the face ABCD cut one another (α contains O, which is not in the face ABCD), so their common section is a straight line [11.3]; since K and M lie in both planes, this common section is the straight line KM. In the same way the common section of β with the face ABCD is LN, the common section of α with the face EFGH is OQ, and the common section of β with the face EFGH is PR. Hence every point of KM or of OQ lies in the plane α, and every point of LN or of PR lies in the plane β.

**Step 3.** Let KM meet AC at U. Since AB is parallel to CD and AC falls upon them, the alternate angles BAC, DCA are equal [1.29]; that is, the angle KAU is equal to the angle MCU. The angles AUK, CUM are vertical angles, hence equal [1.15]. And AK is equal to CM, these being halves of the equal sides AB, CD. Therefore the triangles AKU, CMU have two angles equal to two angles respectively and one side equal to one side, namely AK equal to CM, subtending the equal angles AUK, CUM; hence the remaining sides are equal to the remaining sides [1.26], so that AU is equal to UC. Thus U, which lies on KM and therefore in the plane α (Step 2), is the middle point of AC.

**Step 4.** Join NU and UL. AN is equal to CL, these being halves of the equal sides AD, BC; AU is equal to UC (Step 3); and, since AD is parallel to BC and AC falls upon them, the alternate angles DAC, BCA are equal [1.29], that is, the angle NAU is equal to the angle LCU. Therefore in the triangles NAU, LCU two sides are equal to two sides respectively and the included angles are equal; hence the angle AUN is equal to the angle CUL [1.4]. Now the straight line NU, standing on the straight line AC at U, makes the angles AUN, NUC together equal to two right angles [1.13]; therefore the angles NUC, CUL are together equal to two right angles, and so UN, UL, which lie on opposite sides of UC, are in a straight line with one another [1.14]. Thus U lies on LN, and therefore (Step 2) U lies in the plane β as well as in the plane α.

**Step 5.** In the same manner, if OQ meets EG at S, then ES is equal to SG [1.29, 1.15, 1.26 applied to the triangles EOS, GQS], and S lies on PR [1.29, 1.4, 1.13, 1.14 applied to the triangles RES, PGS]; so S is the middle point of EG and lies in both planes α and β.

**Step 6.** The planes α, β are distinct and have the point U in common, so they cut one another and their common section is a straight line [11.3]. The points U and S both lie in α and in β, and they are distinct, U being in the face ABCD and S in the opposite face EFGH; therefore the common section of the planes is the straight line US.

**Step 7.** AE is parallel to BF, these being opposite sides of the square ABFE, and BF is parallel to CG, these being opposite sides of the square BCGF; and AE, CG are not in the same plane with BF, since C is not in the plane of ABFE. Therefore AE is parallel to CG [11.9]. Also AE is equal to CG, both being edges of the cube. Now AC and EG join the extremities of the equal and parallel straight lines AE, CG towards the same parts; therefore AC is equal and parallel to EG [1.33].

**Step 8.** Since AC and EG are parallel, and U, A are points on AC while S, G are points on EG, the straight lines US and AG both lie in the plane of the parallels AC, EG [11.7]. Let AG and US meet at T. Since AC is parallel to EG and AG falls upon them, the alternate angles CAG, EGA are equal [1.29]; that is, the angle UAT is equal to the angle SGT. The angles ATU, GTS are vertical angles, hence equal [1.15]. And AU is equal to GS, these being halves of the equal straight lines AC, EG (Steps 3, 5, 7).

**Step 9.** Therefore the triangles AUT, GST have two angles equal to two angles respectively and one side equal to one side, namely AU equal to GS, subtending the equal angles ATU, GTS; hence the remaining sides are equal to the remaining sides [1.26]: AT is equal to TG, and UT is equal to TS.

**Step 10.** Therefore the common section US of the planes and the diameter AG of the cube bisect one another at the point T. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 11.39
**Statement:** If there be two prisms of equal height, and one have a parallelogram as base and the other a triangle, and if the parallelogram be double of the triangle, the prisms will be equal.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDEF and GHKLMN be two prisms of equal height. Let the first stand on the parallelogram ABCD as base, its two opposite faces, which are equal, similar and parallel, being the triangles ADE and BCF, and its remaining faces being the parallelograms ABCD, ABFE, DCFE [D11.13]; thus EF is the edge opposite to the base ABCD, and the height of this prism is the perpendicular drawn from EF to the plane ABCD. Let the second stand on the triangle GHK as base, its opposite faces being the triangles GHK and LMN, and its remaining faces the parallelograms GHML, HKNM, GKNL [D11.13]; its height is the perpendicular drawn from the plane LMN to the plane GHK. Let these heights be equal, and let the parallelogram ABCD be double of the triangle GHK. I say that the prism ABCDEF is equal to the prism GHKLMN.

**Step 2.** Let the parallelepipedal solids be completed. Let the solid CP be completed on the base ABCD, having AP, BQ, CF, DE as its parallel edges, so that the triangles ADE, BCF are completed into the parallelograms ADEP, BCFQ, and the solid CP is contained by the six parallelograms ABCD, PQFE, ABQP, DCFE, ADEP, BCFQ, of which the opposite ones are parallel; its face PQFE opposite to the base lies in the plane through EF parallel to the plane ABCD. Likewise let the solid GT be completed, the triangle GHK being completed into the parallelogram GHSK, of which HK is a diameter, and the triangle LMN into the parallelogram LMTN, of which MN is a diameter, so that the solid GT is contained by the parallelograms GHSK, LMTN, GHML, HSTM, KSTN, GKNL, with GL, HM, ST, KN as its parallel edges; it stands on the base GHSK in the plane of GHK, and its opposite face LMTN lies in the plane of LMN.

**Step 3.** In the solid CP the faces ADEP and BCFQ are opposite planes, and AE, BF are their diagonals; the plane ABFE, which is a face of the first prism, passes through both of these diagonals. This plane divides the solid CP into two prisms, namely the prism ABCDEF, whose opposite faces are the triangles ADE, BCF, and the prism ABPQEF, whose opposite faces are the triangles APE, BQF. But a parallelepipedal solid cut by a plane through the diagonals of opposite planes is bisected by that plane [11.28]. Therefore the prism ABPQEF is equal to the prism ABCDEF, and the solid CP is double of the prism ABCDEF.

**Step 4.** Similarly, in the solid GT the faces GHSK and LMTN are opposite planes, with diagonals HK and MN, and the plane HKNM, a face of the second prism, passes through both. This plane divides the solid GT into the prism GHKLMN, whose opposite faces are the triangles GHK, LMN, and the prism HSKMTN, whose opposite faces are the triangles HSK, MTN; and these prisms are equal [11.28]. Therefore the solid GT is double of the prism GHKLMN.

**Step 5.** Since HK is a diameter of the parallelogram GHSK, it bisects the parallelogram [1.34]; therefore the parallelogram GHSK is double of the triangle GHK. But the parallelogram ABCD is also double of the triangle GHK, by hypothesis. Therefore the parallelogram ABCD is equal to the parallelogram GHSK [CN1].

**Step 6.** The solid CP stands on the base ABCD, and its opposite face PQFE lies in the plane through EF parallel to the base; hence the perpendicular from that face to the base ABCD is the perpendicular from EF to the plane ABCD, so that the solid CP has the same height as the prism ABCDEF. Likewise the solid GT has its base GHSK in the plane GHK and its opposite face LMTN in the plane LMN, so that it has the same height as the prism GHKLMN. But the prisms are of equal height; therefore the solids CP and GT are of the same height.

**Step 7.** Thus the parallelepipedal solids CP and GT are on the equal bases ABCD, GHSK and are of the same height. But parallelepipedal solids on equal bases and of the same height are equal to one another [11.31]. Therefore the solid CP is equal to the solid GT.

**Step 8.** Now the solid CP is double of the prism ABCDEF and the solid GT is double of the prism GHKLMN [Steps 3, 4], and the solids CP, GT are equal [Step 7]. I say that the prisms are equal. For suppose, if possible, that the prism ABCDEF is greater than the prism GHKLMN. Since the prism ABPQEF is equal to the prism ABCDEF and the prism HSKMTN is equal to the prism GHKLMN [Steps 3, 4], the prism ABPQEF is also greater than the prism HSKMTN. Then the prisms GHKLMN, HSKMTN are equal to parts of the prisms ABCDEF, ABPQEF respectively; and, these parts being added, the whole solid GT, which is made up of the prisms GHKLMN, HSKMTN, is equal to a part of the solid CP, which is made up of the prisms ABCDEF, ABPQEF [CN2]. Therefore the solid CP is greater than the solid GT [CN5]: which is impossible, since they are equal. In the same manner it is shown that the prism ABCDEF is not less than the prism GHKLMN. Therefore the prism ABCDEF is equal to the prism GHKLMN.

**Step 9.** Therefore, if there be two prisms of equal height, and one have a parallelogram as base and the other a triangle, and if the parallelogram be double of the triangle, the prisms are equal. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.1
**Statement:** Similar polygons inscribed in circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE and FGHKL be similar polygons inscribed in the circles ABCDE and FGHKL, the vertices corresponding in the order A, B, C, D, E and F, G, H, K, L, so that BA and GF are corresponding sides; and let BM and GN be diameters of the two circles. Since the polygons are inscribed, every vertex of each lies on the circumference of its circle (D4.3). I say that polygon ABCDE : polygon FGHKL = square on BM : square on GN.

**Step 2.** Join BE, AM, GL, FN (P1).

**Step 3.** Since the polygons are similar, their angles are severally equal and the sides about the equal angles are proportional (D6.1); hence the angle BAE is equal to the angle GFL, and BA : AE = GF : FL.

**Step 4.** The triangles BAE and GFL therefore have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about these equal angles proportional; hence they are equiangular, and the angles subtended by corresponding sides are equal (6.6). In particular the angle AEB, subtended by BA, is equal to the angle FLG, subtended by GF.

**Step 5.** In the circle ABCDE the angles AEB and AMB are angles in the same segment, both standing upon the circumference AB (E and M lying on the same side of AB); therefore the angle AEB is equal to the angle AMB (3.21). For the same reason, in the circle FGHKL the angle FLG is equal to the angle FNG (3.21). Hence, by Step 4, the angle AMB is equal to the angle FNG (CN1).

**Step 6.** Since BM is a diameter, the angle BAM is an angle in the semicircle on BM and is therefore right (3.31); likewise the angle GFN is right (3.31). Hence the angle BAM is equal to the angle GFN (P4).

**Step 7.** In the triangles ABM and FGN the three angles of each are together equal to two right angles (1.32); the angles BAM, AMB together are equal to the angles GFN, FNG together (Steps 5 and 6, CN2); therefore the remaining angle ABM is equal to the remaining angle FGN (CN3). Thus the triangles ABM and FGN are equiangular.

**Step 8.** In equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, corresponding sides being those which subtend equal angles (6.4). About the equal angles ABM and FGN, the sides BA and GF subtend the equal angles AMB and FNG, and the sides BM and GN subtend the equal right angles BAM and GFN; therefore BA : BM = GF : GN.

**Step 9.** Alternately, BA : GF = BM : GN (5.16); that is, the four straight lines BM, GN, BA, GF are proportional: BM : GN = BA : GF.

**Step 10.** Upon BM and GN stand the squares on BM and GN, which are similar and similarly described figures; upon BA and GF stand the polygons ABCDE and FGHKL, which are similar and similarly described figures, BA and GF being corresponding sides. Since the four straight lines BM, GN, BA, GF are proportional, the rectilineal figures similar and similarly described upon them are also proportional (6.22): square on BM : square on GN = polygon ABCDE : polygon FGHKL.

**Step 11.** Therefore the polygon ABCDE is to the polygon FGHKL as the square on BM is to the square on GN; that is, similar polygons inscribed in circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters. Q.E.D.

Path note: an equivalent route reaches Step 10 through 6.20 (the polygons are in the duplicate ratio of BA : GF) with 6.20 Por. (the squares are in the duplicate ratio of BM : GN) and then equates the duplicate ratios of the equal ratios BM : GN and BA : GF; 6.22 yields the conclusion in one step from the proportion of Step 9, so it was taken as the more direct route.

## Proposition 12.2
**Statement:** Circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters.

Let ABCD and EFGH be circles, and let BD and FH be diameters of them. I say that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the square on BD to the square on FH.

**Step 1.** (Lemma, first part.) Let XY be any straight line fitted into a circle whose centre is Z [3.1], and let W be a point on one of the circumferences cut off by XY such that WX = WY; call the figure bounded by XY and the circumference XWY the segment XWY. Join WX, WY [P1]. Since WX = WY, the angle WXY is equal to the angle WYX [1.5]. Join ZW, and through W draw UV at right angles to ZW [1.11]; since ZW produced is a diameter, UV touches the circle at W and falls outside the circle [3.16]. The angle UWX, which the chord WX makes with the tangent UV, is equal to the angle in the alternate segment, that is, to the angle WYX [3.32]; therefore the angle UWX is equal to the angle WXY [CN1]. But these are alternate angles made by WX falling on the two straight lines UV, XY; therefore UV is parallel to XY [1.27].

**Step 2.** (Lemma, second part.) Through X draw XU parallel to ZW, and through Y draw YV parallel to XU [1.31], meeting UV in U and V. Then XUVY is a parallelogram, and the parallelogram XUVY and the triangle XWY are on the same base XY and in the same parallels XY, UV; therefore the parallelogram XUVY is double of the triangle XWY [1.41]. Again, since UV falls outside the circle [3.16], the circumference XWY lies within the parallelogram XUVY, so that the segment XWY is a part of the parallelogram and is less than it [CN5]. Therefore the triangle XWY is greater than half the segment XWY. This holds for any chord XY and any such point W.

**Step 3.** Let S be the area to which the circle ABCD has the same ratio as the square on BD has to the square on FH (the existence of this fourth proportional being assumed), so that, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the circle ABCD to the area S. I say first that S is not less than the circle EFGH.

**Step 4.** For, if possible, let S be less than the circle EFGH. Let Z be the centre of the circle EFGH [3.1]; through Z draw EG at right angles to FH [1.11], and join EF, FG, GH, HE [P1]; then EFGH is the square inscribed in the circle [4.6], and its sides are all equal [D1.22]. Since EF = EH, the triangle EFH is, by Steps 1–2, greater than half the segment FEH; and since GF = GH, the triangle FGH is greater than half the segment FGH. The two triangles make up the square EFGH, and the two segments make up the whole circle; therefore the inscribed square EFGH is greater than half the circle EFGH.

**Step 5.** Bisect the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE at the points K, L, M, N [3.30], and join EK, KF, FL, LG, GM, MH, HN, NE [P1]. Since the circumference EK is equal to the circumference KF, EK = KF [3.29]; therefore, by Steps 1–2, the triangle EKF is greater than half the segment EKF. In the same way each of the triangles FLG, GMH, HNE is greater than half the segment about it; hence the four triangles together are greater than half of the four segments which remain when the square is subtracted from the circle.

**Step 6.** Now the circle EFGH and the excess by which the circle EFGH exceeds the area S are two unequal magnitudes, of which the circle is the greater. From the circle there has been subtracted the square, which is greater than its half; from the remainder, the four triangles, which are greater than half of it; and, by bisecting the remaining circumferences and joining the points of bisection, this can be continued as often as we please, each time subtracting triangles greater than half of the remaining segments (Steps 1–2, 5). Therefore there will at length be left some segments of the circle which together are less than the excess by which the circle EFGH exceeds S [10.1]. Let such segments have been left, and, to fix the lettering, let them be the segments on EK, KF, FL, LG, GM, MH, HN, NE, so that the remaining polygon is EKFLGMHN (if further bisections are required, the argument is verbatim the same for the polygon with more sides). Then, since the polygon EKFLGMHN together with these segments makes up the circle EFGH, and the area S together with its excess also makes up the circle EFGH, while the segments are less than the excess, the polygon EKFLGMHN is greater than the area S.

**Step 7.** In the circle ABCD, through its centre [3.1] draw the diameter AC at right angles to BD [1.11] and join AB, BC, CD, DA, so that ABCD is the inscribed square [4.6]; bisect the circumferences AB, BC, CD, DA at O, P, Q, R [3.30], join AO, OB, BP, PC, CQ, QD, DR, RA [P1], and bisect further exactly as many times as was done in the circle EFGH, so as to obtain the polygon AOBPCQDR with the same number of sides as EKFLGMHN. In each circle the sides of the inscribed square are equal [D1.22], so the four circumferences they cut off are equal [3.28], and the parts obtained by bisecting them equally often are equal. Hence each polygon is equilateral, its sides subtending equal circumferences [3.29], and equiangular, its angles standing upon equal circumferences [3.27]. Since the polygons have the same number n of sides, and the interior angles of each are together equal to 2n − 4 right angles [1.32], each angle of either polygon is the n-th part of the same sum; so the angles of the polygon AOBPCQDR are severally equal to the angles of the polygon EKFLGMHN. And, all the sides of the one being equal to one another and all the sides of the other likewise, the sides about the equal angles are proportional [5.7]. Therefore the polygon AOBPCQDR is similar to the polygon EKFLGMHN [D6.1].

**Step 8.** Therefore, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the polygon AOBPCQDR to the polygon EKFLGMHN [12.1]. But, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the circle ABCD to the area S; therefore, as the circle ABCD is to the area S, so is the polygon AOBPCQDR to the polygon EKFLGMHN [5.11]. Now the circle ABCD is greater than the polygon AOBPCQDR inscribed in it, the polygon being a part of the circle [CN5]; therefore the area S is greater than the polygon EKFLGMHN [5.14]. But it was proved (Step 6) that the area S is less than the polygon EKFLGMHN: which is impossible. Therefore it is not true that, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the circle ABCD to some area less than the circle EFGH.

**Step 9.** In exactly the same way, interchanging the two circles, it is proved that neither is it true that, as the square on FH is to the square on BD, so is the circle EFGH to some area less than the circle ABCD.

**Step 10.** I say next that S is not greater than the circle EFGH. For, if possible, let S be greater than the circle EFGH. Since, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the circle ABCD to S, inversely, as the square on FH is to the square on BD, so is the area S to the circle ABCD [5.7]. Let T be the area to which the circle EFGH has the same ratio as the area S has to the circle ABCD (again assuming the fourth proportional), so that, as S is to the circle ABCD, so is the circle EFGH to T. Since S is greater than the circle EFGH, the circle ABCD is greater than T [5.14]. Also, as the square on FH is to the square on BD, so is the circle EFGH to T [5.11]; that is, as the square on FH is to the square on BD, so is the circle EFGH to an area T less than the circle ABCD: which was proved impossible in Step 9. Therefore S is not greater than the circle EFGH.

**Step 11.** Since S is neither less nor greater than the circle EFGH, S is equal to the circle EFGH. Therefore, as the circle ABCD is to S, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH [5.7]; and hence, as the square on BD is to the square on FH, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH [5.11]. Therefore circles are to one another as the squares on the diameters. Q.E.D.

Remarks on path choice: (i) In Step 8 the inequality S > polygon EKFLGMHN follows from 5.14 applied directly to the proportion circle ABCD : S = polygon AOBPCQDR : polygon EKFLGMHN (first term greater than third), so alternation (5.16) is not needed. (ii) Tangents at points of the circumference (Step 1) are drawn as perpendiculars to the radius by 1.11 and the porism to 3.16, since 3.17 concerns a point outside the circle. (iii) The existence of a fourth proportional to two squares and a circle (Steps 3 and 10) is assumed, no proposition constructing a fourth proportional to non-rectilineal areas being available; this assumption is inherent in the method.

## Proposition 12.3
**Statement:** Any pyramid which has a triangular base is divided into two pyramids equal and similar to one another, similar to the whole and having triangular bases, and into two equal prisms; and the two prisms are greater than the half of the whole pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let ABC–D be a pyramid with triangular base ABC and vertex D (throughout, "pyramid XYZ–V" denotes the pyramid with base XYZ and vertex V). Bisect the six edges AB, BC, CA, AD, DB, DC at E, F, G, H, K, L respectively [1.10], and join HE, EG, GH, HK, KL, LH, KF, FG [P1].

**Step 2.** Since AE = EB and AH = HD, the sides AB, AD of triangle ABD are cut proportionally at E and H; hence EH is parallel to BD [6.2]. Likewise DH = HA and DK = KB give HK parallel to AB [6.2]. Thus EBKH is a parallelogram, so HK = EB and EH = BK [1.34]. In the same way, in triangle ACD, HG is parallel to DC and HL parallel to AC [6.2], so GCLH is a parallelogram with HL = GC and HG = CL [1.34]; in triangle ABC, EG is parallel to BC and GF parallel to AB [6.2], so EBFG is a parallelogram with EG = BF and GF = EB [1.34]; and in triangle DBC, KL is parallel to BC and KF parallel to DC [6.2], so KFCL is a parallelogram with KL = FC and KF = CL [1.34].

**Step 3.** Since E, F, G, H, K, L are the midpoints, the equalities of Step 2 give [CN1]: HK = GF = EB = AE, each half of AB; HL = GC = AG, each half of AC; KL = FC = BF = EG, each half of BC; EH = BK = KD, each half of BD; HG = CL = LD = KF, each half of CD; and AH = HD, half of AD.

**Step 4.** (Face AEH and face HKD.) Since HK is parallel to AB and AD falls on them, the exterior angle KHD is equal to the interior and opposite angle EAH [1.29]. Also AE = HK and AH = HD [Step 3]. Therefore EH = KD, and triangle AEH is equal and similar to triangle HKD [1.4].

**Step 5.** (Face AGH and face HLD.) Similarly, since HL is parallel to AC, angle LHD is equal to angle GAH [1.29]; AG = HL and AH = HD [Step 3]; therefore GH = LD, and triangle AGH is equal and similar to triangle HLD [1.4].

**Step 6.** (Face EHG and face KDL.) The straight lines HE, HG meeting at H are parallel respectively to DK, DL meeting at D (for HE is parallel to BD and HG to DC), and they are not in the same plane; hence angle EHG is equal to angle KDL [11.10]. Also HE = DK and HG = DL [Step 3]. Therefore EG = KL, and triangle EHG is equal and similar to triangle KDL [1.4].

**Step 7.** (Face AEG and face HKL.) The straight lines HK, HL meeting at H are parallel respectively to AB, AC meeting at A, and are not in the same plane; hence angle KHL is equal to angle EAG [11.10]. Also HK = AE and HL = AG [Step 3]. Therefore triangle HKL is equal and similar to triangle AEG [1.4].

**Step 8.** The pyramid AEG–H is contained by the four triangles AEG, AEH, AGH, EHG, and the pyramid HKL–D by the four triangles HKL, HKD, HLD, KDL [D11.12]. By Steps 4–7 these are planes equal in multitude and respectively equal and similar. Therefore pyramid AEG–H is equal and similar to pyramid HKL–D [D11.10]; and each of them has a triangular base.

**Step 9.** (Similarity of the faces to those of the whole.) In triangles DHK and DAB the sides DH, DK, HK are respectively halves of DA, DB, AB [Step 3]; hence DH : DK = DA : DB, DK : KH = DB : BA and DH : HK = DA : AB [5.15], that is, the two triangles have their sides proportional. Therefore they are equiangular, the equal angles being subtended by the corresponding sides [6.5]; and since their angles are severally equal and the sides about the equal angles are proportional, triangle DHK is similar to triangle DAB [D6.1]. In exactly the same way, since its sides are halves of the corresponding sides, triangle DKL is similar to triangle DBC, triangle DLH to triangle DCA, and triangle HKL (whose sides HK, KL, LH are halves of AB, BC, CA) to triangle ABC [5.15, 6.5, D6.1].

**Step 10.** Hence pyramid HKL–D is contained by four planes similar respectively to the four planes ABC, ABD, ACD, BCD containing pyramid ABC–D, and so is similar to the whole pyramid [D11.9]. The same reasoning applies to pyramid AEG–H, whose faces AEG, AEH, AGH, EHG have sides respectively halves of those of ABC, ABD, ACD, BCD [Step 3]; so it also is similar to the whole pyramid [5.15, 6.5, D6.1, D11.9].

**Step 11.** (The common face HKFG.) HK and GF are each parallel to AB [Step 2] and are not in one plane with it; hence HK is parallel to GF [11.9]. Likewise HG and KF are each parallel to DC; hence HG is parallel to KF [11.9]. Therefore HKFG is a parallelogram.

**Step 12.** (The first prism.) The straight lines HE, HG meeting at H are parallel respectively to KB, KF meeting at K [Steps 2, 11], and are not in the same plane; hence the planes EHG and BKF are parallel [11.15], and angle EHG is equal to angle BKF [11.10]. Also HE = KB and HG = KF [Step 3]; therefore triangle EHG is equal and similar to triangle BKF [1.4]. Thus the solid contained by the two triangles BKF, EHG, which are equal, similar and parallel, and by the three parallelograms EBFG, EBKH, HKFG is a prism [D11.13]; call it the first prism.

**Step 13.** (The second prism.) The straight lines KH, KL meeting at K are parallel respectively to FG, FC meeting at F [Steps 2, 11], and are not in the same plane; hence the planes HKL and GFC are parallel [11.15], and angle HKL is equal to angle GFC [11.10]. Also KH = FG and KL = FC [Step 3]; therefore triangle HKL is equal and similar to triangle GFC [1.4]. Thus the solid contained by the two triangles GFC, HKL and the three parallelograms KFCL, LCGH, HKFG is a prism [D11.13]; call it the second prism.

**Step 14.** The plane EHG cuts off from the pyramid ABC–D the pyramid AEG–H, the plane HKL cuts off the pyramid HKL–D, and the plane of the parallelogram HKFG divides the solid that remains into the first and the second prism. Thus the whole pyramid is divided into the two pyramids and the two prisms.

**Step 15.** (The two prisms are equal.) Triangles GBF and GFC are on the equal bases BF, FC and in the same parallels BC, EG; hence they are equal [1.38]. Parallelogram EBFG and triangle GBF have the same base BF and are in the same parallels BF, EG; hence the parallelogram is double of the triangle [1.41]. Therefore parallelogram EBFG is double of triangle GFC.

**Step 16.** The first prism has the parallelogram EBFG as base and the straight line HK opposite; the second prism has the triangle GFC as base and the triangle HKL opposite. Since HK lies in the plane HKL, which is parallel to the plane ABC [Step 13], the two prisms are of equal height. And the parallelogram EBFG is double of the triangle GFC [Step 15]. Therefore the first prism is equal to the second prism [11.39].

**Step 17.** (The two prisms exceed the half.) Join EF and EK [P1]. The pyramid EBF–K is contained by the triangles EBF, EBK, BFK, EFK [D11.12]; it is a part of the first prism, being cut off from it by the plane EFK, since its vertices E, B, F, K are all vertices of that prism. Therefore the first prism is greater than the pyramid EBF–K [CN5].

**Step 18.** Since EG is parallel to BC and AB falls on them, angle EBF is equal to angle AEG [1.29]; also EB = AE and BF = EG [Step 3]; therefore EF = AG, and triangle EBF is equal and similar to triangle AEG [1.4]. Since EH is parallel to BD, angle EBK is equal to angle AEH [1.29]; also EB = AE and BK = EH; therefore EK = AH, and triangle EBK is equal and similar to triangle AEH [1.4].

**Step 19.** The straight lines BF, BK meeting at B are parallel respectively to EG, EH meeting at E, and are not in the same plane; hence angle FBK is equal to angle GEH [11.10]; with BF = EG and BK = EH, it follows that FK = GH and triangle BFK is equal and similar to triangle EGH [1.4]. Finally, in triangles EFK and AGH, EF = AG, EK = AH and FK = GH; hence angle FEK is equal to angle GAH [1.8], and triangle EFK is equal and similar to triangle AGH [1.4].

**Step 20.** Therefore the pyramid EBF–K is contained by four planes respectively equal and similar to the four planes containing the pyramid AEG–H, and so the two pyramids are equal [D11.10]. Hence, by Step 17, the first prism is greater than the pyramid AEG–H.

**Step 21.** But the second prism is equal to the first prism [Step 16], and the pyramid HKL–D is equal to the pyramid AEG–H [Step 8]; therefore the second prism is also greater than the pyramid HKL–D. Consequently the two prisms together are greater than the two pyramids together.

**Step 22.** The whole pyramid ABC–D consists of the two pyramids and the two prisms [Step 14]. Since the two prisms are greater than the two pyramids, twice the two prisms exceed the two prisms together with the two pyramids, that is, the whole pyramid. Therefore the two prisms are greater than the half of the whole pyramid.

Therefore any pyramid with a triangular base is divided into two pyramids equal and similar to one another, similar to the whole and having triangular bases, and into two equal prisms; and the two prisms are greater than the half of the whole pyramid. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.4
**Statement:** If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and cach of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.

**Statement:** If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and each of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let ABCG and DEFH be two pyramids of the same height, having the triangular bases ABC, DEF and the vertices G, H. From G and H let GZ and HZ' be drawn perpendicular to the planes ABC and DEF respectively (11.11); these perpendiculars are the heights of the pyramids (D6.4), so that by hypothesis GZ = HZ'. Divide each pyramid as in 12.3. In ABCG bisect AB, BC, CA at K, O, L and GA, GB, GC at P, M, N; then ABCG is divided into the two pyramids AKLP and GPMN, equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, namely the prism I whose base is the parallelogram KBOL and whose opposite edge is PM, and the prism II whose base is the triangle LOC and whose opposite face is the triangle PMN (12.3). Likewise in DEFH bisect DE, EF, FD at Q, V, R and HD, HE, HF at S, T, U; then DEFH is divided into two pyramids and into two equal prisms, the prism I' with base the parallelogram QEVR and opposite edge ST, and the prism II' with base the triangle RVF and opposite face the triangle STU (12.3). I say that, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so are the prisms I and II together to the prisms I' and II' together.

**Step 2.** Since CL = LA and CO = OB, the ratios CL : LA and CO : OB are each the ratio of a magnitude to an equal magnitude and are therefore the same ratio (D5.5); thus the sides CA, CB of the triangle ABC are cut proportionally at L and O, and LO is parallel to AB (6.2). For the same reason RV is parallel to DE.

**Step 3.** Since LO is parallel to AB, the angle CLO is equal to the angle CAB and the angle COL to the angle CBA (1.29), and the angle at C is common; so the triangle LOC is equiangular with the triangle ABC, and the sides about the equal angles are proportional (6.4). Therefore the triangle LOC is similar to the triangle ABC (D6.1), C corresponding to C, O to B and L to A, so that LOC and ABC are similarly described upon CO and CB. In the same way the triangle RVF is similar to the triangle DEF and similarly described upon FV and FE.

**Step 4.** BC is double of CO, and EF is double of FV. Since parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order, CO : FV = BC : EF (5.15); and alternately CO : BC = FV : EF (5.16).

**Step 5.** The four straight lines CO, BC, FV, EF are thus proportional; on CO and BC are described the similar and similarly situated triangles LOC and ABC, and on FV and EF the similar and similarly situated triangles RVF and DEF. Therefore triangle LOC : triangle ABC = triangle RVF : triangle DEF (6.22), and alternately triangle LOC : triangle RVF = triangle ABC : triangle DEF (5.16).

**Step 6.** [Lemma: the prisms II and II' are to one another as the triangles LOC and RVF.] First, the prisms II and II' are of the same height. The triangles LOC and PMN are the two opposite faces of the prism II, so the plane PMN is parallel to the plane ABC (D11.13). The two straight lines GC and GZ drawn from G are cut by the parallel planes PMN and ABC, GC at N and C, and GZ at the point Y in which it meets the plane PMN and at Z; therefore GN : NC = GY : YZ (11.17). But GN = NC; therefore GY = YZ (D5.5). Hence YZ, the perpendicular from the point Y of the face PMN to the plane ABC, which is the height of the prism II, is half of GZ. In the same way the height Y'Z' of the prism II', cut off from HZ' by the plane STU, is half of HZ'. Since GZ = HZ', their halves YZ and Y'Z' are equal; so the prisms II and II' are of the same height.

**Step 7.** Through L draw LX parallel to CO and through O draw OX parallel to CL (1.31), meeting at X, so that LCOX is a parallelogram; and in the plane PMN draw PX' parallel to NM and MX' parallel to NP (1.31), meeting at X', so that PNMX' is a parallelogram. This completes the parallelepipedal solid LCOX-PNMX', which has the parallelogram LCOX in the plane ABC as base and PNMX' in the parallel plane PMN as opposite face, and is therefore of the same height YZ as the prism II. The plane PMOL passes through the diagonals LO and PM of the opposite faces LCOX and PNMX'; therefore it bisects the solid (11.28), and the prism II, being one of the two halves, is half of the solid, so that the solid is double of the prism II. Similarly complete the parallelepipedal solid RFVW-SUTW' upon the prism II', of height Y'Z', which is bisected by the plane STVR, so that it is double of the prism II'.

**Step 8.** Parallelepipedal solids which are of the same height are to one another as their bases (11.32); therefore solid LCOX-PNMX' : solid RFVW-SUTW' = parallelogram LCOX : parallelogram RFVW.

**Step 9.** The parallelogram LCOX is bisected by its diameter LO (1.34) and is therefore double of the triangle LOC; likewise the parallelogram RFVW is double of the triangle RVF. Hence triangle LOC : triangle RVF = parallelogram LCOX : parallelogram RFVW (5.15). Again, since the solids are doubles of the prisms II and II' (Step 7), prism II : prism II' = solid LCOX-PNMX' : solid RFVW-SUTW' (5.15). Therefore prism II : prism II' = parallelogram LCOX : parallelogram RFVW = triangle LOC : triangle RVF (5.11), which proves the lemma.

**Step 10.** From Steps 5 and 9, triangle ABC : triangle DEF = triangle LOC : triangle RVF = prism II : prism II' (5.11).

**Step 11.** The prism I is equal to the prism II, and the prism I' to the prism II' (12.3). Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same, and the same has the same ratio to equal magnitudes (5.7); hence prism I : prism II' = prism II : prism II', and prism I : prism I' = prism I : prism II'; therefore prism I : prism I' = prism II : prism II' (5.11).

**Step 12.** Thus prism II : prism II' = prism I : prism I' (Step 11); and since these magnitudes are proportional, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents (5.12): (prism II together with prism I) : (prism II' together with prism I') = prism II : prism II' = triangle ABC : triangle DEF (Step 10, 5.11). Therefore, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so are all the prisms in the pyramid ABCG to all the prisms, equal in multitude, in the pyramid DEFH. Q.E.D.

The bisection of the perpendicular GZ by the plane PMN is taken from 11.17; it could equally be derived from 11.16 together with 6.2 in the plane GCZ.

## Proposition 12.5
**Statement:** Pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as the bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be two pyramids of the same height with triangular bases ABC and DEF and vertices G and H respectively. We must show that as base ABC is to base DEF, so is pyramid ABCG to pyramid DEFH.

**Step 2.** Suppose that pyramid ABCG is not to pyramid DEFH as base ABC is to base DEF. Let W be the solid which is the fourth proportional to base ABC, base DEF and pyramid ABCG, so that base ABC : base DEF = pyramid ABCG : W. Then W is not equal to pyramid DEFH, and is therefore either less than or greater than pyramid DEFH.

**Step 3.** First let W be less than pyramid DEFH. By 12.3, pyramid DEFH is divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, and by 12.3 the two prisms are together greater than half of pyramid DEFH. Divide each of the two pyramids so produced in the same way; the prisms cut off from them are together greater than half of the two pyramids together. Continue this process.

**Step 4.** Pyramid DEFH and the excess by which pyramid DEFH exceeds W are two unequal magnitudes, and from the greater, pyramid DEFH, there is continually subtracted a magnitude greater than its half (the prisms produced at each stage), leaving the pyramids produced at that stage. Therefore, by 10.1, the process may be continued until the pyramids left over are together less than the excess by which pyramid DEFH exceeds W. Let this have been done, and let DQRS, STUH stand for the pyramids so left over.

**Step 5.** Pyramid DEFH consists of all the prisms in it together with the pyramids left over, and the pyramids left over are less than the excess of pyramid DEFH over W. Therefore the prisms in pyramid DEFH are together greater than the solid W.

**Step 6.** Divide pyramid ABCG in the same manner and the same number of times as pyramid DEFH has been divided. Since the two pyramids have the same height and triangular bases, 12.4 gives base ABC : base DEF = (all the prisms in pyramid ABCG) : (all the prisms in pyramid DEFH), the prisms being equal in multitude.

**Step 7.** But base ABC : base DEF = pyramid ABCG : W (Step 2). Therefore, by 5.11, pyramid ABCG : W = (prisms in pyramid ABCG) : (prisms in pyramid DEFH).

**Step 8.** Pyramid ABCG is greater than the prisms in it, the whole being greater than the part (CN5). Hence in the proportion of Step 7 the first magnitude exceeds the third, so by 5.14 the second exceeds the fourth: W is greater than the prisms in pyramid DEFH.

**Step 9.** But by Step 5, W is less than the prisms in pyramid DEFH; which is impossible. Therefore base ABC is not to base DEF as pyramid ABCG is to any solid less than pyramid DEFH.

**Step 10.** In exactly the same way, interchanging the roles of the two pyramids, it is proved that base DEF is not to base ABC as pyramid DEFH is to any solid less than pyramid ABCG.

**Step 11.** Next let W be greater than pyramid DEFH, where base ABC : base DEF = pyramid ABCG : W. Then inversely, by the Porism to 5.7, base DEF : base ABC = W : pyramid ABCG.

**Step 12.** Since W is greater than pyramid DEFH, by the Lemma to 12.2 (whose argument applies equally to solids), as W is to pyramid ABCG, so is pyramid DEFH to some solid X less than pyramid ABCG.

**Step 13.** Therefore, by 5.11, base DEF : base ABC = pyramid DEFH : X, where X is less than pyramid ABCG. But this was shown to be impossible in Step 10. Therefore base ABC is not to base DEF as pyramid ABCG is to any solid greater than pyramid DEFH.

**Step 14.** Since W is neither less than nor greater than pyramid DEFH, W is equal to pyramid DEFH, and therefore base ABC : base DEF = pyramid ABCG : pyramid DEFH. Hence pyramids of the same height with triangular bases are to one another as their bases. Q.E.D.

Path note: in Step 8 the inequality is drawn directly from the proportion of Step 7 by 5.14 (first > third gives second > fourth), which is more direct than first alternating by 5.16; alternation is therefore not used.

## Proposition 12.6
**Statement:** Pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be two pyramids of the same height, the one with the polygonal base ABCDE and vertex M, the other with the polygonal base FGHKL and vertex N. I say that, as the base ABCDE is to the base FGHKL, so is the pyramid ABCDEM to the pyramid FGHKLN.

**Step 2.** Join AC, AD, FH, FK [P1]. The polygon ABCDE is thereby divided into the triangles ABC, ACD, ADE, and the polygon FGHKL into the triangles FGH, FHK, FKL. (If the bases have more sides, join further diagonals from A and from F in the same way; the argument below is then repeated once for each additional triangle.)

**Step 3.** The solid constructed from the triangle ABC to the point M is a pyramid with triangular base [D11.12]; call it ABCM. Likewise ACDM, ADEM are pyramids with vertex M, and FGHN, FHKN, FKLN are pyramids with vertex N. The planes MAC, MAD cut the pyramid ABCDEM into the three pyramids ABCM, ACDM, ADEM, and the planes NFH, NFK cut the pyramid FGHKLN into the three pyramids FGHN, FHKN, FKLN; so each polygonal pyramid is the whole made up of its triangular pyramids, just as each polygonal base is the whole made up of its triangles.

**Step 4.** The height of a pyramid is the perpendicular drawn from its vertex to its base [D6.4]. The bases ABC, ACD, ADE all lie in the plane of ABCDE, and the pyramids ABCM, ACDM, ADEM all have the same vertex M; hence their height is one and the same perpendicular from M to that plane, namely the height of the pyramid ABCDEM. Similarly FGHN, FHKN, FKLN all have the height of FGHKLN. Since the pyramids ABCDEM and FGHKLN are of the same height by hypothesis, all six triangular pyramids are of the same height.

**Step 5.** Since ABCM and ACDM are pyramids of the same height with triangular bases, as the base ABC is to the base ACD, so is the pyramid ABCM to the pyramid ACDM [12.5].

**Step 6.** Componendo, as the base ABC together with ACD, that is the quadrilateral ABCD, is to the base ACD, so is the pyramid ABCM together with ACDM, that is the pyramid ABCDM, to the pyramid ACDM [5.18].

**Step 7.** Again, since ACDM and ADEM are pyramids of the same height with triangular bases, as the base ACD is to the base ADE, so is the pyramid ACDM to the pyramid ADEM [12.5].

**Step 8.** From Steps 6 and 7, ex aequali, as the base ABCD is to the base ADE, so is the pyramid ABCDM to the pyramid ADEM [5.22].

**Step 9.** Componendo, as the base ABCD together with ADE, that is the whole base ABCDE, is to the base ADE, so is the pyramid ABCDM together with ADEM, that is the whole pyramid ABCDEM, to the pyramid ADEM [5.18]. Thus, as the base ABCDE is to the triangle ADE, so is the pyramid ABCDEM to the pyramid ADEM.

**Step 10.** In the same manner, applying 12.5 to the pairs FKLN, FHKN and FHKN, FGHN, then 5.18 and 5.22 as in Steps 5 to 9, it is shown that, as the base FGHKL is to the triangle FGH, so is the pyramid FGHKLN to the pyramid FGHN.

**Step 11.** Inversely, as the triangle FGH is to the base FGHKL, so is the pyramid FGHN to the pyramid FGHKLN [5.7 Por.].

**Step 12.** Since ADEM and FGHN are pyramids of the same height (Step 4) with triangular bases, as the triangle ADE is to the triangle FGH, so is the pyramid ADEM to the pyramid FGHN [12.5].

**Step 13.** From Steps 9 and 12, ex aequali, as the base ABCDE is to the triangle FGH, so is the pyramid ABCDEM to the pyramid FGHN [5.22].

**Step 14.** From Steps 13 and 11, ex aequali, as the base ABCDE is to the base FGHKL, so is the pyramid ABCDEM to the pyramid FGHKLN [5.22].

**Step 15.** Therefore pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.7
**Statement:** Any prism which has a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another which have triangular bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be a prism whose base is the triangle ABC and whose opposite face is the triangle DEF, the vertices D, E, F lying opposite to A, B, C respectively. By the definition of a prism [D11.13], the two faces ABC and DEF are equal, similar and parallel, and the remaining three faces ABED, BCFE, ACFD are parallelograms.

**Step 2.** Join the straight lines BD, EC and CD [P1].

**Step 3.** Since the points B, D, C are not in one straight line, the triangle BDC lies in one plane, and likewise the triangle DEC lies in one plane [11.2]. The plane BDC cuts the prism into two solids. On one side is the solid contained by the four triangles ABD, ABC, ACD, BDC; it is constructed from the plane of the triangle ABD to the one point C, and is therefore a pyramid with triangular base ABD and vertex C [D11.12]. On the other side is the solid contained by the parallelogram BCFE and the triangles DBE, DCF, DEF, DBC. The plane DEC cuts this second solid into the solid contained by the triangles DBE, DBC, DCE, BCE, which is a pyramid with triangular base BCE and vertex D [D11.12], and the solid contained by the triangles DCE, DCF, DEF, CEF, which is a pyramid with triangular base CEF and vertex D [D11.12]. Thus the prism is divided into three pyramids having triangular bases, namely the pyramids ABDC, DBCE and DCEF.

**Step 4.** Since ABED is a parallelogram and BD is its diameter, the diameter bisects it; therefore the triangle ABD is equal to the triangle EBD [1.34].

**Step 5.** The pyramid with base ABD and vertex C and the pyramid with base DEB and vertex C have the same vertex C, and their bases lie in one and the same plane, that of the parallelogram ABED; hence they are of the same height. But pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as their bases [12.5]; and the bases ABD and DEB are equal (Step 4). Therefore the pyramid with base ABD and vertex C is equal to the pyramid with base DEB and vertex C.

**Step 6.** But the pyramid with base DEB and vertex C is the same solid as the pyramid with base BCE and vertex D, for each is the solid contained by the four triangles DEB, EBC, BCD, CDE. Therefore the pyramid ABDC is equal to the pyramid DBCE.

**Step 7.** Again, since BCFE is a parallelogram and CE is its diameter, the triangle CEF is equal to the triangle CBE [1.34].

**Step 8.** The pyramid with base BCE and vertex D and the pyramid with base CEF and vertex D have the same vertex D, and their bases lie in one and the same plane, that of the parallelogram BCFE; hence they are of the same height. Being of the same height with triangular bases, they are to one another as their bases [12.5]; and the bases BCE and CEF are equal (Step 7). Therefore the pyramid DBCE is equal to the pyramid DCEF.

**Step 9.** Now the pyramid ABDC is equal to the pyramid DBCE (Step 6), and the pyramid DCEF is equal to the same pyramid DBCE (Step 8); therefore the pyramid ABDC is also equal to the pyramid DCEF [CN1]. Hence the three pyramids ABDC, DBCE, DCEF are equal to one another.

**Step 10.** Therefore the prism with the triangular base ABC and the opposite face DEF is divided into three pyramids equal to one another, each having a triangular base: the pyramid ABDC on the base ABD, the pyramid DBCE on the base BCE, and the pyramid DCEF on the base CEF (which may equally be regarded as the pyramid having for base the triangle DEF, the face opposite the base of the prism, and vertex C). Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.8
**Statement:** Similar pyramids which have triangular bases are in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.

**Step 1.** Let ABCG and DEFH be similar pyramids with triangular bases ABC, DEF and vertices G, H, the vertices A, B, C, G corresponding to D, E, F, H respectively, so that BC and EF are corresponding sides. I say that the pyramid ABCG has to the pyramid DEFH the ratio triplicate of that which BC has to EF.

**Step 2.** Since the pyramids are similar, they are contained by similar planes equal in multitude (D11.9); thus the triangle ABC is similar to the triangle DEF, the triangle GBC to the triangle HEF, and the triangle ABG to the triangle DEH. Therefore, by the definition of similar rectilineal figures (D6.1), the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF, the angle CBG to the angle FEH, and the angle ABG to the angle DEH; and the sides about these equal angles are proportional: as AB is to BC, so is DE to EF; as BC is to BG, so is EF to EH; and as AB is to BG, so is DE to EH.

**Step 3.** Through A draw AK parallel to BC and through C draw CK parallel to BA (1.31), so that BAKC is a parallelogram on the sides BA, BC; in the same manner complete the parallelogram BCMG on BC, BG and the parallelogram BGNA on BG, BA; and let the parallelepipedal solid BL be completed, having these three parallelograms about the solid angle at B and L as the vertex opposite B, so that its remaining faces are the parallelograms GNLM, AKLN, CMLK, opposite to BAKC, BCMG, BGNA respectively. Likewise complete the parallelograms EDPF on ED, EF; EFQH on EF, EH; EHRD on EH, ED; and the parallelepipedal solid EO with O the vertex opposite E, whose remaining faces are HROQ, DPOR, FQOP, opposite to EDPF, EFQH, EHRD respectively.

**Step 4.** The parallelogram BAKC is similar to the parallelogram EDPF. For the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF (Step 2). The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal (1.34), so the angle AKC is equal to the angle ABC and the angle DPF to the angle DEF; hence the angle AKC is equal to the angle DPF (CN1). Again, since AK is parallel to BC and BA falls upon them, the interior angles BAK, ABC are together equal to two right angles (1.29); likewise the angles EDP, DEF are together equal to two right angles; and the angles ABC, DEF being equal, the angle BAK is equal to the angle EDP (CN3). In the same way the angle BCK is equal to the angle EFP. Thus the two parallelograms have their angles severally equal. Moreover, as AB is to BC, so is DE to EF (Step 2), and the opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal (1.34), AK being equal to BC, KC to BA, DP to EF and PF to ED; hence the sides about all the equal angles are proportional. Therefore the parallelogram BAKC is similar to the parallelogram EDPF (D6.1).

**Step 5.** For the same reason, since the angle CBG is equal to the angle FEH and as BC is to BG so is EF to EH, the parallelogram BCMG is similar to the parallelogram EFQH; and since the angle ABG is equal to the angle DEH and as AB is to BG so is DE to EH, the parallelogram BGNA is similar to the parallelogram EHRD.

**Step 6.** Now the opposite planes of a parallelepipedal solid are equal and similar parallelograms (11.24). Therefore GNLM is equal and similar to BAKC, AKLN to BCMG, and CMLK to BGNA; and HROQ is equal and similar to EDPF, DPOR to EFQH, and FQOP to EHRD. Since figures which are similar to the same rectilineal figure are also similar to one another (6.21), GNLM is similar to EDPF, and hence to HROQ; and likewise AKLN is similar to DPOR, and CMLK to FQOP.

**Step 7.** Therefore the six faces of the solid BL are severally similar to the six faces of the solid EO; that is, the solids BL, EO are contained by similar planes equal in multitude, so that the solid BL is similar to the solid EO (D11.9); and BC, EF are corresponding sides of them, being the sides about the equal angles ABC, DEF in the similar faces BAKC, EDPF.

**Step 8.** But similar parallelepipedal solids are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides (11.33). Therefore the solid BL has to the solid EO the ratio triplicate of that which BC has to EF.

**Step 9.** Next, the solid BL is cut by the plane through AC and NM, the diagonals of the opposite faces BAKC, GNLM; and a parallelepipedal solid cut by a plane through the diagonals of opposite planes is bisected by that plane (11.28), the two halves being prisms with triangular bases. One of these halves is the prism having the triangle ABC as base and the triangle NGM as the opposite face, with AN, BG, CM as its parallel edges. Therefore the solid BL is double of this prism.

**Step 10.** Again, any prism with a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another with triangular bases, so that a pyramid is a third part of the prism which has the same base and equal height with it (12.7). The pyramid ABCG has the same base ABC as this prism, and its vertex G lies in the face NGM opposite the base, so that it has the same height as the prism; hence the prism is triple of the pyramid ABCG. Consequently the solid BL is six times the pyramid ABCG.

**Step 11.** In the same way the solid EO is bisected by the plane through DF and RQ, the diagonals of the opposite faces EDPF, HROQ, into two equal prisms (11.28), one of which has the triangle DEF as base and the triangle RHQ as the opposite face; and the pyramid DEFH, having the same base DEF and the same height as this prism, is a third part of it (12.7). Therefore the solid EO is six times the pyramid DEFH.

**Step 12.** Thus the solids BL, EO are the same multiples, namely sextuples, of the pyramids ABCG, DEFH respectively; and parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order (5.15). Therefore, as the pyramid ABCG is to the pyramid DEFH, so is the solid BL to the solid EO.

**Step 13.** But the solid BL has to the solid EO the ratio triplicate of that which BC has to EF (Step 8); and ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another (5.11). Therefore the pyramid ABCG also has to the pyramid DEFH the ratio triplicate of that which the corresponding side BC has to the corresponding side EF. Hence similar pyramids which have triangular bases are in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides. Q.E.D.
