## Proposition 12.9
**Statement:** In equal pyramids which have triangular bases the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those pyramids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let ABCG and DEFH be two pyramids having the triangular bases ABC, DEF and the vertices G, H. First let the pyramids be equal. I say that, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so is the height of the pyramid DEFH to the height of the pyramid ABCG.

**Step 2.** Through A draw a straight line parallel to BC, and through C a straight line parallel to BA [1.31], and let them meet at M; then ABCM is a parallelogram of which AC is a diameter. In the same way, through D draw a straight line parallel to EF and through F a straight line parallel to ED [1.31], meeting at Q; then DEFQ is a parallelogram of which DF is a diameter. Since the diameter bisects a parallelogram [1.34], the parallelogram ABCM is double the triangle ABC, and the parallelogram DEFQ is double the triangle DEF.

**Step 3.** Through G draw GK parallel to BA and GN parallel to BC [1.31]. Since GK, GN meet one another at G and are parallel to BA, BC, which meet one another at B, and G is not in the plane of ABC (being the vertex of the pyramid), the plane through GK, GN is parallel to the plane through BA, BC, that is, to the plane of the parallelogram ABCM [11.15]. Let the parallelepipedal solid BL be completed, having the parallelogram ABCM as base, BG as an edge, and as the face opposite to the base the parallelogram KGNL lying in the plane through G just described, K, N, L being the vertices over A, C, M respectively (so that AK, CN, ML are parallel to BG). In the same way let the parallelepipedal solid ER be completed, having the parallelogram DEFQ as base, EH as an edge, and as the face opposite to the base the parallelogram OHPR through H, with O, P, R the vertices over D, F, Q.

**Step 4.** The height of the pyramid ABCG is the perpendicular drawn from its vertex G to the plane of its base ABC [D6.4]. The height of the parallelepipedal solid BL is the perpendicular drawn from a vertex of the face KGNL to the plane of the base ABCM; G is such a vertex, and the plane of ABCM is the plane of ABC. Therefore the solid BL has the same height as the pyramid ABCG. In the same way the solid ER has the same height as the pyramid DEFH, namely the perpendicular from H to the plane of DEF.

**Step 5.** The straight lines AC, KN are diagonals of the opposite faces ABCM, KGNL of the solid BL; hence the plane through AC, KN bisects the solid BL [11.28], dividing it into two equal prisms, one of which is the prism having the triangle ABC as base and the triangle KGN as its opposite face. Therefore the solid BL is double this prism. Again, this prism, having a triangular base, is divided into three pyramids equal to one another having triangular bases, one of which is the pyramid having the base ABC and for vertex the point G of the opposite face, that is, the pyramid ABCG [12.7]; therefore the prism is triple the pyramid ABCG. Consequently the solid BL is six times the pyramid ABCG. In the same way the solid ER is six times the pyramid DEFH.

**Step 6.** Now the pyramid ABCG is equal to the pyramid DEFH; hence six magnitudes each equal to the pyramid ABCG are together equal to six magnitudes each equal to the pyramid DEFH [CN2]. But the solid BL is equal to the former and the solid ER to the latter (Step 5); therefore the solid BL is equal to the solid ER [CN1].

**Step 7.** But in equal parallelepipedal solids the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights [11.34]; therefore, as the base ABCM is to the base DEFQ, so is the height of the solid ER to the height of the solid BL.

**Step 8.** Since the parallelogram ABCM is double the triangle ABC and the parallelogram DEFQ is double the triangle DEF (Step 2), the triangle ABC is to the triangle DEF as the parallelogram ABCM is to the parallelogram DEFQ [5.15]. Therefore the triangle ABC is to the triangle DEF as the height of the solid ER is to the height of the solid BL [5.11].

**Step 9.** But the height of the solid ER is the height of the pyramid DEFH, and the height of the solid BL is the height of the pyramid ABCG (Step 4). Therefore, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so is the height of the pyramid DEFH to the height of the pyramid ABCG; that is, in the equal pyramids ABCG, DEFH the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights.

**Step 10.** Next, let the bases of the pyramids ABCG, DEFH be reciprocally proportional to the heights, so that, as the base ABC is to the base DEF, so is the height of the pyramid DEFH to the height of the pyramid ABCG. I say that the pyramid ABCG is equal to the pyramid DEFH. With the same construction (Steps 2, 3), the parallelograms ABCM, DEFQ are double the triangles ABC, DEF, the solids BL, ER have the same heights as the pyramids ABCG, DEFH (Step 4), and the solids BL, ER are six times the pyramids ABCG, DEFH respectively (Step 5).

**Step 11.** As the parallelogram ABCM is to the parallelogram DEFQ, so is the triangle ABC to the triangle DEF [5.15], and, by hypothesis, so is the height of the pyramid DEFH to the height of the pyramid ABCG, that is, the height of the solid ER to the height of the solid BL. Therefore, as the base ABCM is to the base DEFQ, so is the height of the solid ER to the height of the solid BL [5.11].

**Step 12.** Thus the bases of the parallelepipedal solids BL, ER are reciprocally proportional to their heights; but parallelepipedal solids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal [11.34]. Therefore the solid BL is equal to the solid ER.

**Step 13.** Now the solid BL is six times the pyramid ABCG and the solid ER is six times the pyramid DEFH; the solids being the same multiples of the pyramids, the pyramid ABCG is to the pyramid DEFH as the solid BL is to the solid ER [5.15]. But the solid BL is equal to the solid ER; hence the solid BL is to the solid ER as the solid ER is to the solid ER [5.7]; and the solid ER is to the solid ER as the pyramid DEFH is to the pyramid DEFH [5.15]. Therefore the pyramid ABCG is to the pyramid DEFH as the pyramid DEFH is to the pyramid DEFH [5.11].

**Step 14.** The pyramids ABCG, DEFH thus have the same ratio to the same magnitude, the pyramid DEFH; therefore the pyramid ABCG is equal to the pyramid DEFH [5.9].

**Step 15.** Therefore in equal pyramids which have triangular bases the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those pyramids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.10
**Statement:** Any cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height.

**Step 1.** Let the cone have for its base the circle ABCD, with centre O, and for its vertex the point L, so that LO is its axis and is at right angles to the plane of the circle [D11.18]; and let the cylinder have the same circle ABCD for its base and the same height as the cone [D11.21], so that its other base lies in the plane drawn through L parallel to the plane of the circle. I say that the cylinder is triple of the cone, that is, that the cone is a third part of the cylinder. For, if the cylinder is not triple of the cone, it is either greater than triple or less than triple of the cone. Before treating the two cases, some constructions are made in the plane of the circle (Steps 2–7).

**Step 2.** Draw two diameters AC, BD of the circle at right angles to one another and join AB, BC, CD, DA; then ABCD is a square inscribed in the circle [4.6]. Through A, B, C, D draw the tangents to the circle; they form a square PQRS circumscribed about the circle, P being the corner between the tangents at A and B, Q that between the tangents at B and C, and so on [4.7]. In that construction the tangent at A is shown to be parallel to BD and the tangent at B parallel to AC, so that OAPB is a parallelogram; likewise OBQC, OCRD, ODSA are parallelograms.

**Step 3.** The parallelogram OAPB is bisected by its diameter AB, so that the triangle OAB is half of OAPB [1.34]; in the same way the triangles OBC, OCD, ODA are halves of OBQC, OCRD, ODSA. Now the four triangles OAB, OBC, OCD, ODA make up the square ABCD, and the four parallelograms OAPB, OBQC, OCRD, ODSA make up the square PQRS; therefore the square ABCD is half of the square PQRS. Moreover the sides of PQRS touch the circle and do not cut it [D3.2], so the circle ABCD lies wholly within the square PQRS.

**Step 4.** Bisect the arcs AB, BC, CD, DA at the points E, F, G, H [3.30] and join AE, EB, BF, FC, CG, GD, DH, HA [P1]. By the construction of 3.30, E lies on the straight line drawn at right angles to AB from its middle point N, so that AN = NB and the angles ANE, BNE are right. Since NE cuts the chord AB into two equal parts and at right angles, the centre O lies on the straight line NE [3.1, Por.]; hence the straight line through E and O is a diameter of the circle having E as an extremity.

**Step 5.** Through E draw MK parallel to AB [1.31]. The straight line NE falls on the parallels AB, MK, so the interior angles on the same side, ANE and NEM, are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; as the angle ANE is right, the angle NEM is right. Thus MK is drawn at right angles to the diameter EO from its extremity E, and therefore MK touches the circle at E [3.16, Por.] and does not cut it [D3.2]. Through A and B draw AM, BK parallel to NE [1.31], meeting MK at M and K. Then ANEM and NBKE are parallelograms (each having its opposite sides parallel), and together they make up the quadrilateral ABKM. Since MK touches the circle at E without cutting it, the arc AEB lies between the chord AB and the line MK; so the segment AEB of the circle cut off by the chord AB lies wholly within the quadrilateral ABKM.

**Step 6.** The parallelogram ANEM is bisected by its diameter AE and the parallelogram NBKE by its diameter EB [1.34]; hence the triangle ANE equals the triangle AME, and the triangle NBE equals the triangle EKB. Adding, the triangle AEB, which is made up of ANE and NBE, equals the triangles AME and EKB together [CN2]; and these two triangles together with AEB make up the whole quadrilateral ABKM. Therefore the quadrilateral ABKM is double of the triangle AEB. Making the same construction on BC, CD, DA, we obtain quadrilaterals on BC, CD, DA which are respectively double of the triangles BFC, CGD, DHA and which enclose the segments of the circle about BC, CD, DA. The same holds whenever any arc is bisected and the triangle on its chord is formed, as will be done repeatedly below.

**Step 7.** Consider the polygon AEBFCGDH inscribed in the circle (what follows applies equally to any polygon inscribed in the circle by continued bisection of arcs). Join OA, OE, OB, OF, OC, OG, OD, OH [P1]; these divide the polygon into the eight triangles OAE, OEB, OBF, OFC, OCG, OGD, ODH, OHA. Let a prism be set up on the polygon with height equal to that of the cylinder, its lateral faces lying in the planes through the sides of the polygon parallel to the axis LO and its upper face in the plane of the upper base of the cylinder; and let a pyramid be set up on the polygon with vertex L. The planes through the axis LO and the points A, E, B, F, C, G, D, H divide the prism into eight prisms on the eight triangles, each of height equal to the cylinder, and divide the pyramid into eight pyramids on the same triangles, each with vertex L and therefore of the same height. Each of these prisms is triple of the pyramid which has the same triangular base and equal height [12.7, Por.]; therefore all the prisms together, which make up the prism on the polygon, are triple of all the pyramids together, which make up the pyramid on the polygon [5.1]. That is, the prism on the polygon AEBFCGDH with height equal to the cylinder is triple of the pyramid on the same polygon with vertex L. Further, the base of the prism lies within the circle and its height equals that of the cylinder, so the prism is enclosed by the cylinder and is less than it [CN5]; and the base of the pyramid lies within the circle and its vertex is L, so the pyramid is enclosed by the cone and is less than it [CN5].

**Step 8.** First suppose, if possible, that the cylinder is greater than triple of the cone, and let X be the excess by which the cylinder exceeds triple of the cone. On the square ABCD and on the square PQRS set up parallelepipedal solids of height equal to the cylinder, their lateral edges parallel to the axis and their upper faces in the plane of the upper base of the cylinder. Parallelepipedal solids of the same height are to one another as their bases [11.32]; and the square ABCD is half of the square PQRS (Step 3); therefore the solid on ABCD is half of the solid on PQRS. But the circle lies within PQRS (Step 3) and the heights are the same, so the cylinder is enclosed by the solid on PQRS and is less than it [CN5]. Hence the solid on ABCD, the prism on the square ABCD of height equal to the cylinder, is greater than half of the cylinder.

**Step 9.** When the prism on ABCD is taken away from the cylinder, there remain the four segments of the cylinder about AB, BC, CD, DA, namely the parts of the cylinder cut off by the planes through AB, BC, CD, DA parallel to the axis. On the triangles AEB, BFC, CGD, DHA set up prisms of height equal to the cylinder, and on the parallelograms ANEM, NBKE (and on the corresponding parallelograms on BC, CD, DA) set up parallelepipedal solids of the same height. The solid on ANEM is cut by the plane through AE and the diagonal of the opposite face, and is bisected by that plane [11.28]; therefore the prism on ANE equals the prism on AME. In the same way the solid on NBKE is bisected by the plane through EB and the diagonal of the opposite face, so that the prism on NBE equals the prism on EKB. Adding, the prism on AEB, which is made up of the prisms on ANE and NBE, equals the prisms on AME and EKB together [CN2]; and these together with the prism on AEB make up the whole solid on ABKM, that is, the solid composed of the solids on ANEM and NBKE. Therefore the prism on AEB is half of the solid on ABKM.

**Step 10.** The segment of the circle about AB lies within ABKM (Step 5) and the heights are equal, so the segment of the cylinder about AB is enclosed by the solid on ABKM and is less than it [CN5]; hence the prism on AEB, being half of the solid on ABKM, is greater than half of the segment of the cylinder about AB. Likewise the prisms on BFC, CGD, DHA are greater than half of the segments of the cylinder about BC, CD, DA respectively; so the four prisms together are greater than half of the four segments together, that is, greater than half of what was left of the cylinder.

**Step 11.** Thus from the cylinder there has been taken a magnitude greater than its half, and from the remainder a magnitude greater than its half. Bisecting the arcs that are left, joining the chords, setting up on the triangles so formed prisms of height equal to the cylinder (each of which is greater than half of the segment of the cylinder about it, by the argument of Steps 9–10), and continuing in this way, we shall at last leave some segments of the cylinder which together are less than the excess X [10.1]. Let the process be stopped at such a stage, and for definiteness let the polygon then inscribed be AEBFCGDH (the reasoning is the same for the polygon of any stage), so that the segments left are those about AE, EB, BF, FC, CG, GD, DH, HA. What remains of the cylinder when these segments are taken away is the prism on the polygon AEBFCGDH with height equal to the cylinder. Since the cylinder exceeds triple of the cone by X, and the segments taken away are together less than X, this prism is greater than triple of the cone.

**Step 12.** But the prism on AEBFCGDH with height equal to the cylinder is triple of the pyramid on AEBFCGDH with vertex L (Step 7). Therefore triple of that pyramid is greater than triple of the cone, and consequently the pyramid on AEBFCGDH with vertex L is greater than the cone. But this pyramid is enclosed by the cone and is less than it (Step 7) [CN5]: which is impossible. Therefore the cylinder is not greater than triple of the cone.

**Step 13.** Next suppose, if possible, that the cylinder is less than triple of the cone. Then the cone is greater than a third part of the cylinder; let Y be the excess by which the cone exceeds a third part of the cylinder. On the square ABCD and on the square PQRS set up pyramids with vertex L. These are pyramids of the same height (their common vertex L being at the same distance from the plane of their bases) with polygonal bases, and so are to one another as their bases [12.6]; since the square ABCD is half of PQRS (Step 3), the pyramid on ABCD is half of the pyramid on PQRS. But the circle lies within PQRS (Step 3), so the cone is enclosed by the pyramid on PQRS with vertex L and is less than it [CN5]. Hence the pyramid on ABCD with vertex L is greater than half of the cone.

**Step 14.** When this pyramid is taken away from the cone, there remain the four segments of the cone about AB, BC, CD, DA, namely the parts of the cone cut off by the planes through L and AB, BC, CD, DA. On the triangles AEB, BFC, CGD, DHA and on the quadrilateral ABKM (and the corresponding quadrilaterals on BC, CD, DA) set up pyramids with vertex L. The pyramids on AEB and on ABKM have the same height and are to one another as their bases [12.6]; since ABKM is double of AEB (Step 6), the pyramid on ABKM is double of the pyramid on AEB. But the segment of the circle about AB lies within ABKM (Step 5), so the segment of the cone about AB is enclosed by the pyramid on ABKM with vertex L and is less than it [CN5]. Hence the pyramid on AEB with vertex L is greater than half of the segment of the cone about AB. Likewise the pyramids on BFC, CGD, DHA are greater than half of the segments of the cone about BC, CD, DA; so the four pyramids together are greater than half of what was left of the cone.

**Step 15.** Thus from the cone there has been taken more than its half, and from the remainder more than its half. Bisecting the arcs that are left, joining the chords, setting up on the triangles so formed pyramids with vertex L (each greater than half of the segment of the cone about it, by the argument of Step 14), and continuing in this way, we shall at last leave some segments of the cone which together are less than the excess Y [10.1]. Let the polygon then inscribed be AEBFCGDH, so that the segments left are those about AE, EB, BF, FC, CG, GD, DH, HA. What remains of the cone when these segments are taken away is the pyramid on AEBFCGDH with vertex L. Since the cone exceeds a third part of the cylinder by Y, and the segments taken away are together less than Y, this pyramid is greater than a third part of the cylinder.

**Step 16.** But the pyramid on AEBFCGDH with vertex L is a third part of the prism on AEBFCGDH with height equal to the cylinder (Step 7). Therefore a third part of that prism is greater than a third part of the cylinder, and consequently the prism is greater than the cylinder. But the prism is enclosed by the cylinder and is less than it (Step 7) [CN5]: which is impossible. Therefore the cylinder is not less than triple of the cone.

**Step 17.** Since the cylinder is neither greater nor less than triple of the cone, it is triple of the cone. Therefore the cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height. Q.E.D.

Path note: the halving of the solids is obtained directly from 11.32 (parallelepipeds of the same height) and 11.28 (bisection of a parallelepiped by a diagonal plane) for the prisms, and from 12.6 for the pyramids; this is more direct than first deriving the general fact that prisms of the same height are as their bases from 12.7 and 12.6.

## Proposition 12.11
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be cones and cylinders of the same height, whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH [D11.20, D11.23]; let K, M be the centres of these circles, KL, MN the axes of the cones [D11.19], L, N their vertices, and AC, EG diameters of the bases; call the cones AL and EN, and let the cylinders be those standing on the bases ABCD, EFGH with the same height. Because the axis of a cone is the fixed side of the generating right-angled triangle and is at right angles to the side which describes the base [D11.18], the axes KL, MN are perpendicular to the planes of the bases and are the heights of the cones [D6.4]; by hypothesis these heights are equal. I say that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN, and so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH.

**Step 2.** Suppose the circle ABCD is not to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to the cone EN. Then let it be contrived that, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to some solid O, where O is not equal to the cone EN; O is therefore either less or greater than the cone EN.

**Step 3.** First let O be less than the cone EN, and let the solid X be the excess by which the cone EN exceeds O, so that the cone EN is equal to O and X together.

**Step 4.** Inscribe in the circle EFGH the square EFGH [4.6]; by that construction its diagonals EG, FH are diameters of the circle. Circumscribe about the circle a square [4.7]; each side of the circumscribed square is equal to the diameter of the circle [4.7], so the circumscribed square is equal to the square on EG. Since the angle EFG is right, the square on EG is equal to the squares on EF, FG together [1.47], and since EF is equal to FG this is double the square EFGH. Hence the square EFGH is half the circumscribed square. The circle lies within the circumscribed square, because each side of that square touches the circle without cutting it [D3.2]; so the circle is less than the circumscribed square [CN5]. Therefore the square EFGH is greater than half the circle EFGH.

**Step 5.** On the square EFGH set up a pyramid with vertex N, and on the circumscribed square set up a pyramid with vertex N. Their bases lie in the plane of the circle EFGH and they have the same vertex, so they have the same height, namely the perpendicular MN from N to that plane [D6.4]. Therefore the pyramid on EFGH is to the pyramid on the circumscribed square as the square EFGH is to the circumscribed square [12.6]; hence the pyramid on EFGH is half the pyramid on the circumscribed square. The cone EN lies within the pyramid on the circumscribed square, since its base lies within that square and it has the same vertex N; so the cone is less than that pyramid [CN5]. Therefore the pyramid with base EFGH and vertex N is greater than half the cone EN.

**Step 6.** Bisect the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE at the points P, Q, R, S [3.30], and join EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE [P1]. Consider the triangle EPF. By the construction of 3.30, P lies on the straight line drawn from the middle point J of EF at right angles to EF, and this straight line passes through the centre M of the circle [3.1 Por.], so that M, J, P are in one straight line. Draw through P the tangent to the circle [3.17]; it is at right angles to the straight line MP joining the centre to the point of contact [3.18]. Since EF and the tangent are both at right angles to the same straight line MJP, the tangent is parallel to EF [1.28]. Complete the parallelogram on the base EF whose opposite side lies on the tangent [1.31]. The triangle EPF has the same base EF as this parallelogram and lies in the same parallels, so the parallelogram is double the triangle EPF [1.41]. The segment EPF of the circle lies within the parallelogram, since the tangent does not enter the circle [D3.2]; so the segment is less than the parallelogram [CN5]. Therefore the triangle EPF is greater than half the segment EPF of the circle; and in the same way the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE are greater than half of the segments of the circle on which they stand.

**Step 7.** On the triangle EPF set up a pyramid with vertex N, and on the parallelogram of Step 6 set up a pyramid with vertex N; their bases lie in the plane of the circle and they have the same vertex, so they have the same height MN. Therefore the pyramid on EPF is to the pyramid on the parallelogram as the triangle EPF is to the parallelogram [12.6], so that the pyramid on EPF is half the pyramid on the parallelogram. The segment of the cone EN which stands on the segment EPF of the circle, that is, the part of the cone cut off by the plane through N, E, F, lies within the pyramid on the parallelogram, so it is less than that pyramid [CN5]. Therefore the pyramid with base EPF and vertex N is greater than half the segment of the cone standing on EPF; and similarly for the pyramids with vertex N on the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE.

**Step 8.** Thus the cone EN and the solid X are two unequal magnitudes, of which the cone is the greater. From the cone there has been subtracted the pyramid on the square EFGH, which is greater than its half, and from the remainder, namely the four segments of the cone, the four pyramids on the triangles, which are together greater than half of that remainder. Bisecting the remaining circumferences, joining straight lines, setting up on each triangle a pyramid with vertex N, and continuing in this way, we shall at length leave some segments of the cone EN which are together less than the solid X [10.1]. Let such segments have been left, and for definiteness let them be the segments of the cone standing on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE; then the pyramid with the polygon EPFQGRHS as base and vertex N, together with these segments, makes up the cone EN.

**Step 9.** The cone EN is equal to O together with X, and is also equal to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS together with the remaining segments; subtracting the segments from both, the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS is equal to O together with the excess of X over the segments [CN3], and this excess is a magnitude because the segments are less than X. Therefore the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N is greater than the solid O [CN5].

**Step 10.** Inscribe in the circle ABCD, by the same construction, the square ABCD [4.6] and bisect its circumferences the same number of times at U, V, W, Z [3.30], so obtaining the polygon AUBVCWDZ similar to the polygon EPFQGRHS; on it set up a pyramid with vertex L. The height of this pyramid is the perpendicular KL from L to the plane of the circle ABCD [D6.4], which is equal to MN; so the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L and the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N are of the same height.

**Step 11.** Since the polygons AUBVCWDZ, EPFQGRHS are similar and inscribed in the circles, the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS as the square on AC is to the square on EG [12.1]. But the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH as the square on AC is to the square on EG [12.2]. Therefore, as the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS, so is the circle ABCD to the circle EFGH [5.11].

**Step 12.** Since the two pyramids are of the same height and have polygonal bases, the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L is to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N as the polygon AUBVCWDZ is to the polygon EPFQGRHS [12.6], that is, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH [5.11]. But the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to the solid O (Step 2). Therefore, as the cone AL is to the solid O, so is the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L to the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N [5.11].

**Step 13.** In this proportion the first magnitude, the cone AL, is greater than the third, the pyramid with base AUBVCWDZ and vertex L, for that pyramid lies within the cone and is a part of it [CN5]. Therefore the second magnitude, the solid O, is greater than the fourth, the pyramid with base EPFQGRHS and vertex N [5.14]. But by Step 9 that pyramid is greater than O: which is impossible. Therefore the circle ABCD is not to the circle EFGH as the cone AL is to any solid less than the cone EN.

**Step 14.** In the same manner, interchanging the two cones in Steps 3 to 13, it is proved that the circle EFGH is not to the circle ABCD as the cone EN is to any solid less than the cone AL.

**Step 15.** Next let O be greater than the cone EN. Then, inversely, as the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD, so is the solid O to the cone AL [5.7 Por.]. Let it be contrived that, as the solid O is to the cone AL, so is the cone EN to some solid T. In this proportion the first magnitude, O, is greater than the third, the cone EN; therefore the second, the cone AL, is greater than the fourth, T [5.14]. Also, since the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD as O is to the cone AL, and O is to the cone AL as the cone EN is to T, the circle EFGH is to the circle ABCD as the cone EN is to T [5.11], where T is less than the cone AL: which is impossible by Step 14. Therefore O is not greater than the cone EN.

**Step 16.** Since O is neither less nor greater than the cone EN, it is equal to it. Therefore, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cone AL to the cone EN.

**Step 17.** Further, the cylinder on the base ABCD has the same base as the cone AL and equal height, so the cone AL is a third part of that cylinder, that is, the cylinder is triple the cone AL; and likewise the cylinder on the base EFGH is triple the cone EN [12.10]. Since the same multiples of magnitudes have the same ratio as the magnitudes themselves taken in corresponding order, as the cone AL is to the cone EN, so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH [5.15]. Therefore also, as the circle ABCD is to the circle EFGH, so is the cylinder on ABCD to the cylinder on EFGH [5.11].

**Step 18.** Therefore cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.12
**Statement:** Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.

**Step 1.** Let there be similar cones whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH with centres K, M and diameters BD, FH, whose axes are KL, MN, and whose vertices are L, N; call them the cones ABCDL and EFGHN. Since the cones are similar, their axes and the diameters of their bases are proportional (D11.24): BD : FH = KL : MN. I say that the cone ABCDL has to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of that which BD has to FH.

**Step 2.** Each cone is generated by a right-angled triangle turned about one of the sides containing the right angle; the side which remains fixed is the axis, and the other side about the right angle describes the base (D11.18, D11.19, D11.20). As the triangle turns, the moving side, which is always at right angles to the axis, takes the position of every radius of the base. Hence the axis KL is at right angles to every radius of the circle ABCD drawn from K, and MN to every radius of the circle EFGH drawn from M: the angles which KL makes with KA, KB, … and MN with ME, MF, … are right, and all these right angles are equal to one another (P4).

**Step 3.** Since K is the centre, KB = KD (D1.15), so that BD is double KB; likewise FH is double MF. Parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order (5.15), so KB : MF = BD : FH. But BD : FH = KL : MN (Step 1); therefore KB : MF = KL : MN (5.11), and, alternately, KB : KL = MF : MN (5.16). Every radius KX of the circle ABCD is equal to KB and every radius MY of the circle EFGH is equal to MF (D1.15), so KX : KL = KB : KL and MY : MN = MF : MN (5.7); hence for any radii KX, MY we have KX : KL = MY : MN (5.11).

**Step 4.** Suppose that the cone ABCDL has not to the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Then the cone ABCDL has that triplicate ratio to some solid O which is either less or greater than the cone EFGHN. First let O be less than the cone EFGHN.

**Step 5.** Inscribe in the circle EFGH the square EFGH (4.6) and circumscribe about the circle a square (4.7); by the construction of 4.7 each side of the circumscribed square is equal to the diameter FH, so the circumscribed square is the square on FH. In the inscribed square the angle FEH is right and EF = EH (D1.22), so the square on FH is equal to the squares on EF, EH together (1.47), that is, to double the square EFGH. Therefore the inscribed square EFGH is half of the circumscribed square.

**Step 6.** Set up on the square EFGH the pyramid with vertex N, and on the circumscribed square the pyramid with the same vertex N. These pyramids are of the same height, so they are to one another as their bases (12.6); hence the pyramid on the inscribed square is half of the pyramid on the circumscribed square. The circle EFGH lies within the circumscribed square, so the cone EFGHN is a part of the pyramid on the circumscribed square with vertex N and is less than it (CN5). Therefore the pyramid on the square EFGH with vertex N is greater than half of the cone EFGHN.

**Step 7.** Bisect the circumferences EF, FG, GH, HE at P, Q, R, S (3.30) and join EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE (P1). Consider the triangle EPF and the segment of the circle on EF which contains it. In the construction of 3.30, P lies on the straight line drawn at right angles to EF from its middle point; this line passes through the centre M (3.1, porism), so MP is at right angles to EF. Draw through P a straight line at right angles to MP (1.11); it touches the circle at P and otherwise lies outside the circle (3.16, porism). Since EF and this tangent are both at right angles to MP, they are parallel (1.28). Draw through E and F straight lines parallel to MP (1.31) meeting the tangent at E′, F′; then EFF′E′ is a parallelogram on the base EF, and the triangle EPF, being on the same base EF and between the same parallels EF, E′F′, is half of the parallelogram EFF′E′ (1.41). The segment of the circle on EF is a part of the parallelogram EFF′E′ and so is less than it (CN5). Therefore the triangle EPF is greater than half of the segment of the circle on EF; the same holds for the triangles FQG, GRH, HSE and the segments on FG, GH, HE.

**Step 8.** Set up on the triangle EPF the pyramid with vertex N, and on the parallelogram EFF′E′ the pyramid with vertex N. Being of the same height, they are to one another as their bases (12.6), so by Step 7 the pyramid on the triangle EPF is half of the pyramid on the parallelogram. The segment of the cone EFGHN standing on the segment of the circle on EF (the part of the cone cut off by the plane through N, E, F) is a part of the pyramid on the parallelogram EFF′E′ with vertex N, and so is less than it (CN5). Therefore the pyramid on EPF with vertex N is greater than half of the segment of the cone in which it stands; and likewise for the pyramids on FQG, GRH, HSE with vertex N.

**Step 9.** The cone EFGHN exceeds the solid O, and the excess is less than the cone (CN5). From the cone EFGHN subtract the pyramid on the square EFGH with vertex N, which is greater than its half (Step 6); there remain the four segments of the cone on EF, FG, GH, HE. From these subtract the pyramids on EPF, FQG, GRH, HSE with vertex N, each greater than half of the segment in which it stands (Step 8); there remain the segments of the cone on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE. Bisecting the remaining circumferences and continuing in the same way, we subtract at each stage more than half of what is left, so that by 10.1 we shall at some stage leave segments of the cone EFGHN which together are less than the excess of the cone EFGHN over O. For definiteness let this happen at the stage just reached, the remaining segments being those on EP, PF, FQ, QG, GR, RH, HS, SE (the argument is identical at any later stage). Let Π′ denote the pyramid with base the polygon EPFQGRHS and vertex N. The cone EFGHN is composed of Π′ together with these segments, and the segments are less than the excess of the cone over O; therefore Π′ is greater than O.

**Step 10.** In the circle ABCD inscribe the square ABCD (4.6) and bisect the circumferences AB, BC, CD, DA at T, U, V, W (3.30), so obtaining the polygon ATBUCVDW in the same manner as EPFQGRHS was obtained; join its sides (P1) and let Π denote the pyramid with base ATBUCVDW and vertex L. Join KA, KT, KB, KU, KC, KV, KD, KW and LA, LT, LB, LU, LC, LV, LD, LW, and likewise ME, MP, MF, MQ, MG, MR, MH, MS and NE, NP, NF, NQ, NG, NR, NH, NS (P1). The straight lines from K divide the polygon ATBUCVDW into the eight triangles KAT, KTB, KBU, KUC, KCV, KVD, KDW, KWA, and the planes through L and these lines divide Π into the eight pyramids on these triangles with vertex L; similarly Π′ is divided into the eight pyramids on MEP, MPF, MFQ, MQG, MGR, MRH, MHS, MSE with vertex N. Denote by KAT·L the pyramid with base KAT and vertex L, and similarly for the others. Consider the pair KAT·L, MEP·N; the first is contained by the four triangles KAT, KTL, KAL, ATL, the second by the four triangles MEP, MPN, MEN, EPN.

**Step 11.** By Step 3, KT : KL = MP : MN, and the angles TKL, PMN contained by these sides are right and hence equal (Step 2). Two triangles which have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal angles proportional are equiangular, with the equal angles subtended by the corresponding sides (6.6); so the triangles KTL, MPN are equiangular and therefore similar (D6.1). In the same way, from KA : KL = ME : MN (Step 3) and the right angles AKL, EMN, the triangles KAL, MEN are equiangular and similar (6.6, D6.1).

**Step 12.** In the construction of 4.6 the square ABCD is inscribed by means of two diameters AC, BD at right angles, so the angle AKB is right. T bisects the circumference AB (Step 10), and angles at the centre standing on equal circumferences are equal (3.27), so the angle AKT is equal to the angle TKB and is half of the right angle AKB. Likewise the angle EMP is half of the right angle EMF. All right angles being equal (P4), their halves are equal: angle AKT = angle EMP. (In general, whatever part the angle AKT is of the four right angles at K, the same part is the angle EMP of the four right angles at M, both polygons arising from a square by the same number of bisections.) Moreover KA = KT and ME = MP (D1.15), so KA : KT = ME : MP, each being the ratio of a magnitude to a magnitude equal to it (D5.5). Hence, by 6.6, the triangles KAT, MEP are equiangular and similar (D6.1).

**Step 13.** From the similar triangles KTL, MPN we have LT : TK = NP : PM, and from the similar triangles KAT, MEP we have TK : TA = PM : PE (6.4); therefore, ex aequali, LT : TA = NP : PE (5.22). Again, from the similar triangles KAL, MEN, LA : AK = NE : EM, and from KAT, MEP, AK : AT = EM : EP (6.4); therefore, ex aequali, LA : AT = NE : EP (5.22). Taking these two proportions alternately (5.16), LT : NP = TA : PE and LA : NE = AT : EP; hence LT : NP = TA : PE = LA : NE (5.11). The triangles ATL, EPN thus have their sides proportional, so they are equiangular, the equal angles being subtended by the corresponding sides (6.5), and they are similar (D6.1).

**Step 14.** The pyramid KAT·L is therefore contained by four triangles KAT, KTL, KAL, ATL respectively similar to the four triangles MEP, MPN, MEN, EPN which contain the pyramid MEP·N; the two pyramids are contained by similar planes equal in multitude, and so are similar solid figures (D11.9). Similar pyramids which have triangular bases are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides (12.8); hence the pyramid KAT·L has to the pyramid MEP·N the ratio triplicate of that which KT has to MP. Now KT = KB and MP = MF (D1.15), so KT : MP = KB : MP = KB : MF (5.7), and KB : MF = BD : FH (Step 3); thus KT : MP = BD : FH (5.11), and the ratio triplicate of KT : MP is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH (D5.10). Therefore the pyramid KAT·L has to the pyramid MEP·N the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 15.** In exactly the same way each of the remaining pyramids KTB·L, KBU·L, KUC·L, KCV·L, KVD·L, KDW·L, KWA·L has to the corresponding pyramid MPF·N, MFQ·N, MQG·N, MGR·N, MRH·N, MHS·N, MSE·N the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. These eight pairs are all in the same ratio; hence, as one of the antecedents is to its consequent, so are all the antecedents together to all the consequents together (5.12): Π : Π′ = pyramid KAT·L : pyramid MEP·N, that is, Π has to Π′ the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 16.** By hypothesis the cone ABCDL has to O the ratio triplicate of BD : FH; therefore cone ABCDL : O = Π : Π′ (5.11). The pyramid Π has its vertex at L and its base within the circle ABCD, so it is a part of the cone ABCDL, and the cone ABCDL is greater than Π (CN5). In the proportion cone ABCDL : O = Π : Π′ the first magnitude is greater than the third, so the second is greater than the fourth (5.14): O is greater than Π′. But Π′ is greater than O (Step 9), which is impossible. Therefore the cone ABCDL has not to any solid less than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 17.** Interchanging the roles of the two cones throughout Steps 4–16, we see in the same way that the cone EFGHN has not to any solid less than the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of FH : BD.

**Step 18.** Next let O be greater than the cone EFGHN, the cone ABCDL having to O the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Take X, Y such that BD : FH = FH : X = X : Y; then cone ABCDL : O = BD : Y (D5.10). Inversely (5.7, porism; D5.13), O : cone ABCDL = Y : BD, while Y : X = X : FH = FH : BD, so that Y : BD is the ratio triplicate of FH : BD (D5.10); thus O has to the cone ABCDL the ratio triplicate of FH : BD. Now let T be a solid such that O : cone ABCDL = cone EFGHN : T (the fourth proportional, assumed to exist as in Step 4). Since O is greater than the cone EFGHN, the first magnitude in this proportion is greater than the third, so the second is greater than the fourth (5.14): the cone ABCDL is greater than T. Thus cone EFGHN : T = O : cone ABCDL, which is the ratio triplicate of FH : BD (5.11), where T is a solid less than the cone ABCDL. This contradicts Step 17. Therefore the cone ABCDL has not to any solid greater than the cone EFGHN the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 19.** The solid O to which the cone ABCDL has the ratio triplicate of BD : FH is thus neither less nor greater than the cone EFGHN; hence it is equal to it, and cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN = cone ABCDL : O (5.7), which is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Therefore similar cones are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters of their bases.

**Step 20.** Now let there be similar cylinders whose bases are the circles ABCD, EFGH with diameters BD, FH and whose axes are KL, MN (D11.21, D11.22, D11.23), so that BD : FH = KL : MN (D11.24). The cones ABCDL, EFGHN which have the same bases and the same axes (generated by the right-angled triangles KBL, MFN turned about KL, MN) have their axes and diameters in the same proportion and so are similar cones (D11.24); by Step 19, cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH. Each cylinder is triple of the cone which has the same base with it and equal height (12.10). Equimultiples have the same ratio as the magnitudes themselves (5.15); therefore cylinder ABCD·KL : cylinder EFGH·MN = cone ABCDL : cone EFGHN, which is the ratio triplicate of BD : FH.

**Step 21.** Therefore similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.13
**Statement:** If a cylinder be cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so will the axis be to the axis.

**Step 1.** Let AD be a cylinder whose axis is EF and whose bases are the circles AB and CD, with centres E and F; thus AD is generated by the revolution about EF of the rectangle EACF, whose sides EA, FC are radii of the bases and whose side AC is opposite to EF and parallel to it [D11.21, D11.22, D11.23]. Let the cylinder be cut by the plane GH parallel to its opposite planes AB, CD; let this plane meet the axis EF at K and the side AC at G, and let it divide AD into the cylinder BG, whose axis is EK, and the cylinder GD, whose axis is KF. I say that, as the cylinder BG is to the cylinder GD, so is the axis EK to the axis KF.

**Step 2.** First, the axis of any such cylinder is at right angles to its bases. For, since the generating parallelogram is rectangular, the revolving side EA makes a right angle with the fixed side EF in every position [D11.21]; therefore EF makes right angles with every straight line drawn from E to the circumference of the base AB, that is, with all the straight lines in the plane of AB which meet it, and so EF is at right angles to the plane of AB [D11.3]. Similarly FE is at right angles to the plane of CD. Consequently the height of the cylinder, the perpendicular between its bases, is its axis; and any cylinders whose axes are equal are of the same height.

**Step 3.** Next, let any plane parallel to the plane AB be drawn through a point X of the axis EF, or of EF produced [P2], the rectangle EACF being produced as far as necessary. The plane of the rectangle contains X and the radius EA; hence the two parallel planes are cut by it in parallel straight lines [11.16], so that the plane through X cuts the plane of the rectangle in a straight line XY through X parallel to EA, Y lying on AC or on AC produced. Since XY is parallel to EA and XE to YA, the figure EXYA is a parallelogram; therefore XY is equal to EA [1.34]. And since XY is parallel to EA and EA is at right angles to EF, the angle YXE is also right [1.29]. Hence, as the rectangle revolves about the axis, the point Y describes in the plane through X a circle with centre X and radius XY, which is equal to the circle AB, since their radii are equal [D3.1]; and the rectangle is divided by XY into two rectangles which, by the same revolution, generate two cylinders having this circle for a common base and having for axes the two parts into which X divides the axis [D11.21, D11.22, D11.23]. In particular, the plane GH cuts the cylinder AD in the circle GH, with centre K and radius KG equal to EA, which is the common base of the cylinders BG and GD.

**Step 4.** Produce the axis EF in both directions to L and M [P2]; on EL set out any number of straight lines EN, NL, each equal to EK, and on FM any number of straight lines FO, OM, each equal to KF [1.3]; and through the points L, N, O, M let planes be drawn parallel to the plane AB. By Step 3 these planes cut the plane of the rectangle EACF, produced, in the straight lines LP, NR, OT, MV, each parallel and equal to EA and at right angles to LM, the points P, R, T, V lying on AC produced. Therefore LMVP is a rectangle; by its revolution about LM it generates a cylinder PW, whose axis is LM and whose bases are the circles PQ, VW described by P and V about the centres L and M [D11.21, D11.22, D11.23], and of this cylinder the cylinder AD, generated by the part EACF of the same rectangle, is a part. The planes of the circles RS, AB, GH, CD, TU through N, E, K, F, O cut the rectangle LMVP in NR, EA, KG, FC, OT (FC being a side of the rectangle EACF), dividing it into the rectangles LNRP, NEAR, EKGA, KFCG, FOTC, OMVT; hence [Step 3] they divide the cylinder PW into the cylinders QR, RB, BG, GD, DT, TW, whose axes are LN, NE, EK, KF, FO, OM respectively, and whose bases are the circles PQ, RS, AB, GH, CD, TU, VW.

**Step 5.** The radii LP, NR, KG, OT, MV of the circles PQ, RS, GH, TU, VW are each equal to EA [Step 3, 1.34], and the radius FC of the circle CD is equal to EA, being the opposite side of the rectangle EACF [1.34]; therefore all these radii are equal to one another [CN1], and the circles PQ, RS, AB, GH, CD, TU, VW are all equal to one another [D3.1].

**Step 6.** I say further that any two cylinders which have equal axes and equal bases are equal to one another. For let two cylinders have equal axes and equal bases. Since their axes are equal, they are of the same height [Step 2]; therefore, as the first cylinder is to the second, so is the base of the first to the base of the second [12.11]. Now, of four magnitudes in the same ratio, if any equimultiples be taken of the first and third and any equimultiples of the second and fourth, the former alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the latter [D5.5]; taking, then, each of the four magnitudes once, since the base of the first cylinder is equal to the base of the second, the first cylinder is equal to the second cylinder.

**Step 7.** The cylinders QR, RB, BG have the axes LN, NE, EK, which are equal to one another, and their bases are equal circles [Step 5]; therefore they are equal to one another [Step 6]. Hence the cylinder PG, whose axis is LK and which is made up of the cylinders QR, RB, BG, is the same multiple of the cylinder BG that the axis LK, made up of LN, NE, EK, is of the axis EK [D5.2]. For the same reason the cylinders GD, DT, TW are equal to one another, and the cylinder GM, whose axis is KM and which is made up of GD, DT, TW, is the same multiple of the cylinder GD that the axis KM is of the axis KF [D5.2].

**Step 8.** I say that the cylinder PG is greater than, equal to, or less than the cylinder GM according as the axis LK is greater than, equal to, or less than the axis KM. (a) If LK is equal to KM, the cylinders PG and GM have equal axes, and their bases PQ, GH and GH, VW are equal circles [Step 5]; therefore PG is equal to GM [Step 6]. (b) If LK is greater than KM, cut off from KL the straight line KZ equal to KM [1.3], and through Z draw a plane parallel to the plane AB; by Step 3 this plane divides the cylinder PG into two cylinders, one of which, ZG, has the axis ZK and has for bases the circle GH and a circle equal to it. Since the axes ZK, KM are equal and the bases are equal, the cylinder ZG is equal to the cylinder GM [Step 6]; but the cylinder PG is greater than its part ZG [CN5]; therefore PG is greater than GM. (c) If LK is less than KM, then, cutting off from KM a straight line equal to KL, we show in the same way that GM is greater than PG, that is, PG is less than GM.

**Step 9.** Now there are four magnitudes, the cylinder BG, the cylinder GD, the axis EK and the axis KF; of the first and third, BG and EK, equimultiples have been taken, namely the cylinder PG and the axis LK, and of the second and fourth, GD and KF, equimultiples have been taken, namely the cylinder GM and the axis KM [Step 7]; and it has been proved that, if the multiple LK exceeds the multiple KM, the multiple PG exceeds the multiple GM, if equal, equal, and if less, less [Step 8]. Since the number of the straight lines EN, NL and the number of the straight lines FO, OM were any whatever, these equimultiples are any equimultiples whatever. Therefore, as the cylinder BG is to the cylinder GD, so is the axis EK to the axis KF [D5.5]. Therefore, if a cylinder be cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so is the axis to the axis. Q.E.D.

**Note on route.** The equality of cylinders having equal axes and equal bases (Step 6) is obtained directly from 12.11 and the definition of same ratio (D5.5, with the magnitudes themselves as equimultiples); this is more direct than constructing an auxiliary third cylinder of the same height and using 5.7, 5.11 and 5.9.

## Proposition 12.14
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are on equal bases are to one another as their heights.

**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be equal circles with centres H and L. Let EB be the cylinder on the base AB with axis GH, described by the rectangle GHBE (right-angled at H) carried round the fixed side GH, and let FD be the cylinder on the base CD with axis KL, described by the rectangle KLDF carried round KL; thus HB and LD are radii of the bases AB, CD, and KF is a radius of the opposite base of FD (D11.21, D11.22, D11.23). Let ABG and CDK be the cones on the same bases AB, CD described by the right-angled triangles GHB, KLD carried round the same sides GH, KL, so that their vertices are G, K and their axes are GH, KL (D11.18, D11.19, D11.20).

**Step 2.** The height of each of these solids is its axis. For GH makes a right angle with HB in every position which HB takes as it is carried round; hence GH makes right angles with every straight line in the plane of the circle AB which meets it, and so is at right angles to that plane (D11.3). Therefore the perpendicular from G to the base AB is GH itself, that is, the height of the cylinder EB and of the cone ABG is GH (D6.4); in the same way the height of the cylinder FD and of the cone CDK is KL. It is therefore required to prove that cylinder EB : cylinder FD = GH : KL and cone ABG : cone CDK = GH : KL.

**Step 3.** Produce KL beyond L to N (P2) and cut off LN equal to GH (1.3). Produce FD beyond D to M (P2), cut off DM equal to LN (1.3), and join NM (P1).

**Step 4.** The angles KLD, LDF are right, being angles of the rectangle KLDF; hence the adjacent angles NLD, LDM are also right (1.13). The straight line LD falling on KN and FM thus makes the interior angles NLD, LDM on the same side equal to two right angles, so that LN is parallel to DM (1.28); and LN is equal to DM. Therefore NM, which joins their extremities in the same directions, is equal and parallel to LD (1.33), and LNMD is a parallelogram. Its angles at L and D being right, the opposite angles at M and N are also right (1.34); so LNMD is a rectangle with sides LN, LD. Further, KF and NM are each at right angles to KN, so that KF is parallel to NM (1.28), and KN is parallel to FM, as shown; hence KNMF, whose four angles are right, is a rectangle, made up of the rectangles KLDF and LNMD lying on opposite sides of LD.

**Step 5.** Let the rectangle KNMF be carried round the fixed side KN and restored to the position from which it began to move. It describes a cylinder FM, whose axis is KN and whose bases are the circles described by KF and NM (D11.21, D11.22, D11.23). In this same revolution the part KLDF describes the given cylinder FD, and the part LNMD describes a cylinder CM whose axis is LN and whose base is the circle described by LD, namely the circle CD (D11.21, D11.22, D11.23). Thus the cylinder FM is made up of the two cylinders FD and CM, which lie on opposite sides of the plane of the circle CD.

**Step 6.** The straight line KN makes right angles with KF, LD and NM in every position which they take as they are carried round; hence it is at right angles to the plane of each of the three circles described by them (D11.3), and these three planes are parallel to one another (11.14). Therefore the cylinder FM is cut by the plane of the circle CD, which is parallel to its opposite planes, into the cylinders CM and FD, whose axes are LN and LK; consequently, as the cylinder CM is to the cylinder FD, so is the axis LN to the axis LK (12.13).

**Step 7.** The cylinders EB and CM are of the same height, for their heights are their axes GH and LN (Step 2), and LN was made equal to GH. Therefore, as the cylinder EB is to the cylinder CM, so is the base AB to the base CD (12.11). But the base AB is equal to the base CD. In this proportion take of the first and third the magnitudes themselves, the cylinder EB and the circle AB, and of the second and fourth the cylinder CM and the circle CD, each taken once, which is a case of equimultiples: since the circle AB neither exceeds nor falls short of the circle CD but is equal to it, the cylinder EB likewise neither exceeds nor falls short of the cylinder CM but is equal to it (D5.5). Therefore the cylinder EB is equal to the cylinder CM.

**Step 8.** Since the cylinder EB is equal to the cylinder CM, the two have the same ratio to the cylinder FD (5.7): EB : FD = CM : FD. Since GH is equal to LN, likewise GH : LK = LN : LK (5.7). But CM : FD = LN : LK (Step 6). Therefore, ratios which are the same with the same ratio being the same with one another (5.11), cylinder EB : cylinder FD = GH : KL.

**Step 9.** The cone ABG has the same base AB and the same height GH as the cylinder EB; therefore it is a third part of the cylinder EB, that is, the cylinder EB is triple the cone ABG (12.10). In the same way the cylinder FD is triple the cone CDK. Thus the cones ABG, CDK are the same parts (thirds) of the cylinders EB, FD, and parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them taken in corresponding order (5.15); hence cone ABG : cone CDK = cylinder EB : cylinder FD. But cylinder EB : cylinder FD = GH : KL (Step 8); therefore cone ABG : cone CDK = GH : KL (5.11).

**Step 10.** Therefore the cylinders EB, FD on the equal bases AB, CD are to one another as their heights GH, KL, and so also are the cones ABG, CDK on the same bases. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 12.15
**Statement:** In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let AX and EO be two cones, or two cylinders. Let the circle ABCD with centre K be the base of AX and KL its axis, and let the circle EFGH with centre M be the base of EO and MN its axis. Each of the solids is comprehended by a right-angled triangle (for a cone) or a rectangle (for a cylinder) carried round one of the sides about the right angle, which remains fixed and is the axis, while the other side about the right angle describes the base [D11.18, D11.19, D11.20, D11.21, D11.22, D11.23]. Hence the angle AKL at K and the angle EMN at M are right angles, and the axes KL, MN are the heights of the solids. The bases are said to be reciprocally proportional to the heights when, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL [D6.2].

**Step 2.** Let the solids be so named that KL is not greater than MN. If KL is equal to MN, let P be the point N; if KL is less than MN, cut off from MN the straight line MP equal to KL [1.3]. In either case P lies on MN, MP is equal to KL, and the angle EMP, being the angle EMN, is right.

**Step 3.** Let ES be the cone, or the cylinder, of the same kind as AX and EO, comprehended by carrying round MP the right-angled triangle EMP, or the rectangle whose sides about the right angle at M are ME and MP [D11.18, D11.21]. Its axis is MP [D11.19, D11.22], and its base is the circle described by ME as it is carried round M in the plane at right angles to MP [D11.20, D11.23]; since MP lies along MN, this is the very circle EFGH described by ME carried round MN. Thus ES has the base EFGH and the height MP, which is equal to KL. When P is the point N, ES is the solid EO itself.

**Step 4.** The solids AX and ES are of the same height, since KL is equal to MP; therefore, as the solid AX is to the solid ES, so is the base ABCD to the base EFGH [12.11].

**Step 5.** The solids EO and ES stand on the same base EFGH; therefore, as the solid EO is to the solid ES, so is the height MN to the height MP [12.14]. (If P is the point N, ES is EO itself, and EO : ES and MN : MP are each the ratio of a magnitude to itself; any equimultiples of EO and MN then alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of any equimultiples of EO and MN respectively, so that these are the same ratio [D5.5].)

**Step 6.** Since MP is equal to KL, the same magnitude MN has to MP and to KL the same ratio [5.7]; therefore, as EO is to ES, so is MN to KL [5.11].

**Step 7.** First, let the solids AX and EO be equal. Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio; therefore, as AX is to ES, so is EO to ES [5.7]. But as AX is to ES, so is the base ABCD to the base EFGH (Step 4), and as EO is to ES, so is the height MN to the height KL (Step 6); therefore, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so is the height MN to the height KL [5.11]. Thus in the equal cones or cylinders AX, EO the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights.

**Step 8.** Conversely, let the bases be reciprocally proportional to the heights, that is, as the base ABCD is to the base EFGH, so let the height MN be to the height KL. As ABCD is to EFGH, so is AX to ES (Step 4), and as MN is to KL, so is EO to ES (Step 6); therefore, as AX is to ES, so is EO to ES [5.11]. Magnitudes which have the same ratio to the same are equal to one another; therefore the solid AX is equal to the solid EO [5.9].

**Step 9.** Therefore, in equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal. Q.E.D.

Path note: for cylinders the auxiliary solid ES could instead be obtained by cutting EO with a plane through P parallel to its bases, cones then being handled separately through their ratio to the cylinders on the same bases; constructing ES directly on the base EFGH lets a single argument with 12.11 and 12.14 cover cones and cylinders together, and is the more direct route taken here.

## Proposition 12.16
**Statement:** Given two circles about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the greater and EFGH the lesser of the two given circles, and let K be their common centre. Through K draw a straight line and produce it in both directions until it meets the circumference of the greater circle at B and D (P1, P2). Then BD is a diameter of the greater circle (D1.17), and KB, KD, being drawn from the centre to the circumference, are equal (D1.15).

**Step 2.** Let KD meet the circumference of the lesser circle at G. Since EFGH is the lesser circle, its radius KG is less than the radius KD of the greater circle (D3.1); hence G falls between K and D, and KG is a part of KD (CN5).

**Step 3.** From G draw GA at right angles to BD (1.11), and produce it in both directions until it meets the circumference of the greater circle at A and C (P2), G lying between A and C. Then AC is a straight line in the greater circle, and since the angles which AC makes with BD at G are right, KG is the perpendicular drawn from the centre K to AC. Let BAD be the arc of the greater circle cut off by the diameter BD on the side of A; by D1.17 the diameter bisects the circle, so the arc BAD is the half of the whole circumference.

**Step 4.** The arc AD is a part of the arc BAD; therefore the arc BAD is greater than the arc AD (CN5). Bisect the arc BAD (3.30); bisect that half of it which ends at D; bisect again that half of the last arc which ends at D; and continue in this way. At every bisection the arc ending at D is halved; hence, the arc BAD and the arc AD being two unequal magnitudes, by 10.1 (whose argument holds equally when exactly the half is taken away each time) there will at length be left an arc ending at D which is less than the arc AD. Let LD be this arc, so that arc LD is less than arc AD.

**Step 5.** The point L lies on the arc AD. For L is a point of the arc BAD; and if L lay on the arc BA, or coincided with A, then the arc AD would be a part of the arc LD, or equal to it, so that the arc LD would not be less than the arc AD (CN5), contrary to Step 4. Hence L lies between A and D on the arc AD.

**Step 6.** The arc BAD is double of its half, that half is double of its own half, and so on down to the arc LD; hence the arc BAD is measured by the arc LD, that is, it is a multiple of the arc LD (D5.2). Let the arc BAD be m times the arc LD. And the whole circumference of the greater circle is double of the arc BAD (Step 3, D1.17); therefore the whole circumference is 2m times the arc LD.

**Step 7.** Join KA, KL, KC (P1). Since L lies on the arc AD (Step 5), the radius KL falls within the angle AKD, so that the angle LKD is a part of the angle AKD; therefore the angle LKD is less than the angle AKD (CN5). Again, since G, a point of the straight line KD, lies on AC between A and C, the straight line KD falls within the angle AKC, so that the angle AKD is a part of the angle AKC; therefore the angle AKD is less than the angle AKC (CN5). Consequently the angle LKD is less than the angle AKC.

**Step 8.** In the triangles LKD, AKC the two sides KL, KD are equal to the two sides KA, KC respectively, all of them being drawn from the centre K to the circumference of the greater circle (D1.15); and the angle LKD contained by KL, KD is less than the angle AKC contained by KA, KC (Step 7). Therefore the base LD is less than the base AC (1.24).

**Step 9.** From K draw KO perpendicular to LD (1.12). Then KO and KG are the perpendiculars drawn from the centre to the straight lines LD and AC in the greater circle (Step 3). If KO were less than KG, then LD would be nearer to the centre than AC (D3.5), and so LD would be greater than AC (3.15); and if KO were equal to KG, then LD and AC would be equally distant from the centre (D3.4), and so LD would be equal to AC (3.14). Each of these is impossible by Step 8. Therefore KO is greater than KG.

**Step 10.** Since LD is itself a straight line in the greater circle, it is not greater than the diameter (3.15). Beginning at D, fit into the greater circle a straight line DP1 equal to LD (4.1, D4.7); from P1 fit P1P2 equal to LD; and so on continually, each new straight line beginning where the preceding one ends and all proceeding in the same direction round the circumference. Each straight line so fitted, being equal to LD, cuts off from the greater circle an arc equal to the arc LD (3.28). Since the whole circumference is 2m times the arc LD (Step 6), when 2m such straight lines have been fitted the arcs cut off by them together make up the whole circumference, and the end P2m of the last of them coincides with D. Thus DP1P2...P(2m-1) is a polygon of 2m sides, and every angle of it lies on the circumference of the greater circle, since the extremities of each fitted straight line are on the circumference (D4.7); therefore the polygon is inscribed in the greater circle (D4.3).

**Step 11.** All the sides of the polygon are equal to LD, and therefore equal to one another (CN1); so the polygon is equilateral. And the number 2m of its sides is divisible into the two equal parts m and m; therefore it is an even number (D7.6).

**Step 12.** Each side of the polygon is a straight line in the greater circle equal to LD; therefore each side is equally distant from the centre with LD (3.14), that is, the perpendicular drawn from K to each side is equal to KO (D3.4), and hence is greater than KG (Step 9).

**Step 13.** Let S be any side of the polygon, and let KT be the perpendicular drawn from K to S (1.12), so that KT is equal to KO and greater than KG (Step 12). Let P be any point of S. If P coincides with T, then KP is KT, which is greater than KG. If P does not coincide with T, join KP (P1); in the triangle KTP the angle at T is right, so the angle KPT is less than a right angle (1.17), and therefore the side KP, which subtends the greater angle KTP, is greater than the side KT, which subtends the angle KPT (1.19); hence again KP is greater than KG. Thus every point P of the side S is at a distance from K greater than KG.

**Step 14.** Such a point P lies outside the lesser circle. For P is not on the circumference of the lesser circle, since otherwise KP would be equal to KG, both being drawn from the centre to that circumference (D1.15); and P is not within the lesser circle, since otherwise KP produced (P2) would meet its circumference at some point Q with KQ equal to KG (D1.15), and KP, being a part of KQ, would be less than KG (CN5). Hence no point of any side of the polygon lies on or within the lesser circle; no side meets the lesser circle at all, and therefore no side touches it (D3.2).

**Step 15.** Therefore in the greater circle ABCD there has been inscribed the equilateral polygon DP1P2...P(2m-1), having an even number of sides, which does not touch the lesser circle EFGH. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 12.17
**Statement:** Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.

**Step 1.** Let A be the common centre of the two spheres. Every point of the surface of a sphere is at a distance from its centre equal to the radius of the generating semicircle [D11.14, D11.16]. Cut both spheres by any plane through A. In each sphere the section is a plane figure bounded by one line all of whose points are equally distant from A; hence each section is a circle with centre A [D1.15, D1.16]. Let the section of the greater sphere be the circle BCDE, that of the lesser the circle FGH, AB a radius of the greater, and G the point in which AB cuts the lesser circle, so that AG is a radius of the lesser sphere and AG < AB.

**Step 2.** Draw in the circle BCDE the diameter CE at right angles to the diameter BD [1.11], and let H be the point of the quadrant BE in which the straight line drawn through G at right angles to BD [1.11] meets the circle BCDE. By 12.16 inscribe in the greater circle BCDE an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle FGH, taking B as the end of the diameter BD used in that construction. The construction of 12.16 cuts off the side by bisecting continually the arc between the end B of the diameter and the point H (the point where the perpendicular to BD at its intersection G with the lesser circle meets the greater circle), until an arc less than the arc BH is left; the side is therefore a 2^n-th part of the circumference with n ≥ 3, and the vertex K next to B lies on the arc BH. Consequently the vertices of the polygon include B, C, D, E, and each quadrant contains a whole number m ≥ 2 of sides. Let BK, KL, LM, ME be the sides in the quadrant BE, and let s denote their common length.

**Step 3.** Join KA and produce it to N [P1, P2]. From A set up AX at right angles to the plane of the circle BCDE [11.12], X being on the surface of the greater sphere. Draw the plane through AX and BD, and the plane through AX and KN; being planes through the centre A, their sections with the greater sphere are circles with centre A and radius AB (Step 1). Let BXD, KXN be the semicircles of these circles on the side of X. Since AX is at right angles to the plane BCDE, every plane through AX is at right angles to the plane BCDE [11.18]; hence the planes of BXD and KXN are at right angles to the plane BCDE.

**Step 4.** The circles BCDE, BXD, KXN have equal radii and are therefore equal [D3.1]. The angles BAE, BAX, KAX are right (Step 2; AX makes right angles with BA and KA which lie in the plane BCDE [D11.3]), hence equal [P4]; standing at the centres of equal circles they cut off equal arcs [3.26], so the arcs BX and KX are quadrants each equal to the quadrant BE. The quadrant BE is made up of the m arcs BK, KL, LM, ME, which are equal because they are cut off by equal chords [3.28]. Fit into the circle BXD, from B toward X, the chord BO equal to BK [4.1]; it cuts off the arc BO equal to the arc BK [3.28]. Continuing, fit OP, PR, RX each equal to BK, and in the circle KXN fit KS, ST, TU, UX each equal to BK. Since arc BX = arc KX = arc BE, and each is m times the arc BK, these m chords in each quadrant end exactly at X. Join SO, TP, UR [P1].

**Step 5.** In the plane BXD draw OV at right angles to BD [1.12], and in the plane KXN draw SQ at right angles to KN [1.12]. Since the planes BXD, KXN are at right angles to the plane BCDE, and BD, KN are their common sections with it, OV and SQ are at right angles to the plane BCDE [D11.4]. Moreover V falls between A and B: the angle BAO is less than the right angle BAX [CN5], the angle ABO is equal to it [1.5] and therefore acute, and if V lay beyond B (or beyond A), the acute angle ABO (or BAO) would be an exterior angle of the triangle OVB (or OVA), hence greater than the right angle at V [1.16], which is impossible. Likewise Q falls between A and K.

**Step 6.** The arcs BO, BK, KS are equal (Step 4), so the angles BAO, BAK, KAS at the centre are equal [3.27]. The triangles AVO, AQS have the angle OAV equal to the angle SAQ, right angles at V and Q, and the side AO equal to the side AS (radii); therefore OV = SQ and AV = AQ [1.26]. Since AB = AK, the remainders VB, QK are equal [CN3].

**Step 7.** Since BV = KQ and VA = QA, BV : VA = KQ : QA [5.7, 5.11]; therefore VQ is parallel to BK [6.2]. OV and SQ, being at right angles to the same plane, are parallel [11.6], and they are equal; hence VQ and OS are equal and parallel [1.33]. Since VQ is parallel to BK, OS is parallel to BK [11.9]. BO and KS join points on the parallels BK, OS, so they lie in the plane of BK and OS [11.7]; thus KBOS is a plane quadrilateral. In the same way, using the perpendiculars from P and T, and from R and U, to the plane BCDE, the straight lines TP and UR are each parallel to BK, so SO, TP, UR are parallel to one another [11.9], and the quadrilaterals SOPT, TPRU are plane [11.7]; the triangle URX is in one plane [11.2].

**Step 8.** Join AO, AS, AP, AT, AR, AU [P1]. Then on the bases KBOS, SOPT, TPRU, URX pyramids with vertex A are constructed [D11.12]. Make the same construction in the quadrants EC, CD, DB of the circle BCDE, and on the other side of the plane BCDE with AX produced through A. The pyramids so obtained make up a polyhedral solid contained by the plane quadrilaterals and triangles so formed, all of whose vertices lie on the surface of the greater sphere (each lies on a great circle of it); thus the solid is inscribed in the greater sphere. It remains to prove that no base of it touches the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 9.** From A draw AY perpendicular to the plane KBOS [11.11], Y being in that plane. AY makes right angles with YB, YK, YO, YS [D11.3], so AB² = AY² + YB², AK² = AY² + YK², AO² = AY² + YO², AS² = AY² + YS² [1.47]. Since AB = AK = AO = AS, the remainders YB², YK², YO², YS² are equal [CN3]; hence YB = YK = YO = YS.

**Step 10.** Since VQ is parallel to BK, the triangles AVQ, ABK are equiangular [1.29], so AV : AB = VQ : BK [6.4]; and AV < AB, hence VQ < BK [5.14]. But OS = VQ (Step 7). Therefore OS < s, while BK = BO = KS = s.

**Step 11.** The triangles YBK, YBO, YKS have YB = YK = YO = YS and bases BK = BO = KS, so the angles BYK, BYO, KYS are equal [1.8]. The triangles YOS, YBK have YO = YB, YS = YK and base OS less than base BK, so the angle OYS is less than the angle BYK [1.25]. Y lies within the quadrilateral KBOS: otherwise the four points B, K, S, O of the circle about centre Y would lie on one semicircle of it, and the angle at Y subtended by one side of the quadrilateral would be equal to or greater than the sum of the angles subtended by the other three sides, hence greater than each of them, which is impossible since three of the four angles are equal and the fourth is less than them. Therefore the four angles BYK, KYS, SYO, OYB about the point Y together make four right angles [1.15]. Thus three angles equal to BYK together with the angle OYS make four right angles, and OYS < BYK; so four angles equal to BYK exceed four right angles, and the angle BYK is greater than a right angle, i.e. obtuse [D1.11]. Hence in the triangle BYK, BK² > BY² + YK² = 2·BY² [2.12].

**Step 12.** From K draw KZ at right angles to BD [1.12]. As in Step 5, Z falls between A and B (the angle BAK is less than the right angle BAE [CN5], and the angle ABK is equal to it [1.5]). Join KD [P1]. The angle BKD, being in a semicircle, is right [3.31]; KZ is the perpendicular from the right angle to the base, so the triangles DBK, KBZ are similar and DB : BK = BK : BZ, and the triangles DZK, KZB are similar and DZ : ZK = ZK : ZB [6.8]; hence BK² = DB·BZ and KZ² = DZ·ZB [6.17].

**Step 13.** Since Z is between A and B, BZ < BA = AD < DZ. Now DB·BZ = DZ·ZB + BZ² [2.3]; and BZ², being the rectangle contained by BZ and ZB with BZ < DZ, is a part of the rectangle DZ·ZB and so less than it [CN5]. Therefore DB·BZ < 2·DZ·ZB, that is, BK² < 2·KZ².

**Step 14.** From Steps 11 and 13, 2·BY² < BK² < 2·KZ², so BY² < KZ² and BY < KZ. Since AB = AK, AB² = AK². But AB² = AY² + YB² (Step 9), and AK² = AZ² + ZK², the angle AZK being right [1.47]. Hence AY² + YB² = AZ² + ZK², and since YB² < ZK², AY² > AZ²; therefore AY > AZ.

**Step 15.** Since K lies on the arc BH (Step 2), the angle BAK is less than the angle BAH [CN5], so AK falls within the angle BAH and meets GH at a point W between G and H. In the right-angled triangle AGW, AW² = AG² + GW² < AG² + GH² = AH² [1.47, CN5]; so AW < AH = AK, and W lies between A and K. GW and ZK are both at right angles to AB, hence parallel [1.28]; so the straight line through W parallel to the side ZK of the triangle AZK cuts AZ at G, and, W being between A and K, G is between A and Z [6.2]. Therefore AZ > AG [CN5].

**Step 16.** Consequently AY > AZ > AG. Every straight line drawn from A to a point of the plane KBOS other than Y is greater than AY, since it makes with AY a right angle at Y [D11.3] and its square is AY² together with the square on the line joining Y to that point [1.47]. Hence every point of the base KBOS is at a distance from A greater than AG; but the surface of the lesser sphere consists of the points at distance AG from A [D11.14]. Therefore the base KBOS does not meet the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 17.** The same holds for every other base. Every quadrilateral base, such as SOPT, has two opposite sides (OP, TS) equal to s and the other two (SO, TP) less than s, TP being less than KL exactly as VQ is less than BK (Step 10); every triangular base, such as URX, has two sides (UX, RX) equal to s and the third (UR) less; and the bases in the other quadrants and on the other side of the plane BCDE are of these same two kinds. Let AY' be the perpendicular from A to such a base [11.11]. Then Y' is equidistant from the vertices of the base (as in Step 9), the angles at Y' subtended by the sides equal to s are equal [1.8], those subtended by the shorter sides are less than them [1.25], Y' lies within the base (as in Step 11), and the angles about Y' make four right angles [1.15]. Hence twice the angle subtended by a side equal to s, together with the smaller angle or angles, makes four right angles, so that angle is greater than a right angle, and by [2.12] s² > 2·Y'O², O being an end of a side equal to s. Then, as in Step 14, 2·Y'O² < s² < 2·KZ², so Y'O < KZ, and AY'² = AO² − Y'O² > AK² − KZ² = AZ² > AG² (Step 15). Thus AY' > AG, and, as in Step 16, the base lies wholly outside the surface of the lesser sphere.

**Step 18.** Therefore a polyhedral solid has been inscribed in the greater sphere which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface. Q.E.F.
