Then the angles QWV, QWZ, being adjacent angles on the straight line VZ, are together equal to two right angles (1.13); hence the angle QWZ is right. Therefore the square on QZ is equal to the squares on QW and WZ (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius VE and on the side EP of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so QZ = EF. Similarly RZ, SZ, TZ, UZ are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 7).

**Step 13.** Since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle ZVL is right (D11.3), and hence its adjacent angle XVL on the straight line ZX is also right (1.13). Therefore the square on LX is equal to the squares on LV and VX (1.47), that is, to the squares on the radius and on the side of the decagon, that is, to the square on EF (Step 5); so LX = EF. Similarly MX, NX, OX, PX are each equal to EF. Therefore the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX are equilateral, with every side equal to EF (Step 4).

**Step 14.** Hence a solid figure has been constructed which is contained by the twenty triangles of Steps 9, 12 and 13, namely the ten triangles QLR, LRM, RMS, MSN, SNT, NTO, TOU, OUP, UPQ, PQL, the five triangles QRZ, RSZ, STZ, TUZ, UQZ, and the five triangles LMX, MNX, NOX, OPX, PLX. Each of these is equilateral and all their sides are equal to EF, so they are twenty equal and equilateral triangles; therefore the solid is an icosahedron (D11.27), and its side is equal to EF, the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle EFGHK.

**Step 15.** Next, it is to be comprehended in a sphere. Since VW is the side of the hexagon and WZ the side of the decagon inscribed in the same circle EFGHK, and VZ is made up of them, VZ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, and VW is its greater segment (13.9). Bisect VW at Y (1.10). Then, VZ being cut in extreme and mean ratio at W, the square on the lesser segment ZW added to the half WY of the greater segment, that is, the square on ZY, is five times the square on WY (13.3).

**Step 16.** Since VW is bisected at Y, the square on VW is four times the square on WY (2.4). The angle QWY is right, being the angle QWV (Step 12). Therefore the square on QY is equal to the squares on QW and WY (1.47); and QW equals VE, which equals VW; so the square on QY is equal to four times the square on WY together with the square on WY, that is, to five times the square on WY, that is, to the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence QY = ZY. Similarly RY, SY, TY, UY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 17.** Since XV = WZ, each being equal to EP, and VY = YW, the whole XY is equal to the whole ZY (CN2). Again, since VZ is at right angles to the plane of the circle, the angle LVY is right (D11.3); therefore the square on LY is equal to the squares on LV and VY (1.47). And LV is the radius, equal to VW, whose square is four times the square on VY (2.4); so the square on LY is five times the square on VY, that is, five times the square on WY, that is, the square on ZY (Step 15). Hence LY = ZY. Similarly MY, NY, OY, PY are each equal to ZY.

**Step 18.** Therefore the straight lines drawn from Y to all twelve vertices Q, R, S, T, U, L, M, N, O, P, X, Z are equal to YZ (Steps 16, 17). Describe on XZ the semicircle with centre Y and distance YZ (P3, D1.18), and let it be carried round about XZ, which remains fixed, until it is restored to the position from which it began to be moved; the figure so comprehended is a sphere (D11.14), of which XZ is a diameter and Y the centre (D11.17, D11.16). As the semicircle is carried round it passes through the plane containing XZ and any vertex, say Q; and in that plane, since YQ = YZ, the point Q lies on the circle with centre Y and distance YZ (D1.15), that is, on the surface of the sphere. The same holds for every vertex. Therefore the icosahedron has been comprehended in this sphere.

**Step 19.** This sphere is equal to the given sphere. For XZ is bisected at Y, so the square on XZ is four times the square on ZY (2.4), that is, four times five times the square on WY (Step 15), that is, five times four times the square on WY, that is, five times the square on VW (Step 16). But VW equals the radius VE, which equals DB; so the square on XZ is five times the square on DB, which is the square on AB (Step 2). Therefore XZ = AB, and the sphere on the diameter XZ is the given sphere. Thus the icosahedron has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 20.** Finally, the side of the icosahedron is minor. The diameter of the circle EFGHK is double the radius, that is, double DB, so its square is four times the square on DB (2.4). Since the square on AB is five times the square on DB (Step 2), five times the square on the diameter of the circle is twenty times the square on DB, which is four times the square on AB. Hence the square on the diameter of the circle has to the square on AB the ratio which the number 4 has to the number 5; therefore these squares are commensurable (10.6), so the diameter of the circle is commensurable in square with the rational straight line AB and is therefore itself rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 21.** Therefore the circle EFGHK has its diameter rational, and in it the equilateral pentagon EFGHK is inscribed; hence the side EF of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor (13.11). But every side of the icosahedron is equal to EF (Step 14). Therefore the side of the icosahedron is the irrational straight line called minor. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 13.17
**Statement:** To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.

**Step 1.** Setting out. Let the diameter of the given sphere be taken as the assigned rational straight line (D10.1.3). By 13.15 construct a cube comprehended in this sphere; then the diameter of the cube is a diameter of the sphere and the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube (13.15). The cube is contained by six equal squares (D11.25); let ABCD and CBEF be two of its faces with common side BC, so that they are squares (D1.22) whose planes are at right angles to one another.

**Step 2.** Bisect AB, BC, CD, DA, EF, EB, FC at G, H, K, L, M, N, O (1.10) and join GK, HL, MH, NO (P1). Since N, O bisect the equal and parallel sides EB, FC, the lines NB, OC are equal and parallel, so NO is equal and parallel to BC (1.33); similarly MH is equal and parallel to EB, GK to BC, and HL to AB. Let MH, NO meet at P and GK, HL at Q. Then NBHP, PHCO, BHQG are parallelograms, so NP = BH, PO = HC, HQ = BG (1.34). Since BH, HC, BG, BN, OC are halves of equal sides of the cube, NP = PO = HQ = NB = OC = BH = HC.

**Step 3.** Cut NP in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment (6.30), so that NP : RP = RP : RN (D6.3). Cut off PS = RP on PO and QT = RP on QH (1.3). Since PO = NP and HQ = NP, the remainders SO and TH are each equal to NR (CN3). Hence PO : PS = NP : RP = RP : RN = PS : SO (5.7, 5.11), so PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater segment (D6.3); likewise HQ : QT = QT : TH, so HQ is cut in extreme and mean ratio at T with QT the greater segment.

**Step 4.** From R and S set up RU, SV at right angles to the plane CBEF, and from T set up TW at right angles to the plane ABCD, all on the outside of the cube (11.12), and make RU = SV = TW = RP (1.3). Join UB, BW, WC, CV, VU (P1).

**Step 5.** Since NO is parallel to BC and NB falls on them, the angles BNO, NBC together equal two right angles (1.29); angle NBC is right (D1.22), so angle BNR is right. Hence BR² = BN² + NR² (1.47).

**Step 6.** Since NP is cut in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment, NP² + NR² = 3·RP² (13.4). But NP = NB and RP = RU; therefore BN² + NR² = 3·RU², that is, BR² = 3·RU² (Step 5, CN1).

**Step 7.** Since RU is at right angles to the plane CBEF and RB lies in that plane, angle URB is right (D11.3); hence BU² = BR² + RU² = 3·RU² + RU² = 4·RU² (1.47, CN2).

**Step 8.** RU and SV are both at right angles to the plane CBEF, so they are parallel (11.6); being also equal, the line UV joining their ends is equal and parallel to RS (1.33). Now RS = RP + PS = 2·RP = 2·RU, so UV = 2·RU and UV² = 4·RU² (2.4). Therefore BU² = UV² (CN1), and BU = UV.

**Step 9.** Similarly for the other sides. PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater, so PO² + OS² = 3·PS² (13.4); angle COS is right (1.29, as in Step 5) so CS² = CO² + OS² = 3·SV² (1.47, since CO = PO, SV = PS); angle VSC is right (D11.3), so CV² = CS² + SV² = 4·SV² = UV². Again HQ is cut in extreme and mean ratio at T with QT the greater, so HQ² + HT² = 3·QT² (13.4); HL is parallel to AB so angle BHT is right (1.29) and BT² = BH² + HT² = 3·TW² (1.47, since BH = HQ, TW = QT); angle WTB is right (D11.3), so BW² = BT² + TW² = 4·TW² = UV²; in the same way CW² = CH² + HT² + TW² = 4·TW² = UV². Hence UB = BW = WC = CV = VU, and the pentagon UBWCV is equilateral.

**Step 10.** Next, it lies in one plane. From P set up PX at right angles to the plane CBEF on the outside (11.12) and make PX = RP (1.3). PX is parallel to RU (11.6) and equal to it, so UX is equal and parallel to RP (1.33); similarly XV is equal and parallel to PS. Thus UX and XV both pass through X and are parallel to NO; if they were two distinct straight lines they would be parallel to one another (1.30) yet meet at X, contrary to D1.23; hence UXV is one straight line and X lies on UV. Also UV is parallel to NO (Step 8) and NO to BC, these not all lying in one plane, so UV is parallel to BC (11.9).

**Step 11.** Join XH and HW (P1). Since MH is parallel to EB and EB is at right angles to BC, MH is at right angles to BC (1.29); the planes ABCD, CBEF are at right angles with common section BC, so HP, lying in the plane CBEF at right angles to BC, is at right angles to the plane ABCD (D11.4). TW is also at right angles to the plane ABCD, so HP is parallel to TW (11.6). Likewise HL is parallel to AB and AB is at right angles to BC, so HT, lying in the plane ABCD at right angles to BC, is at right angles to the plane CBEF (1.29, D11.4); PX is at right angles to the same plane, so HT is parallel to PX (11.6).

**Step 12.** By Step 3, HQ : QT = QT : TH. But HQ = HP and QT = TW = PX; hence HP : PX = PX : TH (5.7), and inversely PX : HP = TH : PX, that is, XP : PH = HT : TW (5.7). Thus the triangles XPH and HTW have the two sides XP, PH proportional to the two sides HT, TW, they are placed together at the point H, and the corresponding sides are parallel (XP to HT, PH to TW, Step 11). Therefore XH is in a straight line with HW (6.32).

**Step 13.** UV and BC are parallel (Step 10) and so lie in one plane (D1.23). X is on UV and H is on BC, so the straight line XH lies in the plane of the parallels UV, BC (11.7). W lies on XH produced (Step 12), and a straight line cannot be partly in a plane and partly outside it (11.1); therefore W lies in that plane. Hence U, B, W, C, V all lie in one plane.

**Step 14.** Next, it is equiangular. Join BV (P1). Since NP is cut in extreme and mean ratio at R with RP the greater segment, and PS equal to RP has been added to it, the whole NS is cut in extreme and mean ratio at P with NP the greater segment (13.5); hence NS² + SP² = 3·NP² (13.4). Angle BNS is right (Step 5), so BS² = BN² + NS² (1.47); angle VSB is right (D11.3), so BV² = BS² + SV² = BN² + NS² + SP² = NP² + 3·NP² = 4·NP² (1.47, since BN = NP and SV = SP). But BC = 2·BH = 2·NP, so BC² = 4·NP² (2.4). Therefore BV² = BC² and BV = BC.

**Step 15.** Join UC (P1). Since PO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at S with PS the greater segment, and PR equal to PS has been added, RO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at P with PO the greater segment (13.5); hence RO² + RP² = 3·PO² (13.4). Angle COR is right (Step 9), so CR² = CO² + RO² (1.47); angle URC is right (D11.3), so UC² = CR² + RU² = CO² + RO² + RP² = PO² + 3·PO² = 4·PO² = BC² (1.47, 2.4, since CO = PO, RU = RP, BC = 2·PO). Therefore UC = BC.

**Step 16.** In the triangles BUV, BWC the sides BU = BW, UV = WC and the bases BV = BC; therefore angle BUV = angle BWC (1.8). In the triangles CVU, CWB the sides VU = WB, VC = WC and the bases CU = CB; therefore angle UVC = angle BWC (1.8). Thus the three angles BUV, BWC, UVC of the equilateral pentagon UBWCV are equal to one another; hence the pentagon is equiangular (13.7). So UBWCV is an equilateral and equiangular pentagon standing on the edge BC of the cube.

**Step 17.** Making the same construction on each of the twelve edges of the cube, we obtain a solid figure contained by twelve equal, equilateral and equiangular pentagons, which is a dodecahedron (D11.28). This is the required construction.

**Step 18.** Next, it is comprehended in the given sphere. Produce XP through P into the cube (P2). Since P is the centre of the face CBEF and PX is at right angles to that face, the line so produced is the common section of the two planes drawn through the points of bisection of the sides of the cube; hence it meets the diameter of the cube at a point Z at which the two bisect one another (11.38). Thus Z is the middle point of the diameter of the cube, which is a diameter of the sphere (Step 1, D11.17), so Z is the centre of the sphere (D11.16); and PZ, being half of the common section, which is equal to the side of the cube, is equal to half the side, that is, PZ = NP. Join UZ (P1).

**Step 19.** XZ = XP + PZ = PS + NP = NS (CN2), and XU = RP = SP (Step 10). Since UX is parallel to PS and XP falls on them, the angles SPX, PXU together equal two right angles (1.29); angle SPX is right (D11.3), so angle UXZ is right. Hence UZ² = XU² + XZ² = SP² + NS² = 3·NP² = 3·PZ² (1.47, Step 14, CN1).

**Step 20.** The side of the cube is 2·PZ, so the square on it is 4·PZ² (2.4); the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of this (13.15), namely 12·PZ². The diameter is double of the semidiameter, so the square on the diameter is four times the square on the semidiameter (2.4); hence the square on the semidiameter is 3·PZ² (CN1). Therefore UZ² equals the square on the semidiameter and UZ equals the semidiameter of the sphere. Since Z is the centre, U lies on the surface of the sphere (D11.14, D11.16). Similarly each of the remaining vertices of the dodecahedron lies on the surface; hence the dodecahedron is comprehended in the given sphere.

**Step 21.** Finally, the side is an apotome. The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side BC of the cube (13.15), so the square on BC has to the square on the diameter the ratio 1 : 3, which a number has to a number; hence these squares are commensurable (10.6). The square on the diameter is rational (D10.1.4), so BC is commensurable in square with the assigned rational line (D10.1.2) and is therefore rational (D10.1.3). NO = BC (Step 2), so NO is rational.

**Step 22.** NO = 2·NP, RS = RP + PS = 2·RP, and NR + SO = 2·NR (Step 3). Since NP : RP = RP : RN (Step 3), and parts have the same ratio as their equimultiples, NO : RS = NP : RP and RS : (NR + SO) = RP : NR (5.15); therefore NO : RS = RS : (NR + SO) (5.11).

**Step 23.** Cut off NY = RS from NO (1.3); then YO = NO − NY = NR + SO (CN3), so NO : NY = NY : YO (Step 22). Since NO is greater than NY, NY is greater than YO (5.14); hence NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio at Y with NY the greater segment (D6.3). NO is rational (Step 21), so its segment NY is the irrational straight line called apotome (13.6). But NY = RS = UV (Step 8), a side of the dodecahedron. Therefore the side of the dodecahedron is an apotome.

**Step 24.** Therefore a dodecahedron has been constructed and comprehended in the given sphere, and its side has been proved to be the irrational straight line called apotome. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 13.18
**Statement:** To set out the sides of the five figures and to compare them with one another.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the diameter of the given sphere. Bisect AB at C [1.10], and cut off from AB its third part DB at D [6.9], so that AC = CB and AD = 2DB. With centre C and distance CA describe the semicircle AEB on AB [P3, D1.18]; C is its centre. From C and D draw CE and DF at right angles to AB [1.11], meeting the semicircle at E and F, and join AF, FB, EB [P1].

**Step 2.** Since AD = 2DB, AB = AD + DB = 3DB [CN2]; and since AC = CB, AB = AC + CB = 2CB [CN2]. Further, AB = AD + DB where DB is half of AD, so AB is one and a half times AD.

**Step 3.** The angle AFB is in a semicircle, hence right [3.31]; and FD is drawn from the right angle perpendicular to the base AB. Therefore the triangles AFD, FBD are each similar to the whole triangle AFB [6.8], and from the equiangular triangles AFB, ADF and AFB, FDB we have BA : AF = AF : AD and AB : BF = BF : BD [6.4].

**Step 4.** Since BA, AF, AD are three proportional straight lines, BA has to AD the ratio duplicate of that which BA has to AF [D5.9], and the square on BA has to the square on AF that same duplicate ratio [6.20 por.]; hence BA : AD = sq(BA) : sq(AF). But BA is one and a half times AD [Step 2]; therefore sq(AB) is one and a half times sq(AF). Now the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid inscribed in that sphere [13.13]; therefore sq(AF) equals the square on the side of the pyramid, and AF is the side of the pyramid.

**Step 5.** Likewise, from AB : BF = BF : BD we get AB : BD = sq(AB) : sq(BF) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]; and AB = 3BD [Step 2], so sq(AB) = 3 sq(BF). The square on the diameter of the sphere is triple the square on the side of the cube inscribed in it [13.15]; therefore BF is the side of the cube.

**Step 6.** The angle AEB is right [3.31], and EC is the perpendicular from it to AB; so the triangles AEC, EBC are similar to AEB [6.8], whence AB : BE = BE : BC [6.4], and AB : BC = sq(AB) : sq(BE) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. Since AB = 2BC [Step 2], sq(AB) = 2 sq(BE). The square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron inscribed in it [13.14]; therefore BE is the side of the octahedron.

**Step 7.** For the icosahedron: at A draw AG at right angles to AB [1.11], make AG = AB [1.3], and join GC [P1]. In triangle GAC the angle at A is right, so sq(CG) = sq(CA) + sq(AG) [1.47], which is greater than sq(CA) [CN5]; thus CG > CA, the radius, and G lies outside the circle. Since C is the centre, GC cuts the semicircle at a point H between G and C. From H draw HK perpendicular to AB [1.12]; K falls between A and C.

**Step 8.** The triangles GAC and HKC have the angle at C common and the angles at A and K right, hence equal [P4]; therefore their remaining angles AGC, KHC are equal [1.32], and the triangles are equiangular. Hence GA : AC = HK : KC [6.4]. But GA = AB = 2AC [Step 2]; therefore HK = 2KC [D5.5].

**Step 9.** Since HK = 2KC, the square on HK is four times the square on KC, the duplicate of the double ratio [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. And since the angle HKC is right, sq(HC) = sq(HK) + sq(KC) [1.47] = 5 sq(KC). But HC = CB, being radii of the same circle [D1.15]; therefore sq(BC) = 5 sq(CK).

**Step 10.** AB = 2CB and AD = 2DB [Steps 1, 2]; subtracting, the remainder DB is double of the remainder CB − DB = DC [CN3]. Hence BC = BD + DC = 3DC [CN2], so sq(BC) = 9 sq(DC) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. Therefore 9 sq(DC) = 5 sq(CK) [CN1]. Since 9 sq(DC) > 5 sq(DC) [CN5], 5 sq(CK) > 5 sq(DC), so sq(CK) > sq(CD) and CK > CD.

**Step 11.** On CB make CL = CK [1.3]; from L draw LM at right angles to AB, meeting the semicircle at M [1.11]; join MB [P1]. Since CL = CK > CD, L lies beyond D from A; AD is a part of AL, so AL > AD [CN5].

**Step 12.** AB = 2BC and KL = KC + CL = 2CK; therefore sq(AB) = 4 sq(BC) and sq(KL) = 4 sq(CK) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]. And sq(BC) = 5 sq(CK) [Step 9]; therefore sq(AB) = 20 sq(CK) = 5 sq(KL).

**Step 13.** The square on the diameter of the sphere is five times the square on the radius of the circle from which the icosahedron is described [13.16 por.]. AB is that diameter; hence sq(KL) equals the square on that radius, and KL equals that radius, that is, KL is the side of the hexagon inscribed in that circle [4.15 por.].

**Step 14.** AC = CB and CK = CL; subtracting, AK = LB [CN3]. The diameter of the sphere is composed of the side of the hexagon and two sides of the decagon inscribed in that same circle [13.16 por.]; AB = AK + KL + LB, and KL is the side of the hexagon; therefore AK + LB is double the side of the decagon [CN3], and since AK = LB, each of AK, LB is the side of the decagon inscribed in that circle.

**Step 15.** In the right-angled triangles HKC, MLC, sq(HK) = sq(HC) − sq(CK) and sq(ML) = sq(MC) − sq(CL) [1.47]; HC = MC [D1.15] and CK = CL; therefore sq(HK) = sq(ML) [CN3] and HK = ML. But HK = 2KC = KL [Steps 8, 12]; therefore ML = KL [CN1], and ML is the side of the hexagon inscribed in the said circle.

**Step 16.** The angle MLB is right, so sq(MB) = sq(ML) + sq(LB) [1.47], that is, the squares on the side of the hexagon and the side of the decagon inscribed in the said circle. But the square on the side of the equilateral pentagon inscribed in a circle equals the squares on the sides of the hexagon and of the decagon inscribed in the same circle [13.10]. Therefore MB is the side of the pentagon inscribed in the circle from which the icosahedron is described; and the side of the icosahedron is the side of that pentagon [13.16]. Hence MB is the side of the icosahedron.

**Step 17.** For the dodecahedron: cut FB, the side of the cube, in extreme and mean ratio at N [6.30], NB being the greater segment. When the side of the cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the side of the dodecahedron [13.17 por.]. Therefore NB is the side of the dodecahedron. Thus AF, BE, BF, MB, NB have been set out as the sides of the pyramid, octahedron, cube, icosahedron and dodecahedron inscribed in the sphere of diameter AB.

**Step 18.** Comparison of the pyramid, octahedron and cube: sq(AB) is one and a half times sq(AF), double sq(BE), and triple sq(BF) [Steps 4, 5, 6]. Of the parts of which sq(AB) contains six, sq(AF) contains four, sq(BE) three, and sq(BF) two. Hence sq(AF) is four thirds of sq(BE), sq(AF) is double sq(BF), and sq(BE) is one and a half times sq(BF). The squares on AB, AF, BE, BF are all measured by the same area, so these lines are commensurable in square [D10.1.2], and the sides of the pyramid, octahedron and cube are in rational ratios to one another and to the diameter. Also, since four parts exceed three and three exceed two, AF > BE > BF [CN5]; and NB, a part of BF, is less than BF [CN5].

**Step 19.** Let the diameter AB be the rational straight line set out [D10.1.3]. Then MB, the side of the icosahedron, is the irrational straight line called minor [13.16], and NB, the side of the dodecahedron, is the irrational straight line called apotome [13.17]; each is incommensurable with AB both in length and in square [D10.1.3]. Since sq(AF), sq(BE), sq(BF) are commensurable with sq(AB) [Step 18] while sq(MB), sq(NB) are incommensurable with sq(AB), sq(MB) and sq(NB) are incommensurable with each of sq(AF), sq(BE), sq(BF) [10.13]. Thus the sides of the icosahedron and of the dodecahedron are irrational lines of different species, and neither is in a rational ratio to the sides of the other three figures.

**Step 20.** It remains to show that MB > NB. sq(AB) = 3 sq(BF) [Step 5], and AB = 3DB gives sq(AB) = 9 sq(DB) [D5.9, 6.20 por.]; so 3 sq(BF) = 9 sq(DB) [CN1] and sq(BF) = 3 sq(DB). Since AD = 2DB, sq(AD) = 4 sq(DB) [D5.9, 6.20 por.], which is greater than 3 sq(DB) = sq(BF) [CN5]; so AD > FB. And AL > AD [Step 11]; therefore AL > FB.

**Step 21.** AK is the side of the decagon and KL the side of the hexagon inscribed in the same circle [Steps 13, 14]; therefore AL = AK + KL is cut in extreme and mean ratio at K with KL its greater segment [13.9], so AL : KL = KL : AK [D6.3], and rect(AL, AK) = sq(KL) [6.17]. Likewise FB : NB = NB : NF [D6.3], and rect(FB, NF) = sq(NB) [6.17].

**Step 22.** KL > NB. For if NB were not less than KL, then, AL being greater than FB [Step 20], NF = FB − NB would be less than AL − KL = AK; thus rect(FB, NF), having both its sides less than the corresponding sides of rect(AL, AK), would be a part of it and less than it [CN5]; that is, sq(NB) < sq(KL) and NB < KL, contrary to the supposition. Hence KL > NB.

**Step 23.** ML = KL [Step 15]; therefore ML > NB. The angle MLB is right, so sq(MB) = sq(ML) + sq(LB) [1.47], which is greater than sq(ML) [CN5]; thus MB > ML, and therefore MB > NB. So the side MB of the icosahedron is greater than the side NB of the dodecahedron; and the sides of the five figures have been set out and compared with one another. Q.E.F.
